AM ESS A GE from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, Gentle raan-U (her of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries was read the First time.

Bejolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followed; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The open and unnatural Rebellion, which has broke out, and is dill continuing in Scotland, has obliged me to call you together sooner than I intended; and I shall lay nothing before you at present, but what immediately relates to our Security at home; reserving all other Confederations to a farther Opportunity. So wicked and daring an Attempt, in Favour of a Popish Pretender to my Crown, headed by his elded Son, carried on by Numbers of traiterous and desperate Persons within the Kingdom, and encouraged by my Enemies abroad, requires the immediate Advice and AlEdance of my Parliament, to suppress and extinguish it. The Duty and Affection for Me, and my Government, and the vigilant and zealous Care for the Safety of the Nation, which have, with so much Unanimity, been shewn by my faithful Subjects, give me the firmed A durance, that you are met together, resolved to aid with a Spirit becoming a Time of common Danger; and with such Vigour, as will end in the Confusion of all those, who have engaged in, or fomented this Rebellion.

I have, throughout the whole Course of my Reign, made the Laws of the Land the Rule of my Government; and the Preservation of the Conditution, in Church and State, and the Rights of my People, the main End and Aim of all my Actions: It is, therefore, the more aflonishing, that any of my Protedant Subjects, who have knownand enjoyed the Benefits reflating from thence, and have heard ot thq imminent Dangers theft Voi, 25.

Kingdoms were wonderfully delivered from, by the happy Resolution, should, by any Arts and Management, be deluded into Measures, that mud at once destroy their Religion and Liberties, introduce Popery and arbitrary Power, and subject them to a foreign Yoke.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I rely on your Affection to Me, and your Care and Concern for our common Safety, to grant Me such a Supply, as may enable Me intirely to extinguish this Rebellion, effectually to discourage any foreign Power from affiding the Rebels, and to redore the Peace of the Kingdom: For which Purpose, I will order the proper Edimates to be laid before you. Amongd the many ill Consequences of this wicked Attempt, the extraordinary Burden which it mud bring upon my faithful Subjects, very fenlibly affects me. But let those answer for it, whole Treason has occasioned it; and my People be convinced, what they owe to those Disturbers of our Peace, who are endeavouring to make this Kingdom a Scene of Blood and Confusion.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The many evident Proofs this Parliament has given of their Duty, Fidelity, and Affection to Me, and of their deady Adherence to the present happy Establishment, and the true Intered of their Country, make Me repose myself intirely on the Zeal and Vigour of your Proceedings and Resolutions. I am confident you will ad like Men who consider, that every thing dear and valuable to them is attacked: And Iqucltion not, but by the Blelfing of God, we shall, in a short time, fee this Rebellion end, not only in redoring the Tranquillity of my Government, but in procuring greater Strength to that excellent Conditution, which it was designed tofubvert. The Maxims of this Conditution shall ever be the Rules of my Conduct. The Intered of Me and my People, is always the fime, and inseparable. In this common Intered let us unite. And all those, who shall heartily and yigoroully exert themselves in this jud and National Caule, may always depend on my Protection and Favour.

Usual Order*. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right ' to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Pra&iccs, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Com-

Voj,. 25,

mittee thereof; of, directly or indirectTy, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender*

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great ,.

for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House ,is fitting { and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker's Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting;

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning, to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, . during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High-Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the feme put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen, attending the Members of this House, to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall prelume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That to prevent the Intercepting or Losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post-Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster-General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petition for private Bills after the First Day of February next.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves, or by their Agents, within a convenient Time to be appointed either by the House or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard shall be before the House, or the said Committee, deliver to the fitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the fitting Members, giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection; and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to: And that the fitting Members do, by themselves, or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to impower his Majesty to secure and detain such Persons as his Majesty shall suspect are conspiring against his Person and Government.

Mr. Attorney-General accordingly reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill was committed, the Amendments, which the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, Address 04 the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to congratulate your Majesty upon your happy, safe, and seasonable Return to these your Kingdoms.

We cannot sufficiently express our Abhorrence and Detestation of the unnatural Rebellion now raging in North Britain.

Permit us to give your Majesty the strongest Assurances of our Duty and Affection to your Person and Government 1 and to declare. That we will, with Vigilance,

Zeal, and Unanimity, shew a Spirit and Vigour becoming this Time of Danger: In order to make these Sentiments effectual, your faithful Commons will grant such Supplies, and put such Strength into your Majesty's Hands, as, we trust in God, and hope, from your Majesty's Wisdom, cannot fail to defeat the Attempts of those who have already made One Part of the United Kingdom, and would make the other, a Scene of Blood, Rapine, and Confusion.

With Hearts full of Gratitude, we acknowledge. That, under your Majesty's Royal Protection, we have lived in an uninterrupted and secure Enjoyment of our Religion,

Laws, and Liberties.

As all these are now wickedly and openly attacked, we are bound, by every Consideration, human and divine, to exert ourselves in the Defence of your Sacred Person and Government.

Your Majesty may safely rely on the Zeal and Vigour of your faithful Commons, who are resolved to act like Men, sensible of the lilelfings we enjoy, and determined to preserve those Blessings to ourselves and our Posterity.

We beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on the general Concurrence of your Subjects in these Sentiments of Duty to your Majesty, and Zeal for your Service; which happy Union, we doubt nor, will, by your Majesty's Wisdom, be improved to the future Glory and Welfare of your Crown and People; and to the utter Coofufion and Disappointment of the Enemies to both.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That the House do agree with the said Committee in the said Address, to ue presented to his Majesty.

, The Speech of Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, May a, 1745,

W"* upon presenting to his Majesty the several Money printing Bills, when they passed the Royal AlTent.

Jta'i Bills Most gracious Sovereign.

for the Royal Your, faithful Commons do now attend Your Majesty Assent on ad with their last Bill of Supply for the publick Service of Rlay taft. the present Year.

As their Supplies, Sir, are equal to your Majesty's Demand, lb Your Commons have made these Grants to Your Majesty, as they judged them to be adequate also to the Nature, the Importance, and the Necessity of the Services.

What Your Commons have given, the Manner of their Gilt, and the Latitude allowed in the Disposition of great Part of it, are so many Marks of the Sense they have of the Cause it is for, of the Confidence they repole in Your Majesty for the due Application of it, and of the Desire they had also, that our Enemies might conceive no Hopes from our unexpected Disadvantages and most unaccountable Dilappointments the last Year, that this Nation was either unwilling, or yet unable, to maintain its own Rights and Rank, or those of its Allies, against the Dif-turbers of Europe, their Ambition, and Perfidy.

This is, and always has been, the only Object of Your Commons in this War; and although it has been pursued by this Country against One of our Enemies, at an Expence beyond our Proportion of the Danger, compared with that of other States; in Places, and in a Manner not the most natural to the Situation of this Country, or where its principal, and genuine, and less expen-five Strength can be exerted; yet Your faithful Commons, Sir, have enabled Your Majesty to take this large Share in the War upon the Continent, — to be indeed the Life and chief Spirit of the whole; that the Inability offome Powers, and the Slownelsof others, might not make the common Cause to become desperate, and thereby give the common Enemy the Advantage of effecting, without Controul, that Superiority, which must be Tyranny, so long meditated, and cow again attempted, and in which, if obtained, the Independency of Great Britain may looner or later be involved and destroyed.

It is This, Sir, and this alone, that can justify to the People, the imposing upon them the many Millions they have already paid in the Course of this particular Quarrel. — God grant that our Condition, in the further Progress of it, may not call for a Repetition of the same Expence. His Aid we implore, and we rely on Your Majesty's Wisdom and Conduct, and on the expected great

Consequences of Lome late very important Advantages, that the great Armaments Your Commons have again provided for, and the large Subsidies they have enabled Your Majesty to give to Foreign Powers; may have that Success this Year, how much soever it tailed in the last, as to bring our proud Enemies to Reason, and give Your Majesty the Glory of bringing to Your Country, what we are Satisfied is most desired by Your royal Heart, as it is certainly most wanted by Your Subjects, a speedy, an honourable, and a lading Pacification.

To the obtaining of which most desirable End, has the Attention of Your Commons been most earnestly applied,- — recommended to them by Your Majesty, in the strongestand most affectionate Manner, and prosecuted by them, with most distinguished Zeal and Unanimity.

*Twas their first and principal Care: And, when that was done, they applied themselves with the same leriou* Attention to many other very national Concerns — more than has usually ,been the Production of One Session* Among others, there are Bills prepared for Your Majesty's Royal Assent — To regulate Elections of Knights of Shires — To secure the Qualification of Justices of the Peace — To give further Encouragement to the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland — To pursue the suppressing of excessive and deceitful Gaming, that Corrupter of Mind and Morals in the higheit as well as the lowed of a People.

There are other Bills, Sir, to prevent Two very growing and reproachful Evils to the Publick — the Kunning in of Goods and Merchandize to avoid Payment of the legal and accustomed Duties; and the extravagant Use and Consumption of French Cambricks. Both of them enriching our dangerous Rival in Trade and Power. The first of them grown to an Enormity beyond die Controul of all Law, and carried to the most daring and impudent Defiance of all Government. The other to an Expence and clear Loss to the Nation of Two hundred thousand Pounds a Year; of no Necessity, of no particular Conveniency, but the Result of Humour, and Fashion only; and, to our double Shame be it spoken, nimost the only Fashion we do not take from that People of whom we purchase this Commodity.

Some Part of the Session, Sir, has been employed bf Your Commons, not unufefully, we hope, to the Publick, in the most interesting Disquisition of all others to this Nation.

The honour of the British Flag is most justly deemed the chief Honour of the British Empire. It has made us the Envy and the Terror of all other Nations. Our Annals, and those of our Enemies too, bear Testimor.y of its Glory in all Ages. Some other Countries equal, perhaps exceed, us in ether Species of military Strength, — not in Bravery, though in Numbers; but the naval Power of this Island was never exceeded or equalled by any, and is now far superior to the maritime Force of any other Country whatsoever. In the Mediterranean Seas, last Year, we were confcfiedly superior to the united Fleets of France and Spain, conftfting of the Flower ami chief Strength of both their Navies; but, to the Alto-nishment of the World, the Enemy escaped almost with Triumph, when Providence had thrown them almost into our Hands; and the noblest Occasion was thereby loft of establishing the Greatness of the Navy against

all Pretence of Rivalry, and of deciding, perhaps, in our Favour at once, the Fate of the whole War.

Under these Circumstances, Sir, unbecoming and unpardonable would it have been in Your Commons, not to have made this foul Miscarriage the Subject of their ancient, constitutional, and necessary Power of Enquiry into every publick Service. They entered into it, and pursued it wiih an Impartiality, and with a Solemnity, that became their Justice and their Dignity; worthy of tho great national Importance it is of, and worthy the rojal Justice to which they have now appealed. — To You, Sir, Your People in Parliament have deferred this great Cause of their Country, to give it an Examination' in legal Course of Trial, without Distinctioa of Persons

or

i9 Geo. II. 21° — 22* — 230 9

or Degrees; that this Stain upon the Honour of the Kingdom, this Dilgrace that raises Indignation in the Bread of every true Briton, may in forne measure be done away, by doing Right to the Valour and Conduct of those who have done well, and by perpetuating, through exemplary Punishment, the Infamy of the Timorous, and the Treacherous, and of those who in any Manner thus fatally to their Country, have transgressed the Rules, and broken the Discipline of War.

Connected in l'ome fort with this Enquiry, the late Practice of C mrts-Martial in the Sea Service hath fallen under the Observation of Your Commons: In one of which They have found such Defeats and Misbehaviour, as are a Reproach to the Justice of the Nation; and, if generally practised, mud end in the total Overthrow of all Military Discipline at Sea. Towards remedying which so great Evil, and indeed Scandal to the State, a Bill awaits Your Majesty's Royal A dent, to prevent it in feme degree; with our Hopes, that hereafter a more extensive Reformation of thel'e Courts will be made by Parliament — That the Privilege of being tried by Persons of the same Profession, as a Means of protecting the In*-nocent, may not be converted into the base Means of

?rotating the Guilty, because they are of the same rote Hi on; — or for other Realons not less dangerous or dishonourable.

The Bills I have in my Hands to present to Your Majesty, are severally intituled,

An Act for granting to his Majesty the Sum of Eight hundred thousand Pounds, out of the Sinking Fund; and for granting a Sum remaining in the Exchequer (arilen by the Surplus of the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder and Perry 1, for the Service of the Year 1745; and for the further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and for giving further Time for the Payment of Duties, omitted to be paid for the Indentures or Contracts of Clerks and Apprentices; and for the further enforcing the Payment of the said Duties.

An Act for repealing the present Inland Duty of Four Shillings per Pound-weight upon all Tea fold in Great Britain; and for granting to his Majesty certain other Inland Duties in lieu thereof; and for better securing the Duty upon Tea, and other Duties of Excise; and for purluing Offenders out of one County into another.

To which your Commons, with all Humblcness, bc-feech Your Majesty's Royal Assent.

Reflations Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

n Papers jn Parliament assembled. That the Two'printed Papers paWifliedby jespectively signed James R. and dated at Rime, the 23 d *ee e Day of December, 1743; and the Four printed'Papers signed Charles P. R. dated respectively the 16 th Day of May, 1745, Augufl22d, 1745, the 9th' Day of October, 1745, and the 10th Day of 1745, are

false, scandalous, and traiterous Libels, intended to poi-fen the Minds of his Majesty's Subjects; containing the most malicious, audacious, and wicked Incitements to them to commit the most abominable Treasons, ground-id's and infamous Calumnies and Indignities, against the Government, Crown, and sacred Person, of his most Excellent Majesty King George the Second, our only right-

fal and undoubted Sovereign, and seditious and pft-sumptuous Declarations against the Oonstitution of this united Kingdom; representing the High Court of Parliament, naw legally assembled by his Majesty's Autho-thority, as an unlawful Afi'embly, and all the Acts of Parliament passed since the late happy Resolution, as null and void; and that the said printed Papers are full of the utmost Arrogance, and insolent Affronts to the Honour of the British Nation, in suppofntg, that his Majesty's Subjects are capable of being mipoled upon, seduced, or terrified, by false and opprobrious Invectives, insidious Promises, or vain and impotent Menaces , or of being deluded to exchange the free Enjoyment of their Rights and Liberties, as well civil as religious, under the well* established Government of a Protestant Prince, for Popery and Slavery, under a Popish bigotted Pretender, long fitice excluded by the wisest Laws made to secure our excellent Constitution, and abjured by the most l'olemn Oaths.

Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament afi'embled, That, in Abhorrence and De-testation of such vile and treasonable Practices, the said several printed Papers be burnt by the Hands of the common Hangman, at the Royal Exchange, in London, on Tuesday the Twelfth Day of this Instant November, at

One of the Clock in the Afternoon; and that the Sheriffs of London do then attend, and cause the same to be burnt there accordingly.

A PETITION of the Persons, whole Names are Crediton thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and Arrears of several others. Inhabitants of Crediton, in the County of L*1-'1* Devon, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, that on Sunday the 14th Day of August 1743, a sudden and most terrible Fire happened in the West Town and Borough of Crediton aforesaid, by which the said Town, excepting a very few Houses, was consumed to Allies; which unhappy Accident necessarily occasioned a considerable Deficiency in the Land Tax, from Midsummer 1743, to Lady-day 1744, amounting to the Sum of Fifty-four Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence Three Farthings; all which laid Sum was charged on the said Houses and Stock in Trade, lo consumed, and Hill remains in Arrear, and unpaid: And that, by Means of the Poverty of the said Inhabitants, who were intirely unprovided with Materials for building, and also from the Scarcity and excessive Price of Timber for building, from abroad, far the greatest Part of the said Town Hill remain* unfinished} by which Means, there happens a Deficiency in the Land Tax on the Grid Houses for the Year 1744, and for the present Year 1745, amounting to the further Sum of One hundred Forty-five Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Six Pence, as will appear by the Account to the Petition annexed: And expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that, in Companion to the distressed Circum-llances of the Petitioners, and also to prevent any Procel* from issuing out of his Majesty's Court of Exchequer against the atfling Commissioners of the Land Tax for the said County and Division, on account of such Arrears, the House will take into Consideration the same of the unhappy Sufferers; and that they may be excused from paying the said Arrears incurred in the Year 1743 and 1744, and also from the Charge on the said Houses and Stock in Trade, for the present Year 1745; and that no Process may issue against the said ailing Commissioners, on account of such Deficiences; or will give such other Relief, as the House shall think fit, to the Petitioners, under their present Circumstances.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1746, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause or Clauses, for the Relief of the Petitioners, upon their said Petition.

To this end it is agreed. That all the preceding Treaties, chiefly of Guaranty, shall be deemed to be renewed and confirmed, by the present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses; and shall be of the same Force as if they were inserted here. Word for Word; so far forth as they are not derogated fresh by the present Treaty.

III.

His Swedish Majesty, as Landgrave of , having still, in consequence of the last Treaty, some extraordinary Expences to demand, on account of the said 6000 Men of his Troops, during the Campaigns of the Years . 1742 and 1743, his Britannick Majesty engages, that he will take care that the Demand of his Majesty,

.on the Account of the said extraordinary Expences, be , fully satisfied on his Part, as soon as the necessary Vojich-ers and Documents shall have been produced, and that the Amount of that Debt shall have been duly ascertained and settled.

IV.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having desired . that his Majesty the King of as Landgrave of

Hejfe, would be pleased to hold in Readiness a Body of his Hejfian Troops, for the Service of his Britannick Majesty, in case the Welfare of his Kingdoms and States demanded this Succour, his Majesty the King of Sweden has been pleased to comply therewith; promising and engaging, by virtue of this Article, to hold in Readiness, for this Purpose, during the Term of Four successive Years, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty, a Body of 6000 Men; to wit. Twelve hundred Cavalry or Dragoons, and Four thousand Eight hundred Infantry, provided with General Officers and Subalterns, properly mounted, and armed, in a Condition to march for the Service of his Majesty the King of Grecft Britain, Two Months after that the Requisition shall have been made; or (ooner, if it should be possible; unless the immediate Defence of the Kingdpms and States of his Britannick Majesty should require them; in which case they shall march forthwith, after the Requisition shall have been made: And the said Troops shall take the Oath of Fidelity to his Britannick Majesty, when they shall havepafied the Frontiers of without Prejudice to that which they have taken to his Majesty the King of Sweden, as Landgrave: His said Majesty reserving farther to himself the filling up of all the Vacancies which shall happen in the said Body, asalfothe Administration of Justice.

V.

notwithstanding what is stipulated in the precedin Article, with respect to the Time of the Requisition, it is agreed, considering the present Circumstances, That his Swedish Majesty shall cause to march, in a Month, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of this Treaty, from the Country of Hejfe, towards the Netherlands, the said Body of 6000 Men, in order to join there forthwith the confederate Army, under the Command of his Royal Highness the Duke of or to repair

to such other Place as his Britannick Majesty shall appoint them: Saving always, the Exceptions which are contained in the Eighth Article of this Treaty; and to serve there as long a Time as his Britannick Majesty shall have Occasion for them, pursuant to the present Engagements.

VI.

His Britannick Majesty promises to pay to his Majesty the King of Sweden, to commence from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty, and to be continued as long as these Troops shall be really in his Pay, an annual Subsidy of a Hundred- Fifty thousand Banco Crowns; and for the Time that they shall not be any longer therein, but shall be.sent back, and placed again to the Charge 22

of the Finances of his Swedish Majesty, his Britannick Majesty shall augment this Subsidy to the Currency of Two hundred Fifty thousand Banco Crowns: The Payment of the one and the other to be regularly made without Deduction, and Quarterly, in the Town of Cajfel, into the Military Chest of his Swedish Majesty, authorized for the Receipt thereof.

vn.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having already paid in full, by virtue of the preceding Treaty, the Levy of the said 6000 Men, will charge himself with the Pay and Entertainment, as well ordinary as extraordinary, of the Officers, Troopers, and Foot-Soldiers, of this Body, from the Day that the said 6000 Men shall be assembled in a Body, and shall begin their March from the Country of Hejfe towards the Netherlands, for his Service j and this Pay, as well ordinary as extraordinary, shall be settled upon the Foot of that of the Hejfian Troops, granted by the Treaties of 1702, Article 5th and 6th; and of 1726, Article 6th; and by that of 1740: And it shall be remitted into the Military Chest, without any Deduction or Abatement, in order to make the Distribution thereof: And if it should happen, unfortunately, that any of the Regiments, or Companies, of the said Body, should be ruined or destroyed, in the Whole, or in Part, his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall cause to be paid, without Delay, into the above-mentioned Chest, the Expences of the necessary Recruits and Remounts, in order to reinstate (peedily die Regiments, or Companies: And theft: Recruits and Remounts shall be regulated in like manner, on the Foot of those which were fumilhcd to the HeJJian Officers, in virtue of the Treaty of 1702, Article 5th, to the end that this Body may be always kept up; and sent back hereafter in as good a Condition as it was delivered.

VIII.

It shall depend on his Britannick Majesty to keep this Body of Troops in his Service all the Time of the Duration of this Treaty, to serve wherever he may have Occasion for them; provided that it be not in the Fleet, or on the other Side of the Sea, as soon as it shall once depart the Hereditary States of his Swedish Majesty; excepting, nevertheless, for the Defence of the Kingdoms of Great Britain and of Ireland; in which case these Troops shall enjoy wholly, and without any Restriction, the feme Pay and Emoluments which the English Troops enjoy: And when his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall be pleased to (end back the said Troops, he shall make it known to his Majesty the King of Sweden Three Months before-hand; and shall cause to be paid them One Month's Pay for their Return; providing them with the necessary Transport-Ships gratis. It is farther agreed. That the said Hejfian Troops shall not be employed neither against the Kingdom of Sweden itself, nor against any of the Provinces thereto belon^ng.

In case that his Majesty the King of Sweden should find himself attacked, or disturbed in the Possession of his Hereditary States, his Britannick Majesty promises and engages to fend him back, immediately, the said Body of Troops; paying them not only a Month's Pay, but providing them also, gratis, the Transport-Ships requisite for their Return; and to give also to his Swedish Majesty as Landgrave of HJfe, all the Succour of Troops which the case shall require; which Succour shall be continued to him till he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace: As his Majesty the King of Sweden, in quality of Landgrave, on his Part, promises also, that in case that his Majesty the King of Great Britain should be attacked, or disturbed, in his Kingdoms, States, Lands, Provinces, or Towns, he will give him also all the Succour which the case shall require; which Succotir shall be in like manner continued till he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace.

X.

In order to render this Alliance an Union the more perfect, and not to leave any Doubt to the Parties upon the

Cer-

Certainty of the Succour which they have to expect the One or the other, it is e*pressly agreed, That, in order to judge lor the future, if the Caleof this Alliancy, and of the ft pulated Succour exist or not, it shall suffice that One of the Parties be actually attacked by force of Arms, without having used before, open Force against that which attacks it.

XI.

In case that his Britannick Majesty should have Occasion, during the Continuance of this Treaty, of another Body of the HJJian Troops of his Swedish Majesty, his said Majesty proniifes and engages to furnish it to him. On the (amc Conditions, with respect to the SubGdy, and to the Pay, in proportion to the effective Number of this ne.v Body, concerning which they shall hereafter agree; provided that in that Calc as his Majesty will have

incurred many considerable Expences to mount, and put into a good Condition, such a Body, his Britannick Majesty, to relieve him therein, shall cause to be paid, on account of the Levies, to his Majesty the follow-

ing Sums; that is to say, for each Trooper duly armed, and mounted, Four-score Banco Crowns; and for each Foot-Soldier, Thirty; One Half to be paid immediately after the Signature of the new Convention which shall be made then for this Purpose, and the other Half when the said Second Body of Hejfian Troops shall be delivered.

XII.

This Treaty shall last the Term of Four Years, io be reckoned from the Day of the Signature: And if their Majesties should think proper to continue, prolong, or alter it, they shall, in that Cafe, treat about it Three Months before it expires, according to the Exigence of Affairs.

XIII.

The Ratifications of this Treaty shall be exchanged at Hanover, within a Month after the Signature; or looner, if it can be done. In Testimony whereof, we the underwritten, furnished with the full Powers of the most serene Kings of Great Britain and of Sweden, have signed the present Treaty, and have set thereto the Seals ot our Arms. Done at Hanover the T'r Day of the Month of June 1745.

A Motion being made, and the Question being prepared, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty our Thanks for communicating to this House the Advices he has received of the Preparations making at Dunkirk, and other Ports of France, for invading this Kingdom, in Support of a Po-pish Pretender, and of the actual Landing of some French Troops in Scdtland; to express our Detestation and Abhorrence of this daring Attempt, and of the insolent Declaration of the Person who takes upon him the Command of those Troops; to return his Majesty our Thanks for his paternal Care for the Security and Safety of his People, in directing the Hejfia Troops, taken into his Majesty's Service last Summer, to be brought into this Kingdom, in order the more effectually to repel the said Invasion, and to suppress the present most unnatural Rebellion; to allure his Majesty, that this House will make good any Expence incurred on that Account; that we will, with our Lives and Fortunes, support his Majesty's most sacred Person and Government, and heartily concur in such further Measures, as shall be found necessary to put a Strength in his Majesty's Hands, sufficient, by the Blelfing ot God, to deter our avowed Enemies from prosecuting their ambitious DeGgns, totally to extinguish the present wicked Rebellion, and to refeue these Kingdoms from all ApprehenGons of Popery and arbitrary Power;

That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty. was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent M iftakes, obtai ned a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

At the Opening of this Session of Parliament, I did not think it proper to lay any thing before you, for your Consideration, but what immediately related to the present unnatural Rebellion, and our Security at Home: The daring Attempt, which the Rebels have since made upon this Part of my Kingdom, has been happily disappointed: And as their precipitate Flight before a small Number of my Troops, must greatly dispirit their Followers, so that inviolable Duty and Loyalty, which have been so univerlally and steadily shewn by my faithful Subjects, and shall never be forgotten by me, must convince them, how vain and ill-grounded their Hopes were of any Addition of Strength from such an Enter-prize. 1 have not only sent a considerable Body of our h&tional Forces into Scotland, and ordered Troops, in my Pay, to be landed there; but have also made such a Disposition of the rest of my Forces, by Land as well as by Sea, that I hope, by the Bldfing of God, this Rebellion will, in a short time be extinguished; and our Enemies, who have so long menaced us with an Invasion, be deterred by the fealonable Preparations made for our Defence.

The Election of the Emperor, which I very Zcaloufiy promoted, was an Event of great Importance, not only to the support of the House of but to the Li-

berties of Europe in general. I did also, during the Course of the last Year, exert my earned endeavours to bring about an Accommodation between the Emprels, the King of Poland, and the King of Prussia; and laid a proper Foundation for it, by the Convention made between me and the King of u This great Work

The States»General have made the most pressing Indances to fne, to assist them in this difficult Conjuncture. The imminent Dangers to which they are at present exposed, which do lo nearly affect the Safety of Great Britain, as well as the very Being of call for our moll

serious Attention; for the Interests of the Two Nations re so united, that whatsoever brings Ruin upon the One, mull, in consequence, be attended With the most fatal Mischiefs to the other. These Reasons have induced me to assure the States, that I will, to the Utmost of my Power, according to the Circumstances of my own Dorn inions^co-operate with them towards opposing the further Progress of our Enemies in the Netherlands, and procuring a proper Security for the Republick, against the ambitious and dedruftive Dfsigns of France. In order to this necessary End, Measures are now aiflually concerting between me and the States, for furnishing this Affidatice, on my Part, as early and effectually as poi-fible; ind for their making such an Augmentation of fheirpresent Forces, as their own immediate Preservation, and the Necessity of Affairs, absolutely require.

The great Advantages which we have received from bur Naval Strength, in protecting the Commerce of my Uubjedts, and intercepting and dillreffing that of our Enemies, have been happily experienced by the former, and severely felt by the latter. I am therefore determined to be particularly attentive to this important Service; and to have such a Fleet at Sea early iti the Spring, as may be sufficient to defend ourselves, and effectually to annoy our Enemies.

Gentlemen of the Houfj of Commons,

It is with much regret that I find myself obliged to ask any further Aids of ray People: I am so fe.ffiole of the Burthens they endure, that nothing could give me so sincere a Pleasurt as to lighten them: But the Coh<-, federations 1 have laid before you, are so necessny to our own Preservation, that, I doubt not, you will grant me such a Supply as shall be sufficient for these Purposes. The proper Estimatet shall soon be laid before you; and I eaineflly recommend it to you to take the most effectual Methods to maintain the publick Credit in this Conjuncture.

Mv Lords and Gentlemen,

Sir John Crojfe reported, from the Committee appointed to consider of Methods to prevent the Spreading of ths Distemper now raging among the homed Cattle in this Kingdom, and to report the fame, with all convenient Speed, to the House, That the Committee had considered of the same accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the feme were read; and are as followeth; viz.

_ Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the most likely Method to prevent the Spreading of the Distemper, will be, to inflict proper Puniftiraents on all Persons who shall buy or fell, or offer to buy or fell, any Cattle, or the Hides, Horns, or any Part of any Cattle, which are infected; or shall open, skin, or flay, any Cattle, knowing them to be infected.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a proper Punishment should be inflicted upon all Persons, who shall knowingly buy, fell, or expose to Sale, the Meat or Milk of any such infected Cattle; or who £hafl give the same to Hogs, Calves, Lambs, or any other Animals.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Owners of infected Cattle should be obliged to buty them Ten Feet deep, where the Ground will admit of it; and to leave Six Feet in Depth above the upper-most Bead.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Owners should be obliged to fence round the Place where such Cattle shall be buried, in order to prevent any other Cattle feeding the re, for a Time to be limited; and that it is necessary to prevent the driving infected Cat tie from the Place where they are infected to another where there are any Cattle feeding or grazing j or from felling any Cattle out of infected Herds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Provision should be made more effectually to prevent the Importation of Cattle, or Hides, from foreign Parts.

The Three first Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by inserting, after the Word felling," the Words " or exposing to Sale:"

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That the Owners should be obliged to fence round the Place where such Cattle shall be buried, in order to prevent any other Cattle feeding the re, for a Time to be limited; and that it is necessary to prevent the driving infected Cattle from the Place where they are infected to another where there are any Cattle feeding or grazing; or from felling, or exposing to Sale, any Cattle out of infected Herds*

*4

And the said Proposal was read; and is as follotys:

To the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled:

The Governor and Company of the Bank of England; in order to facilitate the Raising of the Supplies for the Service of the Year t746, humbly propose.

That they are willing, apd copfent, that the Sum of Nine hundred Eighty-six thousand Eight hundred 1 Pounds in Exchequer Bills, remaining unfinished, on the Duties for Licences to sell Spirituous Liquors and Strong Waters, by Retail, and upon the Sinking Fund, may be cancelled, provided they may have an Annuity of Thirty-nine thousand Four hundred Seventy-two Pounds, being the Interest on the said Sum, at the Rate of Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, granted to them upon the same Securities; and that they may have a Power to Create and dispose of the Sum of Nine hundred Eighty-six thousand Eight hundred Pounds of Bank Stock (to be joined and incorporated with their present Capital) in such Manner, and at such Times, as they shall think proper; with such further Powers, Privileges, and Advantages, as have been usually granted them by former Acts of Parliament, on the like Occasions: They then humbly further propose to advance the Sum of One million upon the Malt and Land Tax, for the Service of the Year 1746, at Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, for Exchequer Bilk, to be issued for that Purpose.

By Order of the Court,

Robert Lewin, Secretary.

Regulating A Petition of several Persons urtder the DenOmi-I1a*'on of Pawnbrokers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and several others, within the Cities of London and the Bills

of Mortality, following that Business, and no other, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That the Petitioners have, for many Years, carried on no Other Business than that of lending small Sums of Money Upon Pledges, great Numbers of whom have served regular Apprenticeships, and have, for a long time, been settled as Masters in the said Business, having large Families which depend on them for* their Support; and, by long Experience, find, that a Business of this Nature is of indii'penfable NeceflUy, where Trade and Commerce flourish: That the Petitioners have long laboured under the publick Reproach and Infamy of being Extortioners, and great Encouragers of Thieves; the latter of which Imputations, the Petitioners apprehend, is owing to their not being distinguished from Persons keeping Gin-Ihops, Chandlers-lhops, and other such like Businesses, who, likewise lending Money upon Pledges, do, whenever they are discovered to have taken in Pawn any Goods which are stolen, aflame the Name of Pawnbrokers; the Petitioners themselves being so far from encouraging Thieves,

. that they very frequently detect them, and could much

oftener, il authorized to stop lufpected Persons, which they many times dare not attempt, though even under the moil suspicious Circumstances, left by mistaking Persons, they should subject themselves to vexatious and CXpenfive Law-Suits: That the Petitioners conceive their being deemed Extortioners, proceeds from Misrepresenta-tions of the Nature of their Business, by comparing their T teputed or leaning Profit with the legal Interest of Money, without considering the great Expence, Labour, and Care, attending the fame; that their whole Time is taken up therein; which Cjrcumstances considered, the Petitioners Profits will not be found superior, if equal, to those of other middling Tradesmen; nor can their Business be carried on at a lower Rate, unlessaTiine was settled and limited for the Redemption of Pledges, by which the Petitioners would be discharged from the Expence of keeping great and perishing Stocks by them; in which same they could afford, and willingly would supply, the honest and industrious Poor, at a much cheaper Rate than they at present can: That the Petitioners not being legally justified in taking more than after the Rate of Five Pounds for the Loan of One hundred Pounds for One Year, and not being allowed any Considerttion for Warehouse-room* or other Expences attending the negotiating Business, or -authorized to fell the Goods pledged with them, though Of ever so perishable a nature, many vexatious and txpenfive Law-Suits are daily commenced, and prosecuted, against the Petitioners in respect thereof: That if

, the Business was regulated, by limiting a Time for the

Redemption of Pledges, and allowing a reasonable Profit to the Pawnbroker, and only such Persons were admitted to follow the Business as should be licensed by proper Authority, after an Examination into their Characters and Reputation, it would not only be of much greater Service to the honrft and industrious Poor, by considerably reducing the Premiums they now pay for the Loan of

Money, but likewise of public Benefit, by hindering

Persons of ill Fame and Reputation from acting the rein;

‘ which is at present but too much practised, and is the

principal Cause of the Mischiefs complained of: That the Petitioners Were, the last Session, permitted to lay open the Nature of their Business and Practices, before a Committee of this House; by means whereof, the Difficulties the Petitioners at present labour under, have been so far made publick, that, they apprehend, it will be impossible for them, under their present Circumstances, to follow that Profdfion for the future, notwithstanding the y were, as they hope, so fortunate as to remove the publick Prejudice conceived against them; and that, inConfe-

quence thereof, a Bill passed through this House, whereby the Publick would have been secured, and the Petitioners enabled to carry on their Trade with Credit and Reputation; but the Time that then remained of the Session being very short, the same did not pals the House of*

Lords: That the Petitioners apprehehd it appeared to the said Committee, that a Business of this Nature was of indispensable Necessity in Places where Trade and Commerce flourish; and that a Regulation thereof was absolutely requisite: And therefore praying. That this House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief; as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opiniorl thereupon, to the House:

The House being informed, That One of the Sheriffs of London attended at the Door;

He was called in j and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled:

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was read, setting forth. That by an Act of Parliament, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, An Act for regulating Elections within the City of London; and for preserving the Peace, good Order, and Government, of the said City; it is, among other things, enacted, " That no Act, Order, or Ordinance, whatsoever, at any "Time, from and after the First Day of June One " thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-five, shall be " made or passed in the Common Council of the said " City, without the Assent of the Mayor and Aldermen present at such Common Council, or the major " Part of them; nor without the Assent of the Commons present at such Common Council, or the major " Part of them That the Petitioners can, with great Truth, inform this House, That the said Act has by no means answered the good Ends and Purposes thereby said to be intended; neither has the fame, in anywise, preferred the good Order and Government of the City of London; but the exercising the negative Power thereby given to the Mayor and Aldermen, has occasioned great jealousiesand Discontentsamong the Citizens of London, highly obstructed the Proceedings of the Common Council, and tended greatly to destroy the Peace and good Order of the said City: That by this Law, the Commoners in Common Council, though composed of no less than Two hundred and Thirty-six Citizens, should they be unanimous, may, by the negative Votes of the Mayor, and Two or Three Aldermen, be restrained from making any Act, Order, or Ordinance, however advantageous or beneficial to the said City: That the Petitioners conceive, that so great a Power lodged in few Hands, may in time prove subversive of the Rights and Privileges of the Citizens of London, and destructiveof the very Elfence

and Being of Common Councils: And therefore praying this House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to repeal so much of the said Act as relates to the Making 17

A. 1745.

or Passing of Acts, Orders, or Ordinances, in Common Council; or to give the Petitioners such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read > setting forth. That the Petitioners are, by several Acts of Parliament passed in his present Majesty's Reign, appointed Commissioners for building a Bridge crots the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey; and are, by Two Acts passed in the lath and 13th Years of his pvefent Majesty's Reign, impowered to make, design, and lay out such Ways, Streets, and Passages, as they shall find proper to make, open, and lay out, on each Side the River Thames, to and from the said intended Bridge, the Courts of Justice, both Houses of Parliament, and the Parts adjacent; and to agree for, and purchase such Houses and Ground, within certain Limits by the said Acts prefer ibed, as they shall find necessary for them to be possessed of: That the Petitioners have made a considerable Progress in building the said Bridge, and have purchased foveral Houses, and Parcels of Ground, for opening, widening, and rendering convenient the said Ways, Streets, and Passages; in doing of which they have expended almost all the Monies hitherto granted them foF the said Purposes, notwithstanding the y have proceeded with the utmost Care and Frugality; and are Hill under Contracts for several Parts of the Works which are now carryingon, and which will amount to a greater Sum than is now in the Hands of the Petitioners: That the Petitioners find themselves under a Necessity of applying to this House, for such further Sums of Money as this House shall judge proper; that a Work so ufelul, and advantageous to the Publick, may not be Hopped for want thereof: And therefore praying, That this House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such further Sums of Money as to this House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, who are respectively Owners and Proprietors of Common Field Lands, lying and being in Ripen, Littlethorpe, and Bondgate, in the County of York;

andof certain ancient Burgages and Tenements (landing and being in Ripon, Littlethorpe, and Bondgate aforesaid, for themselves, and on the Behalf of several other Owners and Proprietors of common Field Lands, Burgages, and Tenements in Ripon, Littlethorpe, and Bondgate, respectively, was presented to the House, and read; reciting Part of an Act of Parliament, made in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for extinguishing a Right of Common claimed by, and belonging to, the Owners and Proprietors of ancient Burgages and Tenements in Ripon, Littlethorpe, and Bondgate, in the County of York; and for settling and providing an Equivalent for the said Common Right; And setting forth, That the Commissioners appointed by the said Act, did, in pursuance of the Power and Authority thereby veftedin them, cause a Survey, Admeasurement, and Valuation of the common Field Lands therein mentioned to be made; and to be laid down, delineated, and described, in a Map; and also a Survey and Lift to be made and taken of the Burgages and Tenements intitled to Right of Common, as aforesaid; and of the Stint and Number of Cattle-gates, belonging to the same; and the Names of the respective Owners of the said Burgages and Tenements: And that the said Map, Lift, and Survey, was laid before the said Commissioners, at one of their Meetings, held within the Time limited by the said Act for that Purpose; but that, by various and unavoidable Accidents, the said Commissioners have been prevented from ascertaining and determining the Rent or Value of the whole Stint and Number of Cattle-gates, belonging to the said Burgages and Tenements; and the Shares and Proportions of the Rent to be contributed by the Owners of the common Field Lands; and the Distribution of the said Rent amongst the Owners of the said Burgages and Tenements, within the Time limited by the said Act: And that the Peti-

tioners, being highly sensible of the great Advantages that would have accrued to them, and all other Parties concerned, by means of the said Act, are desirous the same should be carried effectually into Execution: And therefore praying the House, to give Leave that a Bill may be brought in, forgiving such further Time to the Commissioners for the executing the Powers and Authorities of the said former Act, now remaining unexecuted, as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr.

Wortley, Sir John Cuji, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Yane, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufac- M«nufcftore turers of Sail-cloth, Sail-makers, Rope-makers, Flax of and Hemp-growers, Inhabitants of and the Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for further encouraging and regulating the Manufactures of British Sail-cloth, and for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail-cloth imported into his Majesty's Kingdoms; it was Enacted, "That after the 24th " Day of June 1736, all foreign-made Sail-cloth, or " Canvas, usually entered as Hollands-Duck, or VitreryCanvas, for making of Sails for navigating Slvps and " Vessels, which shall be imported to Great Britain, by " way of Merchandize, and for which Duties have been

granted, shall be stamped at the Time of the Landing thereof, when such Duty is paid: And that every " Ship built in Great Britain, or in the British Plantalionsin America, not having a complete Set of Sails of British Sail-cloth, are, upon Conviction, to forfeit " Fifty Pounds for the same But that forasmuch as there is no Duty mentioned, or fixed, in the said Act, upon Sails made up in foreign Parts, of foreign Sailcloth, the Generality of Mailers of Ships purchase Abroad, and bring with them into these Kingdoms, full Sets of Sails, as the Petitioners are well informed: w hereby they are furnished not only with a Supply for their own Ufc, but frequently furnifH their Neighbours and Friends; and these they bend to their Yards, when they arrive at tire Ports they are respectively bound fqr in these Kingdoms; and thereby elude the Design of the aforesaid Act, and have their Sails made up of foreign Sail-cloth, without paying any Duty at all: And further setting forth. That the Duty payable upon the Importation of foreign Sail-cloth has been eluded, by importing them under the Name of broad Russia Linens; and that, as the Petitioners are capable to make appear, from the Bills of Lading, Frauds of this Kind have amounted to Three hundred Pounds in a single Ship; and that several Sloops, of Forty or Fifty Tons, built upon the River Trent, have beenentirely fitted out with foreign Sail-cloth, and have navigated to without any Exceptions taken at them by the Officers of the Customs; the Owners of such Sloops pleading the y are not within the Cognizance of the Act; which the Petitioners apprehend to be attended with many Inconveniencies; such as diminishing . his Majesty's Revenue, prejudicing the Merchants, Importers of Flax, Hemp, and foreign Sail-cloth; and that it likewise affects the landed Interest, by discouraging all further Essays towards Improvement of Husbandry, as far as respects the cultivating Hemp and Flax (of which none better than our own Growth, and few Countries afford so good) obstructs the Progress of Sail-cloth Manufactories in these Kingdoms; and, in consequence, multiplies the Poor, who want Work and Bread: And that several, who trade in these Commodities, have large dead Stocks of Sail cloth now lying uuon their Hands; which, taking an Estimate from the Sale

Palatine of Lancaster, to the Town of Prefcot, in the said County, leading through the Towns of West Derby, Huy ton cum Picby, and Knowsley, being above Seven Miles in Length; as also the Road from Blacklowbrow through Roby Town, and through Twigg-Lane, into the said Road between Liverpool and Prefcot, being about One Mile; and alfi of the several Persons living near, or usually travelling through the said Road from Liverpoole to Prefcot aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by the said Act several Tolls and Powers were granted to the Trustees therein mentioned, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, commencing from the First Day of June 1726, for repairing the said Roads: And that the said Trustees, the better to enable them to answer the Intention of the said Act, by carrying on the Repairs of the said Roads with Effect, have, from time to time, taken upat Interest considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Act, and have duly appl'ed the lame, together with the Money arising by the said Tolls, to the several Purposes by the said Act directed; notwithstanding which, the said Roads are, from the many, and heavy. Carriages which daily pass thro* them to Liverpoole aforesaid, continually breaking up in

different Places, and thereby rendered very bad, especially in the Winter Season; and such Parts thereof as have been already amended, will, in a short Time, become ruinous again, if Care be not taken constantly to repair the same: That the Petitioners find that the Repairs of the Roads directed to be amended by the said former Act cannot, during the Term aforesaid, be compleated, and the Debt now due be repaid, unless the Term and Powers granted by the said Act be enlarged; nor can the said Roads, when compleated, by the ordinary Method provided by the Laws, be effectually kept in Repair, with-VroL. 25.

out a further Aid be granted, and applied for that Purpose: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted in and by the said Act; and that a Provision may be made in the said Bill, for repairing and amending the Road leading from the Town of Prefcot aforesaid to the Chapel of Saint Helen, in the Hamlet of Archie, in the Township of Windle, in the said Ceunty of Lancaster, being about the Distance of Three Miles and One Quarter of a Mile, or thereabouts, further on the great Road leading to the Market-Towns of Bolton and dale, and also to the County of York', and opening a Way to several Ranks of Coal-Pits, whereby all the Country adjacent, and particularly the Inhabitants of the Town of Liverpoole (now become very numerous) and also the Shipping of the said Port, may be commodiously served, both in Winter and Summer, with Coals; by the want of which they have greatly suffered of late, a great Part of the said Road being, in many Places, always in Winter, and frequently in Summer, lb bad, that Carriages cannot pass.

Dorchester in the County of Dorset, lying within, and being Parcel of the Manor of Forthington in the same County; which Manor belongs to his Royal Highness Frederick Prince of Wales, as Part of the Post'eftions of the Duchy of Cornwall: That such of the Petitioners as are Tenants of the said Manor are entitled to Right of Common for their Cattle, in and upon the said Moor or Meadow, and some of them to the Math, or Crop of Grass, growing upon Part of the same Moor or Meadow respectively: That the Common Highway, or publick Road, from Blandjord into the Town of Dorchester, lieth over Part of the said Common or Moor, and through a Ford, at the Sluice or Tail of a Mill erected on the River Froom, which is a very dangerous Passage both for Horses and Carriages, and in Times of Floods and High-Waters utterly unpaflable: That the Petitioner Lora Pitt hath proposed, and is willing, to open and make a new Way or Road to branch out of the said common Highway or publick Road between Stockingbridge and Londonbridge, in the said Road, and to be carried over Forthington Moor aforesaid, and through Part of a Garden called Glover's Cloje, or Segar's Orchard, into the Town of Dorchester, and to erect a Causeway, and a Bridge or Bridges, upon the said new Way or Road, so as to render the same passable at all Seasons of the Year; and to maintain and repair the said Road for Three Years at her own Expence, in order that the same may thereafter be made a common Highway and publick Road for all his Majesty's Subjects: But that although the making such new Way or Road would be a great Benefit and Advantage to the Inhabitants of Dorchester, and of publick Utility; yet, from the Nature of the several Interests, and Property of the several Persons in the Lands upon, and through, which the said new Way or Road is pro-pefed and intended to be made and erected, the same cannot be effectually done without the Aid and Authority of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to give Leave that a Bill may be brought in, for impowering the said Lora Pitt to make such new Road, with such Powers and Authorities for establishing and maintaining the same as shall leem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the ConsideratioR of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition;

The Agent for the Petitioners called,

Regulating Mr. Richard Grainger; who salt!. That he had, for Pawnbrokers' Sixteen or Seventeen Years pad, followed the Bufinets of Traoe. Pawnbroking, and no other; which Business chiefly con-fists in lending small Sums upon Pledges: That from Lady-Day 1744 to Lady-Day 1745, he had taken in 24,328 Pledges; upon which, at a Medium, he had lent Three Shillings apiece: That the Petitioners were Persons who had been long settled in tire Business, and had, most of them, large Families depending on them for their Support: That he himself had served a regular Apprentice-strip; and it was cudomary for the Professors of the Business to do the fame: That a Business of this Nature was of indispensible Necessity within the Bills of Mortality, to Persons falling under the following Descriptions.

Fird, To the yery poor Sort of People, such as Persons who cry Fish, Fruit, or other Wares, about the Streets, and other People who may be reckoned in the lowed Class of Life, who, not having any personal Credit, are obliged to have Recourse to the Pawnbrokers, and by the Money borrowed from them, are enabled to purchase the several Commodities they deal in; and, by the Profits arising from thence, to support themselves and Families: That it is of such singular Service to Numbers of these poor People, that it is very usual, besides maintaining themselves and Families the whole Week, to get diffident to make a comfortable Provision for Sunday.

Another Class of People to whom the Business was of Service, were the middling Sort of Tradesmen, who, from the Nature of their respective Businesses, are under a Necessity to employ a great Number of Journeymen; these People, by the Money borrowed of the Pawnbrokers, are enabled to pay their Journeymen's Wages, support their Credit, and maintain their Families, which, lie conceived they could not do, were there no such Bu-liness; by reason of the great Credit they are obliged to give their Customers,

That it was likewise of great Benefit to these Journeymen, who, having nothing but their Wages to depend on, must perish when sick, or out of Employment, if there were no such Profession.

And lastly, To Artificers and Handycraftfmcn, who, by the Money borrowed of the Pawnbrokers, were enabled to buy Materials to carry on their Businesses; and which few of them could otherwise do, by reason of their not having any personal Credit; and even those few who might have Credit for their Materials, can better afford to pay the Pawnbroker the Interest he takes, and go to Market with ready Money, than'to take up their Materials upon Trust; the Difference of buying Goods with ready Money, and upon Trust, being more in Proportion than the Pawnbroker takes.

Mr. James Wilson confirmed the Evidence of Mr.

Grainger, as to the Nature and Necessity of the Bufi-nels; and said, That he looked upon it as a distinct Business; that he himself had served an Apprenticeship to it; and since he had been a Mailer, he had taken Two Apprentices: That the Number of Pledges taken in by him were, upon an Average, 70 a Day, *ths whereof were under the Value of Ten Shillings.

Mr. Nathanael Brown informed your Committee, That he had served a regular Apprenticeship, and has been many Years a Master: That he always used the utmost Caution, and stricteft Enquiry, before he took in a Pledge of the most trifling Value from a Stranger; for that it was always his Method to enquire who the Person was, and where he lived; and if the Goods offered were not suitable to the Appearance which the Person m ide, that he always enquired into the Property; and if Goods of Value, always sent home with the Party who offered them, to be satisfied therein; and whenever he had Reason to suspect that the Goods were not honestly come by, it was his constant Practice to rejett the Pledge, or to (top the Party and Goods.

He then proceeded to give several Instances to the Committee, wherein he had flopped Persons and Goods;

and delivered in an Account of the feme; which is annexed in the Appendix N* I.

He said. That Jie constantly toeik in the Daily vertifer, being the Paper wherein Lolfes and Robberies are usually advertised, that he might receive as early Intelligence-as possible, out of which he constantly tran-feribed the Advertisements of such Losses and Robberies into a Book; by which means he could directly find when any Pledge offered to him had been advertised: That he could and would oftener flop Persons and Goods, if he durst; but the Law not authorizing him to flop fuf> petted Persons, he was many times afraid to do it, left he should happen to mistake the real Owner for a Thief, and thereby bring himself into Trouble; and several Persons, whom he has had the greatest Reason to suspect, have even dared him to flop them at his Peril.

But he gave several Instances to your Committee, and delivered in a List of Persons who keep Ale-houses, Gin-fliops, Chandlets-shops, and Coal-cellars, who likewise take in Pledges; and who, when detetted for any mal Practices, fereen themselves under the Name of Pawnbrokers, without mentioning their other Professions; and that he apprehends the Mischiefs complained of, chiefly arose from such Persons being permitted to take in Pledges.

And he tnflanced a Journeyman to a Salefimn, who having received in Pawn a Watch which was stolen, being committed to New Prison for receiving it, knowing it to be so, passed under the , and was publickly advertised to be a certain Pawnbroker, although his Master dealt in nothing but Buying and Selling; the Reproach of which, by that means, fell upon the Pawnbrokers: And that many more Instances might be given of the like Nature.

Mr. Jonathan Beez/ey confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Brown. And,

Mr. fVilJon, being further examined, said. That the Profits of the Pawnbrokers are not superior, if equal, to those of other middling Tradesmen; and acquainted the Committee with the Nature and Profits of his Business; and delivered in an Account of the Value of his Capital, and the Amount of the Profits arising thereupon; which is annexed in the Appendix, N* II. whereby it appeared that he did not return his Capital above twice in a Year; and that he did not make above 16 per Cent, per Annum upon his whole Capital; out of which was to be paid House-rent, Servants Wages, and every other Expence attending the negotiating such a Business.

That for every Pledge of the Value of 1 s. he took a Half-peny for every Calendar Month; and for Two Months a Peny: And though the Profits on these small Pledges appear exorbitant, yet it would be impossible to live upon Pledges of that Value only, since the Profit will not answer the Charge of transacting the Business: For upon every Pledge taken in, he is obliged to make an Entry'of the Sum lent, and the Person to whom, and the Nature of the Pledge, in a Day book; that he likewise ticket ted or billed every such Parcel; and the feme was then to be folded up, and disposed of in the proper Place in the Warehouse for its particular Sortment; that upon its being re-demanded, it was fetched out of the Warehouse, which is usually up Two Pair of Stairs, and delivered at a Minute's Warning; that the Entry in the Book, and the Bill, were both to be discharged, in order to balance the Account; that the Pledge must always be inspected as to the Value, when taken in; and if the Pledger is a Stranger, great Trouble and Caution is required in being satisfied as to the Property: That this engrosses his whole Time and Attention, so that he cannot follow any other Business for his Livelihood.

Mr. George Curtis confirmed the Account of Mr. fVi/fon, as to the Nature and Profits of the Business; and likewise delivered in to your Committee, an Account of his Capital and Profits from the Year 1741 to the present Time; whereby it appeared he had made about 17 per Cent, per Annum grols Produce, on his whole Capital;

lal; out of which the Charges of Management, and other incident CiiargeS are to be deducted as aforesaid. The Account delivered in by him is annexed in the Appendix N' 111.

The Two last Witnesses being asked, What Profit they thought the Generality of Pawnbrokers made upon their Capitals at a Medium ? They severally answered, That they believed about 16 Cent, per Amtu*.

Mr. Grainger being f urther examined, as to vexatious Law-Suits brought against the Professors of this Business, said. There was lcarce a Term wherein Actions of Usury, and Actions of Trover, were not brought against them; and that the Actions of Trover were generally for Goods which have been pledged above Two Years; and that he himself had an Action of Trover brought against him for felling Goods which be had been possessed of Six Years.

Mr. Beezley confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Grainger, as to the vexatious Suits brought against the Profession; and said further, That he himself had an Action of Trover brought against him for Goods pledged in October 1739; that he had kept them above Four Years, for lear of being sued; that being of a perishable Mature, and much damaged, he was obliged to fell them for 40*. less than the Money he had lent upon them; that he was afterwards sued for those very Goods, in the Nameof a Person who he did not know; and not being able to make a Defence in Point of Law, he was obliged to give Ten Guineas to make it up.

That very lately he had a laced Waistcoat pawned to him for Two Guineas, which the Person who pledged to him (who was not the Owner) afterwards informed him, was pledged for more Money than he could get for it by Sale; and that it was never intended to be redeemed; upon which he with Difficulty fold it for the Money he had lent: That by some means the Owner of the Waistcoat coming to the Knowledge of the Sale of it, has since demanded Eleven Pounds; and threatens him with an Action, uniris he comply with that extravagant Demand.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the better Regulating of Pawnbrokers.

A PETITION of John Elwick Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That his -present Majesty, by Letters Patent, bearing Date the 21st Day of November, in the Eighth Year of his. Reign, did

grant to John Tuite of London, Goldsmith, the foie fcxer-cife and, Advantage of an Engine for making Stone Pipes; but that, because the said John Tuite could not carry such Invention into Execution, for want ol a Suin of Money sufficient for that Purpose, he did, for a valuable Consideration, assign all his Property in the same to divers Persons, of whom the Petitionerwas one; but that the other Parties concerned in such Purchase, not complying with their several Agreements in relation to carrying on the said Undertaking, it stood unprosecuted till the Year 1743; when the Petitioner, finding so useful an Inventu n likely to drop, after expending many Thousand Pounds in the Purchase and Prosecution thereof, applied to Parliament for a Renewal of the Term granted by the Letters Patent; and obtained an Act of Parliament for vesting in him the sole Property of the said Engine, and to enlarge the Term granted by Letters Patent for the fame; which Term, by such Act, was extended to Fou.teen Years beyond the Expiration of the then subsisting Patent; That the Petitioner, hath, with great Labour, and at a very large Expence, improved this Engine in such Manner, that he can therewith bore, and at the feme time polish. Cannons, Mortars, and Musquets, of any Size, for the Use of his Majesty's Army and Navy, or any other Purposes, at much less Expence, and with more Certainty and Expedition, than the feme can possibly be
