A.Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Art or Mystery of Butchers, of the City of don, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That King Charles the First did, by his Letters Patent, bearing. Date the 31st Day of July, in the Thirteenth Year of his Reign, incorporate the Petitioners, by the Name of, The Mafier, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Art or Mystery of Butchers, of the City of London:

and directed. That there should be annually, for ever thereafter, on a Day for that Purpose mentioned in the said Letters Patent, elected a Master, Wardens, and Assistants; which said Master, Wardens, and their Successors, for the Time being, are, by the said Letters Pa-, tent, impowered to insped, govern, and regulate, the Persons therein described, exercising or tiling the Art or Mystery of Butchers, in such Manner as therein mentioned: That the Election of a Master, under the express Words of the said Letters Patent, has been attended with Difficulty; and such Election is now rendered impradi-cable: And that, by that, and other means. Informations and Actions have been exhibited and commenced against the Petitioners, touching Matters done, as the Petitioners conceived, under the Meaning of the said Letters Patent; whereby the Petitioners, and the Public, are deprived of the Benefit thereby intended: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, and rendering more effectual, the said Letters Patent.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Fane, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions, which the Committee had directed him to report r the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Seventy-seven thousand Five hundred Thirty-seven Pounds Three Shillings and a Half-peny, be granted to his Majesty, for continuing Two Regiments of Horse, and Thirteen Regiments of Foot, now in his Majesty's Service, under the Command of several Noblemen, for the further Time of One hundred Twenty-two Days.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding One hundred Ninety-eight thousand and Forty-eight Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Three Pence be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary 22

of the Navy, including Half-Pay to Sea-Officers, for the Year 1746.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum not exceeding Sixteen thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, towards carrying on the Building of the intended Hospital for sick and wounded Seamen, near. Gosport, for the Year 1746.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, towards the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, for the better Maintenance of the Seamen of the said Hospital, worn, out, and become decrepit, in the Service of their Country.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second tjme, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are sub- ChariraWe feribed, being Members or Proprietors of the Charitable Corporation. Corporation for Relief of industrious Poor, by assisting them with small Sums upon Pledges, at legal Interest, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Proprietors of the said Corporation, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That her late Majesty Queen Anne, in the Year 1707, did grant unto the said Corporation a Charter, with divers Privileges and Powers, and, in particular, a Power to raise, by voluntary Subscription, a Fund of £.30,000, and that the Members thereof should receive a Benefit proportionable to their Shares therein; and also a Power to make By-laws: That the said original Fund, beingjudged too small to carry on the Design of this In-stitution, his late and present Majesty were pleased to grant the said Corporation, by Three several Royal Licences, a Power to increase their Fund or Capital to £.600,000, by means whereof, the said Corporation having raised several Hundred thousand Pounds, they carried on, for several Years, a fair and successful Trade, and always supplied Persons who made Pledges with them at a moderate Rate, and carefully preserved such Pledges, and ever faithfully restored them, or the Surplusses due upon them, to the Borrowers, without Fraud or Imposition:

And having thus, in all Respects, during the whole Course of their Dealings, acted uprightly, according to the Design for which they were incorporated, their Trade at length extended to all Degrees of People, until, by a most infamous Confederacy between feme of the Directors, Officers, and Servants, the said Corporation were defrauded of near their whole Capital; and great Part of what was left has (ince been spent in Litigations, to recover Satisfaction; but with very little Effect: That these Litigations being now almost finally ended, the Court of Committee of the said Corporation, in Conjunction with many of themost considerable Proprietors, taking into Consideration the present calamitous Situation of the Corporation, who are left without a Fund sufficient to trade withal, yet are exposed to a Forfeiture of thek'

Charter, unless they do trade, have concerted together in what Manner a new Fund might be raised, for the Purposes of their Charter, as the only Means left to save the Company from total Destruction: That accordingly a Scheme was prepared, by Order of the Court of Committee of the said Corporation; which was drawn with all the Ten-derness towards the Circumstances of the Proprietors that could confidently be, with the Nature or the same:

That the Court of Committee likewise provided a System of By-laws, so greatly rectified from the former Methods used in this Corporation, that the Petitioners apprehend no considerable Frauds can again ever happen therein; and that the said Corporation have taken all adviseable Means to render both the Scheme and Plan publick, not only by causing them to be printed, and delivered to the Proprietors, but by publishing frequent Adv.rtisements in the publick Papers of these Transactions: And that, after about Twelve Months had been spent in public and private Meetings, to regulate Measures necessary to restore the Company, a General Court

N

19 Geo. II.

i° — 3° Fe

of the Proprietors was duly called, and held, the iath of March last; at which, and at several other ensuing General Courts, the said Scheme was established; and a Call of Twenty Shillings a Share on each Proprietor was made, to be paid by Four Instailments, of Five Shillings each; and an exa<ft and just Appraisement was, at the same time, ordered to be made of the present Effects, Debts, and Rights, of the said Corporation, except the Charter and Licences; and that all Proprietors, who did not think fit to contribute to the new Fund, might receive their distributive Share of those Effects, upon executing Releases of their Right and Interest in the said Corporation; with divers other Clauses, for the Eafeand Benefit of the Proprietors: That notwithstanding what the General Court had thus done for the Preservation of the whole Company, yet, upon taking the Opinion of divers of the most eminent Counsel, both at Law and in Equity, they found, that the Powers in their Charter would not warrant any Call compelling the Payment of Mopey; but that Proprietors who were Defaulters, and run no Risque, would have an equal Benefit by the Profits of a new Fund with those that ventured their Money, and restored the Company: That therefore, as many of the ' Proprietors could not be prevailed on to answer the Call, those who were desirous to do la, would not in Prudence make their Payments; sincethey could have no superior Interest in the Charter than those who did not: That, besides this, another unfortunate Circumstanceis, That Thirty thousand of the Corporation Shares, and upwards, arc veiled inTiruftces, Executors, Administrators, Infants, and Lenders, before the nth of October 1731; and that several Thousand other Shares belong to Proprietors known to be dead, who either have no legal Representatives, or such as will not veil t hem selves with their Shares, or concern themselves therewith; and that several Thousand more Shares (land in the Names of Persons who are not known, nor do appear, but are supposed to be dead; all which Executors, fYuftees, and Mortgagees, according to the Opinion of the said Counsel, would not be justified, if they obeyed the said Call; a Consideration, which ofitself is sufficient to repel every Attempt that might be made to re-establish the said Corporation, without the Affillance of the Legislature: That the Situation of the said Corporation is more grievous, in regard they have no Course at Law to extricate themselves; but they mull inevitably fink, unless the House will be pleased to interpose so far towards their Relief, as to give all Proprietors of Shares in this Corporation, and their legal Representatives, their Option either to conform with such a Call as to a General Court shall seem expedient, or take their full distributive Share of the present Effects, and release the said Corporation of their Interest and Shares therein: And representing to the House, That the Corporation apprehend such a Compuifion will be a real Benefit, not only to the conforming Proprietors, but likewise to those who chuse to be Defaulters; because, unless a new Fund is raised, that Part of the old one that is left, must be wasted in necessary Charges; and then the present Shares, having no in-trinsic Value, will consequentlyproduce nothing; whereas if a new Fund is raised, the Proprietors of the old may

5

forthwith take their Part of it, or dispose of their Shares to such Persons as are willing to contribute to a new Fund; which if they do not before the Weight of Expences swallows up the Calli in Hand, many of the Rights and Credits belonging to the Corporation will be loft; because the Recovery of them depends upon the Ability of the Corporation to go through the Courts of Justice: That the said Corporation, in the Way of their Trade, have been found to be of general Use to the Inhabitants of these Two great Cities of and

minster-, and, as being a Corporate Body, must be able to lend upon far easier Terms, and with greater Security to the Borrower; apd conseqyeptly cannot fad to prove a principal Remedy against the Oppressions and Frauds of private Lendersupon Pledges: And therefore praying, That in Companion to the present perplexed Situation of the Petitioners, Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the said Corporation to make a- Call on the Proprietors of Shares in the said Corporation, towards carrying on the Business of their Charter, of so much Money on each Share as a General Court of the said Corporation shall find necessary; with such Powers, Conditions, and C'laufes, as the House shall think proper, to regulate and enforce the said Call; and to make a full and just Distribution of the said Company's Effects as shall be judged expedient; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morn-, ing, Nine of the Clock.

Froome Mr. John Pitt reported from the Committee, to whom Bridge, Stc. the Petition of Lora Pitt, Widow, and of the several other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribid, as well for themselves, as on the Behalf of divers other Persons, who are Tenants of the Manor of Forthington, in the County of Dorset, and Inhabitants of the Town of Dorchester, in the same County respectively, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follow; viz.

That by the Evidence of several Persons, it appeared to your Committee, that there is a Common or open Ground called Forthington Moor, or Forthington Meadow, near the Town of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, lying within, and being Parcel of, the Manor of Forthington, in the said County; which Manor belongs to his Koval Highness Frederick Prince of Wales, as Part of the Possessions of the Duchy of Cornwall i and many of the Petitioners, who are Tenants of the said Manor, are - inttried to Right of Common for their Cattle, in and upon the said Moor or Meadow; and several of them to the Math, or Crop of Grass, growing upon the same respectively.

And it also appeared, that the common Highway or publick Road from Bland ford to the Town of Dorchester lieth over Part of the said Common or Moor, and through a Ford, at the Sluice or Tail of a Mill cre&ed on the River Froome-, which is a dangerous Passage for Horses and Carriages, and in Times of Floods and High Waters utterly unpalfable.

And by the same Evidence it further appeared to the Committee, that Mrs. Lora Pitt hath proposed to open and make a new Way or Road, to branch out of the said common Highway or publick Road between Stocking bridge and Londonbridge in the said Road, to be carried over Forthington Moor aforesaid, and through Part of a Garden called Glover's Close, or Segar's Orchard, into the Town of Dorchester-, and to make a Causeway, and erect a Bridge or Bridges upon the fame, so as to render the new Way or Road commodious at all Times; and to maintain arid repair such Road for Three Years, at her owp Expence, in order that the same may hereafter be made the common Highway or publick Road.

And it likewise appeared, that although the making such new Way or Road will be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Inhabitants of Dorchester, and of publick Utility; yet, from the Nature of the several Interests and Property of the Persons in such Lands through which the said new Road is intended to be made, the same cannot be rendered effectual without the Authority of Parliament.

And a Motion being made, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to impower Lora Pitt, Widow, to erect a Bridge or Bridges over the River Froome; and to make a Hoad or Causeway to the East End of the Town of Dorchester, over 1 unds in the Manor of Forthington, in the County of Por/et, belonging to his Royal Highness the Pr ince of U ales, a> Parcel of his Duchy of Cornwall}

Sir Thomas Bootle, Chancellor to his Royal Highness the

Petition respecting a Scheme for

Smuggling.

A Petition of Robert Bonell was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That fevftal Laws have been made to prevent the Running of prohibited and uncustomed Goods, and Wool and Woollen Yarn, from Great Britain and Ireland, to Parts beyond the Seas: That yet the same is still notoriously continued, to the great Diminution of the public Revenue, and the manifest Prejudice of the Trade of these Kingdoms: And that the Laws now in being have not been found sufficient to remedy these great and growing Evils: That the Petitioner has, with great Labour and Cost, prepared a Scheme, which, if carried into Execution, he apprehends, will effectually prevent all manner of Smuggling, Frauds, and Abuses in the Customs, and the pernicious Practice of running Wool and Woollen Yarn, fr#m Great Britain and Ireland, to Parts beyond the Seas, by proper and cafy Checks and Restraints, suitable to the Laws and Constitution of these Realms: And praying, That the Petitioner may have an Opportunity of submitting the same to the Judgment of the House; and that he may be heard thereon, byhiir.self, or Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the *4

Committee, who are appointed to enquire into the Causes of the most infamous Practice of Smuggling; and considerof the most effectual Methods to prevent the said Practice; and to report their Opinion therein to the House.

A Petition of the Land-Owners, Farmers, and Growers Manu&fiura of Hemp and Flax in Marsh Land, in the West Riding in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by an Act passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for further encouraging and regulating the Manufactures of Sail-cloth, and for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail-cloth imported into his Majesty's Kingdoms; it was enacted. That, after the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1736, all foreign-made Sail-cloth or Canvass, ufuilly entered as Hollands Duck, or Yittery Canvas, which shall be for Making of Sails for navigating Ships and Vessels, which shall be imported to Great Britain by way of Merchandize, and for which Duties have been granted, shall be stamped at the Time of the Landing thereof, when such Duty is paid; and that every Ship built in Britain, or in the British Plantations in America, not having a' complete Set of Sails of British Sail-cloth, are, upon Conviction, to forfeit Fifty Pounds fur the fame: That as there is no Duty mentioned or fixed in the said Act, upon Sails made up in foreign Parts of foreign Sail-cloth, the Generality of Matters of Snips purchase abroad, and bring with them into these Kingdoms, full Sets of Sails, as the Petitioners are well in-, formed; whereby they are furnished not only with a Supply for their ownUfe, but frequently furnish their Neighbours and Friends: That thcle they bend to their Yards, when they arrive at the Ports they arc respectively bound for in these Kingdoms; and thereby elude the Design of the aforesaid Act, and have their Sails made up of foreign Sail-cloth, without paying any Duty at all: That the Duty payable upon the Importation of foreign Sail-cloth has been eluded, by importing them under the Name cf Broad Russia Linens: And alleging. That the Petitioners are capable to make it appear, from the Bills of

Lading, Frauds of this Kind have amounted to Five hundred Pounds, in a single Ship: That several Sloops of Forty or Fifty Tons, built upon the River have been entirely fitted out with foreign Sail-cloth; and have navigated to Hull, without any Exceptions taken at thetn

by the Officers of the Customs; and the Owners of such Sloops plead they are not within the Cognizance of the

19 Geo. ii. f 70 Februarii.

Act j which the Petitioners apprehend to be attended with many Inconveniencies: such as diminishing his Majesty's Revenue, prejudicing the Merchants, Importers of Flax, Hemp, and foreign Sail-cloth: That it likewise affects the Landed Interest, by discouraging all further Essays towards Improvement of Hutbanary, as far as respects the cultivating Hemp and Flax, of which none better than our own Growth, and few Countries afford lo good, obstructs the Progress of Sail-cloth Manufactories in these Kingdoms, and in consequence multiplies the Poor, who want Work, and Bread: And that several, who trade in thel'c Commodities, have large dead Stocks of Sail-cloth now lying upon their Hands, which, taking an Estimate from the Sale, and present Demands of their Markets, will be sufficient to supply the Course of Commerce, for several Years to come; and that thereby the worthy and valuable Ends proposed in the aforesaid Act, arc rendered of no Effect: And therefore praying for such Relief, as shall to the House appear most suitable and fitting.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers of Sailcloth, Sail-makers, Rope-makers, Flax and Hemp-growers, Inhabitants of Gainsborough, and the Places adjacent, is referred: And that the Committee do examine, and (late to the House, the Matter of- Fast contained in this Petition.

Prayers.

A PETITION of several Yeoman and Farmers, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves, and many others, concerned in the Growth of Com, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Legislature was so sensible of the great Advantage that would accrue not only, to the Revenue of the Malt-duty, but to the Landed Interest ingeneral, by the Consumption of malted Corn: That several Laws have been made for the Encouragement thereof; particularly in the Second Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, and in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King William the Third; whereby -it was Enabled, That such as make low Wines, Spirits, or brew from Corn, should cause their Corn to be made into wholesome Drink; and from such Drink, without any Mixture, should draw their low Wines, &c. and fee they be made from malted Corn entirely: And if Distillers, or others, mix other Materials, the Gaugers should charge the low Wines drawn, from Drink lo mixed, per Gallon; t"he Duty on low Wines being id. per Gallon only: And that in the 10th and utlvof the same Reign, an Act passed, prohibitingMelaffesto be used in the Brewery, to encourage the Consumption of malted Corn; but that notwithstanding the se, and other Acts, made to encourage the Consumption of malted Corn, Distillers, and others, in preparing Spirits, and other Liquors, use considerable Quantities of unmalted Corn, or Corn not sufficiently malted; whereby much less Corn, as well as Malt, is consumed: And further setting forth the Lois of the Duty of Sea Coal and Welsh Coal, used in the Making of such large Quantities of Malt, that would be further consumed in the Distillery, if Distillers were to make their Spirits in the manner prescribed by the Act of the Seventh and Eighth of King William the Third: And therefore praying, in Behalf of the Petitioners themselves, and many others, thus prejudiced by the Use of unmalted Corn, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and give Relief to the Petitioners, as so considerable a Benefit will arise to his Majesty's Revenue, and the Landed Interest will be greatly promoted, by in forcing the Laws heretofore made for the Consumption of malted Corn; or by such other Means, as to the House shall Teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Petition of several Yeomen and Farmers, in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves, and many Othert concerned in the Growth of Corn; and also the Petition of several Grafiers and Farmers, in the County «of Bucks, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in Bejialf of themselves, and many others, concerned in the Growth of Corn, and the Breeding and Fatting of Cattle.

Manufac- A Petition of the Makers of Sail-cloth in the Port of

_ ‘-'f* London, was presented to the House, and read; felting

al c ‘ lords, That by an Act of Parliament, made in the 12th

Year of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better Encouragement of the Making of Sail-cloth in Great Britain, it is enacted, That over and above all Duties already payable upon foreign-made Sails and Sailcloth, or C nival's, usually entered as Hollands Duck, it Vitterv Canvass, which shall be fit to be made use of for Making of Sails for Ships, and which shall be imported into Great Brit, by way of Merchandize, except Canvass of the Product and Manufacture of Ireland, there should be paid unto her Majesty a further Duty of One Peny per Ell: And that, by another Act, made the Ninth of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for furl her encouraging and regulating the Manufacture of British Sail-cloth; and for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail-cloth imported into this Kingdom; it is enacted, That all so.eign-made Sail-cloth, which shall be imported, and for which Duties are payable, shall be stamped at the Time of Landing; And that by the said Act it is likewise enacted, That no Person shall make into Sails or Turpawlins, any foreign Sail-cloth imported after the 24th of June 1736, not damped, under a Penalty therein mentioned: And further setting forth, That several Merchants, Importers of Sail-cloth, have imported the same und?r the Denomination of Linen, by which they have evaded Payment of half the Duty; and have a'lo been entitled thereby to a Drawback upon Exportation, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all others. Manufacturers of Sail-cloth, in Great Britain: And that several Sail-makers make up into Sails such Canvass so entered as Linen, although undamped, contrary to the express Words of the said Act of Parliament; which the Petitioners apprehend they venture to do, by reason of the Stnallness of the Penalty contained in the said Act: That several Masters of Ships and Yeft'els have brought in ready-made Sails, for which they have never paid any Duty, in Defiance of the aforesaid Acts; and that the several Acts made for the Encouragement of this Trade, have of late been greatly evaded: That, if a tpeedy Relief is not given to the Petitioners, this valuable Branch of Trade, so beneficial to this Kingdom, by employing lb many Thoutands of Poor ot both Sexes, from the Age of Seven to Seventy, which mud otherwise become burthensome to their Parishes, will be entirely ruined, and the Revenue very much lessened: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Relief to the Petitioners, as to the House shall fcvr.i meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers of Sail -cloth. Sail-makers, Rope-makers, Flax and Hemp-growers, Inhabitants of Gainsborough, and the Places adjacent, is referred: And that the Committee do examine, and date to the House, the Matter of Fad contained in this Petition.

DU)illation A Petition of several Graziers and Farmers, in the

from Corn. County, of Northampton, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, concerned in the Growth of Corn, and the Breeding and Fatting of Catile, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That by an Act of the Second Year of King William and Queen Mary, for the Encouragement of the Making of Brandies, Strong Waters, and Spirits, from malted Corn, and for the greater Consumption of Corn, and the Advantage of Tillage, a Durv ot One Peny only was laid on every' Gallon of Low Wi ucs of the First Extraction, drawn and made from Drink brewed with any Sort of malted Corn; and the l'everal Duties of Eight Pence, Twelve Pence, and Three Pence, were imputed upon every Gallon of such Low VOL. 35.

73

Wines, made or drawn from the other Materials therein-mentioned; and all Distillers are obliged thereby to draw their Spirits of the Fird Extraction from clear Drink, made of malted Corn only, without any Mixture whatever; and as an Encouragement for drawing and making Spirits or Brandies from malted Cofn, for Exportation, a Drawback was allowed of Three Pence Gallon of Brandies, and Spirits drawn from Drink brewed from malted Corn, without any Mixture; which said Duties were continued, and the Provisions and Drawbacks were-re-enacted by an Act of the Seventh and Eighth Year of his said Majesty King William: That by an Act of the Twelfth and Thirteenth Year of the said King William, which laid several new Duties on Low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extradion, the like Drawback is allowed on Exportation of Spirits, or Brandy made from malted Corn only, as aforesaid; but that, notwithstanding the Laws made to encourage the Consumption of malted Corn,

Distillers, and others, in preparing Spirits, and other Liquors, use great Quantities of unmalted Com, or Com not sufficiently malted, the said Distillers pretending the y are licensed to do so by the Act of the Sixth of his present Majesty, whereby to encourage Spirits drawn from Corn in Great Britain, a Drawback on Exportation is allowed of £. 4. 18 s.o d.for every Tun of such Spirits: and for every Tun of Spirits drawn from Barley malted, or other Corn, the Bounty of Thirty Shillings is also directed to be paid to the Exporter, when Barley is at One Pound Four Shillings the Quarter, or under; which Ad, nevertheless, doth not, as the Petitioners apprehend, repeal any of the Provisions made by the before recited Acts, for obliging Distillers to draw their Low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesome Drink, made of malted Corn entirely: That by the using unmalted Corn, much less Corn, as well as Malt, is confomed; and than with the Grains of unmalted Corn, now used in brewing and preparing Spirituous and other Liquors, Distillers, and others, feed and fat a great Number of Hog % which would otherwise be better ted and fatted in the Country, by Farmers and Graziers, or would consequently consume a ^reat Quantity of Pease and Beans, and coarse Com, mixed with Grains, if the Distillers, and others, were obliged to use malted Corn only: And therefore, in behalf of the Petitioners themselves, and many others, thus prejudiced by the Use of unmalted Corn, which tends greatly to the Diminution of the publick Revenue, lessening the Consumption of Corn, and discouraging the Breed- ing and Fatting of Cattle, praying the House to take the i Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioners Re-, lief, by enforcing the said Laws, heretofore made, for the Consumption of malted Com, or by such other Means as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Petition of several Yeomen and Farmers, in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others concerned in the Growth of Corn; and of several other Petitions.

A Petition of A Bon Brown, of London, Distiller, was Distilhtloo presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That fe°m Conu the Petitioner hath found, by long Experience in the Trade of Distilling, that Spirits may be made of malted Corn, very near as good, if not equal, in Taste and Fla-your to any foreign Spirits, drawn from the Grape, or any other Materials; but that, by a lately devised Method of mixing raw Corn with that which is malted, the Spirits so produced are rendered both unwholesome and unpalatable, and not of half the intrinsick Value as if they were made of malted Corn only, in a proper Manner: That if the making Spirits intirely from malted Corn, in afkil-ful Way, were encouraged, his Majesty's Navy, and the other Confu.mers thereof, might constantly be supplied with Spirits of a true vinous Flavour, without any let id Smell or Taste, and to answer all thCpurposes that foreign Brandy can do, and superior to any Spirits drawn from Melaues or Sugar, which,'as the Petitioner alleges, he is able, at. anytime, to demonstrate, by ocular and expert* mental Proof: That it is now become almost an universal Practice to add Two or Three Bushels of raw Corn, and so in larger Proportion, to One Bushel of malted Corn; Liverpool* Mr. Brereton reported from the Committee, to whom &c. ' the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto

Road*, fub.scribed, for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign- of his late Majesty King George, for repairing the Roads from the Borough or Port of in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to the Town of in the said

County, leading through the Towns of West Derby, ton cum Roby, and Knozvjley, being above Seven Miles in Length; as also the Road from , through

Roby Town, and through Twig-Lone, into the said Road, between Liverpool and being about One Mile;

and of the several Persons living near, or usually travelling through the said Road, from to Prefcot

aforesaid; was referred; 1'hat the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Part of an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, for repairing and enlarging the Road from Liverpool to Prefcot, and other Roads therein mentioned, in the County Palatine of Laiicaster, was read; whereby it appeared. That several Tolls were granted for repairing the said Roads, to continue from the First Day of June 1726, for the Term of Twenty-one Years.

It further appeared, by the Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Trustees appointed to put the said Act in Execution, ligned by several of the said Trustees, upon the 14th of this instant February, and also by an Abstract of the said Receipts and Disbursements, both which were produced and attested by Mr. John Eyes, That the Sum of Two thousand Three hundred Pounds had been taken up at Interest; and also the further Sum of £.9,894. 1 raised by the Tolls,

making together £. 12,194. v§s. gld. That £. 11,8:6. 6s. lid. Part of the Sum last mentioned,.had been expended by the Trustees; and that the Sum of £.400 If ill remains due upon Bond; towards discharging which, the Trustees have in their Hands the Sum of £.368. 9 7 d.lb that there was, upon the ad of this Instant February, a net Debt of £.31. 10 due upon the Credit of the said Act.

The said John Eyes, being examined, as to the Condition of the Road, said, That the Lane called Twig-Latte, being about Three-quarters of a Mile, still remains unrepaired; and that the Expence of amending the same will amount, upon Computation, to about £.750. That the Cauley already made betwixt Liverpoole and Prefcot, is at present much out of Repair, occasioned by the late Frosts; and that the Charge of amending the same will amount to a considerable Sum, over and above the Statute-work.

Being further examined, he said. That he had heard the Trustees intimate a Design to widen the said Cauley, the same being at present too narrow for Carriages to pass each other; and believed, that the Charge thereof would amount to about £.4,000; but that, if the Caa-fey was to remain as it is at present, he did not apprehend it could be kept in Repair by the ordinary Methods appointed by the Laws in being.

Being asked, Whether the Road was not of late much damaged, by the great Number of Carriages which pals from Liverpoole to Warringtonf he said, That since the Commencement of the War with France, Cannon, and other Military Stores, are frequently carried to Liverpoc/e by Land; but that the Manufactures of Liverpoole, except such as are sent upon Pack-horses, are mostly conveyed to Warrington by Water; but he acknowledged. That there are some Goods carried in Waggons, which commonly go the Prefcot Road, because it is better than that through Roby, though the latter is the nearest Way.

Being examined, as to the Utility of repairing the Road from Prefcot to St. Helens, proposed by the Petitioners to be amended; he said. That the said Road leads to Bolton and Rochdale, and also into the County of Turk, and opens a Way to several Coal-pits at St.; and that the Repairing of the same will be great Advantage to the Country adjacent, and particularly to the Town of Liverpoole, which would, by that means, be more certainly and commodiously supplied with Coals than they noware: That if-any Accident should happen to the Collieries at Prefcot, Liverpoole could not be served with Coals, other than from St.Helens', and that the Road between the said Places is at present so bad, that, in Winter, Carriages cannot pass: That before the Road to Prefcot was repaired, the Inhabitants of Liverpoole usually furnished themselves in Summer with Coals for the whole Year, if they could get. them; but that that Method was attended with gfeat Incoovenicncies, People being often obliged to wait a.coriudurable time at Prefcot, before they could be supplied; there not being, in general, a sufficient Quantity of Coals upon the; Bank to answer the Demand; and many poor People not being able to lay in such a Stock as would serve them all the Year: That since the Making of the said Act, there has been a great Increase of Trade and Manufactures, as well as af the Inhabitants, of fiverpoo/e; and consequently, that the Demand for Coals tnuft be much larger than it was at that time.

Being further examined, he laid. He apprehended that the Town of Liverpoole would reap the gneateft Benefit from the proposed Amendment of the Road to St. Helens 1 but that nfverthelels he believed the same would be of Advantage to the whole Country adjacent; and he added. That the Inhabitants of alone pay fths

of the Money raised by the Tolls now collected.

Being asked. Whether the Opening of this Road would not be a Detriment to the Collieries at Prefcot f he said. He did not'believe it would; because Prefcot being Three Miles nearer to Liverpoole than St. , Persons will naturally go to the former Place for Coals, if they can be supplied as well, and as cheap there, as at the latter.

And he added, in general, That, notwithstanding the Statute-work, should be constantly done, and the Money payable by Law towards the Repair of Highways, be duly levied, yet neither could the Road to St. Helens be made passable for Carriages, nor could that to Prefcot, already amended, be continued in Repair, without the

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Security of Commonalty of the Society of Merchants Adventurers Trade <jur-in the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was ‘"8 'Vjr-presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Interruption of the Navigation and Commerce of these Kingdoms has greatly increased, especially of late, by the frequent Captures of our Enemies, to the great Lois and Impoverishment of many of his Majesty's faithful Subjects, and the Diminution of the publick Revenue; and representing to the House, that unless the same be prevented for the future, it will be impossible for the Petitioners to carry on their Commerce; and that as many of our Ships have been taken by the Enemy near our own Coasts, the Petitioners apprehend that many of the Losses already sustained might have been prevented, if a sufficient Number of Ships of War had been constantly kept cruizing in proper Stations, and more frequent Convoys granted; which was Evident by the Experience of former Times, when an Act of Parliament, made in 1707, intituled, An Act for the better Securing the Trade of this Nation, by Cruizers and Convoy', was still in Force; and, as the Honour, Security, and Wealth of these Kingdoms, depend upon the Protection and Encouragement of Trade, and the improving and increasing the naval Strength; therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

That the House will take thele Things into their Consideration, and afford such Relief as may seem most proper.

Memorandum: The Duties in the above-mentioned Act were granted for a Term of Ninety-nine Years, subject to pay to the several Contributors certain Annuities for Lives: Those Annuities were of a two-fold Nature; that is to lay, Every Contributor had his Option, either to have' an Annuity of £. 14. per Annum only, or an Annuity of £.7. per Annum with the Benefit of Survivorship, for and during his own or any other Person's Life, to be named by him:

Far the greatest Number of the said Annuitants chose to take£. 14. per Cent, certain; the rest thought it would turn to better Account to take £.7.

Cent, with the Benefit of Survivorship.

The Number of Nominees that have died, from the first Nomination to Christmas 1745, upon the Annuities, with the Benefit of Survivorship, is set forth in the above Account; but as to the Nominees upon the £.14. per Cent, who have died within that Time,

'tis impossible to ascertain their Number, for the Realbns following; viz.

Soon after the granting the aforesaid jf.14. per Cent.

Annuities for Lives, several Acts of Parliament passed, which gave Liberty to purchase the Rever-lions of those Annuities.

The Purchasers of such Reversions had Orders made out to pay them such and such Annuities as were mentioned in the Life-orders after the Death of the Nominees for Life; and, as many of those Purchasers were also Proprietors of the Orders for Life, they chose rather to receive their respective Annuities, upon, and by virtue of, their reversionary Orders, than be at the needless Trouble of producing Certificates of the Lives of their several Nominees, every time their Annuities became due, having, after such Reversionary Purchase, a just Claim to those Annuities for a long Term of Years then and yet to come; so that from thenceforward no Cer- -

tificates, either of Life or Death, were, or could be, required at the Exchequer; and consequently no Return can be made of the Deaths that never came to Knowledge.

Exchequer, 13th March 1745. J. Dawson.

Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the Table,-to be perused by the Members of the House.

Manufacture Mr. fVhichcote reported from the Committee, to whom

of Sail-cloth, Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manufacturers of Sail-cloth, Sail-makers, Rope-makers, Flax and Hemp Growers, inhabitants of and the Places adjacent; and also the Petition of the Land Owners, Farmers, and Growers of Hemp and Flax in Marsh Land, in the West Riding in the county of ; and also the Petition of the Makers of Sail-cloth in the Port of London; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House $ and he read the Report in his Place: and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Evidence was as follows:

By an Act of Parliament, made in the 12th Year of Queen Anne, for the better Encouragement of the Mak-

ing of Sail-cloth in Great Britain, and continued by several subsequent Acts, it is enacted, That over and above all other Duties already payable upon foreign-made Sails and Sail-cloth, or Canvas, usually entered as Hollands-Duck, or Vitery Canvas, which shall be fit to be made use of for Malang of Sails for Ships, and which shall be imported into Great , by way of

Merchandize, except Canvas of the Product and Manufacture of Ireland, there should be paid unto her Majesty a further Duty of One Peny per Ell.

The Act, made in the Ninth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, for encouraging and regulating the Manufacture of BritiskSail-cloth, and which has since been continued by subsequent Acts, directs. That, after the 24th of June 1736, all foreign-made Sail-cloth or Canvas, usually entered as Hollands-Duck, or Vitery-Canvas, proper for the Making of Sails for navigating Ships and Vessels, and imported byway of Merchandize, and for which Duties have been granted, shall be damped, at the Time of Landing, with a Stamp denoting the Place or Country from whence the said foreign-made Sail-cloth or Canvas was imported, and with such an Impression as should be durable, and the least liable to be counterfeited; and that, after the 29th of September 1736, every Ship or Vessel built in Great Britain, and after the 25th of December 1736, every Ship or Vessel built in the Plantations, should, upon her first setting out, or being first navigated at Sea, be furnished with One compleat Set*of Sails, made up of British Sail-cloth, on Vol. 25.

Pain of the Forfeiture of Fifty Pounds; and that no Sail-maker should, after Michaelmas 1736,'make or work up into Sails or Tarpawlins any foreign-made Sail-c'oth or Canvas, not flampt, on Pain of forfeiting the said Sails and Tarpawlins, and also the Sum of Twenty Pounds: And ailb ascertains the Number of Pounds-weight contained in each Sortment of Sail-cloth, from N° 1 to N° 10, inclusive.

To prove that Sails are purchased Abroad, and brought

into this Kingdom;

Mr. Samuel Atkinfcit said. That, since the Commencement of the lati-mentioned Act, he has known several Masters of Ships bring home for others, as well as themselves, foreign Sails, acknowledged to be such: That, about Three Weeks since, a Master of a Ship lately arrived, fold a Main-Sail (bene only, as he said, when he came to the English Coast) for One-third less than it could have been fold for, if manufactured at Home; which Sail was brought to the Witness to alter; and that the same was not Ramped, pursuant to Act of Parliament, nor are many others which, the Witness said, he had seen: That it is the common Practice of Matters of Ships to bend Sails to their Yards, and, by that Method, bring over great Quantities yearly, to elude paying the Duty.

Mr. Ephraim Heydon, Sail-maker, being examined, said. That he never knew any Ship return from the Bal-tick, or the Coast of Norway, and the East Country, without bringing One or more, oftentimes Four, Five, or Six, foreign Sails, of which, none that he had ever seen were stamped; and that Ships from Riga and Petersburgk usually bring home double Sets.

That in the Northern Ports of this Kingdom it is usual to fend Orders abroad for Sails to be made of particular Dimensions, and which pay no Duty, when brought here: That he had given Information of this Practice to the Inspector of the Customs; who answered, That Masters ot Ships alleged, that, without buying such Sails, they could not bring home their Ships.

To prove that foreign-made Sail-cloth hath been imported under the Denomination of Broad Linens, without paying the Duty charged thereupon by Law';

There was produced, an attested Copy of a Judgment obtained for his Majesty in the Court of Exchequer, in Hillary Term, in the 18th Year of his Reign, at the Suit of George I. ot thigh am, against Henry Vogeh, on Account of several Parcels of Russia Sail-cloth seized by the said 1‘ottingham, for Non-payment of the said Duty; whereby it appears. That the said Goods were adjudged to be forfeited.

The said George Tottingham, Deputy-Waiter in the Port of London, being examined, laid, That in 1742, Three Bails of Sail-cloth being imported, and entered, ad valorem, as Russia Linen, by one Courteen, he, the

Witness, found that the said Linens were fit to be made use of for Sails, and accordingly seized them, for Two Reasons; the one, their being entered ad valorem at 7 though worth 10 d. per Ell; the other, because they were in reality Sail-cloth: That he gave Information of this Seizure to the Commissioners of he Customs; who, upon hearing their Officers, and the Manufacturers of Sail-cloth, ordered the Examinant to deliver the Cloth to the Owner, unless the Examinant would carry on the Prosecution of the said Seizure at his own Expence, which he declined; and thereupon delivered the Goods to the Merchant, who was admitted to amend his Entry from 7 d. per Ell, ad valorem, to ip which is 25

Cent. Difference; and the Examinant averred. That the said Goods were really Sail-cloth.

That in 1744 he made another Seizure of Sail-cloth; entered as Broad Brown Russia Linen, and gave Information thereof to the Commissioners of the Customs; who did not care to carry on the Prosecution at the Expence of the Crown; but said, That if the Examinant chose to prosecute, they had no Objection to it; if net, he was ordered to deliver back the Goods.

But this Examinant said, That being allured by the Dealers in Sail-cloth, that the said Goods were Sail-cloth, he undertook the Prosecution at his own Charge, and obtained the Judgment before-mentioned: He added further. That upon his making this Seizure, the Land-Surveyors made report to the Commissioners of the Customs, That the Cloth seized was not Sail-cloth; but the Examinant declared to the Committee, That it was equal in Quality to British Sail-cloth of the Sortment N® 5, or betwixt the Sortments N® 5 and 6.

Being further examined, he laid, That at the Trial, several Officers of the Customs gave Evidence, That it was a Practice to enter, under the Denomination of Broad Brown Russia Linen, Canvas equal in Goodnels to what the Examinant seized; and this Practice, he said, was daily increasing.

Peter de CAngle, One of the Jerkers at the Custom-

house, having produced the Report and Papers relating to the Cargo of a Ship called 'The Mary, from burgh, Thomas Jackson Matter; by which Papers it

appeared, that 1,92a Pieces of Goods, Part of the said Snip's Cargo, were entered as Broad Russia Linens, at 9 id.8 d.and 7 d. per Ell, ad valorem, and were seized by the Officers of the Customs, as being Sail-cloth, and therefore liable to the Duties thereon; which Duties exceed, to the Amount of£.310. iu. o the Duties payable on Russia Linens; and that Deposits were made of the Duties for all the said Goods, except Four hundred Pieces, by the Owners, in order to try the Legality of the said Seizure.

The said George Tottingham was further examined; and

said. That theie Goods being imported I'ubsequent to the Trial, and the Commissioners of the Customs having given Orders to their Officers to be very careful in the Inspection of Goods of the like Sort, they were flopped by the Officers, who made Reports to the Commissioners, That they were such like Goods as were seized by the Examinant; but he said, The Owners having made the said Deposit as before-mentioned, in order to Hand Trial, it was ordered by the Commissioners, that the Goods should be discharged, and the Deposits returned; they judging, as the Examinant believes, the Demand of the Officers, in that Instance, a Hardship, considering the Practice had been to enter such Goods as Linens.

Mr. John Pr eft wick. Manufacturer of Sail-cloth, said. That he saw and compared the Goods seized on board the said Ship Mary, which, he said, were Canvas, fit for Sails; and that they answered, in Weight and Quality, to British Sail-cloth of the Sortments N® 6 and 7, used in the Royal Navy, and are fit for any Ships: That the Sortment N° 7. is used in a first Rate Ship of War.

Mr. Heydon produced, before the Committee, a Piece of Linen unstamped, entered, as he was told, by Thomas Fowell, of whom he bought the fame, as Brown Russia Linen, and which pay only a Duty of 3s. 6 the Piece; that the Vender made him a Bill of Parcels of this Linen for Ravens-Duck: That the Witness asked him the Reason of the blue Threads, wove near the Middle and Edges of the Warp; who answered him. That it was a Piece of the Sort of Cloth used in the Navy of; that after their Navy was furnished, the Residue was not permitted to be sold in that Country; but was exported; And the Witness said. He knew the Piece produced by him to be of that Sort; and that the same was equal in Quality to the Sortment of British Sail-cloth N® 6, of which he said, a considerable Quantity is imported; and that he paid 32*. for this Piece, being 38 Yards, which is about 10 d.per Yard: And he laid, further. That British Sail-cloth of the Sortment N® 6, cost is. or 13^. per Yard.

JoJitihWallis, Sail-maker, being ffiewn the said Piece of Cloth, he said. That it came from Ruff a, is entered as Brown Linen, and sold as Ravens-Duck; this, he said, he knew to be a Practice; and that Sails for the Russia Navy are made of the same Sort; and likewise, that Sail-makers make Linen unstamped into Sails, which 22

he attributes to the Smallness of the Penalty in that Cafe.

John Robinson, Maker of Sail-cloth at Warrington, laid, That the Stamp used at the Custom-house, pursuant to Act of Parliament, makes a very obfrure Mark; and that this is one Cause of the Laws being evaded:

And a Piece of Sail-cloth stamped, being produced before the Committee, upon View thereof, the Stamp appeared to be as the Witness had described it.

And Mr. Gee laid. That not one Piece in Fifty was plainer stamped than the Piece produced; and that as the Mark was fixed so near the Edge, a great Part of it must necessarily be much hid, in making the Cloth into Sails. '.

He said also. That he was told by a Matter of a Ship, that whatever Law was made, foreign Sails would be bought; and that he, the said Matter, could get too Pieces of Cloth stamped for a Bottle of Wine.

Four different Pieces of foreign Canvas, proved beforte the Committee to be Sail-cloth, but unstamped, were produced before the Committee.

Mr. Heydon said, that the Navy of England does not consume above 4-th Part of the Sail-cloth used in this Kingdom; and that not above 4-th Part of foreign Sailcloth pays Duty; but that in general the British Sailcloth is better than the foreign.

With regard to foreign Sail-cloth being made use of by Vessels navigating on the River Trent;

Mr. Samuel Atkinson said. That about 130 Sloops, Keels, and Ketches, are navigated upon the said River; the Owners whereof urge they are not comprehended within the Meaning of the Act of the 9th Year of his present Majesty, by reason the said Vessels arc not navigated to the Sea; and therefore they make use of foreign Sail-cloth.

Mr. Joseph Gee being examined, gave Evidence to the tame Purpose with Mr. Atkinson.

Then, in order to prove the Decrease of the Manufacture of Sail-cloth, which is attributed to the before-mentioned Causes;

Mr. Wallace said. That the Cheapnels of foreign Canvas is in some degree owing to the low Price of Flax, as well as the Price of Labour, abroad; that British Flax is better, stronger, and cleaner, than foreign; and that in Dressing of the first, there is greater Loss than in the latter; the Flax imported from Russia being so badly drafted, that the Lois by Waite (whereof no use can be made) amounts to 14 or 15 per Cent.

And, in Confirmation of their Evidence, they produced to the Committee Samples of British and foreign Flax; and described in what Particulars the one was preferable to the other.

Mr. Gee said, That foreign Hemp being soft and spungy, it requires more Tar in the Making of Ropes than British, which is a more solid Body, but will take

Tar enough to preserve the Rope; and that British-Hemp makes by much the stronger Cords.

Then, to shew the Prejudice the said Manufacture receives, by the Importation of foreign Sail-cloth;

Mr. George Bryerly, being examined, said, That he makes about 600 Bolts of Sail-cloth in a Year: That he has now 300 Bolts lies on his Hands, 120 whereof is fit for the Navy, and 200 for Merchants: That this Manufacture has been declining for the last Four Years; which the Examinant attributes to foreign Sail-cloth being imported under fictitious Denominations.

Mr. Thomas Cartivright said. He has employed Eight hundred Persons in spinning Flax; Part whereof was for making Sail-cloth: That he has now 1,400 Bolts by him (though be has left off Trade) undisposed of, which is fit for the Navy, and Merchant Ships; but that Merchants get Ruff a Canvas cheaper than the British can be sold for.

Then the Committee examined Stephen Theodore Jansen Esquire, who said, That the Act for reducing the Excise upon Tea, has, since the Commencement thereof, which was MidsummerJaft, lessened the Practice of Smuggling,

with regard to that Commodity; for that the Accounts at the Custom-house and Excilc-office, shew that the Tea for which Custom and Excise have been paid since Mid-Pummer last, is much more than double to what paid the Duty in any the like Period of Time preceding.

He said, He apprehended the great Quantity of Tea, W'hich appears to have paid Duty in the First Quarter after the Commencement of the present Act, was not all fold out by the Dealers within that Time; but was bought by them, to replenish their Stocks thenexhaufted, by their having postponed such Buying till after the said Act took place; and is the Occasion of the great Disproportion in the Produce of the Duty, within that and the succeeding Quarter; and that it is much more probable, after the Dealers had so supplied themselves in those Two Quarters, that the Tea they have taken out of the Ware-houses since Christmas last, is the Quantity which in reality has been disposed of for Consumption; which Quantity, from Christmas last, to the 17th February following (being Seven Weeks and Four Days) appears, by the Excise, to be 306,662 Pounds-weight; so that, according to this Proportion, within the whole Year, Duty will be paid for upwards of 2,000,000 Pounds-weight of Tea.

He said, That the Smugglers purchase their Goods with Wool and Money, carried from hence; and that the Money so carried, he believes, may amount to^.200,000 annually; though not so much, perhaps, this Year, by reason of Commodore Barnet's making Prizes of the French Tea: That, besides the aforesaid Evil, another pernicious Consequence arisesfrom this Practice; for the Smugglers are, at this Time, admitted into the French Ports, to carry on their illicit Trade, and give our Enemies Information of the Situation of publick Affairs: That the Witness received Advice by Letter (now destroyed! that the Day after Admiral Martin failed last from Plymouth., a supposed Smuggling-vessel went to Su Malo, or Brejly and the Enemy probably knew immediately of the Sailing of that Fleet j and that he sent this Letter to One of the Lords of the Admiralty.

He further said. That he has made particular Enquiry, and has been informed, that the Inhabitants in the of Man (where no Customs are paid, or Duties levied) carry on a constant Trade with France, even in Time of War; that the French bring thither Teas, other India Goods and Brandies; which are deposited in Magazines, and conveyed from thence to and other Ports

By Accounts laid before the Committee, from the Commissioners of the Customs, of Representations made by their Officers relating to the Practice of Smuggi ng; the Instances of that Practice since the Commencement of the Act made in the last Session, appear to be as follows:

From Cardigan, in July 1745, the Surveyor-General of South Wales acquainted the said Commissioners, That Smuggling is carried on to a great Height between England and Ireland. — From Tarmouth, in August 1745, the Collector and Comptroller represented, That they had received Information, that on the 1 ith of July preceding, Fifty Smugglers run a Cargo of Tea and Brandy at Benacre-Warren, in Suffolk; and on the 25th of the same Month, Sixty Smugglers landed another Cargo at the same Place; and a Gang of Forty landed another Cargo at Kejland Haven; and that on the 3 ift of that Month, Seventy Smugglers passed through Benacre-street with a large Quantity of Goods, having with them a Breast-cart with Four Horses; and that Forty Smugglers, with Fifty Horses, landed at Haven a

Cargo of Tea and Brandy, which they carried off — From Wells, in October 1745, the Collector represented, That on the 18 th of that Month, about Two Miles Northward of Yarmouth, between 50 and 60 Horses were laden with

Run-Goods, and carried off by a Gang of armed Smugglers. — From Yarmouth the principal Officers gave Account, That on 2 2d October, 112 Horses were laden on the Beach near Benacre with Dry Goods, by upwards of 90 Men, guarded by Ten Persons with Fire-arms; and that on 20th of the same Month, Forty Horses were laden with Dry Goods at Kirtl, by Riders well armed. — From Chichester it was represented. That on January 1745, Nine Smuggling-Cutters failed from Rye in that Month for Guernsey, in order to take in large Quantities of Goods, to be run on the Coast; and that they had Intelligence, that One of the Cutters had landed her Cargo. — From lpfwichthe Surveyor-General informs the Commissioners, That he had received Accounts, that at different Times, between the 30 th of and 2 8 th of December, there have been run; on several Parts of the Stffo/k Coast, 1,835 Horse-loads of Tea, with some other Goods, and 1,689 Horse Loads of Wet and Dry Goods, besides great Quantities of Wet and Dry Goods landed out of several Vessels; all which were conveyed away in Waggons, and other Carriages, and by great Numbers of Smugglers, loaded: With regard to the First of these Representations, the said Commissioners ordered a Vessel to cruise on the Coast of Wales; and with regard to the others, they gave Directions to intercept the Goods: And as to what related to the Surveyor-General's Account from lpfwich, they ordered Proofs of the said Frauds to be procured; but all Endeavours proved ineffectual.

By the said Account it appears likewise. That the Teas, and other Goods so conveyed, were guarded by formidable Gangs of Smugglers, armed; and that the Officers of the Customs durst not attempt to make any Seizures; and that there have been several other Instances since the late Act, wherein the Officers of the Customs have been obstructed and prevented in searching for, and seizing of, prohibited Goods on Shore, and on great Number of Vessels at Sea; and that where they have attempted it, they have been beaten, and cruelly wounded.

Mr. Richard Sclater, Dealer in Tea, being examined, said. That he is of the same Opinion with Mr. as to the Increase of the Quantity of Tea which will pay Duty; and as to the great Gain of the Smugglers.

That he computes the Tea consumed in this Kingdom to be near 4,000,000 of Pounds-weight per Annum; and as the annual Quantity which paid Duty was not, till the present Act commenced, above 8oo, oco Pounds-weight, therefore 3,000,000 Pounds-weight at least must have been run every Year.

That the Smugglers now trade, and have always Admittance, into the Ports of France: That they buy some Teas of the Danes and Swedes, and run great Quantities from Middleborough and Fluffi; but that he believes

there is not so much smuggled in general, since the present Act passed, as before; which he attributed to Commodore Barnet's making Prize of the French Tea in the

Indies; for he laid. If that Tea had been brought to France, it would have occasioned as much Smuggling now as formerly; but as the Dutch have bought it, though it may be run from Holland, yet it must be run with greater Difficulty, by reason of the Distance of the Dutch Coasts.

That the Running of Goods into the Counties of and Sussex (the Counties where commonly this Practice was mollly canied on) has met with great Interruption, and been in some Places totally prevented, by the Fleet upon that Coast, and the Forces on Shore; and that several Perlims, who were never known to lell Tea before, have, since the Commencement of the present Act, bought large Quantities of the fair Traders, and disposed of it upon those Coasts, where Smuggling was at a stand: But he added. That since Smuggling has dccreased on the Kent and Sussex Coasts, it has increased, to a great degree, on the Coast of Suffolk.

That the French, Dutch, Swedes, and Danes, deal chiefly in low-priced Tea; and, upon a Medium, for several Years past, he believes there has not been above 60,000 Pounds-weight yearly of fine Tea brought into Europe, except into this Nation, wherein the Quantity annually imported, is about 150,000 Pounds-weight: That the smugglers run only coarse Teas, purchased, abroad lor is. or is. 4 d.and loid here for 4*. 6 or 5/. per Pound: As to fine Tea, their Package would spoilit; nor could they, if they bought a Quantity, dispose of it: That he thinks the French do not consumc above -rV"* Part of their Tea, nor the Dutch any Quantity equal to what they bring; and as the Germans, and other neighbouring Countries, consume very little, in comparison to our Consumption, he apprehends that the greatest Part of the Dutch and French Teas must be sold to Per-fions who run them into this Kingdom.

He laid likewise, That the Smugglers pay for their Goods with ready Money, or Wool; and that he believes this clandcstine Trade brings France more Specie than all Vol. 25.

their Trade in Europej and must in time bankrupt this Nation.

He said further. That the Smugglers in the Country, by their Numbers, and their Outrages, intimidate several of the Civil Magistrates from granting Warrants to apprehend them, and the Officers of the Customs and Ejc-cile from venturing to do their Duty: And the Witness attributes it to this Terror, that so few Seizures are made.

He laid likewise, That the East India Company having, besides their Importation from the Indies, lately bought in Holland a great Quantity of Tea, this large Supply may, in some degree, prevent Smuggling; but then the Company must fell it at lo low a Price, as that the Smuggler cannot under-fell the Dealer; for otherwise, let them-import ever so much, it will be to no Purpose.

Mr. Samuel Wilson, Grocer, being examined, owned. That formerly he had been greatly concerned in Running of Tea; but took the Benefit of the Act of Indemnity, made in 1736; and said. Three or Four Miles from our Coasts, By Boats, which bring the Goods a-ftiore; and before the present Act, he believes 20 or 30 Cargoes were run in a Week: That the Smugglers buy their Goods abroad with Money, or Wool; and that the principal Commodity they run is Tea.

That for the Three or Four Years preceding last -fnmmer, therewasfeldom less than Three millions Pounds-weightofTea clandestinely imported every Year; and of this, he said, he was lately informed, by one Robert Hanning, who supplied the Smugglers with Tea formerly at Dunkirk*and since the War with France, at Flushing;

and has been several times in England: And which Fast Hanning told the Witness he could make appear.

That the Dealers in Tea gave to the Smugglers, in 1728 and 1729, Eight Shillings per Pound for run Tea; but that since the Danes, French and Swedes, have traded to the Indies, the Price has gradually decreased.

That Tea run into London, is put into Warehouses, under the Care of Agents; and if any is seized, all the Parties concerned are Sufferers alike.

That the Smugglers give more abroad for their Tea now than formerly: That the present Price of such Bohea as is imported by our Company is about zs. 10 a Pound/; and a great Quantity is now supplied, at that Price, by one Andrew Her fey, at Middleburgh: That their Expences are, for Freight £. 1. is. per Hundred-weight; for their

English: That he has been informed by Smugglers, that they do not now get clear above zos. per Hundredweight; and he himself believes their Profit cannot amount to 3d. per Pound.

As to the Loss which Smugglers sustain by Seizures, he said, it is a mere Trifle: That he formerly dealt with a considerable Trader in run Tea for Six or Seven Years, who never had any Goods seized in all that time; and that although the Danger of Seizures is greater at Sea than on Land, yet the Smugglers most commonly efoape the Custom-house Sloops, by means of Intelligence sent from the Inhabitants on the Coast, when those Sloops fail out of Port; and that the generality of the People on the Coasts are bitter Friends to the Smugglers than to the Custom-house Officers: He added likewise. That Smugglers, to escape being seized at Sea, frequently make out their Clearance from the foreign Port, at which they took in their Lading, to some other foreign Port; so that if they are not met at Sea by the Custom-house Sloops, within Six Miles of the Coast, they are not liable to Seizure; and that he has known several Smuggling Vessels escape by this Contrivance.

As to the Seizures on Land, he said, They very seldom happen; for when Tea is landed, it is carried by 10 or 12 armed Persons in a Body, on Horseback into the inland Counties, where there is no Danger of having it seized; and it is disposed of, at certain Markets, to People, who take 1,000 Pounds-weight at a time: That

there arc likewise a Number of Men called Duffers, who go on Foot, and have Coats in which they can quilt a Quarter of a Hundred-weight of Tea, and bring it to London in that manner, undifeovered; and that these Duffers supply the Hawkers, who carry it about the Town, and fell it to the Consumers.

That Tea is now seldom brought in great Quantities to London-,or when brought, is scarcely ever seized, with-

out the Assistance of Soldiers; in which Cafe, the Smugglers commonly have Knowledge of the intended Seizure time enough to remove their Goods.

That the Informations of Places where Tea is lodged in the Country are commonly given to the Inspectors of the Customs, who fend for Soldiers to feiae it; but they are generally unsuccessful Three times in Four; For the Smugglers have timely Intelligence of such Informations from their Agents.

That they likewise employ an Agent (one Norton) to defend them against Prosecutions; and he searches to fee when Capias's are taken out in the Exchequer against any of his Clients, and accordingly apprizes them to get out of the way: That this Norton was formerly Clerk to the late Mr. Metcalf, Solicitor of the Customs; and that the Witness believes he then might fee all the Informations that were given in at the Custom-house against Persons for running Goods; and it is not impossible but that he may now come at the Knowledge of the like Informations, by means of the Solicitor's Clerks: The Reason why he thinks so is, because that himself had come to the Knowledge of several Informations the same way; That the Smugglers have such Intelligence, and use such artful Management, and are withal so resolute and defpe-rate, that the Witness believes, notwithstanding all the Care of the Custom-house Officers, not One round in Twenty of run Tea is seized.

As to the Number of People who follow this Practice, he said, they are not less than 20,000: That they affem-ble together at Ports and Places the most convenient for their Purpose, particularly at Folkstone, where there is a great Number; but their chief Place of Resort is -hurst in Kent: That they go armed; and although they are well known. People dare not venture to molest any of them; and that if Soldiers are ordered to take them, they have Intelligence either from their Agents, or perhaps from some of their Relations or Friends: And the Witness owned, that he himself actually did apprise one Tomkins of his being advertised in the Gazette, with a Reward for his Apprehension, early enough for the said Tomkins to make his Escape.

Being asked the Question; he laid. That Smugglers purchase Teas with Money and Wool: That when they get any Wool, they put it on board such Vessels as are ready to put to Sea; but that a Ship never stays for that Sort of Lading; for if no Packs are ready, the Vessels frequently go without; and he believes that there is carried out of this Kingdom at least One million Pounds per Annum, in Specie, to purchase the various Goods run in here; and he was the more confirmed in his Opinion, because that the said Hanning, formerly a Smuggler in this Kingdom (and who wasindifted for a Murder, and absconded, and was afterwards pardoned, on Condition of his making certain Discoveries in relation to the Practices of Smuggling) wrote thereupon to at

to make Enquiry amongst his Correspondents at other foreign Ports, what the Money received from Smugglers might amount unto; and Hanning delivered a private Account thereof to Sir Robert feme time before

the Year 1736; by which Account it appeared, that the same amounted to £. 1,000,000 or £. 1,100,000 per Annum; of which £.800,000 per Annum was paid for Tea: But the Witness said. That at that time the Smugglers gave for their Tea a much larger Price than they give at present.

Mr. John Scrivener, Dealer in Tea, being examined, said, That since the present Act commenced, the Practice of Smuggling has greatly decreased; for that the fair Traders now fell much more Tea than they did formerly; but that (till a great Quantity is run: That the Swedes fell Tea to the Smugglers; and that it is a common Practice to fend Tea to the Isle of Man, from whence it is run into England and Ireland; and that if the East India Company cannot supply the Dealers with a sufficient Quantity of Tea, at a low Price, the Smugglers will continue to run it; and if they cannot supply the coarse Teas at at. 9 d.per Pound, the Dutch will.

That when the Company puts up only a small Quantity to Sale, several Persons buy in a speculative way, in order to fell it again at large Gain, when Tea is wanted: That the Price of Teas is, by this means, often raised, and the Smugglers thereby encouraged to run this Commodity.

Mr. Bamaby Bland, Officer of the Customs, being

examined, laid. That he judges by the great Decreale of Informations in the Port of London, that the Quantities of Tea run are much less than before Jail.

That the East India Company had always more Tea, before the Commencement of the present Act, than they could dispose of; but the Demands since being much larger, they had not enough to supply the Dealers; and that till the Company can bring in a sufficient Quantity, if there were no Duty at all. Smuggling would continue.

He said. That the Smugglers Profit is much less now than it was before the Act; for that their Journies are less frequent, and more expensive: That they formerly came to London about Two or Three o'Clock in the Morning, and could fell to particular Dealers from 1,000 to 2,000 jfOunds-weight, and be out of Town again by Six the same Morning: and, by this quick Return, they generally made a Voyage every Ten Days; but as the said Dealers have refilled to buy since the said Act, the Smugglers have had great Difficulty in disposing of their Tea; and that now a Dozen or Twenty of them in a Gang carry each of them Half a Hundred or a Hundred-weight from the Coast, and separate, and dispose of the same in the inland Counties in small Parcels of Six, Seven, and Eight Pounds, and sometimes in what they call Dollets, which are about 13 Pounds; so that their Returns are very uncertain, being regulated by the Succels they have in disposing of their Tea: And he added. That he believes there is not now so much Tea run as was within Three Months after, the Commencement of the present Act.

Mr. George Barrington, being examined, said, That he believes not lets than 5,000,000 Pounds-weight of Tea is yearly consumed in this Nation, Ireland, and the British Plantations: That the Dutch and Danes bring great Quantities of Tea to the lllands of St. Eufiafiia, Sabea, and St. 'Thomas, in the West , from whence the British Settlements in the West Indies are fopplied: That Ships go from the British Northern Colonies into the French Ports, and carry small Yards, Malls, and Arms, and sometimes Horses; for which they barter either in Money or Sugars; and if not for the Whole, they dispose of the Remainder at the Engliftt Settlements; and in their way home, they call at the Dutch and Danish Islands, and buy Teas, and Other Goods, with Money; whereby England is prevented from supplying those Colonies with Tea.

That the Tea brought into the North-East Part of England, and East Part of Scotland, comes from Denmark, Sweden, and Holland, and is conveyed in Scotch Vessels, which load Wine and Brandies in That

the Teas brought from Sweden and Denmark, are purchased with our Specie and Manufactures; the Scotch lend

feme Lead and Salmon, which dre exchanged for Brandies, Tea, and Wine; but not to the Amount of the 20th Part of the Value of the Wines and Brandy they bring; the rest being paid for in Specie.

That Tea run into the South Part of England is brought by Vessels, employed in Smuggling, from Hot-land, France, Jersey, and Guernsey; and that great Quantities are brought by Lime Vessels, which come to Devonshire: That he believed not a Ship went from to Holland or France, but what run prohibited and French Goods; the Witness having bought Hundreds of Dozens of Claret, with the Bottles, for i6J. the Dozen, and French Brandy at 35. 6d. per Gallon.

That many Vessels, from Liverpoole and Whitehaven, carry Tobacco to Holland (which is a great Trade in the North-West Ports, because of the Opportunities to avoid the Duties) and run large Quantities of Tea, and other Goods; and that the same is practised from Glasgow in Scotland.

He said likewise. That prohibited Goods are carried from France to the Iste of Man, and' the West Coast of Scotland; and are sent to Ireland, Chester, and Cumberland.

That the Officers in the East India Ships carry out what Money they can raise, and buy Goods in the Indies, and' run almost all the Goods they bring into this Kingdom; they take up'Money on Bottomry, which the Company must be apprised of, because they pay £. 15 per Cent, for Liberty to Trade.

Then the Committee examined Evidence, with regard to some Defects in the Act, made the last Session, for indemnifying Offenders for Running of Goods.

"M.v.Richard Sclaterand Mr Sseverally laid,

Thata Number of Persons willingly embraced the Pardon granted by the said Act; and accordingly left off Smug-' gling, and settled themselves in Farms, and other Occupations; but One of those, whole Name is Murton, being apprehended, and indicted upon a former Statute, for riding with Fire-arms near the Coast (which Offence is not included among those pardoned by the said Act of Indemnity) most of the Smugglers who had embraced that Pardon, being equally culpable, absconded, upon an Apprehension they were liable to the like Prosecution; and upon Conviction of the said Murton, at the last Summer Assizes at Rochester, all those Persons, finding the ni-selves not safe, returned again to their former Practices of running Goods.

Mr BarnabyBland, an Officer in the Customs, confirmed what had been said, in regard to this Defect in general; and that the Continuance of the Running of Tea, since Midsummer last, is in some measure to be attributed to that Defect: He added, That a great Number of Smugglers, and Receivers of run Goods, who had not rid with Fire-arms near the Coast, had embraced the Pardon offered by this Act, and have accordingly left off; apd that he believes most of the wealthy Importers have left off; but that some of them, who have rid with Firearms (notwithstanding the y have accepted the Pardon) are now afraid to come to London, from an Appreheri-fion of being prosecuted; and that he has observed, that most of the Persons affected in that Particular, continue their former Practices.

M r. Samuel Wilson said. That he apprehended the most effectual way to prevent Smuggling of Tea, is to reduce the Price of that Commodity io low as to make it not worth any Person's while to run it; but thinks it impossible to attain that End, without a.Reduction of the Duty, especially as the , Swedes, , and
