He also added. That Robert Hanning, before-mentioned iii the Course of the Examination, told this Witness, that if the Price of Tea was lessened 6d. in the Pound, it would put an entire Stop to Smuggling.

' He then proceeded to prove, that by such Reduction the Revenue would be considerably increased; viz.

That upon a Supposition of Three millions of Pounas-weight of Tea is consumed annually' in this Kingdom, and that Quantity £. paying a Duty of 6 d. per Pound, would produce - 75,000

The Duty, ad valorem, supposing each Pound to be sold at the Company's Sale for 4on a Medium, would produce - - - - 150,000

The Custom o*f £.14 per Cent, paid by the Company, would produce - - - 84,000

Which makes in the Whole - 309,000

From Whence he inferred, That if the Duty of is. per Pound was reduced to 6 d.and Smuggling thereby prevented, the Revenue Would be increased £.75,000 per Annum more than the present Duty, upon a Calculation of what already appears will produce.

And this Reduction would certainly prevent the Running of Tea at present, by reason that the East India Company have, with their own Stock, and a large Quantity of inferior Teas they lately purchased in Holland, sufficierst to supply all present Demands; and as they have great Quantities coming from the , and may buy Cheap in foreign Markets, he had no Doubt of their Applying the whole Consumption of this Kingdom for the future; and in this same the Revenue would be increased much above his Computation; because he has great feafotl to believb, that the annual Consumption of Tea in this Kingdom greatly exceeds 3,000,000 Pounds-weight.

That Smuggling Vessels sometimes take in Brandies as Ballast; but the Witness has heard the Smugglers fey. That, as Brandy is a heavy Commodity, if Smuggling of Tea was prevented, it would not be worth while to bring Brandies; and that as there is, by the Vessels that bring Tea, an Opportunity of fending Wool out of this Kingdom (and by which means a great Quantity is actually Conveyed) he apprehends, that if no Tea was run, it would, in a great degree, lessen the Smuggling of Wool; for it would not answer for any Persons to employ Vessels merely in the Carrying of Wool, by reason of the long time they mud wait between their Voyages to get a Loading, and of the great Hazard they must run of being seized while they arc in Waiting.

And he added. That Tea is by far the most considerable Commodity that is run; and as Running most of the

other Species of Goods depends upon, and are encouraged* to be run merely from, the Opportunity of running them with Tea, he apprehends, that this Reduction of the Duty on Tea, accompanied with a free and general Pardon, will be a more effectual means to prevent Smuggling in general, than any other Methods that ever he heard proposed.

Being asked, Whether fending on board Ships of War People taken in the Practice of Running Goods, would not greatly discourage them ? and whether they might not be made very useful there ? He answered, he believes it would, in some degree, discourage them; and that they might be made useful; but then he thinks, that the practising that Method would make them more desperate; and that he is confident, from his being well acquainted with their Disposition, that if a Law was made to pardon them, on Condition of their enlisting for Soldiers or Sailors, they would not accept it; and that ifcompulfory Methods be attempted, they will assemble together in a Body to defend themselves: That he believes if the Duty was reduced, and a free and general Pardon was granted, they would disperse; and in that Cafe, several of them. might be induced to enter into the Army and Fleet, and be extremely useful, particularly at Sea; they being extraordinary good Sailors.

With reference to the Mitigation of Penalties, he said. That if by Law there was no Power of Mitigation for receiving run Tea, and felling Permits, in the manner before described, he believes it would be a great Discouragement to the Smuggler and the Receiver; but if the Power of Mitigation was wholly taken away, he thinks withal, that some Laws relating to the Excise would be extremely severe, particularly One, whereby a Penalty of £.100 is inflicted upon Dealers who neglect to set down in their small Books, every Day, the Quantity of Tea they fell without Permits; and if a Dealer forgets, or happens to be ill, or engaged in other Business, and trulls to his Servants to enter Tea fold, and they neglect it, and the Officer comes in the Morning, and by Survey of his Stock, finds that he hath fold a Quantity for which he rieither sent to the Officer for Permits, nor entered it in his Book, this Penalty of £.100 is recoverable; but added, that if this, and some other Penalties, were lessened, the Power of Mitigation (very detrimental to Trade) might be taken away.

Mr. Matthew Blakifion said. That the taking away (he Temptation of Smuggling by lowering the Price of Tea, would be the mosteffectual Method to prevent it; but apprehends, that by a Reduction of the present Duty, that End would not be attained; for that, as the India Company do not bring home a sufficient Quantity, the Dealers, by bidding one above another, would give the said Company an advanced Price equal to the Reduction of the Duty.

That he apprehends the Running of Tea may be prevented, without reducing the present Duties, if the said Company were obliged to supply Dealers with a Quantity equal to the Consumption of this Kingdom, and their Two Sales in the Year v. ere fixed to certain times.

That if a free Pardon was granted to Persons concerned in the Practice of running this Commodity, he believes that many of them, particularly most of those who have acquired large Sums of Money, would accept it; and that if they be not effectually pardoned, they will keep together in Bodies, for their own Security, and continue their Practices, though attended with very little. Profit.

Being asked the Question; He said, he apprehends if some Method were contrived to employ these Persons on board the King's Ships, it would greatly prevent the carrying on the said Practice.

Evidence with Mr. Adams, is to the Method of preventing the Smuggling of Tea, by reducing the Duty, and granting a free Pardon for Offences for Running of Goods; and in the Reaions why Redtidion of the is. per Pound is preferable to an Abatement in the £ per Cent, ad valorem; and added, That it will always be in the Power of the East India Company to affect the Practice of Smuggling more or less; for if they do not bring in a Quantity sufficient to supply all Demands, whatever Laws are made against it. That he is of Opinion, That were the East India Company to fopply the Trade with a sufficient Quantity, at a low Price, and 6 d.per Pound Duty taken off, the Deale's would then be enabled to fell JBohea Tea for per Pound, and Green for $s. which would not only ruin the Smugglers, but the Company might in time engrossalmost all the Trade to themselves, and fell to several of thol'e Nations who now fell to usj for then, as the Danes, Swedes, and French, would not bring near the Quantities they do at present, they must be driven out of the Trade; because it would not be worth their while to go to the Indies to supply their own Consumption.

The Witness said further, That he has been twice in

China; and is fore, that if the Company would give £.25 per Cent, more for the fine Teas, they might secure the whole Quantity to themselves.

Then the Committee came to the the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the high Duties charged upon Tea, and other Commodities, have been One Cause of the infamous Practice of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Act of Indemnity, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for Persons guilty, of the infamous Practice of Smuggling, was not extensive enough for the Pardon of several Persons therein concerned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the not efTedually prosecuting Owners of Vessels used in carrying on the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, is another Cause of that infamous Practice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of tins'Committee, That the exposing to Sale the Boats, and other Vessels, taken from Persons carrying on the Practice of Smuggling, by means of which, such Boats, or Vessels,' are often bought by the same or other Persons carrying on the faihe pernicious Practice, is another Cause of the Continuance, and an. Encouragement of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the ealy Composition of the Penalties incurred by Persons convicted of Running, or being concerned with" others, in Running; Landthg; or Ditpofing of uncuf-. tomed Goods, is another Cause of the said pernicious Practice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this: Committee, That the want of proper; Penal ties and Punishments to be inflicted upon Officers--of the Excise and Custonrts, for Neglect of Duty, or Misbehaviour in their respective Offices, is another Cause of the said pernicious Practice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That lowering the Duties on Tea, and other Commodities, would be One Means to prevent the said pernicious > Practice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a general Ad of Indemnity to all Persons guilty of any- Crimes again (I the Laws for preventing the running uncustomed Goods (except such as have been guilty of Murder) will be One other Means to put a Stop to the infamous Practice of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the burning the Boats, and other Vessels, belonging to, and taken from, Persons concerned in the infamous Practice of Smuggling, will be One other Means to prevent the said Practice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the compelling Seamen and Seafaring-men, taken

on board any Ship or Vessel employed in Running uncustomed Goods, or otherwise concerned in Landing or Dif poling of the lame, to serve for a certain T>me on board his Majesty's Ships of War, would be One other Means to prevent the infamous Practice of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the giving a Reward for the discovering and apprehending all such Persons who have followed the infamous Practice of Smuggling, either by Sea or Land, or as Riders, would be another Means for putting an End to the infamous Practice of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the incapacitating all Persons who shall hereafter be convicted of Running uncustomed Goods, from voting at Elections for Members of Parliament, will be another Means of preventing the infamous Practice of Smuggling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the prosecuting such Subjects of his Majesty who shall resort to the Ports of France, and carry with them Sums of Money, or Wool, or give them Intelligence, in Time of War, as guilty of High Treason, would be another Means of preventing Smuggling.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Tomorrow Fortnight.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the several subscribing Merchants of the City of London, and other Persons interested in the Trade from this Kingdom to Ireland, and his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in America, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by several Acts of Parliament, now in force, all Teas imported into Great Britain are subjected, upon the Importation, to divers Subsidies and Imposts, amounting to near f. 14. per Chut which Subsidies and

Imposts have constantly, ever since the 12th of his Majesty King Charles the Second, to the 25th of June last, been drawn back, and repaid, upon Exportation, except only half the Old Subsidy; and that the Duties thus drawn back amount to£. 12. 31. id. per :That byjan Act, passed in the last Session of this present Parliament, in lieu of the former inland Duties payable to his Majesty on Teas, a new Duty is imposed thereon, of 1 per Pound, and of £. 25 for every £. 100 Value of Tea, at the Gross Price at which it is sold at the India Company's Sales, o\er and above all Customs, Subsidies, and Duties, payable on the Importation; which Duty is to be paid 18

down on all Tea, before it can be taken out of the Company's Warehouse, for any Purpose whatsoever: And it is thereby further enacted, That no Drawback shall be allowed for any Tea to be exported or shipped, to be exported after 24th June 1745, when the said Act took place: That the Eaf-India Company have the Privilege of importing Tea into Great Britain, and the only legal Supply which Ireland, and his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in America, can have of that Commodity, mud be from the Importation here: That several re-strictive Claufts have been, from time to time, inserted in all the Acts of Parliament, which have allowed the Drawback on Tea, to prevent any Frauds or Abuses, either against the Revenue, or the fair Trader; and particularly by an Act, passed in the 10th Year of his late Majesty, for repealing certain Duties therein mentioned, and payable upon Coffee, Tea, £sV. and for other Purposes therein mentioned; it is enacted, That no Tea shall be delivered out from the Warehouses for Exportation, until Security first given that the same shall be exported, and not re-landed in Great Britain: That by the Encouragement of the Drawback Ireland and the Plantations have hitherto taken for their Consumption, large Quantities of Teas, imported into Great; and

that the' Consumption of Tea, in those Parts of his Majesty's Dominions, has, for forne time past, considerably increased; inso much, that in 10 Years time the Quantity exported from hence to tvas doubled,

and That to the Plantations trebled; the annual Export having arisen to near 400,000 lb. of Tea, before the Act of the last Session of Parliament was passed: That in Ireland and the Plantations, clandestine Importations are morse practised than in Great Britain; and that by their natural Situation, and the necessary frequent Intercourse they have with Foreigners, they are particularly exposed to Temptations of this kind; and that, even whilst they enjoyed the Benefit of the Drawback, there was no Ids than Two-thirds of the whole Consumption clandestinely imported to Ireland, to evade paying the Duty of tid. per Pound, to which all Tea is subjected, immediately upon the Importation there; and that, though the precise Quantity illicitly imported into the Plantations cannot be ascertained, the amount must have been very considerable: That all Teas font from hence, being at present burdened with the Inland Duty and Custom, and no Drawback being received here on the Exportation, foreign Teas are now introduced into Iteland and the Plantations, for less than One hundred per Cent, of what they can be imported from Great Britain; which makes the present Law amount to a Prohibition of English Tea in those Parts: That the Exportation of Teas being thus Itopt, the Importation into this Kingdom from mwft necessarily decrease in proportion, and thereby many valuable Advantages be loll to the Nation, in respect to Trade and Navigation: That by discontinuing the Drawback, and subjectingall Teas exported to the Payment of the Inland Duties here, the Irish will open the Door wider to a foreign Vent for their Wool and Woollen Manufactures, which will no longer be brought hither as Returns for Tea, to be exported from hence; the Trade of the Plantations, which, from the Policy of all Nations, should be confined to their Mother Country, will fall into the Hands of the Dutch and French, who will supply them with all European Commodities, which are now lent from hence; our declared Enemies, and most watchful Rivals in Trade, will only reap the Advantage of the Commerce of those his Majesty's Dominions; and the Mischiefs which this Part of the Act was calculated to rcdiefs, and which are already become more pernicious than ever, will be further extended to the great Fraud and Prejudice of the Revenue, and fair. Trader: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter into their Consideration; and to grant the Petitioners such Relief, as the Nature of the Circumstances requires, and the House shall fee fitting.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Agents for the British Sugar Colonies in America, and of the subscribing Planters and Merchants, interested in and trading to America, was presented to the House, and read; representing. That the British Sugar Islands being unable to subsist by their own Productions, depend absolutely for their Subsistence on the Provisions of North America, both as to Bread, Corn, Fish, and many other Necessaries of Life, which they constantly receive from thence, having seldom a Supply on their Islands for more than Two Months; so that every Interruption or Difeouragement to the Trade and Commerce carried on between the British Sugar Islands, and the British Northern Colonies in America, threatens his Majesty's Subjects in those Parts with Famine: That the said Colonies, not having Timber of their own Growth fit for the purpose of making Calks, cannot remit their Produce of Sugar and Rum to this Kingdom, without large and constant Supplies of Lumber from North America; and that whatever therefore obstructs that Trade, inevitably puts the Sugar Colonies under the greatest Distress: And further representing to the House, the destructive Consequences of impressing Seamen in the Sugar Colonies; and reciting several Provisions for the effectual Prevention of these Evils, made by an Act of the 6th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the Trade to America; and alleging, that these Provisions, made

by this Act, were of the greatest Benefit, not only to the Sugar Islands, but also to the Navigation, Trade, and Commerce, of this Kingdom, and, in consequence thereof, to the Revenue of the Crown; and that no inconveni-cncy was thereby brought on the Ships of War in those Parts: And setting forth, That, as the Petitioners apprehend, that Part of this Act which restrains the Impressing of Seamen in the British Colonies is perpetual, not only from the Nature of the Provision itself (which is equally necessary in Time of Peace as in Time of War- but from the Obligation all Ships are now under, before they can have their Clearances to fail from the Su-^gar Islands, to deliver in at the Custom-house the Lift of their Men, required by the 1 ith Section of the said Act, and which is done in pursuance of the said Act; but that the Admirals, and other Commanders of his Majesty's jKavy Rationed in America, ppon a Supposition, that the Voc. 2J.

said Act of Parliament expired with the last War, have revived the Practice of impressing Seamen iri those Parts, as well out of Privateers as out of Merchaht Ships; and particularly have, in Jamaica, impressed Hands but of the Northern Vessels, who came toiupply the Inhabitants of Jamaica with their daily Bread: And further representing to the House the Distrcls which this Practicehath brought upon the British Sugar Colonies, and the Benefit received in consequfence thereof, by our greatest Enemies and Rivals in Trade, the French, to the great Injury of the British Navigation and Commerce, and to the occasioning the Course of Trade to the Spanish Main being alfcr turned into thb Channel of the neutral Ports of St. EuJiatia and Curacoa: And setting forth, That the Royal Navy receives very little, if any. Benefit therefrom, and would be much better manned, without impressing, by the Me-, thod prescribed by the 13th Section of the said Act of Parliament: And therefore praying the House, That they will be pleased to take the Premises into theirferious Consideration; and that they will, by a Law to be passed for that Purpose, either declare That Part of the said Act of the 6th of Queen Anne, prohibiting the Impressing of Seamen in the British Colonies and Plantations to be in full Force; or that the same Provisions made by that Act may be re-enacted; or that such other Remedy and Relief may be provided, for the effectual preventing the impressing Seamen in his Majesty's Colonies in America, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to considerof the said Petition.

And the Titles of the said Papers were read.

The laid Copy of the said Memorial is bound up w th the other Papers of this Session.

And the said Proposals and Translation of the said Memorial, are as follow; viz.

Proposals for furnishing a Body of the Troops of,

to be employed in the Low Countries, for the Service

of the Year 1746.

WHEREAS his Majesty has maintained in the Low Countries, from the 25th Day of December last, a Body of his Electoral Troops, consisting of 3,000 Horse, and 5,000 Foot: And whereas it is found necessary, that a further Body of Troops should be procured, to act in the Law Countries in Conjunction with the Aufirian Troops, and those of the States General of the United Provinces; his Majesty, in Consideration of the great Difficulties there are to obtain a sufficient Number of Troops for that Purpose from other Princes or States, does propose to continue the said 8,000 Troops; and to fend forthwith, into the Low Countries, a further Body of his Electoral Troops, consisting of Eight thousand Foot, and Two thousand Horse, on the following Conditions; viz.

That there be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Expence of the Pay and Subsistence of the said Two Bodies of Troops (making in the whole a Body of Eighteen thousand Men) the Sum of Three hundred thousand Pounds Sterling.

That the said Troops be allowed to march back into his Majesty's Electoral Dominions, on the 25th Day of November in this present Year, in case no previous Agreement shall be made for their remaining in the Low Countries.

That in c^fe his Majesty's Electoral Dominions shall

Translation of a Memorial delivered by the Baron

Wafner, Minister Plenipotentiary from their Imperial Majesties, to the Earl of Harrington, on the 2d of April 1746.

THE under-written Minister Plenipotentiary from their Imperial Majesties, having given an Account to his Court of the strong and earnest Representations made by Order of his Majesty the King of Great , to convince his Court of the indispensable Necessity, by reason of the evident and extreme Danger to which both the Au/lrian Netherlands, and the Republick of itself,

was exposed, by the great Superiority of the French Armies, That her Majesty the Empress Queen should immediately fend into the said , and maintain

there, during the next Campaign, a very considerable Body of her Troops, to act in Conjunction with those of his Majesty and the States General, against the common Enemy; the Emprels Queen has ordered the under-writ-' ten Minister to acquaint the King, That nobody can have a truer Sense than The has of the Endeavours, and indefatigable Cares, which his Majesty continually took, for tire Preservation of the Liberty of , and that of his faithful Allies; and that, in order to co-operate thereto, on her Part, Ihe had resolved to exert herself to the utmost, as well for the Defence of the Republick of Holland, as of the Netherlands; and to have there, against the next Campaign, a Body of 50,000 Men, of 7ier own Troops: But ihe has, at the same time, ordered the under-written to acquaint his Majesty, That

in spite of all her good Intentions, she was not in a Con-‘dition, by reason of the very exhausted State of her Finances, to support, upon her own Account, the whole Expence of so considerable a Corps: especially considering the extraordinary Efforts which (he was obliged to make in other Parts, for the Good of the common Cause, and particularly in Italy, where her Majesty was, at this very time, making One of the most useful Diversions, even to the Service of the Netherlands That her Majesty was therefore very much mortified, at finding herself under the TCeceflity of requesting the King, and infilling, that, in order to assist her in maintaining the (kid Body of 50,000 Men, his Majesty will be pleased to grant her a Subsidy 0*

400,000 Pounds Sterling, for the present Year.

London, 2 April 1746. De Wafner.

Translation of Lord Harrington's Letter to Messieurs de Boetfiaer and Hop, of the 3d January 1745-6.

Gentlemen,

The King having maturely considered the Represen-tations and Demands on the Part of the States General, contained in their llesolution of the 25th November N. S.

I am commanded by his Majesty to acquaint you, by this Letter, with his Sentiments thereupon; desiring you to make them known, without Lois of Time, to their High Mightinesse.

You will pleats. Gentlemen, to allure them, at the same time. That the King's having deferred till now the returning an Answer in Form to the said Resolution, has not proceeded from any Want of Regard to the Security of the Republick (which his Majesty has always extremely at Heart) nor to any Difference in Opinion, with Respect to the Importance and Necessity of procuring an early Superiority next Spring in Flanders, but from thcahnoft dclperate Situation to which publick Affairs had been reduced; on one Hand, by the Continuance of the Prrffir.tWar; and on the other, by the very dangerous Circumstances of his Majesty's own Dominions.

Ic is true, that the latter of those Two Caufos of his Majesty's Silence does still fubiut, and is even every Day increasing. by the vast Preparations now making by France to support the Rebellion in this Country; but the former being now happily at an End, by the Peace concluded ti.e 25th pad at Drefde; the King, who has always declared to the States his Readinets to join with them in proper Measures, for the Defence of their own Frontiers, and of the Remainder of the , lays

hold of this first Appearance of a more hopeful Prospect to open to their High Mightinesse his own Sentiments, as to what may be still done for the Benefit of our common Interest; and to explain to them what be is able and willing to contribute thereto on his own Part.

But, in the First place, with regard to this Point, his Majesty desires it may be considered how greatly the same is altered, lines the Concert entered into with the States the last Winter; at which time, there being nothing to be apprehended, with respect to the Security of his own Kingdoms, the King was enabled to transport a large Body of British Troops mto Flander, and to maintain theua there, during the whole Campaign, over and above the foreign Troops which he took into his Pay; whereas Vox.. 25.

now, by reason of the Rebellion in his Majesty's Dominions, and the Invasions threatened, and on the Point of being executed, by foreign Powers, it has been necessary not only to recall all our national Force; but to lend for the 6,000 Hejftans besides, for our domestick Safety; the former are an equal Charge to the Nation; whilst employed here, as when abroad; and the latter a much greater here; the additional Load of Expence now incurred for the necessary Protection of our Sea-Coasts against the Fleets of France and Spain, and the great and burthen-some Augmentation which his Majesty has been obliged to make in his Land Forces, upon account of the Rebellion, must be likewise brought to Account; and all this at a Time when the publick Revenues are exceedingly diminished, by the almost total Stagnation of our inland Trade, and the Difficulties arising trom the War to our foreign Commerce, and when the publick Credit is, as may well be imagined, l'o greatly ajfe&ed by these internal Disturbances, and Apprehensions from our foreign Enemies, that it cannot be practicable to raile Money, in the same proportion as before, for the Service of the Continent.

In the mean while, the States General are in a very different Situation from that 0 the Security of

the Netherlands, which is to us a foreign, but indeed very

important Object, is to them in a manner a domestick one; inso much, that whatever Troops or Money they raise for that Service, are in fact employed for their own immediate Protection: And as, by having hitherto declined to declare War against France, as the King has a Right to expect they should do, in pursuance of the Treaties, they have kept themselves clear of all Hostilities by Sea, their Trade, and consequently their Revenues, are not exposed to the same Diminution as those of his Majesty; notwithstanding which, their High Mighti-nesses have recalled the Troops which they had sent to his Majesty's Assistance; and, after having first reduced their Naval Succour from Twenty to Ten Ships, they just now, in the Time of our greatest: Necessity, have withdrawn the Whole; both which Articles must be replaced by the King: And thus, what is laved thereby to the States, becomes a fresh Charge upon his Majesty.

This, however, is not laid by way of Complaint; but for the fake of shewing in how much better a Condition their High Mightinesse are than England to contribute to the Expence of the War in Flanders: And theqeccf-lary Conclusion froqi the Whole is; That, at this Juncture, when they now apprehend so great Danger iron? the Arms of France to their own Republick, it is reason-

able that they should redouble their Efforts for the next Campaign, but unreasonable to expect even equal Effort? to those of the last Campaign, from his Majesty:

The King is persuaded, fron? the known Equity of the States General,-that they will give all dye Weight to theft; Considerat ions; and does not hesitate to allure them. That be will, to the utmost of his Power, according to the present Circumstances of his Dominions, co-operate with them towards opposing the further Progress of the French Arms in the Netherlands, and defending the Frontiers of the Republick; and that as soon as the Situation of our domestick Affairs will admit of it, his Majesty will be disposed to give his Assistance, in such further Proportion as may then become practicable: But as the joint Efforts of the Maritime Powers do not appear sufficimt to answer the Ends which they propose to themselves, it is necessary to be informed, without Loss of Time, what we have to e^pect from the Em-prels, as Sovereign of the Netherlands, now (he is free from her Silejian War, towards their Defence and Pre-

servation.

As to what concerns the King in particular, l am ordered to say, Tlxat his Majesty, having feeruhe Planprp. posed by the Prince of Waldccby which it is represented, that an Army of Ninety-live thousand Men isne-ccflary to b employed the next Year in the j

lands, his Majesty does, for his own Part, approve the fame

If the States will, therefore, furnish 40,000 of their Troops to the Service of the Netherlands, as there is rea-ion to believe it is their Intention, from what Monsieur Boetflaer has declared, and make such an Addition to their present Forces as their own immediate Preservation, and the Necessity of Affairs, absolutely require, and join with his Majesty in taking the Saxons, as above mentioned, it only remains, that the Empress's Intentions be known, in order to settle the Whole upon this Foot, by an Agreement between the Three Powers, that we may immediately proceed to the Execution of it.

I have hot touched, in this Letter, upon what relates to the Defence of the Empire; because his Majesty is not in a Condition to contribute to it; and cannot doubt of the Emperor and Empress taking all proper Measures, in Conjunction with the Princes and Circles, for that Purpose: And with regard to Italy, the King ought to believe, that the Empress will now give that Attention to it which Ihe is obliged to, by the Treaty of Worms, and enabled to do, by the Conclusion of That of;

his Majesty being, oh his Part, still disposed to fulfil the Engagements which concern him, with the feme Exact-ness as he has hitherto, provided that be done.

The King having thus explained his Ideas and Intentions to the States General, and opened to them, in the greatest Confidence, the true Situation of his Affairs, his Majesty flatters himself, that their High Mightinesse will be equally frank and explicit in their Answer to him; and that he shall receive it as loon as possible; his Majesty not doubting, but that, as the Object of the War in Flanders is no longer the Assistance of the Queen of Hungary only, but extends to the Independence and to the very Being of the Republick itself, which has been treated with the moll infblent and indecent Menaces by France, the States General will be ready (as indeed they have of late often insinuated it to be their Intention) to exert their utmost Power, by Augmentations in their Land and Sea Forces, and all other Means, for the Preservation of their Religion and Liberties, by keeping the Enemy at a due Distancefrom their Frontiers; in like manner as his Majesty, whose Dominions are in a still greater State of Danger, being already actually invaded by France, in Support of the Pretender to his Crown, has been obliged to increase his Forces, and subject himself to many new and immense Expences; and that their High Mightinesse, -now that the same is become directly their own, and that they have thought it necessary to have Recourse to his Majesty's Assistance against the common Enemy, will no longer helitate to put themselves upon the same Foot with the British Nation, by declaring War against France', by this means they will support the Honour of the Republic, injuriously, and even contemptuously, treated by France; fulfil their Treaties towards their Allies; and encourage his Majesty's Subjects to exert tftemselves to th© utmost, in their Defence.

Translation of the Extract of the Register of the Resolur tions of their High Mightinesse the States General of the United Provinces of the Countries.

Friday, 21 January 1746. The Report has been heard of Mefiieurs de wyck, and other Deputies of their High Mightinesse, for foreign Affairs; who, in Consequence of the Coin-million which was given them by the Resolution of Today, Date of these Presents; and, in order to satisfy the fame, have examined a Letter of Mefiieurs de and Hop. the respective Minister Plenipotentiary and Envoy Extraordinary df their High Mightinesse at the Britannick Court, written at London, the 14th of the current Month, addressedto the Secretary Fagel-, giving Advice of the Pains which they had continued to take in order to obtain a speedy and sufficient Succour in the Austrian Netherlands, and of what they had learnt upon this Subject; this Letter being accompanied with a Letter from Lord Harrington, wrote in the Name of his Britannick Majesty, in order to serve for an Answer to the Resolution of their High Mightinesse of the 25th of November last, concerning the same Subject: Whereupon, it having been deliberated, it was found fitting and re-lolved to write to Mefiieurs de Boetzlaer and That their High Mightinesse have seen, with a great deal of Satisfaction, by the Letter which the Lord Harrington had wrote to them, the cordial Declarations which his Majesty had been pleased to make, of his Inclination to co-operate with the Republick, in order to prevent the further Progresses of the French in the Austrian Netherlands, and to cover the Frontiers of the Republick; and the confidential Overture which it had pleased his Majesty to make of his Sentiments, with regard to the Means which, as the moll proper, ought to be employed for that Purpose: That they should have very much wished that Circumstances had allowed to do this sooner, considering the little Time which remains for to be able to take Measures jointly, and considering the present dangerous Situation to which Affairs are reduced; and that it had pleased his Majesty to explain himself further upon what his Majesty will contribute thereto.

That their High Mightinesse are too much attached, and have too great an Interest, in the Welfare of Great Britain, not to feel with his Majesty the considerable Alterations which have happened since last Winter, by the unhappy Rebellion, and the Invasion, with which the Kingdoms of his Majesty have been menaced, on the Part of France: And they acknowledge also willingly the Difficulty to which these Two Objects reduce his Majesty, and the Necessity which he has been under to oppose thereto the necessary Precautions; but that, at the feme time, they cannot dispense with themselves from considering. That the Affair of the Rebellion being Hopped, in its first Progress, and the Rebels being driven back, even into Scotland, there is Hopes that, by good Measures, these wicked Projects may be entirely dissipated and annihilated; and that the present happy Government of his Majesty will be, from thence, more firmly established: That hitherto their High Mightinesse have neither learnt nor received any News, upon which they can depend that France has made such great Preparations as those which have been given out, in order to undertake an Invasion of the Kingdoms of Great Britain-, and that, at all Events, the Forces which his Majesty has at present at Hand, joined to the Zeal of his own faithful Subjects, appear more than sufficient to prevent such precarious Undertakings.

That on the other Side, the Situation of Affairs in the Republick cannot be looked upon, by a great deal, so favourable as they seem to represent it to themselves in England', and that the Security of the Austrian Netherlands cannot be considered as a mere domestick Object, for their High Mightinesse than for Great Britain', for if it is true, that the Attention which they have for the Au-Brian Netherlands, as being more contiguous to them,

That the Plan upon which his Majesty has fixed his Contingent for the fendingan Army into Flanders against next Spring, seems to be the Project of Prince;

by which he requires an Army in the Field of 95,000 fighting Men; which Projefl supposes there must be an Augmentation of 40,000 Men over and above what is at present there: But that the said Prince IValdeck, having afterwards learnt, that the Hessian Troops were to pais over into England, and having moreover considered, that

certainly, in the present Si tuat ion, byjudging of the exterior Appearance of Things, might be done, without neglecting the Safety of Great Britain, That would give provisionally some Ease for the present; whilst, without these

6,000, the Remainder of the Low Countries, is even now, and even before the Opening of the Campaign, exposed to a great deal of Danger: That with regard to what his Majesty further offers by the said Letter, to take into the Service of the Maritime Powers the 10,000 Saxons which, are granted to them by the Treaty of their High

Mightinesses have already caused to be made, by their Minister at the Court of Saxony, the provisional Requi-fition to that Effeifl; and are ready to expedite, in Concert with his Majesty's Minister, who is here, the Orders for making the forma] Demand of them, and to assist in making the necessary Dispositions for that Purpose: That for what regards the Offer which his Majesty makes, to put, by a suitable Subsidy, her Imperial Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia in a Condition to augment her Troops in the Aujirian Low Countries to the Number of 30,000 Men, betides the Garrison of Luxembourg, their High Mightinesses must inform his Majesty,

That the Ministers of her Imperial Majesty have communicated here in a Conference, First, That her Majesty was actually fending into the Low Countries the Troops which she had withdrawn from thence the last Year, and Two Regiments of Hussars, which altogether may be reckoned at about 10,000 Men: Secondly, That she was ready to fend thither a further Corpsof 21,400 Men, in Consideration of proportionable Subsidies, to the Number of these Troops: And lastly, That as soon as Great Britain shall have paid the Remainder of the Convention, which was made for the 8,000 which are now in the Low Countries, she will not fail to

Translation of a Memorial presented by Monsieur , Envoy Extraordinary from the King of Sardinia.

London, April -jVh 1746.

The under-written. Envoy Extraordinary of his Majesty the King of Sardinia, does himself the Honour, in Execution of the pressing and repeated Orders of his Court, to represent most humbly to his Britannick Majesty, That the King his Master, who desires only to fig-nalize more and more his Zeal for the common Cause of Europe, being firmly relblved always to act in Concert with her Majesty the Empress Queen, and his Britannick Majesty, in the Pursuit of every thing that shall be judged proper for the Support of the same Cause, fees, with great Concern, the absolute Impofiibility he is under of providing for the necessary Expences for seconding vi-gorously, on his Side, their wife Measures for that Purpose, unless he be immediately assisted with an extraordinary Sum of Money, proportioned to the Occasion; for -after the great Efforts which he has hitherto made for supporting himself against the powerful Enemies that have attacked him, and after all the Losses he has suffered, it is evident, that his Finances cannot but be totally exhausted, as well as all the Resources that he could think of, to answer his Necessities, especially after the Misfortunes of the last Year; in Consequence of which, nothing was left to him, but some Fortresses: And the Enemy, being Matters of the Field, did freely overrun and ravage his whole Country, even almost to the very Gates of Turin; where he has been upon the Point of being obliged to shut himself up, without having any Communication with any foreign Country, not even to receive Letters.

Debtor. A Petition of the Prisoners confined for Debt in the

I'ctition. prisons of the King's Bench and Fleet, in behalf of them-

selves, and the rest of the Prisoners in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That at the Time the late Act for Relief of Insolvent Debtors took place, a great Number of the Petitioners were excluded the Benefit thereof, by reason that the Day the said Act commenced was precedent to the Day of their Confinement: That the Petitioners the Prisoners in the Fleet have received Accounts from several Gaels

in this Kingdom, whereby it appears, that some Thousand Persons are now confined as Debtors, many of whom are in a starving Condition: That the Decay of Commerce, and the Stagnation of many Branches of Inland Trade (unavoidable Consequences attending War) have not a little contributed to inercafe the Number of unhappy Debtors: That in the First Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, when this Nation was at War with France, the Legislature thought proper to recruit the Army and Navy, by passing an Act to let at Liberty such Insolvent Debtors as should enter into the Service of the one or the other, or find a fit Person so to do: and that the Relief given by that Act was, by an Act, made in the Second and Third Years of the said Queen's Reign, further extended: And that there are some Thousands of able-bodied Men (several Hundreds of which are able Seamen) confined in the Prisons of Port Towns and Coast Counties, and in the other Gaols of this Kingdom, who might be useful to their Country in the Army or Navy; and who, upon a Surrender of all they have to their Creditors, and their inlisting as Soldiers or Seamen (if adjudged fit and able) would most gratefully and thankfully receive their Liberty: And repreieming to the House the State of their present melancholy Situation; and praying. That this House would be pleased to take the same into Consideration, and bestow such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

It is with Hearts full of Duty and Gratitude, we acknowledge Your Majesty's Wisdom and paternal Attention to the Interest and Welfare of Your People, so strongly expressed by Your Majesty, in the Choice of that General, whose Birth, and tried Abilities, marked him out to defend the Liberties and Constitution of Great Britain, and so fcnlibly felt by Your People, in the happy Consequences of that Choice.

And as we think the Defeat given to the Rebels an Event which must immediately produce the most desirable Effects upon the whole State of our Affairs at home and abroad; ,so we doubt not, but, in its remoter Consequences, it will tend to the future Peace and Tranquillity of Your Majesty's Reign, to the firm Establishment of Your Majesty, and Your Royal Posterity, upon the Throne of these Kingdoms, and to the effectual Security of the Religion, Laws, and liberties, of Great Britain.

Thus, by a Fate, not uncommon to the Devices of Rebels and Traitors, those wicked Attempts, which have been levelled against the Protestant Succession, and the happy Constitution of this Country, will, under the Blessings of Providence, prove, in the Result, the most effectual Means of confirming both.

We beg Leave to assure Your Majesty, That Your faithful Commons, truly sensible of the great Benefits this Nation has received, from the eminent Courage and

towards the Support of the Royal Hospital at wich-t and to oblige Agents for Prizes to register their Letters of Attorney; and for enlarging certain Powers in the said several Acts; and for making the same more effectual.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Gentlemen,

I return you my hearty Thanks for this Address, so full of Affection to Me and my Family: The Satisfaction I feel at the Success of my Arms against the Rebels, is greatly increased by your kind Expressions towards my Son the Duke; and your Approbation of his Services, on this Occasion. I will not fail to improve this Advantage to the utmost of my Power, towards establishing, upon a lasting Foundation, the Future Security and Happiness of my People.

Mr. Bennet accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Author, Printer, and Publishers, of the said printed Paper; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee find, by the Evidence of Mr. Walter Moffett, Door keeper to the House, That the Paper complained of was brought to him by a Porter, from one Thomas Allen, a Butcher in Newport market-, and that Mr. Samuel Johns afterwards gave him Seven more of them.

The said Thomas Allen, being examined, confelfed. That he was the principal Person concerned in getting the said Paper written; and that he applied to Mr. Johns to draw up a Paper, to be presented to the Members of the House, containing Reasons against a Bill, now depending in the House, concerning the Admeasurement of Coals: That Mr. Johns drew up the Paper complained of; and that he (Allen) carried it to the House of one Mr. Hughes, a Printer.

The said Samuel Johns, being examined, confessed. That he was the Author of the said Paper.

The said John Hughes, being examined, said, That the said Paper was printed by his Directions; but that he did not read it over.

The House was moved, That the Resolution of the House, of the said 30th Day of April last, in relation to the said printed Paper, might be read.

And the said Resolution being read accordingly;

Ordered, That Mr. Samuel Johns, Solicitor in Chancery, do attend this House, upon Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That Thomas Allen, Butcher in Newport-market, do attend this House, upon Tuesday Morning next.

Ordered, That John Hughes, Printer, do attend this House, upon Tuesday Morning next.

GEORGE R.

The Desire which his Majesty's faithful Commons have expressed, to shew some publick Mark of their Approbation of the Services performed by his dearly beloved Son the Duke of Cumberland, towards suppressing the Rebellion, and preserving our happy Constitution in Church and State, has given his Majesty the greatest Satisfaction: His Majesty is therefore persuaded, that, upon this Occasion, he complies with the Inclination of this House, in recommending to their Consideration the settling an additional Revenue upon his laid Son, and his Issue Male, with such Provisionsas shall be judged proper.

Then the said Mr. Samuel Johns was called in: And Mr. Speaker having acquainted him with the Resolution of the House, of the 30th Day of April lad, in relation to the printed Paper then complained of; and with the Report, as far as it relates to him, of the Committee ap-finted to enquire who are the Author, Printer, and ublifhers, of the said Paper; and to report the same to the House;

He alleged, in his Excuse for writing the said Paper, That, in drawing it up, he had no Intention to offend the House; and that it was drawn up, and carried to the Press, in a Hurry, without an Opportunity of revising it; but acknowledged, That he had acted without proper Caution; and asked Pardon of the House for his Offence.

And then he was directed to withdraw.

Ordered, That the said Samuel , being the Author of the said Paper, be now brought to the Bar of this House; and be, upon his Knees, reprimanded by Mr. Speaker for his said Offence.

He was brought in accordingly; and, upon his Knees, reprimanded by Mr. Speaker; and discharged, paying his Fees.'

Ordered, That the said Thomas Allen be dismissed from any further Attendance upon this House.

Ordered, That the said John Hughes be dismissed from any further Attendance upon this House.

Ordered, That the said Thomas Paulin be dismissed from any further Attendance upon this House.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, in Obedi- Duke of ence to their Commands, he had transmitted the Thanks Cumberlaad* of this House to his Royal Highness the Duke, for the All*wer to eminent and very important Services performed by him to his Majesty, and the Kingdom, against the Rebels, particularly in the late great Defeat of them in Scotland, by his Majesty's Forces, under his Royal Highness'sCommand: To which his Royal Highness had been pleased to return the following Answer; which Mr. Speaker said he received upon the Saturday after the last Adjournment of the House.

Mr. Speaker, Inverness, May the 7th, 1746.

I desire you would acquaint the House of Commons with the just Sense 1 have of the Regard they have been pleased to shew me upon this Occasion; and to allure them, that nothing can be more agreeable to me than their Congratulation upon the Success of his Majesty's Arms, which is so authentick a Testimonial of their steady Zeal and Loyalty for his Majesty's Person and Government.

Their Esteem and Approbation of my Endeavours in the Publick Service, fill my Wishes; and it will always be my Study to deserve the Continuance of their good.

Opinion.

I cannot enough extol my own good Fortune, in being placed by his Majesty at the Head of an Army, which expressed all along the best Affections, and the greatest Ardour; and crowned all by the Resolution shewn by every Officer and Soldier in the Day of Action: To which, under God, our Success was owing.

I return you my Thanks for the Cordiality and Affection, with which you have executed the Commands of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker,

Your most-affectionate Friend,

William.

Lowndes' A Petition of Thomas Lowndes, together with several Preparation Papers thereunto annexed, being offered to be presented affriae Salt. House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Confederation of the House, to do therein as they shall think fit.

' Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; re-

presenting to the House, That every State in Europe justly yields the Pteference to Great Britain, and for being always able to supply their Inhabitants, in a most plentiful Manner, with all the Convenienciespf Life, good Salt only excepted; but that, for the said Commodity,

we are forced to have recourse to foreign Nations; and that authentick Vouchers will plainly prove, that from abroad we purchase about Thirty thousand Tons of Salt yearly; That the Petitioner has been at great Expence, both of Money and Time, in endeavouring to improve the Brine Salt of this Kingdom; which he hopes, by his Means, is now brought to that Perfection, as to equal, if not excel, the best French Bay Salt: That, by Order of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, Specimens of \hc Petitioner's Salt have been laid before the College of l*byficians; and that the said learned Body, upon mature Consideration, have made a favourable Report; a Copy of which is annexed to the said Petition: That the Petitioner, on the 7th Day of March last, did by a Letter to Mr. Corbett, Secretary to the Admiralty, propose certain conditional Terms, which, if complied with, the Petitioner offered to disclose his Method of making the said Salt; but that the Lord* of the Admiralty, by a Letter of the 28th of the said Month, declare. That it is not in their Power to agree to those Terms;,both which Letters are annexed to the said Petition; and submitting to the House the Terms mentioned by the Petitioner to this House.

The laid Papers annexed to the said Petition, were also read.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-flight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Ditto. A Petition of the Merchants, Commanders of Slops, ard others, concerned in foreign Trade, from the Port of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of was

presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend, that the Bill, now depending before this House, to regulate Insurance on Ships belonging to the Subjects of Great Britain-, and on Merchandizes or Effects laden therein; if it pals into a Law, as it now dands, would be highly prejudicial to the foreign Trade of these Kingdoms, and, in a particular manner, must inevitably, in Time of War, ruin that Share which they in these Northern Ports have therein: That the Petitioners Apprehensions are principally founded on that Clause in the said Bill, wherein it is enacted, " That the Master or Officers belonging to any Ship, on " Proof of his or their having wilfully Separated from their " Convoy, shall, in case the Ship be afterwards taken, destroyed, or run a there, by Means of, or from Apprehension of, any Enemy, be responsible to the Owners, " Freighters, or Aflurers, for the Loss they shall severally " sustain thereby, and may be prosecuted accordingly for " the fame, in the Court of AdmiraltyThat this the Petitioners think is so severe a Clause, that no Captain of Vol. 25.

a Ship can be lafe under it; but is liable to be ruined at all times, byexpenfive Prosecutions: And further representing, That this Clause must have a most pernicious Influence upon all Trade from these Northern Ports, in Time of War: And therefore praying. That if the Bill must pass into a Law, this Clause may be left out, or amended, that the Petitioners may not be under the hard Necessity of either losing all the Benefit they have of Convoys in America, and abroad, or else of losing the main Security they have of their foreign Trade, by Situation, in the Return of their Ships home; or that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises, as to this House shall l'eem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is re-committed.

Your Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined Mr. Samuel Powell; who, upon being asked.

What were tire Fees he took, whilst Jie was Serjeant at Arms attending the House of Commons, for bringing a Person to the Bar, in order to his being reprimanded by Mr. Speaker ? said. That if the Person was not in Custody, he was intitled only to the Sum of 6s. 8 and never took more, during the Time he was Serjeant at Arms, which was 16 Years.

That when he has brought a Person to the Bar, when in Custody, in order to his being discharged, he never look the Fee of 6s. 8 d.for bringing him to the Bar, as he thought he was not intitled to it.

Your Committee also proceeded to enquire into the Fees taken by the MefTcngers of the House, for serving the Orders of the House upon Members who, upon the House being called over, were ordered to attend upon a future Day.

The Deputy Serjeant informed your Committee, That he thinks it is his Duty, when a Member is ordered by the House to attend, to get such Order signed by the Clerk of- the House, and deliver it to the Messengers, who are to serve the fame; for which Service they are intitled to the Sum of 6s. 8d and 6 per Mile for riding Charges: And that he had the Speaker's Order for lo doing.

Then the said Mr. Powell was asked, That when the

House has been called over, and an Order made for absent Members to attend on a future Day, did he fend the Messengers to serve such Orders? He said, No; for as those Members had Time allowed them by the House for their Attendance, and an Order was usually made, that they were to be taken into Custody, if they did not attend, he never lent a Messengerto serve such Order; not thinking it was his Duty so to do.

Upon the whole the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House is intitled to, and ought to take and receive, a Fee of Six Shillings and Eight Pence, from every Person not in his Custody, who shall be brought to the Bar of this House, to be reprimanded by Mr. Speaker.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That neither the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, or any Messenger thereof, are intitled to any other Fee or Sum of Money, to be paid by such Person so brought to the Bar, to be reprimanded by Mr. Speaker, other than the said Sum of Six Shillings and Eight Pence.

fracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of 'arliament, as followeth; viz.

The King* Speech.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot put an End to this Session of Parliament, without expressing to you my entire Satisfaction in your Proceedings. The Zeal and Vigour which you have so unanimously shewn for the Support of my Government, for suppressing the late Rebellion, and for bringing the Guilty to Justice, in which you have been so universally seconded by my good Subjects, have not only fully answered my Expectations, but give Me the best AtTurance, that you are determined to perfect this good Work, by settling our Tranquillity at home upon (olid Foundations, and extinguishing the Hopes of the Pretender, and all his Adherents.

The Powers which you thought fit to repose in Me on this Occasion, have been employed in the most proper and effectual Manner, and made strictly subservient to those Purposes only for which you intended them: And it has pleased the Divine Providence, in a most signal Manner, to bids the Measuries we have taken with Success. I am very sensible there are Matters of great Moment still behind, which are necessary for our lading Security, and preventing the like Calamities for the future: But as a Foundation is prudently laid for your proceeding upon them in the next Session, I was unwilling to detain you longer out of your respective Countries at this advanced Season of the Year.

I have the Sat'sfaflion to acquaint you, that the Posture of Affairs abroad appears more favourable than when I last spoke to you. As soon as the Safety of my own Kingdoms would permit, I sent such a Body of Troops as could be spared from hence to (Lengthen the allied Army in the Netherlands, for the Defence of the United Provinces, and opposing the further Progress of France on that Side. By means of this Succour, and the other powerful Aflistances which you have enabled Me to furnish, that Army has been very considerably augmented, and is become much stronger than was expected at the Beginning of the Year.

188 12° August, — ^o° Septembris. A. 1746.

This Event, together, with the happy Succefies of the Avf-trian and Sardinian Armies in Italy, and tome other Incidents which have happened, to the Advantage of the common Cause, give us a better Prospect of bringing our Enemies to Reason, and procuring a safe and honourable Peace; which is my great End and Aim.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The great Readiness and Chearfulness with which you have granted Me the Supplies for the current Year, require my particular Thanks. I am very sensible of the extraordinary Difficulties which the Circumstances of the Times brought upon this important Service, and upon the publick Credit in general; and which nothing but your Prudence and Firmncls could have overcome. What you have given shall be strictly applied to the Purposes intended: And you cannot bijt have observed my Desire to leti'en the publick Expence, as far as possible, by taking the first Opportunity to disband those Regiments which the laudable and act ive Zeal of several of my faithful Subjects, of the First Rank and Distinction, had added to our Strength on this Occasion.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have had such ample Experience of your unshaken Fidelity, and of your Affection and Attachment to Me

and my Family, that I rely, with the utmost Confidence, on your future Conduct. 1 cannot doubt, that during this Recess, you will, in your several Stations, use your utmost Endeavours to restore and preserve the Peace of the Kingdom; to heal the Wounds which this unnatural Rebellion may have made; and to encourage and cultivate in my Subjects that Spirit of Loyalty, and of Zeal for the present Establishment, which has so remarkably appeared. The Impressions of it shall ever remain upon my Mind, and be demonstrated by the Continuance of my Vigilance and Endeavours to make them a happy People.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command, said;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal-Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to the 30th Day of

September next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the 30th Day of September next.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as follow-cth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have called you together as early as the late Conclu-fion of the last Session of Parliament, and the Situation of publick Affairs, would permit. During this Recess, I have been particularly attentive to extinguish any Remains of the late Rebellion, and to re-establish and secure our Tranquillity at home, so far as depended upon me. The rest I have reason to expect from your Zeal, and prudent Deliberations; of which the Foundation already laid gives me well-grounded Hopes.

In the mean time, the State of the War abroad has received a considerable Alteration. Though France has made some further Progress in the Netherlands, yet the United Provinces, whose interests are so ftriCUy connected with ours, have been preserved from that Danger which threatened them at the Opening of the Campaign, and a considerable Army remains there for their Defence. It has pleated God to bless the Arms of my good Allies the Empress Queen of Hungary, and the King of Sardinia, with signal success in Italy. The Acquisitions made there by our Enemies, have been recovered from them; their Forces broken, and almost ruined, have been obliged to evacuate that Country; and an Irruption is now actually making into France; whereby the Distresses of Vol. 25.

that Kingdom must be greatly increased, and a proportionable Diversion made in Favour of the Low Countries.

1 have often assured you, that my foie Aim in carrying on this just and necessary War, is a safe and honourable Peace. In this View, I have shewed a sincere Disposition towards a general Pacification. 1 have consented to the Holding of Conferences at Breda, in order to try whether our Enemies will, in the Event, agree to fitch Terms and Conditions as may be consistent with the Honour of my Crown, the Security and true Interests of my Kingdoms, and my Engagements to my Allies; whom it is my firm Resolution not to abandon.

But whilst we are treating of Peace, Reason and good Policy demand that we should be prepared for War. I am therefore actually concerting with my Allies the proper Measures for vigorously pursuing the War in another Campaign, in case the.Obstinacy of our Enemies should render it necessary. My desire is to adjust these Measures as speedily as possible; that our Preparations may be early; that the Confederate Army in the Netherlands may be augmented in time; and the Operations on the Side of Italy carried on with Effect. It shall also be my particular Care to exert our Strength at Sea, in the most effectual manner, for the Defence of my Kingdoms and Possessions, the Protection of the Trade of my Subjects, and the Annoyance of our Enemies.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the ensuing Year to be prepared, and laid before you: And desire you to grant me such Supplies as shall be requisite for your own Security, and for carrying on such Measures as it shall be ne-ccssary for Great Britain to pursue, in the present important Conjuncture.

It gives me much Concern to be obliged at the same time to acquaint you, that by reason of the unavoidable Accidents and Consequences of War, the Funds appropriated for the Support of my Civil Government, have, for some Years part, fallen greatly short of the Revenue intended and granted by Parliament: I therefore rely on your known Affection to me to find out some Method to make good this Deficiency.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Nothing is so valuable and essential to me as your vigorous Support: On this I depend; and I trust you will demonstrate it by the Zeal, Unanimity, and Dispatch, of your Proceedings.

Address on Mr. Campbell of Pem reported from the Com-the King's mittee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be peech. presented to fils Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return our humble Thanks for Your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We are truly sensible of Your Majesty's particular Attention to extinguish the Remains of the late Rebellion: And we beg Leave to allure Your Majesty, That we will not fail, on our Parts, to answer Your just Expectations, by taking all such further Measures as shall appear conducive to re-establish, upon a lading Foundation, the Security and Tranquillity of Your Majesty's Government.

We most heartily congratulate Your Majesty upon the signal Success with which it has pleased God to blels the Arms of Your Allies in The wile and vigorous

Measures they are jointly purluing to improve it, by the Irruption now actually making into France, give us just Ground, to hope, that by the happy Consequence of chat *5

Operation, the DistrelTes of our Enemies may be so increased, and such Advantages gained over them, as may balance, in a great measure, the Losses sustained in the other Part of the Continent.

We acknowledge, with the deepest Sense of Gratitude,

Your Majesty's great Care, and paternal Tendernels, for Your People, expressed in Your Majesty's Endeavours to procure a general Pacification: And we do, at the same time, with the greatest Duty and Affection, allure Your Majesty, That Your faithful Commons will-grant such timely and adequate Supplies, as may, with the hearty Concurrence, and united Efforts, of Your Allies, enable Your Majesty, either to cany on the War in the most effectual manner, both by Sea and Land, or to obtain such a Peace as may be consistent with the Honour of Your Crown, Your Engagements to Your Allies, and the true interest of Your People.

We do humbly alfure Your Majesty, That wc will take into our Confederation, and make good, whatever Deficiencies shall appear to us to have arisen in the Funds appropriated for the Support of Your Majesty's Civil Government: And in this, and all other Matters recommended to us by Your Majesty, we will proceed, with that Zeal, Dispatch, and Unanimity, as shall manifest to the World our dutiful Attachment to Your Majesty's Person and Government, and our constant Attention to the Welfare and Prosperity of Your Kingdoms.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemitie contrudicente, That t he House do agree

with the Committee in the said Address, to be presented to his Majesty.

MR. Brampston reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Trustees, appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the Roads leading from the Western Part of the Parish of Shctifield to Harwich, in the County of Essex-, and the Road leading from Chelmsford, in the said County, to Sudbury, in the County of and

from Margaretting to Malden, in the County of EJj'ex; and from Colchester to Langham, in the same County; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it-appeared to them, to the House; andiie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read4 and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Part of the said Act, of the Twelfth Year of King George the First, was read; by which a Power is given to the Trustees therein named to erect Turnpikes, and

raile

Shenfield

Road*'

20 Geo. II 40 — 50 Decembris. 201

raile Tolls, for the Term of 21 Years, from the ift of A Jay 1726.

Then the Committee examined Mr. William May hew, who said. That the Money arising by the said Tolls had been duly applied, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act; and that great Progress had been made in the Repair of the Roads; but that it was impossible sufficiently to amend the fame, during the subsisting Term, which expires in less than Five Months: And though the Roads should be amended, it would be impossible to continue to keep them in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law for amending the Highways of this Kingdom.

The same Evidence proved to the Committee, That by a Standing Order made by the Commissioners, no Money collected at the Turnpikes is to be applied in the Repair of any Part of the Road, till the Statute-work shall have been performed by the respective Parities; which Order has been punctually observed; and the Tolls and Statute-work have been found barely sufficient to keep the Roads in tolerable Repair, but that a large Sum will be necessary immediately to be laid out to put the same into such a Condition as may render them safe and commodious for Wheel Carriages.

The Evidence of Mr. May hew was confirmed, in every Particular, by several Gentlemen present;

Then the Committee proceeded to examine Witnesses, as to the Condition of the additional Roads mentioned in the Petition.

And Mr. Nath. Bowcer and Mr. John Lodozcick were severally examined; and said, That the Roads leading from the Pound at Run fell, in , to Alitiiorne

Church, in the County of and also the Road leading from the Eagle and , in the Parish of Sheffield, by Billericay, to Rayleigh; and from thence to Rockford-, and from Rayleigh to Leigh, in the Hundreds of Rockford, and Barnstaple, in the said County; were

contiguous to the Road directed to be repaired by the Act of the 12th of King George the First, as mentioned in the said Petition: And that those Roads, in several Places are not passable for Wheel Carriages, in the Winter Seaton: That One Man was drowned in endeavouring to pass the said Roads; and Cattle have frequently been loft.

They further said. That *tis impossible for the Parishes through which the Roads lead to amend the fameeffectu-ally, and to keep them in Repair, by the Work directed to be done by the ordinary Course of Law.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the Roads leading from the Western Part of the Parish of Shenfield to Harwich, in the County of Essex; and the Road leading from Chelmsford, in the said County, to Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk; and from ling to Malden, in the County of Essex; and from Col-chef er to Lang ham, in the same County; and for repairing other Roads adjoining to the same Roads: And that Mr. Bramston, Sir Robert , and Mr. Gray, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

of the Commission Officers of his Majesty's Navy, who are now in Commission, with the Dates of their several Commissions; and also a List of those who are upon Half Pay.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of Four Shillings in the Pound, and no more, be raised in the Year 1747, upon Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offices, and personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called , Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed; and that a proportionable Cess, according to the Ninth Artic'e of the Treaty of Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

MR. Fane, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1747, was committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were once read throughout; and then a well taken care of, as since they were in your Hands:

Honourable and Dear Sir,

I Received, with vast Pleasure, the Honour of your Letter of the 31st October, by the Bearer, who has the Honour to be known to you: He is my Relation, and was my Secretary for several Years; and he is now Captain-Lieutenant in the First Battalion of my Son's Regiment. He gave me great Joy, in letting me know, at this Time, as well as when he came from,

some Weeks ago. that you was in perfect Health, notwithstanding of the ext ream Fatigue, and constant Hurry, that the essential Affairs of the Royal Prince keeps you in Day and Night.

I do allure you, dear Sir, that no Man in Scotland is better pleased to hear of the Continuation of your Health, and the Prosperityof your Person, in every Shape, than lam; as I always found you a worthy Gentleman, full of good Scnfe and Politeness, full of true Loyalty and Valour, and faithfully zealous for the Interest of the Royal Family; and in the mean time mighty civil and obliging to me, when I had the Honour to fee . on the Subject of the King's Affairs, which never was so

Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Sir William Tonge reported from the Committee ap- Lord pointed to draw up Articles of Impeachment, and pre- Lovat's pare Evidence, against Simon Lord Lovat, impeached of I"p*"chn, eut‘ High Treason, That the Committee had drawn up Articles of Impeachment accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table:

YVhere the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Articles of Impeachment of High Treason against Simon Lord Lovat.

WHEREAS the Imperial Crown and Government of these Kingdoms have been long duly and happily established in the Royal Family of his present Molt Sacred Majesty, upon Principles equally conducive to the Honour and Safety of the Crown, and to the Protection and Liberty of the Subject; whereby settled Laws ard made the common Measure of Justice to both; and a Prerogative wifely calculated to promote the greater Good of the People, and answer the Exigencies of Government, has been ascertained and secured:

And whereas the Reigns of his present Majesty, and his Royal Father, have given the Itrongeft and most i*-luftrious Proofs of the happy Effects of those Principles, in the Exercise of their legal, mild, and equal, Administration, under which every Subject, from the highest to the lowest, has had his Religion, his Person, and his Property, fully protected, by the moll inviolable Observance of the Laws, which have had their free Course, without the least Interruption on the Part of his Majesty, or of his Royal Father.
