A Petition of the Matters of Ships, and other Officers and Seamen employed in the Merchants Service, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the other Seamen in the said Service; together with Two Representations of several Merchants, and others, in favour of the said Petition, thereunto annexed; were presented to the House; and the said Petition and Representations were read; the said Petition setting forth, That the Seamen employed in the Merchants Service are cx-poled to great Hazards and Dangers, especially in Times of War; and frequently lose their Lives and Limbs, and are otherwise maimed and disabled in defending the Ships which they lerve in when attacked by, as well as in attacking and taking, the Ships belonging to the Enemies of this Kingdom, and often in working such Ships in violent Storms and bad Weather; and are sometimes worn out by Age, and disabled by the Severity of Heat and Cold in certain Voyages, l'o that they are rendered incapable of any future Service at Sea, and of providing for themselves and Families: That by an Act, made in the 7th and 8th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, for the Increase and Encouragement of Seamen, certain Encouragements are given for Seamen to register themselves in and for his Majesty's Service; and Six Pence per Month is thereby to be deducted out of the Pay of every Seaman employed in the Merchants Service, as well as of those who served in the Royal Navy, for the better Support of Greenwich Hospital, to make Provision for such of the said registered Seamen, who, by Age, Wounds, or other Accidents, should be clifabled for future Service at Sea; and for the Children of such disabled Seamen, and they Widows and Children of such of them as should happen to be flam, killed, or drowned, f > far forth as the said Hospital should be capable to receive them, and the Revenue thereof would extend for or towards their Relief or Support: That by an Act, made in the 10th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the better collecting and recovering the Duties granted for the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, and for the

further Benefit thereof, and for preferring her Majesty's Harbour Moorings; and by an Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the F.states forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of and

Charles Radcliffe, it is Enacted, That Seamen on board Merchants Ships, who shall be maimed or hurt in Fight against any Enemy of this Kingdom, shall be admitted into the said Hospital in like manner as any other Seamen wounded or disabled in the Service of the Royal Navy; and that by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for the more effectual Suppression of Piracy, every Seaman on board any Merchant Ship, who is maimed in Fight against any Pirate, is likewise to be admitted into the said Hospital: That, the said Hospital not being capable to receive, nor the Income tlier of being sufficient for the Relief and Support of, the disabled and worn out Seamen, and the Widows and Children of such as have been killed, llain, or drowned, in the Service of the Royal Navy, the Seamen maimed or disabled in Fight in the Merchants Service against the Enemies of this Kingdom, cannot be admitted into the said Hospital; and there is no Provision at all made for those who shall be maimed or disabled by accidental Misfortunes, or for those worn out by Age, or for the Widows or Children of those who are killed, llain, or drowned, in such Merchants Service; wherefore the Petitioners are desirous and willing that Six Pence per Month should be deducted out of their Pay, and be applied towards the erecting, founding, and endowing, an Hospital for the Reception and Support of maimed and disabled Seamen, and the Relief of the Widows and Children of those who shall be killed, llain, or drowned, in the Merchants Service; but the fan\e cannot be effected without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief and Support of maimed and disabled Seamen, and the Widows and Children of such as shall be killed, llain, or drowned, in the Merchants Service. And the said Representations alleging. That, if an Act of Parliament should pass for the Purposes mentioned in the said Petition, it will be attended with many Consequences useful and beneficial to this Nation; particularly it will greatly tend to the Increase of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, by encouraging our Sailors to undertake difficult and dangerous Voyages, to venture their Lives and Limbs in the vigorous Defence of the Ships they serve in, as also in attacking and taking Ships of superior Force, render such Sailors more obedient to Command, and prevent them entering into the Service of Foreigners, whereby his Majesty's Royal Navy will be the sooner manned upon any Emergency; and that it will likewise be a great Ease to the respective Parishes where Seamen have Settlements, by preventing them, when rendered incapable of Service, and their Families, when they are killed, from becoming burdenlome to such Parishes; and submitting the same to the Consideration of this House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Brookfbank, Mr. Burrell, Admiral Vernon, Sir Edmund Thomas, Mr. Cooke, Mr. Sydenham, Mr. Pratt, Mr. Wilkinson, Mr. Hume, Sir Nathanael Curzon, Sir John Philipps, Lord Doneraile. of the several Gentlemen, Tradelinen, Freeholders, Farmers, and Mariners, residing in and near to the said Borough, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and bad directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations contained in the said Petition,

John Steel, Pilot, being examined, said, That he had known the Harbour of Southwould many Years; and that formerly the Depth of Water upon the Bar, at the Mouth of the said Harbour* being about Eight Foot at a

Sp.ing

do Geo. it. ti° PebrudriL

Spring Tide, was sufficient for Coafiing Vessels; but that at present the Entrance is so choaked up with Sand, that the Depth of Water is not at any time above Four Feet; by which means even very small Vessels arc prevented from getting in:

That about Ten Years ago, when the said Harbour was open, a considerable Trade was there carried on, to the great Benefit of the said Borough and the neighbouring Country; and that he (the Witness) had frequently piloted out Timber Hoys belonging to the Crown, which had been loaded there for the Use of the Government; but that now more than Half the said Trade is loti to the Town, upon account of the Inconvenience and Charge which attends the putting of Goods brought there into Boats, in order to their being carried to or from the Ships which lie wthout the Bar:

That all the Trade from the Northward comes by this Harboui, which, if open, would be a safe Port for Ships in Time of War to put into, when chafed by Privateers, to which they are very much exposed; and that the making of a Sluice, and scouring of the Haven, would not only be very beneficial to the Town and Country adjacent, but would all'o contribute to the Draining of the Marshes, which are now frequently overflowed.

Being further examined, he laid, That the Corporation of Southwould had expended more than the annual

Revenue of the Town (which is about £. 80 )

in endeavouring to scour the Bar, and keeping the said Harbour from being totally stopped up; but that the Charge of eflfedually clearing and opening the same will, by Estimate, amount to about £. 2,000, which Sum the said Corporation cannot raile without the A Alliance of Parliament; and that if a small Duty was laid only upon such Goods and Vessels as Ihrdl come or be brought into the said Harbour, he (the Witness) apprehends a sufficient Fund would be thereby established for raising the said Sum, and also for preserving the said Harbour open for the future.

The House proceeded to the further Hearing of the Matter of the Petition of Luke Robinson Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Hedon, in the County of York:

And the Counsel were called in:

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded in their Evidence:

And they having proposed toestablish the Vote of a Person who voted for the Sitting Member at the last Election for the said Borough, and whom the Counsel for the Petitioner had endeavoured to disqualify, as having received the Benefit of a publick Charity in the said Borough, and as having been threatened by the Mayor to be deprived of the said Charity if he did not vole for the Sitting Member, and as having been induced by those Threats to vote for the Sitting Member;

Part of the Copy of the Will of the Donor of the said Charity, entered in One of the publick Books of the said Borough, was read:

And a Witness was examined, in order to prove that the Person, who so voted for the Sitting Member, did vote at former Elections in the said Borough; and that Persons who have had the same Benefit from the said Ciiarity, have been constantly allowed to vote in all Elections in the said Borough.

The Counsel for the Sitting Member also examined several Witnesses, in order to prove an Attempt to corrupt several Burgesses of the said Borough to vote for the Petitioner at the said Election:

And having examined a Witness, in order to prove that the Petitioner himself had made an undue Application to him for his Vote at the said Election;

They also examined a Witness, in order to prove that the Person, who made that Attempt to corrupt those Burgesses, was an Agent for the Petitioner:

They also examined another Witness, in order to prove that the Petitioner himself had made an undue Application to him for his Vote at the said Election:

They also examined a Witness, in order to discredit the Proof offered by the Counsel for the Petitioner, That the Sitting Member haddeposited a Sum of Money for the U(e of a Burgess of the said Borough, upon Condition of voting for him:

They also examined a Witness, in order to prove that a Burgess of the said Borough confessed, after the said Election, that he was influenced by the Promise of a Gratification made by the Petitioner, to vote for him: They also examined a Burgess of the said Borough, in order to prove that an undue Application had been made to him for his Vote in favour of the Petitioner; and that upon his Refusal to vote for the Petitioner, he was solicited by the Promise of a Gift to forbear to vote for the Sitting Member:

They also examined a Witness, in order to prove that the Burg- fs, who so confessed that he was influenced to vote for the Petitioner by the Promile of a Gratification so made by the Petitioner, did receive the Gratification so promised.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member having proposed to prove, that the Sitting Member is duly qualified by his Ellate to be c-leded a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough;

The Counsel for the Petitioner admitted, That the Sitting Member was so qualified.

A Petition of the Royal African Company of England being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the find Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are legally possessed of sundry Forts and Settlements on the Coast of,

which for many Years they supported and maintained at their own foie Cost and Charge, for the Protection and Security of the Trade of this Nation in Negroes for the Use of the British Colonies and Plantations in , and

in Gold, Ivory, Bees-wax, Dyeing-woods, and many other valuable and necessary Commodities for the Use of our Home Manufactures; and that it hath appeared to this House, that the said Forts and Settlements cannot be maintained and supported, upon the Foot of a free and open Trade, without the Aid of Parliament; and that the House hath been pleased to grant sundry Sums of Money, for several Years past, towards the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements; and that the Petitioners have found by Experience, that the annual Allowances hitherto granted by Parliament for this Service, are not sufficient to enable the Petitioners to support and maintain the said Forts and Settlements in a defenfible Condition against the unwarrantable Encroachments of other rival Nations, and the open Attacks of declared Enemies: And therefore praying. That the House will be pleased to take the preTent dangerous State and Condition of this most valuable Trade into Consideration; and to purchase the said Forts and Settlements of the Petitioners, or to make such effectual Provision for enabling the Petitioners to support and maintain them, as the Nature and Importance of this Trade requires; or to grant the Petitioners such other Relief as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace of the County of Norfolk, assembled at their General Quarter-Sessions of the Peace held the 17th Day of January 1746, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Shire House on the Castle Hill, in the said County, where the Summer Assizes, and the Quarter-Sessions for the Peace for the said County, have been always held, was lately intirely burned down: That it is absolutely necessary that a new Shire House should be erected there for the Purposes aforesaid, but that the same cannot possibly be done Time enough for the next Summer Assizes; and that there is no Place so convenient for the holding the said Assizes and Sessions, for the said County of Norfolk, as the City of Norwich, which lies in the Centre of the said County; That, as the said City is a County of itself, the Assizes and Sessions for the said County of Norfolk cannot be held there by any Law now subsisting: That it is doubtful whether the Laws now in Force are sufficient to authorize the railing Money on the said County of Norfolk for the Rebuilding of the said Shire House: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the holding the Assizes and Sessions of the Peace, for the County of Norfolk, in the said City and the County of Norwich, until a new Shire House can be built for the said County of Norfolk, and for the building a Shire House on the said Castle Hill; and for the railing Money on the said County of Norfolk for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Wear River and Sunderland Fort.

Mr. Bowes reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners of Lands and Grounds adjoining on, or lying near to, the River Wear, in the County of Durham, and the other Gentlemen, Merchants, Trades-men, and Inhabitants, within the said County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said lYtition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the.Housejand he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act of Parliament, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, was read; whereby it appeared, tint certain Powers were granted to the Commissioners thereby appointed, and certain Duties imposed and made payable, from and after the 24th Day of June in the Year of our Lord 1717, for the space of 21 Years, to be applied for the Purposes mentioned in the said Act:

And also an Act of Parliament, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his laid late Majesty, was read; whereby several further Powers were granted to the said Commissioners during the said Term, and for the same Purposes.

Then the Committee examined Mr. Mark Burleigh: Who laid, That the Commissioners appointed to put the said Acts in Execution had expended a considerable Sum of Money in building a Pier on the South Side of the said Haven; which Pier is 333 Yards long, and 30

Then your Committee proceeded to examine into the present State of the said River and Haven, and whether the Works already performed were sufficient to secure and improve the Navigation of the fame, or what further Works might be necessary for those Purposes.

And Mr. Burleigh and Mr. Thompson severally informed your Committee, That, notwithstancfing the Works already done, a dangerous Sand hath collected itself at the Mouth of the Harbour: That One of the Witnesses measured the said Sand about Two Months ago, and found it to extend a Hundred Yards from the Pier; That it stretches out in an irregular F igure, and is in most Places about a Hundred Yards broad: Thar the said Sand is daily increasing; and must in a little time totally obstruct the Navigation of the said River and Port, which is already rendered so difficult thereby, that several Mailers of Ships have abf dutely refilled to come into the said Harbour, on account of the Danger thereof, to the great Detriment of the said Town of Sunderland, and Parts adjacent.

The said Witnesses, being asked what Methods were proper to be taken to remove the present Obstructions, and to prevent the same or any other for the future, severally said.

That the proper and only Method, as they apprehended, for obtaining those Purposes, was, by lengthening the Pier already built on the South Side, and by erecting a Pier or Piers, Jettce or Jettees, on the North Side of the said Port or Haven, which Works the Commissioners appointed by the former Acts proposed to have performed; but the Duties collected by virtue of those Acts (as appeared by the Accounts before-mentioned) were infuffi-16 cient

20 Geo. II. 20* Februarii. 297

cient for that Purpose; and that it would be impossible to prefen'e the Navigation of the said River and Harbour without the further Aid of Parliament.

what had been acknowledged to be due from Great Britain to Spain-, which Sum of £. 60,000, together with the Balance of£. 95,000, which was to have been paid by the Crown of Spain, as aforesaid, was designed to have been appropriated to the paying the Demands of the said Sufferers, and the rest of his Majesty's Subjects who were Sufferers by the unjust Seizures and Depredations of the Spaniards: That the King of Spain not having complied with the Terms of the Convention, his Majesty was pleased to order Reprifels to be made on the Crown and Subjects of Spain; in consequence whereof, several rich Spanish Ships were taken before the Declaration of War against Spain: That, in the Year 1743, his Majesty was graciously pleased to grant a Commission for the Distribution of the Moiety of such Sums as had arisen from Reprifels, among such of It is Majesty's Subjects as had sustained LolTes by Spanish Depredations since the 2d of June 1721; whereby the Petitioners were excluded from any Relief under the said Commission, notwithstanding that their Losses constituted a great Part of the Demands made by the British Commissaries on the Crown of as aforesaid: That, in the Year 1743 and 1744, the said suffering Merchants, or their Representatives, petitioned this House, praying to be relieved out of the £.60,000 granted, as aforesaid, for the Uses of the Convention; and Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, then acquainted the House, That his Majesty had been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, and was graciously pleased to recommend it to the Confi- -deration of the House, who thereupon referred it to a Committee; and that the said£.6o,coo remained undisposed of: That, by reason of the late Rebellion, it was conceived improper to renew any Application to the House, for Relief in the said Matters, the ensuing Session; but that Rebellion being now happily suppressed, and Great Britain being restored to perfetft Tranquillity at home, praying, That such Relief maybe granted to the said suffering Merchants out of the said £. 60,000, or in such other manner as the House shall judge proper.

MR. Delme reported from the Committee, to whom Southarrproa

the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, Burgesses, and Waterwcri*. Inhabitants, of the Town and County of Southampton, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. 1

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. John Ruffen said. That the Town of Southampton is supplied with ffelh Water by Four Conduits of great Antiquity, which arc open to all Persons coming to draw Water: That these Conduits are supplied by Leaden Pipes from Conduit Heads, and Springs, about a Mile distant from the Town: That in Gosling Lane there is a Conduit, in which is a Pump, which is often used in dry Seasons to supply the said Town with Water: That at a small Distance from the Town there is a Water-house called Houndwell-koufe, where Two Pipes are constantly running, and the Poor of the Town used to walh their Clothes; from whence the Water runs to a large Pond without Eafi-gate, where all the Horses of the Town are generally watered; and in dry Seasons there is no Pond but this within a Mile of the Town, to water Horses.

That the Conduits are not only of great Use to the Inhabitants, but also to Matters of Ships, who frequently water at these Conduits, the Water being better for most Uses than Pump-water.

That these Conduits and Pipes were repaired, ever since his Memory, by Rates upon the Inhabitants and Occupiers of Houses in the said Town (except in the Tything of Portswood, and on the Estates of Padwell and Northani) until 1735, when, upon a Rite being made, several of the Inhabitants refused to pay to it, and, there being no Power to compel them, no Rate has been since made; and nothing has been laid out in repairing the said Conduits and Pip* s, but what arose by voluntary Contributions of Gentlemen: That the same are now l'o much out of Repair, that, if some Provision is not made, effectually to repair them, it will be a great Prejudice to the Inhabitants and Matters of Ships trading the re; and may be of the utmost ill Consequence in case of Fire, most of the Houses in the said Town confiding of Timber and Plaister Buildings.

Mr. Thomas Foy confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Jo'n Ruffen.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and maintaining the publick Conduits, and other Water-works, belonging to the Town of Southampton: And that Mr. Delme, Mr. Sydenham, and Mr.

Edward Gibbon, do prepare, an J bring in, the fame.

Mr. Oswald reported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the Burgh of Bruntisland, in North Britain, was referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

In Support of the Allegations contained in the said Petition,

Part of an Act, made in the 6th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, was read; whereby a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, was laid upon every Scots Pint of Beer or Ale fold within the said Burgh, and Liberties thereof, for railing Money to defray the ‘necessary Charges of maintaining and improving the Harbour belonging to the said Burgh, and for repairing the Church and Town-house, and also for discharging the publick Debts then due from the said Burgh; which Duty was to have Continuance, from the 24th Day of 1720, for the Term of25 Years; which Term is now expired.

Patrick Scotland James Mill, Ship-masters in Dundee, being severally examined, said, That the said Harbour, which is the only one upon the Firth of is now

going to decay for want of Money to keep the same in Repair; and that the Reviving of the said Act would be very beneficial to the said Town.

Then, in order to shew that the Revenue of the said Town is not sufficient to repair and maintain the said Harbour, a Slate of the said Revenue, with the annual Salaries, Stipendiaries, and Debts, payable out of the fame, since the Ijixpiration of the said Duty, attested by the Magistrates and Town Clerk of the said Burgh, was produced: whereby it appeared, that the said annual Salaries and Stipendiaries amount to the Sum of . 68. 4 11 \d. whereas the annual Revenue amounts only to the Sum of£. 59. 4*. 2 d.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for reviving and continuing an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Beer or Ale vended or sold within the Town of Bruntisland, and Liberties thereof, for increasing the publick Revenue of the said Town; and for other Purposes therein mentioned: And that Mr. Oswald, Mr. Lyttelton, and Sir Hugh Dalrympdo prepare, and bring

in the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty of the City and County of Norwich, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, that the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, have presented a Petition to the House, setting forth, That the Haven and Piers belonging to the said Town have many Years been maintained and repaired by several fhcceflive Acts of Parliament, the last whereof, which was passed in the 9th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, is determined and expired, and praying, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for clearing, depthening, repairing, maintaining, and improving, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth; and for preserving Ships wintering in the said Haven from Accidents by Fire; by an Imposition on Coals, and other Goods, to be imported into the said Haven; and that these Petitioners, the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City and County of Norwich, have a just Sense of the Necessity of railing Money for repairing, amending, and altering, the said Piers, and for depthening and cleansing the said Haven and the Chanel o and the Rivers

emptying themselves into the said Haven, which were provided for by the said late-expired Act: That the last mentioned Petitioners have for several Yearspaft, from time to ,time, aj>i>ointedDeputiestomeetotherDeputiesappointed

said Haven and Piers, and preventing such ineffectual Application of Money to be raised for the said Haven and Piers for Time to come, it was proposed, That the Twelve Commissioners to be appointed, as by the said late-expired Act, for the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, City of Norwich, and Burgh of Great Yarmouth, should be impowered to direct the raising a Sum of Money by Duty on Coals, and other Goods, imported into the said Haven, to be by them, or the major Part of them, applied to the amending and altering the said Piers in the most expeditious and effectual manner, in order to remove a Bax, which frequently gathers to such a degree, before the Entrance into the said Haven, as to obstruct the Passage of Ships out of, or into, the said Haven, for many Weeks together, to the very great Damage of the Merchants and Manufacturers of the City of Norwich, who export their Goods to foreign Parts, and also of Exporters of Corn into foreign Parts, or to other Ports of this Kingdom, through the said Haven: That it has allb been proposed, that further Sums of Money Ihculd be raised for keeping the said Piers, so amended and altered, in Repair, and for depthening and cleansing the said Haven and the Channel of Bray don, and the Rivers emptying themselves into the said Haven. And further reprefeating to the House, That about One-half of the Money raised by a Duty on Coals, and other Goods, imported into the said Haven, will be paid by the City and, County of Norwich And therefore praying. That, if Leave be given to bring in a Bill for raising Money upon Coals, and other Goods, to be imported into the said Haven, which shall be brought up to the City and County of Norwich, the Petitioners, the Mayor, Sheriff, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City and County of Norwich, may be authorized to appoint Commissioners, who, with Commissioners to be appointed lor the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, and Burgh of Great Yarmouth, may have Power to dispose of all Monies to* be raised for the said Haven and Piers} and to contract with Workmen for executing such Work as they, or the major Part of them, shall think proper to be done to the said Haven and Piers, in order to prevent the Bar gathering at the Entrance into the said Haven; and to gain such a Depth of Water as will admit therein not only such flat-bottomed Ships as of late Years have been built for the Trade of that Port, but also Ships of greater Burthen, which, for want of such a Retreat in stormy Weather, have been obliged to lie in Yarmouth Roads during such Storms, where many Ships of late Years have been loft inSight of the said Town; which might have been laved, if they could have put into the said Harbour for Shelter, as formerly: And further praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against any Bill, applied for by the Burgh of Great Yarmouth, for raising Money upon Coals, and other Goods, brought through the said haven to the City and County of Norwich, to be by the said Burgh applied

Mr. Brookjlank reported from the Committee, to whom Support of

the Petition of the Matters of Ships, and other Officers and Seamen employed in the Merchants Service, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the other Seamen in the said Service, was referred,

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Fetition; and had directedhim to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations contained in the said Petition,

Part of an Act, made in the 7th and 8th Year of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act for the Increase and Encouragement of Seamen, was read; which, after reciting, that his then Majesty, and the late Queen Mary, in order to encourage the Subjects of this Kingdom to continue in, and betake themselves to, the Service of the Royal Navy, did, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of England, bearing date the 25th Day of October then last past, found and endow a Hospital at Greenwich, for the Relief of disabled Seamen, their Widows and Children, enacts. That all able Mariners, Seamen, Watermen, Fishermen, Lightermen, Bargemen,

Keelmen, or Seafaring-men, being the King's Subjects, and above the AgeofEighteen Years, and under the Age of Fifty, who shall voluntarily register themselves to serve on board the Fleet in the Manner directed oy the said Act; and who by Age, Wounds, or other Accidents, shall be disabled for future Service at Sea; shall be admitted into, and provided for in, the said Hospital, during their Lives; and that the Children of such disabled Seamen, and also the Widows and Children of such as shall be killed or drowned in the Sea Service, shall like-wife be received into the said Hospital, and there be provided for; all which is to be done so far forth as the said Hospital shall be capable to receive them, and the Revenues thereof will extend: And it is also further Enacted, That every Seamen in the Service of the Crown, or belonging to any Merchant Ship or Vessel, shall allow*

Six Pence per Menfem out of his Wages, for the better Support of the said Hospital, and to augment the Revenues thereof for the Purposes aforesaid.

Part of another Act, made in the 10th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better collecting and recovering the Dutiesgranted for the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, and for the further Benefit thereof; and for the preserving her Majesty's Harbour Moorings; wasalf) read; which, after alleging.

That no Seamen had been admitted into the said Hospital, but only such as hadfervedin the Royal Navy, n >twith-

{landing great Sums had been constantly paid towards the Support of the said Hospital, from the Wages of Seamen employed in the Merchants Service, enacts, That any Seaman, who shall ofler himlelfto he admitted into the said Hospital, and shall produce an authenrick Certificate of his having been wounded, maimed, or hurt, in defending any Ship, belonging to the Subjects of this Kingdom, against the Enemies of the Queen, her Heirs or Successors, or in taking any Ship from the Enemy, and being thereby disabled for Sea Service, shall be considered as fully qualified for an Admission into the said Hospital.

Part of another Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Suppressing of Piracy, was also read; which, (or a further Encouragement to Seamen to light, and defend their Ships against Pirates, enacts, That every Seaman or Manner on board any Merchant Ship or Vessel, who shall lac maimed in Fight against any Pirate, shall, upon due Proof thereof, not only receive the Rewards appointed by a Statute made in the 22d and 23d Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act to prevent the delivering up of Merchant Ships, and for the Increase of good and serviceable Seamen, but shall also be admitted into, and provided for in, Greenwich Hospital, preferable to any other Seaman or Manner who is diiabied from Service, or getting a Livelihood merely by his Age.

Part of another Act, made in the 8th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of and Charles Radcliffe, was also read; which, after taking

Notice, that the Encouragement given by the said Act, made in the 8th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, extends only to such Seamen or Mariners on

board any Merchant Ship or Vessel as shall be maimed in Fight against any Pirate, enacts, That every Seaman or Mariner, on board any Merchant Ship or Vessel belonging to the Subjects of this Kingdom, who shall be maimed in Fight against any Enemy whatsoever of his Majesty, his Heirs or Successors, shall be admitted into, and provided for in, the said Hospital, in like manner as any other Seaman or Mariner wounded or disabled in the Service of the Crown; but no Provision at all is made for such Seamen in the Merchants Service as shall be maimed or disabled by accidental Misfortunes, or worn out by Age, or other Infirmities.

Then, in order to prove that the said Hospital is not capable to receive all the Seamen who are disabled and worn out in the Service of the Royal Navy,

In order also to shew, that the Revenue of the said Hospital is not sufficient for the Purposes intended thereby, a State of the yearly Revenue and Expence of the said Hospital, dated the 19th of February 1744, and contained in the Journal of the House of the 20th of February 1744, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Revenue of the said Hospital is £.3,323. 131. 8 let's than the annual Expence of maintaining 1,000 Seamen, with the Officers, Servants, and Nurles, upon the present Establishment, and the ordinary Repairs in and about the said Hospital.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Cojnmittee, That the allowing of Six Pence per Month out of the Wages of every Seaman in the Merchants Service, to be applied for the Relief and Support of such Seamen as are rendered incapable of Service by Sickness, or by Wounds or accidental Misfortunes, either in defending, fighting, or working, the respective Ships to which they belong; and for the Relief and Support of l'uch of them as shall be worn out by Age, and of the Widows and Children of those who shall be killed, (lain, or drowned, in the said Service; will not only be a great Encouragement to such Seamen, but be a publick Utility.

Jordan attended at the Door;

Leverland since that time; and that he (the Witness) has also seen him since that time, and has converted with him upon the Subject of the said Order, and that the said W. Leverland said he would attend this House, according to their Order.

And then he withdrew.

He was again called in; and, being examined, acquainted the House, That he gave Notice to the said W. Leverland of the said Order, and saw the Copy thereof in his Hand; and that the Christian Name of the said Leverland is William.

And then he again withdrew

APetition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Exporters of Corn, and other Inhabitants, of the City and County of Norwich, was presented to the House, and read; reciting a Petition presented to this House from the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Great Tarmouth, in the County of Norfolk; and representing to the

Yarmouth

Harbour.

so Geo. It. 50 — 6° \ i t

House, That more than Twenty thousand Pounds was raiied, by an Act made in the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, fer the Use of the said Haveri and Piers, and was at the absolute Disposal of the said Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Great Yarmouth, subject to an Inspection of their Accounts only*. That, notwithstanding the Petitioners have paid a large Share thereof, they have not received the Benefit that might have been expected therefrom; but have laboured, and do (till labour, under many and great Difficulties and fuss-r great Damages, by reason that One of the said Piers is in so bad a Condition as to let the Haven Ebb pass through it, instead of being by it forced out Kail to Sea; and the other so extended, as to keep the Flood from having a proper Direction into the said Haven; which frequently occasions such a Bar at the Entrance into the said Haven, as obstructs the Pillage of Ships out of, and into, the fume, for many Weeks together; during which time it has happened that Ships laden with the Manufactures of the said City, to the Amount of not less than Fifty or Sixty thousand Pounds, and with great Quantities of Com, to be exported into foreign Parts, and ailo Ships laden with Corn for other Ports of this Kingdom, have been there detained; and the Goods and Corn have received much Damage, and been prevented arriving in Time at their intended Markets, to the great Disappuintment and Loss of the Petitioners: That, for want of Water to carry out of the said Haven even those ftnall Ships which the Petitioners are obliged to venture so much P rope tty in when fully laden, such Ships have been obliged to go out with Part of their Lading only, and the Remainder thereof to be lent to them in l'mall Boats, and to b. hoisted thereout into such Ships, to the great Hazard of falling into the Sea, and thereby of receiving much Damage, or being intirely loft: That, during the present War, Ships appointed for Convoy have waited a longtime in Yarmouth Road fora Fleet of Ships so detained in the said Harbour, and have at last been obliged to depart without them; and that such Fleets of Ships have been detained not only until there was a sufficient Dcptn of Water, but until another Convoy could be obtained; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Money to be raised for the future upon Goods imported into the said Haven, for the Use of the said Haven and Piers, was to be at the Direction of Commissioners tobe chosen out of the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, and City of Norwich, which are so greatly interested therein, as well as out of the Burgh of Great

mouth, such Commissioners, Actuated by Views for the publick Good, might so apply the said Money, as to restore the said Haven to as good a Condition as formerly, when Ships of much greater Burthen than can now come into the said Haven, were constantly made use of for the Trade thereof: And therefore praying, if Leave be given to bring in a Bill according to the Prayer of the said Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Great Yarmouth, that Monies to be raised for the Use of the said Haven and Piers, by a Duty upon Coals, or other Goods, which may act'eft the Petitioners, may not be at the absolute and uncontroulable Direction of them the said Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty only.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Burgh and Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common-Council assembled, is referred: And that they do examine the Mutter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Commonalty, and Wear River trading Inhabitants, of the City of Durham, and of many and Sunder-Gentlemen interested in the Navigation of the River Wear, knd *>orfe was presented tothe House, and read; setting forth, That the

Petitioners

Sontharaptofe

Water-works,

3 iv

6° Martii 1746'.

Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending in the House for the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Wear-, in which is contained (or proposed to be inserted) a Clause, granting Powers to Commissioners, to be named in a future Bill, for making the River navigable

from a Place called Blacksford, or from Newbridge upwards, to the City of Durham, or so far as can be effected: That the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the Words " or so far as can be effected" are unreasonable, unnecessary, and dangerous: That, in the former Adb of Parliament relating to the River Wear, it was always presumed and declared, that the Improvement of the Navigation of the River above Newbridge might and should extend absolutely up to the City of Durham: That in the Year 1730 the River was surveyed, from Durham to Sunderland, by Men of great Skill and Experience,

who judged that the River might be made navigable from Newbridge to the City of Durham, by the Expence of a Sum for which the Duties of Tonage, proposed to be laid on Coals, and other Commodities, conveyed upon that Part of the lliver, would raise an Interest sufficiently high to encourage Undertakers: That the Petitioners doubt not the speedy Success of such an Undertaking, whenever proper Powers thall -be granted by Parliament: That thereby the Trade of the said City would be increased, because the Expence of the Carriage of Goods would be diminished, and because the said City is conveniently situated for an extensive and profitable Commerce: That whenever such Design shall beeffedted, the Price of Coals will be much reduced in London, and other Parts of the Kingdom, because many very large Mines of Coal, which are now unopened on account of the Difficulty of procuring an Expence of maintaining Way-leave to the Part of the River at present navigable, might then be wrought, and the Coals exported probably at a much lower Rate than from any of the present working Collieries: That the Petitioners are earneftlydefirous the said Words shall not be inserted, because they seem to admit aPrefumption that the Design of extending the Navigation of the River up to Durham is impracticable, and will be pleaded in Opposition to any future Application to Parliament fora Bill granting Powers for the Execution of that useful Design , at a time perhaps when the Persons who surveyed the River, and who are now ready and willing to confirm the Truth of their Allegations by their Testimony, may not be living; and when, perhaps, from some fatal Causes, the true Interest of Trade, and of this City, may not be properly represented and afierted, against Adversaries so rich and so powerful: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That the said Words " or so far as can beeffedted" will be omitted from the Clause.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the better Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, is committed.

Inns, Coffee-houses, and Ale-houses, on paying Twenty-Shillings per Annum for every Licence; and, in the same Act, laid a double Duty on all British diddled Spirits; but die Petitioners were thereby totally excluded the Benefit of-retailing: That the Petitioners apprehend the Redrift ion laid upon them only (when so many different Sets of Traders were permitted by Law to retail the smalled Quantities) did not in the lead answer the good Intention of the Legislature in redraining the exorbitant Use of Ipiiituous Liquors; and that if the Petitioners were admitted to retail, in common with those now authorized by b v so to do, it would be a Means of suppressing the Iniquities practised in unlicenled Places; for then thol'e who now retort thither would purchase in a reputable Manner of the Petitioners, who, living in open Streets, could not suffer any Enormities to becotn-niitied in their Shops, without the Observation of the Civil Magistrate; and that the Petitioners hope they shall be the rather deemed worthy of the Favour and Countenance of the Legislature, as they at all Events are obliged to pay the large Duties on spirituous Liquors Monthly, though they are forced to give long Crctlir, and at a small Profit, to the present lawfully authorized Retailers, and are frequently great Sufferers by such of them as come to Misfortunes in Trade; by which means the Profits arising by the wholesale Trade are become insufficient foe the Support of the Petitioners, and their Families: And further representing to the House, That the Petitioners labour under inexpressible Hardlbips, and pay large Sums i f Money, arising from t he Informations daily commenced against them, and prosecuted by a Sort of the most abandoned Part of human Race, who, having no other visible Method of Subliilence, make a Livelihood by this Trade of informing, without any Regard to Truth, or Distinction between the Guilty and the Guiltless; and against which it is a1 most impossible to make any Defence, be the Party accused ever so innocent; as ihefe Informations, though laid wit hin a Month alter the Offence supposed to be committed, are so numerous, that they frequently do not come in course to be heard before the Commissioners of Excise till Four, Five, or Six Months alter exhibited; and die Day upon which the Offence is charged, and the Name of the Informer, being concealed from the Accused till the Time of Tryal, by that Length of Time the Party is-deprived of an Opportunity of recollecting and proving Circumstances, which would in many Cales totally dil-prove the Charge; and, for want of knowing in whole Name the Information is laid, it is impofiib.e to offer Evidence (which could be done in most Cafes) to prove such Informer a Person of vile Character, and no such credible Witness as ought to affect the Character or Property of any free-born Eaglif:Subject: That the Petitioners are willing lo be retrained, under the fevered Penalties', differing any Private Tippling, or other Disorders ik'L. 25.

Tented to the House, and read; setting "forth, That it appears by the Votes of this House, that a Bill is now depending in Parliament, intituled, A Bill for the naturalizing of foreign Protestants; and that the Petitioners, too fenlible of the Mischiefs by Introduction ot Foreigners into this Nation (experienced Mischiefs, solemnly so declared by the Legislature) cannot but be alarmed at this new Attempt; which, if it passesinto a Law, mult divide and weaken the pureftestablished Church, and endanger the belt Syftetn of Government that human Judgment is capable of forming; and that the Petitioners, recolleding the Examples or their Ancestors, ever jealous of the lead Innovation of British Liberty, and whole Applications for Redress have merited and received the Countenance and Support of their Constituents in perilous Times, and most imminent Dangers, beg Leave to implore this House to take this their Petition into Consideration; and that a Bill, in its Nature so dangerous to the Liberty and Property of the rightful-born Subjects of this Nation, incompatible with the Honour of a free People, and subversive of our happy Constitution in Church and State, may not pass into a Law.

Mr. Fane, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it. was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Refblution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Five hundred thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to enable his Majesty to carry on the War with Vigour, both by Sea and Land, and to make good such Treaties as are, or shall be, made with his Majesty's Allies, for the Year 1747.

The said Resolution, being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Complaint being made to the House, That John Williams, Keeper of the White Horse Inn in,

was, upon Thursday last, at a publick Assembly, assaulted, and severely treated, upon a publick Assertion made by feme Persons in that Assembly, that Frafer, said by them to be One of the principal Witnesses against the Lord Lovat, was in his Custody;

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to inquire into the Matter of this Complaint.

Ordered, That the Members, who were appointed a Committee to be Managers of the Impeachment against

Simon late Lord Lovat, be this Committee: And they are to meet this Afternoon at Six of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber: And they have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and to adjourn from time to time, and from Place to Place, as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Committee be impowered to examine, in the most solemn Manner, such Persons as they shall think fit to examine upon the Subject-matter of their Inquiry.

Ordered, That Five be the Quorum of the said Committee.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That all that come to the said Committee have Voices;

It paired in the Negative.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, Relief i» resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for Relief of such of his Majesty's Subjects, in

that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, whole Title by Scotch Deeds and Writings were destroyed or carried off by the Rebel*. Rebels in the late Rebellion.

And then the House adjourned till To morrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Fane, according to Order, reported, from the way» Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred and M* s. to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same Were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One million, out of such Monies as have arisen, or shall or may arise, of the Surplusses, Excesses, or Overplus Monies, commonly called the Sinking Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, his Majesty be enabled to raise a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred thousand Pounds, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged on the First Aids or Supplies to be granted in the next Session of Parliament.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Union of Mr. Scot reported from the Committee, to whom the Leonard Petition of David Young, Professor of Philolbphy, in be-

Collegcg. half of himself, and of the Provost or Principal, Mailers

and Professors, in the Colleges of St. Salvator and St.

'Leonard ',in the University of St. was referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petition laid before the Committee, Pro-pofals and an Agreement, dated 1 ath Day of December 1746, under the Hands of the Principal, Mailers and Pro-selfors in both Colleges; whereby they (after setting forth the Meannefe of the Salaries of the present Principal, Mailers and Professors, and the ruinous Condition of One of the Fabricks, and that the same cannot be repaired and supported, without an Expence far exceeding what the publick Fund can afford) have agreed to apply to Parliament, for an Act to unite and incorporate the Two Colleges, and their Rents and Revenues, under One common Management; and likewise for uniting the correspondent Professorships in the Two Colleges, as the same shall become vacant, by Death or Resignation, upon such Terms and such Manner, as may be for a general publick Benefit, and for promoting the Advancement of Learning.

And the said Report was read: and is as followeth; viz

The Act, of the 22d Year of King Charles the Second (which is the first Act made for repairing the Pier and Haven of Great Yarmouth)lets forth the Importance of the said Borough in f. veral Particulars, especially in respect of the Preservation of the Fishery.and the Breeding and Employing of many Thousands of skilful Mariners and Seamen, the Truth whereof, by long Experience, had been sufficiently evinced; and that the Revenues of the said Borough had been walled in defraying the daily great and unavoidable Charge of repairing and maintaining the Haven and Piers, and the Inability of the said Town to maintain the lame; lb that the great Benefit accruing by the said Haven mull of Necessity be loll, unless timely prevented; and therefore enacts. That for Ten Years, from Midsummer then following, there should be granted for every Chaldron of Coals, Lall of Wheat, Rye, Barley, Malt, or other Grain, and for every Weigh of Salt, and every Ton of any other Goods and Merchandizes whatsoever, which should be imported and unladen in the said Haven (Cod-fish, Ling, Herrings, and other Fish, only excepted) such Sum of Money, not exceeding

V

nd. as the Bailiffs, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Great Yarmouth, in Common-Coucil assembled, should from time to time order and appoint; with Power to them to nominate the Collectors of such Duties, which Collectors were to pay the Money into the Hands of the Chamberlain of the said Borough.

And to the Intent the Money collected might be employed towards repairing the said Haven and Pier, Eight Commissioners were to be nominated and appointed tQ have the Inspection, and take Account, of the Receipts and Disbursements of all the Monies to be collected during the Term aforesaid; Two of which Commissioners were to be yearly appointed by the Bailiffs, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the said Borough, in Common-Council assembled; Two l>y the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of Norwich, in Common-Council assembled; Two by the Justices of the Peace, at the Quarter Sessions for the County of,

and the other Two by the Justices of the Peace at the Quarter Sessions for the County of Suffolk; which Commissioners, or any Five or more of them, should and might from time to time, during the said Term, call before them the Collectors, Receivers, or others intruded with the Collection, Receipt, or Employment, of the said Monies, who were thereby required to render to the Com -missioners, or any Five or more of them, a true Account thereof, and of all Money which should red due upon such Account; and the said Commissioners, or any Five or more of them, should and might order and appoint all such Monies, which should rest due upon such Account, to be laid out and expended for and towards the Uses and Purposes aforesaid, as there should be Cause; and the Bailiffs of Yarmouth were to administer an Oath to every Collector, for the true and faithful Execution of his Office in and about the Premises, according to the true Intent of the said Act.

And to the end the Haven and Pier aforesaid might be repaired and maintained with as much Thrift and good Husbandry as might consist with the effectual and substantial Performance thereof; and that all Parties, who were made contributory to the fame, might be satisfied therein, Three Persons were to be chosen by the Justices of the Peace for Norfolk, at their then next Quarter-Sessions, and the like Number at the Quarter-Sessions for Suffolk, as also Two Persons by the City of Norwich, and Two by the Town of Great Yarmouth, who were to meet at Michaelmas then following, and to adjourn to such other Time and Place as Occasion should require; which Ten Persons, or any Five or more of them, meeting as aforesaid, upon Consideration and Examination upon Oath to be had of the State of the Haven and Pier, and of the Repair necessary for the fame, might treat and contract with Persons, fitly qualified, for the Repair of the said Haven and Pier, and maintaining the same in good Repair for the Space of Seven Years; and the said Persons to be obliged, at the Determination thereof, to leave the same in good and sufficient Repair, in such Manner, and under such Covenants and Conditions, as they should think fit; and, if the Ten Persons aforesaid, or any Five or more of them, should find it convenient to make any such Contraft, as aforesaid, before Christmas then following, the Imposition to be levied, as aforesaid, should be continued no longer than till the Sum necessary for Performance of such Contraft, together with the necessary Charges of levying the same, to be accounted and allowed, as aforesaid, should be raised and paid; but if the said Ten Persons, or any Five or more of them, should not make such Contraft before Christmas then following, then the said Haven and Pier should be repaired by the Direction and Care of the Bailiffs, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of Yarmouth, in Common-Council assembled; and the Money raised and levied should be accounted for as in the former Part of the Act was directed; and if the Pier should be repaired within lets than Ten Years, then the Imposition lhou;d cease, when the Sum lo employed in the Repair of the Pier should have been raised thereby.

Another Act was made in the loth and nth Years of King William the Third, which, amongst other Things, lets forth, That the Haven and Piers of Yarmouth have been of late much more than heretofore, and ftiii continue, obstructed by Sands thrown up by the Sea, in such fort, as the Benefit accruing thereby must be wholly loft, if not prevented and preserved by daily clearing, repairing, and maintaining, the fame; The other Evidence, produced on behalf of the Petition of the Town of Yarmouth, is as follows:

The laid Mr. James Millifon, Deputy-Master of Tri-

nity-house, and employed by them in laying the Buoys, and surveying the Sands, being examined, laid. That he hath known the Haven and Piers of Yarmouth above 30 Years: That in the Year 1744 he was Chamberlain, at which time the Piers were in as good Repair as they had been for many Years; but that the Haven, up at the Quays, was in a very indifferent Condition, and wanted to be dideled, that is, to have the Mud taken away by an Engine made use of for that Purpose: That the Depth of Water at the Entrance of the Haven, upon the Bar, was from Nine to Eleven Feet at High-water; which Bar, he said, sometimes lay 150 Fathom off from the Pier Heads, and sometimes shifts from the S. S. E. to the N. N. E. in different Chanels.

That the Winds, which blow from W.N.W. to N. W. scour the Manure away from the Bar, and make good Tides; but when they blow from the S. S. W. to S. W. they make the Bar very bad; and that any Wind blowing to the Southward of the West makes the Bar so

340

30 Jprilis.

A. 1747.

Yarmouth bad, that sometimes no Flood comes into the Ha-Harbour. yen.

That no great Depth of Water can be had at mouth, by reason that, as the Flood comes from the Northward, the Sand, called the Cockle , is dry, and as the Flood comes up, it meets with such Obstruction from that Sand, that it is Half-Flood before it comes over it; so that instead of going into Yarmouth Road, it paflea over a Sand called Scrooby.

That at present the Piers are but in indifferent Repair and the Haven was never in worse Condition, for Vessels drawing no more than Four Foot Water, can now scarce come up to the Quay; whereas, about Six or Seven Years ago, Ships drawing Eight or Ten Foot Water could come up close to the Quay, with all their Loading, which he imputes to the Manure brought down by, the Three Rivers, and which lodges in the Haven close to the Quay; that when the Engine before-mentioned worked, it answered the End intended; and had it continued working, the Witness apprehends the Haven would not have been in so bad a Condition; and that he believes the Working of it Two or Three Years would clear the Haven.

That the bed Method, in the Witness's Opinion, to remove the Bar at the Entrance of the Harbour, would be to make the South Pier so tight as to prevent the Water passing through it; by which means the Tide would have a true Course to scour the Manure away; and that he believed the Methods used by , for

repairing the Haven and Pier, have been the most effectual that could be used for that Purpose; though lately they have varied their Method, and endeavoured to make the Pier tight, by sinking Trunks full of Chalk, Robbifli, isV. between the Piles, to prevent the Water from running between them.

Being, cross-examined, he laid. That, at the Commencement of the last Act, he believes at high Water the Depth was from Nine to Eleven Feet; and that he believes if the North Pier was shortened, and the South Pier extended, it would be a great Help to the Clearing of the Bar.

Being asked, Whether, if the North Pier was shortened, and the South Pier extended, the South Pier would not be more exposed to the North-West Wind than it is at present ? he said, That it would; but that he did not conceive it would be in any Danger, because it must be built stronger, in Proportion to the Length.

Being also asked. Whether, if the Outsides and Sea-End of the South Pier were lined with Oak Plank, that would not prevent the Trunks, filled with Marl and Lime as before-mentioned, from being washed away ? he said. That it would be of Service; but could not say that he had ever heard, that that Method had been proposed.

Being further examined, he said. That the South Pier was tight, till the Badness of the Weather lately washed away the Trunks; so that the Water now goes between the Piles, to the great Prejudice of the Haven, and Detriment of the whole Pier, which will sometimes (hake, and when the Wind blows hard from North-weft to North-east, is in Danger of being wholly washed away.

That he believes, in the Year 1743, the Water ran through the Piles, and was then stopt, and continued in pretty good Order for Two Years; but has fiace broke out, and now continues to run through the fame.

Being asked, Whether, if the Pier and Haven were once effectual!v repaired and made good, they might not be kept so at a small Charge? he said. That, in his Opinion, the Pieis would always require a great deal of Money to keep them in Repair; for that very often Ships run against the Piles, and break them; morcefpe-cially in Gales of Wind, which, at several Times of the Year, blow great Holes in the Piers, so that the Manure is washed away from them, and that it would sometimes take a Month to repair them.

Being asked, Whether, if proper Works were erected, the Bar might not be made and kept so clear, that Ships of Burthen might go in and out of the Haven, with Sarety ? he answered in the Negative; and the Reason he 1 6

gave for that Answer was, That sometimes there were Eleven Feet Depth of Water upon the Bar, with North-weft Winds, and the next Day, if the Wind came to the South-east, the Manure would fill up the Harbour, so that there would not be Four Feet Depth of Water: That he believes a strong Back-water, if it could be procured, would be of Use, especially if the Haven was once cleared; but he does not think it possible to clear the Haven, but by the Engine; there being fb weak a Current of Water from the Rivers, that it was necessary to, keep the Rivers as clear as possible, to prevent the Manure from washing into the Haven j and that he has known the Freshesfrom the Three Rivers; when the Wind has blown Westerly, clear the Bar of Sand at the Haven's Mouth, in 48 Hours; which he attributes partly to the Freshes, and partly to the Westerly Wind.

Captain James Spurrell being examined, said, That he had been Master of a Veflc), using Yarmouth Trade, 2£ Years; that, at the Expiration of the last Act, the Piers and Haven were in pretty good Order, in comparison to what they are at present; and the Piers were in better Repair than he had known them for Twenty Years before; and the Haven was in better Condition than it had been for Five or Ten Years preceding: That there was then from Nine to Eleven Feet Dq>th of Water at Spring Tides, at the Mouth of the Haven, with an Off-Shore Wind; but that at present the greatest Depth of any Tide is but Eight or Nine Foot.

That whenever the Winds are Easterly, the Sands block up the Mouth of the Harbour, so that the Tides run through the Piers to the Southward; and the bed Method, in the Witness's Opinion, of procuring a better Entrance into the Haven, is to make the South Pier tight, which would scour the Harbour right out to Sea.

That the Haven at present is in a worse Condition that it has been fof 20 or 25 Years past; and that while the Engine was employed in scouring it. Ships could come up to the Quays; but that the same has not been worked these last Three or Four Years for Want of Money, as he apprehends.

Then being asked. Whether the said Engine was frequently used during the Continuance of the late Act of Parliament? he said, He had known it used for Two Years together, sometimes at Braydoti, and sometimes upon the Quays; and that he had known it lie still for a Year oc Two together.

"Being cross-examined, he said, That the Haven, according to his Belief, was ina better Condition in 1744, than it had been for Six or Seven Years preceding that Time; and that at that Time the Water did not run through the South Pier so much as at present, because there was a Bank of Sand thrown up at the Back of it, which set the Tide out truer to the Sea.

That if the Three Rivers are kept clean, the Waters of those Rivers, together with a Westerly Wind, would at all times greatly contribute to scour the Harbour more right to Sea.

The said Captain Spurrell being further examined, said. That during the Time the Watch was kept, called the Clapper-man, the same was of Utility in preventing Accidents by Fire on Board the Ships which lay in the Harbour.

The Witness being required to acquaint the Committee with the Reasons why Application was not made to Parliament, in pursuance of the said Agreement, said. That feme Gentlemen, who have Estates upon the North Ri- ver\ thinking that the Allowance of a Half-peny per Ton was not sufficient for the cleansing and depthening of that River, applied to the Deputies of the County of Norfolk (of whom the Witness was One) and acquainted them, That if a further Allowance was not made for the said River, they would oppose the Draught at the Quarter-Session: Whereupon it was agreed between the Deputies of the County of Norfolk, and the said Gentlemen, That, as the Boats going up the North River have no Passage over the Chanel of Braydon, the said Gentlemen should not be at any Expence about the same; but that when the Money for Braydon should be raised, they should be allowed a Half-peny of that Money, to be applied in the Clearing of the North River: That upon this express Condition, and not otherwise, the Bill was agreed to at the Sessions for the County of Norfolk; but that some Time after, he (the Witness) received a Letter from Mr. Ferrier, Town-Clerk of Yarmouth, dated the

That the (jlentlemen who were appointed a Committee to go to London, for getting the Haven and Pier Act pafietl, were not a little surprized, that, after Minutes had been signed, and a Draught of an Act approved by all Parties, a new Matter should be offered; and that they (the said Committee) desired him to acquaint the Witness, that it is their Opinion that the said Propoful would never be agreed to by Yarmouth; and that if any Obstruction should be put to the Palling of the Bill, in the Shape it then was, the Corporation would never again consent to a new Act on the like Terms (very many there being difliitisfied with what had been done); and that the Committee then desired the Witness to inform them, as soon as he could, whether the Bill, as it then flood, would be consented to at the Norfolk Sessions qr not; and that if it should nut, they said they should think themselves released from the Agreement they had made, as it was not to be doubted their Constituents would also. *7

That afterwards the Witness received another Letter-from Mr. Ferrier, dated the 11th of March 1741, acquainting him, That, at the Assembly of the said Corporation, he had the Day before read the Order made at the Jail Session for Norfolk, relating to the Haven and Pier Act; and that the Assembly would not come to any Determination thereabout; and had referred it to be considered at some succeeding Assembly: Upon which, the Witness said, the Affair dropt.

With regard to what was transacted at the other. Meetings of the Deputies of the said Four Places, since the Year 1741:

' Mr. Meadows being examined, said, That he was present at all the said Meetings, the First of which was upon the 13th of November 1744, the Second aboit Six Weeks after, and the last upon the 16th of January 1746; and that they all broke up without coming to any Agreement about an Application to Parliament, which was . the End of the said Meetings; because the Deputies for Yarmouthconstantly inlisted, That the said Corporation should have the Direction of the Application of the Six Pence per Ton, as they had under the former Act; alleging, as the Reason of such Demand, that lets than the said Sum would not besufficient to keep the Haven and Piers in Repair; whereas the Deputies for Norfolk and Norwich infilled, That Four Pence would be sufficient for that Purpose; the Quantum being the only Matter in Dispute between them.

Being asked, If any thing passed at any of those Meetings, in relation to the Eight Pence proposed to be raised by the Draught of the Bill before:mentioned ? he Lid, That the Commissioners for Norfolk and Norwich had agreed among themselves, that 8 d. more should be raised for Seven Years, provided the Majority of the Twelve Commissioners to be appointed should judge it necessary, for putting the Haven and Piers into immediate Repair; and that 2 d.more should be raised, during the Remainder of the Term, to be under the same Direction; but that nothing relating to this Matter passed at any of the said Meetings, as a Subject of Debate.

Being asked. Whether he apprehended that the giving of the uncontroulable Dispoficion of Six Pence per Tun, to the Corporation of Yarmouth, would have been attended with any ill Consequences ? he said, That both his Constituents and himself were of that Opinion; and that though they had consented to the giving of to be disposed of in that manner, yet it was because they found a joint Application could not goon without their making that Concession; and they thought That the lead; Evil of the Two.

Being further examined, he said. That he apprehended the Power of inspecting the Accounts only, given to the Commissioners by the last Act, to be, as far as regarded the Execution of the Works, no Power at all; because they only signed what appeared to them to be a true Balance; the Act having, as was conceived, expressly given the Direction of the Works to the Corporation of Yarmouth -, and that though he was far from thinking all which they did wrong, yet that, in general, the Manner of applying the Money under the said Act, was the Foundation of his Opinion, that the giving of the uncontroulable Disposition of the Money, to be raised by any future Act, would be attended with ill Consequences: And the Witness added. That he apprehended it would be better if the whole Money, to be raised by any fub-sequent Act, was to be under the Direction of the Commissioners at large.

Being asked. Whether, in case of any sudden Damage done to the Harbour by a Storm, or otherwise, the Commissioners at large could be of Service, in directing the Works necessary upon such an Emergency ? the Witness said, That he thought they might, because they might be summoned together in a lliortTime; and that in case of any such accidental Mischief, as afore-mentioned, if an Engineer, properiy authorized by the Commissioners, was upon the Spot, he (the Witness) thinks such Engineer would be at lead as able as the Corporation of Yarmouth to direct what might be proper to be dune.

Year 1739 he remembered, that the great Frod and Eaderly Winds, which continued for near Three Months, occasioned a large Bank of Sand to be flung up before the Mouth of the Haven, during the Continuance whereof the Navigation was extremely hazardous; but that, in the Summer following, the Wederly Winds blew, which removed the said Bank, and Ships went in and out as usual, and upwards of 40,000 Chaldron of Coals were imported that Summer: That the following Winter was very severe; and, by Means of the Eaderly Wind?, the Entrance of the Haven was again blocked up with Sand; and, to the bed of the Witness's Remembrance, a Chanel was cut through the Bar by People belonging to the Haven and Piers, and the next Day, or the Day after. That he apprehends, that the Bank of Sand thrown up on the South Side of the South Pier in 1742, prevented the Water running through the Piers; and that from 1739 to 1742 the Water foinctimes did, and sometimesdid not, run through the Piers.

Sir John Cust reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are lit to be revived, or continued; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the *7

House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the feme was read; And the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth, viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for prohibiting the Importation of Books reprinted abroad, and first composed or written, and printed, in Great Britain; and for repealing lb much of an Act, made in the 8 th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, as impowers the limiting the Prices of Books, as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Books reprinted abroad, and first composed or written, and printed, in Britain (which was to continue in Force, from the 29th Day of September 1739, for the Space of Seven Years, anti from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament) is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 3d Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for reviving and amending an Act, made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Weirs upon the River of Thames, West-ward; and for ascertaining the Rates of Water-Carriage upon the said River (which was to continue in F ree, from the First Day of May 1730, for the Term of Nine Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for continuing several Laws therein mentioned, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of June which shall be in the Year of our Lord 1747) is near expiring, and fit ro be continued.

3.
