Mr. Fane, according to Order, reported from the Way* Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred and to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, from and after the 24th Day of June 1747, the Sum of Five Pounds yearly shall be paid to his Majesty, for a Licence to be taken out yearly by every Distiller who shall vend, barter, or utter, any spirituous Liquors by Retail, in less Quantity than Two Gallons, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, or Weekly Bills of Mortality.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Resolution, reported upon the 26 th Day of March last, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Petition of the several Distillers within the Cities of Westminster, Borough of Southwark, and Weekly Bills of Mortality,-whole Names arc thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others exercising the Distilling Trade, which Resolution was then agreed to by the House;. he now read:

And the said Resolution was read accordingly j and is as followeth; viz.

" Resolved, That the several Distillers within the Cities " of London and Westminster, Borough of Southwark, or " Weekly Bills of Mortality, be permitted to take out " Licences, with a Duty payable thereupon, for retailing " spirituous Liquors in their own publick Shops only;

" and that they be restrained from suffering any Persons " to drink or tipple in their Shops, or other Places to

them belonging."

Ten thousand Pounds South-Sea Stock, after the Death of his Wife (which has lately happened) unto his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, to be applied to the Use of the Sinking Fund, in such Manner as should be directed by Parliament: That the Petitioners apprehend it is evident, that it could not be the Intention of the said Sir Joseph Jekyll to provide for the Payment of Part of the publick Debt out of his private Estate, and leave his nearest, and some of his most necessitous Relations defti-tute of Support; but that he intended to make Provision for them, more ample and sufficient than what lie had allotted to his distant Relations; which Provision, by reason of his mistaken Opinion, with regard to his Power of granting Leases for Forty-one Years, is reduced to little Value, and consequently the Petitioners mutt suffer great Distress, unless this House shall grant them some Relief: And therefore submitting this their distressed same to the Consideration and Companion of the House; and praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

The said Mr. Hunt, One of the Vestry-men of the said Parish, being examined, said, That he had been Overseer of the Poor of the said Parish in the Year 1705, and Churchwarden in 1723; and that the general Opinion of the Parish was, that this Piece of Ground was to be laid into the Church-yard, for the Benefit of the Parish: That when he was Churchwarden the Burial Fees amounted to above £.392; but that now they are much less, by reason of the Smallnefsof the Church-yard; and that the Want of this Piece of Ground is a Detriment to the Parish. A Memorial of the Bishop of , to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, in the Year 1740, was also produced; wherein the Memorialist represents, That by virtue of an Act, made in the First Year of King James the ad, he and his Successors, Rectors of the said Parish, are intitled to the Reversion in Fee of a Piece of Ground, whereon some Stables and Tenements are erected, in Piccadilly, adjoining to the Church-yard of the said Parish, after the Determination of a Lease made thereof, by the late Lord Jermyn and others, to Sir Thomas Bond, which would expire at Michaelmas then next ensuing: And that in perusing the said Act, and other Deeds relating to the Premises, it appears there is a Mif-take in the Description of the Grounds; and that the Memorialist had laid the said Act, with the same and other Papers relating thereto, before his Majesty's Attorney-General, and another of his Majesty's Counsel, for their Opinion, whereby the Validity of the Memorialist's Title appeared; and that he was apprehensive, that the Reprc-fentatives of the said Sir 'Thomas Bond, or others, might be induced to apply to their Lordships for a Grant of Part of the Premises, to the Prejudice of the Memorialist and his Successors; and therefore he prayed. That their Lordships would giveDirections for such Entries or Caveats to be made in the proper Offices, as might discourage any Attempt to disturb the Memorialist, or his Successors, in the peaceable Possession of this Part of the Endowment of the said Church; or at least that no Grant thereof might pass, without first hearing Counsel on behalf of the Memorialist and his Successors.

Which Memorial being referred to the Surveyor General, he, in his Report in Answer thereto, after reciting the before-mentioned Clause in the said Act, observes, That it appears, upon examining the Premises, that this Piece of Ground of 40 Foot by 25 Foot, does not abut East on the Church-yard, there being another Piece of Ground of 25 Feet Front, and 76 Feet deep, which interferes between them; so that of Necessity either the Front Dimension of 40 Foot, or the Eastern Boundary on the Church-yard must be mistaken; and that the Question will then be on the Construction of the Act, where the Mistake lies: That although the learned Counsel above-mentioned seem to think that the Mistake lies in the North Dimension, rather than the Eastern Boundary, and consequently that the 25 Feet Front, as well as the 40 Feet Front, are included in the Act; yet as the same on which they gave their Opinion wasftated only on the Act of Parliament, and the contemporary Demise of the Premises to Sir Thomas Bond, without any Retrofpcft to the Grant of King Charles the 2d, of the same Parcel, and to the same Uses, immediately preceding the Act, and from whence the Description of the Premises, and even the Mistake is copied, the Surveyor-General conceived it might be prop.r to consider how the Matter -flood under that Grant; and if a certain and necessary Construction of the Crown in the Letters Patent, notwithstanding the Mistake, could be come at, he apprehended it would naturally lead to the Construction of the same Words in the Act of Parliament.

Then after reciting the Contents of the Grant before-mtoiipood, under the Great Seal, bearing Date the 31st

May 1684, as far as they relate to the Matter in Question, the Surveyor-General observes. That there is the same Mistake in the Grant as in the Act of Parliament; and in order to discover where the Mistake arose, fays, he has traced the Proceedings in the Offices as far as he could, and finds that the Grant did not pass by Reference from the King to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, and thence to the Offices under them, but by Warrant immediately from the King, drawn at the Secretary of State's Office, and directed to the Attorney-General, to prepare a Bill (or Draught of the intended Grant) which Bill is the First Instrument he (the Surveyor-General) could find relating to this Matter; so that what the Crown intended to convey by it, can only be learned by the Description of the Premises in the Grant itself, or from Circumstances attending them, about the Time of passing.

He further observes, That the Premises under Consideration were held and deemed, at and after the Time of passing the Grant, as Two separate Estates, devised by the Earl of St. Alban's to Two different Tenants, and under different Rents: That the First Parcel of 40 Foot by 75 Foot, was leased to one Joseph Thompson, under a Rent of Six Pounds per Annum, and was assigned over by him to Bond, subject to the same Rent; and that the other Parcel of 25 Feet by 76, was devised by the said Earl to one Sir Cafar Wood, in Trust for Bond, under a Rent of £.5 per Annum: That being thus possessed of both Parcels, did not use them separate, but together, as his OccafioBSrequired; so that the Stable-yard extended over the South Part of both Parcels; but that this promiseuous Use of them did not alter the Tenure, they being held still as Two Parcels, and Two Rents paid for them: And the Alignment from Lord Jermyn to Bond, dated 27 February 1684, which was after the Grant, calling them Two separate Parcels: And as the essential Parts of the Description in the Letters Patent, are express and certain, that what was granted was One Parcel containing in Front next Piccadilly 40 Foot, and in Depth 75 Foot, with Two Front Houses erected thereon, One in Possession of Hayburne, and the other of Clifton; and some Stables erected on the other Part thereof; and as there was a distinct Parcel, exactly corresponding with all these Particulars, the Surveyor-General submits to their Lordships, whether a new and separate Parcel of 25 Foot in Front, and 76 Foot in Depth, not therein mentioned, can be included in the Grant, from the single Circumstance of the Eastern Boundary; and whether the Boundary ought not to be governed by the more essential Parts of the Description; and the rather so, because, in the same of Lord Portland's Grant of the Dog Field in Soko, which was under their Lordships Consideration in the Year 1731, the Name of the Field and Number of Acres were mentioned in the Grant, but excluded by the Boundary; and the present and late Lord Chancellors, thenAttorney and Sollicitor-General, gave their Opinions,

hat the Grant included the Field, notwithstanding the Boundary.

That what (as the Surveyor-General apprehends) will render the Construction of the Letters Parent certain and necessary, is, that the Eastern Boundary on the before-mentioned Church-yard is no where to be found: That neither of the Parcels under Consideration could possibly abut Eastward on the aforesaid Church-yard, which lay intirely upon the South, and no Part thereof upon the East; that which lies on the East being the Ground whereon the Church was erected, and a quite separate. Thing, as evidently appears, on a careful Perui'al of the said Letters Patent; the necessary Consequence whereof will be, that the Western Parcel, of 40 Foot by 75, was granted to Lord Jermyn, and his Heirs, for the religious Uses above-mentioned; and that the Eastern Parcel of 25 Foot by 76, remained in the Crown.

The Surveyor-General concludes with observing, That the Construction of the Letters Patent being the refore certain and unavoidable, the Construction of the Act of Parliament which was immediately consequent to it, and

This Memorial being aho referred by the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury to the Surveyor-General, he, in his Report, in Answer thereto, dated the 25th of February 1746, after reciting the before-mentioned Clause in the said Act of the First Year of Ring James the Second, observes, That there is a Mistake in the Description of the Premises contained in the said Clause, either in the North Dimension of 40 Feet, or in the Eastern Boundary; for, if the Piece of Ground intended to be granted be rightly bounded on the present Church-yard, it mud contain 65 Feet, instead of 40 Feet mentioned in the Grant, which is the Construction the Memorialid would have established; whereas if the Ground intended to be granted contains only 40 Foot in Front, then the Eastern Boundary is wrong, which ought to have been on another Piece of Ground in Possession of Sir Thomas Bond, indead of the Church-yard: That the Description of the said Piece of Ground, as contained in the Act, is taken from the Description of the same Piece of Ground

contained in the Letters Patent of the 3 id of May 1684, both as to the Dimensions of the Front, and Depth of the Ground, the Names of the Occupiers, the Buildings etefted thereon, and also in all the Abuttals and Boundaries; and that even the Mistake itself, wherever it lies, is copied from the Letters Patent; and whatever the Crown intended to grant by the Words and Descriptions contained in the Signet Bill and Letters Patent before-mentioned, the same Construction, he apprehends, will be put upon the same Words and Descriptions in the Act, preluming that it was the Intention of the Legifla-ture, in passing the said Act, that whatever the Parcel was which was vested in Lord Jermyn by the Crown, as Part of the Minister's Endowment, should be taken from Lord Jermyn, and vested in the Rector, and his Successors, and nothing more.

Then, after reciting the Words of the Signet Bill and Letters Patent before-recited, the Surveyor-General observes, That it appears, upon the Face of them, that the Description of the Parcel under Consideration is perfect and complete without the Eastern Boundary, it containing in Front 40 Foot, and in Depth 75 Foot; abutting on Piccadilly North, South on the Church yard, and West on Anthony Hart Bricklayer; and the Two Tenements were. A Petition of the Commissioners of the Land Tax for the . Sheriffdom of Dumfrieswhich comprehends the Stewartry of Annandale, assembled together at Dumfries upon the 18th Day of April 1747 Years, for putting in Execution an Act, passed in this present Session of Parliament, for granting to his Majesty certain Rates and Duties upon Houses, Windows, or Lights, was presented to the House and read; letting forth, That the Petitioners being informed, that a Bill is depending in this House for taking away and abolishing the heretable Juril'dictions in that Part of Great Britain called , and for making

Satisfaction to the Proprietors thereof, and for restoring such Jurisdictions to the Crown; and for making more effectual Provision for the Administration of Justice throughout that Part of the united Kingdom, by the King's Courts and Judges there; and for rendering the Union of the Two Kingdoms more complete; beg Leave to acquaint this House, That having in no Instance, that the Petitioners can recoiled, found the Exercise of the Jurisdiction of the Sheriffof Dum, Stewart of Annandale,

or of the Judges of the several Regalities within the same, injurious or oppressive to their Persons or Properties; but having, on the contrary, received many Ad vantages from the (peedy, impartial, and easy, Administration of Justice, within their own Precincts; and those Advantages, as they flatter themselves, fully secured to them by the Treaty of Union between the Two Kingdoms; they cannot but be greatly alarmed at any Attempt to innovate or alter a Constitution which the Petitioners and their Ancestorshave lived happily and quietly under, all Innovations being attended with many unforeseen Inconvenk encies: That the Petitioners think themselves no less interested in the Fate of the said Bill, than the Owners of the Jurisdictions thereby intended to be taken away, all being equally affected, though not in the same Shape; the Petitioners not foreseeing that Justice would be administeredn upon the Plan of this Bill, with so much Ease and Convenience as at present, or with greater Impartiality to the People: That, if the late wicked and unnatural Commotions in the Kingdom have given Rife to this Bill, the Petitioners must beg Leave to observe, that these cannot be charged upon the Powers acifing from heretable Jurisdictions, but upon thelnfluence the Highland Chiefs have over their several Clans; an Authority founded upon no Law, norconnefted with the Power of any legal Jurisdiction granted by the Sovereign, but established by ancient Custotn, blindly submitted to by the People in that Part of the Kingdom, and which has upon many former Occasions been the Object of the Attention, of the Legislature: That the Petitioners hope to be excused for observing, that they consider the Custom of taking down and reducing into Writing the Evidence given in capital and criminal Causes, and Prosecutions before the Court of Judiciary, and the Circuit Courts in Scotland, a6 a greater Security to the Subject, in regard the Jury have the Evidence more fully before them, and can consider the same more deliberately than the Evidence of Witnesses examined in a Hurry viva voce: And therefore, for these Realons, submitting their Sentiments of this Bill, and praying that it may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town-Council, in Name of the Community, of the Borough of in

18

the County of Air, subscribing, was presented to the Scotch House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, H«ewhle being informed that a Bill is depending in the House for taking away and abolishing the heretable Jurisdictions in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, for making Satisfaction to the Proprietors thereof, and for restoring such Jurisdictions to the Crown; and for making more effectual Provision for the Administration of Justice throughout that Part of the united Kingdom, by the King's Courts and Judges there; and for rendering the Union of the Two Kingdoms more complete; beg l^eave to acquaint the House, That all the inferior Jurisdictions are extremely beneficial to the Subjects, as they obtain Justice at their Door, and at a small Expence, these Jurisdictions creating no Dependence in the People upon the Judges; and that as the Petitioners never experienced any Tyranny, Oppression, or intended Partiality or Injustice, in the Administration of the inferior Judges, fb neither have they any Apprehensions thereof for the future, as an easy and effectual Remedy can be had from the Court of Session when any Mistakes in Judgment happen, to which every Mortal is liable; and that as these Jurisdictions and Offices, whether heretable or for Life, are by the 18th and 20th Articles of the Union facrodly secured to the then Possessors, the Petitioners apprehend it will be esteemed a Breach of the publick Faith, and an open Violation of that sacred Treaty, as well as equal to oblige the Proprietors of fbefe Jurisdictions to fell their Eftatfs'; and will involve the Subjects in immense Trouble and Expence beyond what they are now put to, or are abl.e to bear, and render the Administration of Justice more ineffectual and flow, should the said Bill be allowed to pass into a Law,; and that this and many other Boroughs will be dripped of the Benefit they now enjoy, by being the Seats of the Courts of Justice, the only Amends they have for the Expence of building and supporting publick Prifoar houses: And therefore, for these several Reasons, submitting their Sentiments of the said Bill unto" the House^ and praying that it may not pass into a Law,

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Archibald Esquire, heretable

Sheriff of the Sheriffdom of R, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That this Jurisdiction of heretable Sheriff of the County of , now

verted in the Petitioner, has for many Ages part been possessed by his Predecessors; and that in no Instance did ever either he or they exercise it to any other Purpose than to the Good of the Subjects living in that Part of the Country over which it extends: lhat a it appears to have been the Sense of the Legislature, even in ancient Times, when the Liberty of the Subject was not so well secured as it is at pitfent, that these heretable Jurisdictions were Rights of Freehold, of which the Possessor could not be deprived without his own Content, or the Commifrton of a Crime; so the only Attempt that ever was made, not indeed to abolish, but to in pair, them by a Statute passed in the Year 1681, was, by the Parliament called at the late happy Resolution, represented as One of the Grievances of the Nation, and accordingly repealed; and that since that time these Rights have been secured to the Porte flora by the Treaty of Union, upon the Faith of which they relied; and that in no time thereafter they could be disquieted, unless they should be found to deserve it by their own Fault or Offence; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioner apprehends that he, and many other loyal Subjects, would be deprived of their Property and Freehold, which he thinks himself more bound to infifr upon, that he is fully persuaded thcle Jurililiftions, when legally exercised, tend greatly to the Advantage of the Subjects of that Part of the united Kingdom; and that when they are so exercised, as that of the Petitioner's has always been, he is advised they cannot be taken away from the Proprietor without his own Consent: And therefore praying the House, That he may be heard, by his Counsel, againfr parting this Bill into a Law; an Indulgence which he hopes will never be refuted to any Subject, whose Pro|>erty is to be affected by any Bill depending in this House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of the several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, of Roxburghe, whose Name? are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners observing a Bill brought into Parliament, intituled, A Bill for taking away and abolishing the heretable Jurisdictions in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and for making Satisfaction to the Proprietors thereof, and for restoring such Jurisdictions to the Crown; and for making more effectual Provision for the Administration of Justice throughout that Part of the united Kingdom, by the King's Courts and Judges there; and for rendering the Union of the Two Kingdoms more complete; think themselves obliged, in Duty to their Country, themselves, and their Posterity, to represent against it, and petition the House, That it may not pass into a Law, for the following Reasons: — Because it appears to them. That heretable Jurisdictions, intended to be taken away by the Bill, were, by the 20th Article of the Treaty of Union, secured to the Proprietors thereof as Rights of Property j that therefore any Infringement upon them might justly alarm every Proprietor in that Part of the united Kingdom, as this is an Attack upon private Property, without Consent of the Proprietor: — Because, by the 18th Article of the said Treaty of Union, it is provided. That no Alteration be made in the Laws which concern private Property, except for the evident Utility of the Subjects within Scotland-, and these heretable Jurisdictions, as being private Rights of Property, ought not to receive any Alteration, but for the evident Utility of Scotland -, and the Petitioners cannot observe any Utility arising to Scotland from this Act; for as they have hitherto had Justice administered to them in that Country by an heretable Sheriff, there nevey occurred to them any Reason of Complaint of such Jurisdiction, but on the contrary liaVe found the Sheriff always ready and willing to administer Justice in the most equal and impartial Manner: — Because this Infringement of the Articles of Union mull certainly alarm that Country, as that most solemn Treaty is the only Security they have for their Rights and Privileges: — Because they are not Satisfied, that vesting the Nomination of Sheriffs in the Crown can beof any Advantage to the Constitution of that Country, as it leems to be an unnecessary Addition to the Power of the Crown; and as the Sheriffs are the returning Officers, it may be attended with bad Consequences in Elec-ons: — Because, by this Bill, great Alterations are intended to be made in the Administration of Justice \n that Part of the united Kingdom, and the Petitioners are sensible that such Alterations mud be attended with unavoidable Difficulties, and will rather tend to distract the Subjects rhan to make the Administration of Justice more easy; the Petitioners are well Satisfied with the Administration of Justice in its present 'Form; and such an Alteration as is intended will require new and unusual Forms of Procedure, which will naturally produce great Confu-Ijon, and, as the Petitioners are afraid, may be made a

Precedent for greater Alterations in the ancient Laws of that Part of the united Kingdom, which were Solemnly reserved to them by the sacred Treaty of Union; besides, by the 19th Article of that Treaty, the Court of Session is stipulated to remain in all Time coming within Scotland, as then constituted by the Laws of that Kingdom, and with the Authority and Privileges as before the Union; and as this Bill incroaches in divers Respects upon the Jurisdiction of the Court of Session, it becomes thereby an evident Infringement of that Article: And therefore praying, That, for these Reasons, the House will not pals this Bill into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against it.

Ordered, That the Said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Consumers of Coals in the City Fraiidi in and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, on behalf '*

of themselves, and several other Consumers, was presented Coa to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners will be obliged, by the Bill now depending in the House, to explain, amend, and render more effectua', an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled,'

An Act more effectually to prevent the Frauds and Abu-fes committed in the Admeasurement of CoaJs, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining thereto, and the several Parishes of St. Giles in the Fields, St. Mary leBon, and such Part of the Parish of St, Andrew Holborn, as lies in the County of Middlesex j and to indemnify Persons, who have acted under the said Act, in certain Cafes; to pay an unnecessary Charge for the Metage of their Coals, in Cales where there is no Occasion for any Admeasurement, there being no Probability of Fraud: That the Petitioners apprehend there are Sufficient Powers in the before-mentioned Act, and several former Acts, to remedy any Frauds or Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, in case the same were duly put in Execution; and that the said Bill, should it pals into a Law, will greatly inhance the Price of Coals; and will, instead of being of Service, be both oppressive and burdensome to the Petitioners, and the other Consumers within the said Limits: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

and that in the same Session of Parliament an Act passed, for prohibiting the Wearing and Importation of Cambricks and French Ixwns, whereby the importing them into Great after the First Day of August 1745, is prohibited: That, encouraged by the said additional Bounty, great Numbers of Looms have, since the granting of the fame, been let at Work in Great Britain and Ireland, for making coarfo Linens, intitled to the said Bounties, in which many thousand poor People, old and young, are employed: And that several of the Petitioners, on the Credit and Expectation of receiving such Bounty, have bought large Quantities of such Linens, and shipped the same for Exportation to America, and other Places: That the said additional Duty on foreign Cambricks, between the First of August 174a, when it commenced, and the First of August 1745, when the Prohibition of the Importation of Cambricks took Place, amounted to Twenty-five thousand Nine hundred Twenty-six Pounds Three Shillings and Two pence Three Farthings; and the Bounties already paid thereout amount only to Ten thousand Nine hundred Twenty-six Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence Three Farthings; and the Residue of the said Money, being Fifteen thousand Pounds, hath been, by Orders of the Lords of the Treasury, pursuant to the Di-red ions of the said Act, paid into his Majesty's Exchequer to the Sinknig Fund, by the Title of Duty on Earn-bricks, by the Act of the 15th and 16th George the Second: That there is unpaid to the Petitioners and several other Exporters, in respect of the said Bounties, I'ere-ral Sums, amounting to Two thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-one Pounds, for which Debentures have been prepared at the Custom-house; but such Debentures have not been signed, in regard a Doubt hath arisen, whether the said Bounties are payable since the Time the said Duty on the Importation of foreign Cambricks ceased: That unkfs Provision be made for paying the said Bounties, which are or shall become due on the Exportation of the said British and Irish Linens, the Exportation thereof will be intirely at a Stop; and the Petitioners, who purchased great Quantities thereof, on a Belief they were intitled to such Bounties, will be great Sufferers: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir Henry Liddell reported from the Committee, tct whom the Petition of ! Thomas Jekyll, Edward Richard Blacket Jekyll, and Hamah Jekyll, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Twelve residuary Legatees named in the Will of Sir Joseph Jekyll Knight, late Matter of the Roll's, deceased, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad; contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Examination of the Matters of Fa<tt contained in the said Petition, the Committee find. That by an Act: made in the 12th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for impowering the Matter of the Rolls for the Time being, to make Leases for Years, in order to new build the old Houses belonging to the Rolls (whichAd recitcs.That the M an fion-house, Ground, and Tenements, belonging to the Matter of the Rolls, were much out of Repair, and not capable of Improvement, in regard the Matters of the Rolls were not enabled to grant such Leases, and for such Terms as might encourage Tenants to build and to repair) it is enacted, That the Matter of the Rolls for the Time being, and his Successors, Matters of the Rolls, flin.ll have good Right, full Power, and lawful Authority, during the Time he or they shall continue Matters of the Rolls, by Writing indented under Hand and Seal, to grant and make Leases for One-and-Forty Years, or for any lefferTerm, to commence from the Making of any such Leases, of all and singular the Premises, or any Part thereof (the Chapel of the Rolls, with a convenient Mansion-house, Courtyard, Garden, and other Appurtenances, fit for the Habitation of the Matter of the Rolls only excepted); and it is provided. That the Matter of the Rolls, for the Time being, or any succeeding Matter of the Rolls, after the Premises had been once let ten, according to the Power given as aforesaid, should not grant or make any new or concurrent Lease, until within Seven Years of the Expiration of the Lease then in being, nor for any letter Rent than was reserved upon the former Lease, nor for any longer Term than Twenty-one Years, from the making such new Lease.

That upon Inquiry made, none of the Leases granted by Sir Har bottle Grim Hon can be found; but Charles

Frewen, Esquire, an Officer in the Rolls the Time Sir Joseph Jekyll was Matter of the Rolls, has seen several Counterparts of those Leases, which were granted for the Term of Forty-one Years, particularly those granted to Sir Beversham Filmer, One of the Matters in Chancery, and which bore Date a Year or Two after the said Act was made.

That on the 13th of July 1717, Sit Joseph Jekyll was appointed Matter of the Rolls; and the Houses belonging to the Rolls being in a very ruinous Condition, in or about the Year 1719 he rebuilt Nine of the said Houses, according to a Plan designed by Colin Campbell Esquire, deceased; and within a few Years after, Thirty other of the said Houses were rebuilt by the said Sir Joseph Jekyll, under the Direction and Survey of Mr. Biggs deceased, and his Nephew William Biggs: That the Expence of rebuilding the First Nine Houses was 5 or £.6,000, and the I'x pence of the 30 Houses was about £.25,000.

That the said Sir Joseph Jekyll, from the Opinion he expressed, did not doubt his having a Power, under the above-recited A<tt, to grant Leases for the Term of 41 Years, of Houses rebuilt; and when the Plan and Elevation of Ten of the Thirty Noufes were laid before him, for his Approbation, he inquired. How long Houses builc according to those Plans would (land ? and being informed they would continue longet1 than 41 Years, he said. He would luve them built as strong and as well as if they were his own Inheritance s whereupon the Plan was altered, the Walls made thicker, the Timber of larger Dimension, an additional Story was added to each House, and the Height of the other Stories raised 18 Vol. 25.

Inches, and Vaults were built, and the Extent of each of the said Houses was enlarged backwards, which cauled a Difference of Expence, in the Articles of Brick and Tiin-ber only, to the Amount ol £.200 each House; betides Marble Chimney-Pieces, Brals Locks, and other Decorations, which amounted to £.150 more each House.

That the Account of the Expence of building the said Houses was stated by Mr. Frewen, who was Steward to Sir Jof ph Jekyll, in the Year 1734; and the Vouchers being then delivered to Sir Joseph Jekyll, cannot now be found, but are supposed to have been deftreyed as useless Papers, Sir Joseph not regarding Papers of that Nature, after he had settled Accounts.

Thar of Six of the aforesaid 39 Houses, Sir Joseph Jekyll granted Leases for the Term of 41 Years, from Lady-day 1718, the Rents whereof amounted to £.255 per Annum; and for Three others for the like Term, from Lady-day 1720, the Rents whereof amounted to £164 per Annum-, and of Two othefs for the like Term, from Midsummer 1723, the Rents whereof amounted to £.131 per Annum; and of Four Houses for the like Term, from Midsummer 1728, the Rents whereof amounted to £.133 per Annum; and of Six others for the like Term, from Michaelmas 1728, thellents whereof amounted to £.189 per Annum; and of Two others for the like Term, from Lady-day 1728, the Rents wdiereof amounted to £.62 per Annum; and of Twelve others for the like Term, from Midsummer 1729, the yearly Rents whereof amounted to £.632; and of Three others for the like Term, from 28th August 1729, the yearly Rents whereof amounted to £.183; and One other for the like Term, from 6th May 1732, at the yearly Rent of £.31; the whole of which Rents amount to£. 1,780 per Annum.

That Sir Joseph Jekyll died in the Year 1738; and after having given by his Will several large pecuniary Legacies to feme, and Annuities for Life to other of his Relations,

He directed, That the East India Stock and South-Sea Stock which he should be possessed of at the Time of his Death, should not be transferred or altered by his Executor, during the Life of his Wife; and after her Death, he gave his said East India and South-Sea Stock to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, Kings or Queens of England, to be applied to the Use of the Sinking Fund, in such manner as should be directed by Act of Parliament: And after having bequeathed several other Legacies, he devised the Residue of his real and personal Estate to Thomas Jekyll, John Jekyll, Joseph Edward Jekyll, Richard Blacket Jekyll, Mary jekyll, and

Hannah Jekyll, the Children of John Jekyll, late of Neva England, deceased; and to Joseph Jekyll Grocer, the Son of Thomas Jekyll-, and to Nicolas Thomas Hester,

Tryphena Baldwyn, and Tryphofa Sanders, as Tenants in common; and gave a Power to his Executor to renew, from time to time, Leases of the Houses held of the Maf-terof the Rolls, with his Successoror Successors, Matters of the Rolls for the Time being.

That the East India Stock devised by Sir Joseph Jekyll as aforesaid, amounted to £.10,000 capital Stock; and the South-Sea Stock which helikewife deviled, amounted

to £.10,000 Capital.

That Mr. John Jekyll, late of New England, Father to Seven of the Legatees as before-mentioned, and Mr. Thomas Jekyll, the Father of Mr. Joseph Jekyll Grocer, deceased. One other of the said Legatees, were Nephews to Sir Joseph Jekyll, by the Father's Side; and Mr. Nicolas Robarts, One other of the said Legatees, is the Son of Mr. Robarts deceased, who married Mary Jekyll, Niece to the said Sir Joseph Jekyll, by the Father's Side; that

For his Maintenance; and on his making a Journey to England, purposely to pay his Respects to the said Sir Joseph, he received him very affectionately, and took him down to his Seat in; and the said Sir Joseph Jekyll fending him afterwards upon his Travels, he resided in France Two Years, where he had the Misfortune intirely to lose his Sight, having before loft the Sight of One Eye by the Small-pox; and during the Time he was in France Sir Joseph paid £. 686 on his Account, and gave Directions for a Person to be sent to fetch him from thene, and expressed great Concern at his Misfortune of losing his Sight, which Sir Joseph said rendered him unfit to enjoy what he intended for him.

That Mr. Joseph Jekyll, another Son of the said John Jekyll, was at the same Time in England, under the Care of Sir Joseph Jekyll, who was at the Expence of improving his Education, and took him to his own House, and made him his Companion: That the Second Son of the said John Jekyll succeeded his Father as Collector of the Customs in New England.

That Sir Joseph, about Two Months before his Death, in Discourse with Mr. Thomas Sand ford, expressed a high Regard for the Children of the said Mr. John Jekyll, and declared, That he intended to make a handsome Provision for them; and that, upon his Return to Town, he intended to (end Blacket Jekyll to New England, with a Cargo to begin Trade; and also expressed a great Regard for Mr. Robarts, mentioned before.

That Mr. John Jekyll of New England, at his Death, did not leave his Children £. 30 a-piece; and they had no Support but what they received from Sir Joseph Jekyll.

That upon Sir Joseph JekylTs Death, John Verney Esquire, deceased, who succeeded him in the Office of Matter of the Rolls, denied that the said Sir Joseph Jekyll had Power under the Act of Parliament, to let Leases of the Ground on which the said Houseswerc built, for any longer Term than One-and-twenty Years; and infilled that such Leases as were granted for 41 Years were absolutely void: Upon which Disputes, States of the same were drawn up by the said Mr. and the Legatees,

A Petition of the principal Consumers of Coals in the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, on . behalf of themselves, and several other Confymers, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That by the Bill, now depending in the House, to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act more effectually to prevent the Fraudsand Abuses committed in the Admeasurement of Coal? within the City and Liberty of minster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaftct1 adjoining thereto, and the several Parishes of Giles hi tie Fields, St. Maty leBat, and such Part of the Par

rith of St. Andrew Hollow, as lies in the county of .

Middlesexj and to indemnify Persons, who have acted under the said Act, in certain Cafes; the Petitioners will be obliged to pay an unnecessary Charge for the Metage of their Coals, in Cafes where there is no Occasion for any Admeasurement, there being noProbability of Fraud; and that, as the Petitioners apprehend, there are sufficient Powers in the before-mentioned Act, and several former Acts, to remedyany Frauds or Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, in case the same were duly put in Execution; and that the said Bill, should it pal's into a Law, will greatly inhance the Price of Coals; and will, instead of being of Service, be both oppressive and burdenlbme to the Petitioners, and the other Consumers within the said Limits: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Consumers of Coals in the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, on behalf of

themselves, and several other Consumers, was also presented to the House, and read; containing the same Allegations and Prayer as are in the last mentioned Petition.

Ordered, That this Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the several Owners of the Ships Andrezv Nicholson, Master; the Volunteer, John,

Mailer; and the U/ke Galley, junior. Ma-

iler; Three Ships fitted out last Year for the Greenland Seas, to catch W-hales and other Creatures, agreeable in every respect to the several Acts of Parliament made for that Purpose; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Three Ships were Turveyed by the proper Officers of his Majesty's Customs, and a proper Certificate given, to the Satisfaction of the Commissioners of his Majesty's Customs, and Bonds executed by Two of the Owners and Master of each Ship, for Treble the Penalty of the Bounty, likewise Oath made by them, that they were to proceed directly for those Seas, and on no other Account whatsoever: That thereupon a Licence was granted by the said Commissioners for that Purpose; and the said Three Ships were cleared 20

out at his Majesty's Custom-house in London the 27th of March 1746, and proceeded directly for the Greenland Seas, and arrived there the Firstof May following; and that each Master and Crew of the said Ships used their utmost Endeavours to kill Whales and other Creatures, as appears by the Oath of the said Mailers and Officers which were delivered in a Memorial to the Commissioners of his Majesty's Customs; but that on the 20th Day of the said Month of May, about Four of the Clock in the Morning, by a moll violent Storm of Wind, the said Three Ships were unavoidably and intirely loft, with Eight Whales killed, and that with much Difficulty the Crews of the said Ships saved their Lives; by which Misfortune the said Petitioners lost their whole Properties in the said Ships, which Hood them in upwards of Tea thousand Pounds, and not One Shilling inlured by any of the Proprietors: That by Two several Acts, made the Sixth and Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty, for the Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, a Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton was granted, in order to enable his Majesty's Subjects to fit out Ships for that Voyage; which laid Bounty is directed to be paid, at the Return of the Ships, by the Commissioners of his Majesty's Customs; but that, as this great Misfortune hath happened, the Petitioners are wholly deprived of the said Bounty, without the Aid and Assistance of this House; and that as this House hath beenpleased to encourage the Undertaking of carrying on this Fishery, which mull consequently be a very great Benefit to the Nation in general, in not only saving a great many Thousand Pounds paid to the Dutch every Year for Whale fins imported from Holland to England, but also the Means of training up a large

Number of good and able Seamen for his Majesty's Service; and as there was a great Probability of making a successful Voyage, if the said Ships had arrived safe in the River, the Petitioners then should not only have received the Bounty, but also saved their Property of Ships and Cargoes: And therefore, as the Proceedings of the Petitioners were just and honourable in carrying on this Whale Fishery, praying, That the House will take their unfortunate same into Consideration.and relieve them in such manner as to the House shall teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House wPl, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Bennett:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed (o the Amendments, made by this House, to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prevent the Return of such Rebels and Traitors concerned in the late Rebellion, as have been or shall be pardoned on Condition of Transportation; and also to hinder their going into the Enemies Country: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to revive, continue, and amend an Act, made in the 9th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for clearing, depthening, repairing, extending, maintaining, and improving, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth; and for depthening and making more navigable the several Rivers emptying themselves at the said Town; and also for preserving Ships wintering in the said Haven from Accidents by Pire; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue several Laws for prohibiting the Importation of Books reprinted abroad, and first composed or written, and printed, in Great Britain; for preventing Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Wears upon the River of Thames, Westward, and for ascertaining the Rates of Water-carriage upon the said River; and for better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty's Subjects to and from the Raft-Indies, and for the more effectual preventing all his Majesty's Subjects trading thither under foreign Commissions; and relating to Rice, to Frauds in the Customs, to the clandestine Running of Goods, and to Copper Ore of the Britishi Plantations; and for the free Importation of Cochineal and Indico; and for Punishment of Persons destroying Turnpikes or Locks, or other Works, erected by Authority of Parliament; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lord* have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act' for the Relief and Support of maimed and disabled Seamen, and the Widows and Children of such as shall be killed, flain, or drowned, in the Merchants Service, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to indemnify Persons who have omitted to register their Letters of Attorney, appointing them Agents for Prizes, within the Time limited by Law; and for allowing further Time for that Purpose; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Ease of Sheriffs with regard to the Return of Process, without any Amendment.

Clause A: " And whereas the InfranchiZing of Vassals of Subject Superiors, by causing them to become immediate Vassals of the Crown, is a Matter of publick " Benefit which ought to be encouraged: Be it therefore " Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That it shall and " may be lawful for any Person seised in, or possessed of, a tailzied Estate in Scotland, comprehending Lands-or " Superiorities of Vassals under or holding of him, to fell " to such Vassals, or any of them, the Superiorities over " their respective Lands, at such Prices as the Parties shall " agree for; and thereupon to resign such Lands, for " new Infeftment to be granted to such Buyer, of his " own Superiority, which shall be good and valid; any " Law, Charter, Tailzie, or other Act or Deed, ro the " contrary notwithstanding."

Clause B: " Provided always, That the Monies paid '* as the Price of such Superiority or Superiorities, being " Part of a tailzied Estate, shall be laid out and settled " to the same Uses, and with the same Limitations and " Restrictiorts, as such Superiority was settled before the " Sale thereof, as aforesaid; or applied for Payment of " the Debts, if any fych there be, of the Maker of the " Intail, or other Debts that arse effectual Burdens on the " tailzied Estate, not contracted by such Vendor himself; and, for that Purpose, the Monies shall be paid " into the Hands of Trustees, who shall be appointed " by the Vendor of such Superiority or Superiorities, and " the Purchaser or Purchasers thereof, respectively; and " such Trustees, and the Survivor and Survivors of them, 22

" and the Executors and Ad mini ft razors of such Survivor, " shall lay out the Monies arising from such Sale in the " Purchase of other Lands or Heretages, and settle, or " procure the same to be settled, as aforesaid; or such " Monies to be applied for Payment of Debts on the " tailzied Estate, in the Manner herein before directed.-'

Clause C: " And whereas it has been frequently practised in Scotland, to lett Lands to Tenants or Taclcfmen, referring and expressing (over and above the " certain Kents and Duties payable for the lame) Services used and wont, or Services indefinitely, or other " general Words of the like Nature, without specifying " or ascertaining the fame, which Practice is liable to be " abused, is productive of Disputes between Landlord " and Tenant, and subject to divers Inconveniences: Be " it therefore Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That, " from and after the First Day of July, in the Year of " our Lord 1747, no Tenant or Tacksman of any Lands " or Heretages in Scotland, by virtue of any Lease or " Tack which shall be made in Writing, or by verbal " Agreement, tacit Relocation, or otherwise, after the " said First Day of July, or by virtue of the Prorogation of any Lease or Tack made before the said First " Day of July, or any Assignee of any such Lease or " Tack, shall be obliged or liable to perform any Services whatsoever to his Heretor or Landlord, other than " such as shall be expresslyand particularly reserved and " specified, and the Number and Kinds thereof enumerated and ascertained in some written Lease or Tack, ct or by some Agreement made in Writing, and signed " by the Parties thereto, or feme Persons authorized by " them; any former Law or Usage to the contrary notwithstanding."

Clause D: " Provided always, That nothing herein " contained, relating to Services to be performed by any " Tenant or Tacksman after the said First Day of July, " shall extend, orbe construed to extend, to any Services " by Law or Custom due to Mills, or any Matter or Thing " relative thereto."

Clause E: " Provided, always, That nothing herein " contained, relating to Services to be performed by any " Tenant or Tacksman, after the said First Day of July, " shall extend, or be construed to extend, to the Stewartry " of Orkney and ZetlandT or any Lands or Heretages *5. lying within the lame."

The Ggnal Success, which, by the Blessing of God, has already attended my Fleet, has happily dii'appointed Tome very pernicious Projects of our Enemies, and given a considerable Blow to their Naval Strength, as well as to their Commerce, which will be the most probable Means of reducing them to Reason: This is the great Object which I have at Heart, the foie View of all my Measures being to put an End to the Calamities of War by a safe and honourable Peace.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I mud acknowlege in a particular manner the Zeal and Application with which you have raised the necessary Supplies for the Service of the current Year: And your Readiness in making good the Deficiency of the Civil Lid Funds, arising from the unavoidable Consequences of War, is a fresh Instance of that Regard and Affection which I have always ex| erienced from you: To be able to effectuate all this immediately after the Suppressing of an unnatural and expensive Rebellion, and under the Burdens of War, must let the Strength and Credit of the Nation in the highest Light, and secure to the Crown of Great Britain that Weight and Respect, both with its Friends and Enemies, which justly belong to it.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

After the Examples 6f Justice which have been found necessary, 1 have with Pleasure taken the very first Opportunity of doing what is more agreeable to my own Inclination, the passing an Act of Grace: The good EftcCt I promise myfelt from hence, is to heal in some measure those Wounds which have been made, and re-establish the Quiet of the Kingdom; since, by this Act, the Generality of those, who have been deluded from their Duty, will find themselves restored to Security, and to the Protection of those Laws which they had endeavoured to subvert: A just Sense of this early Mercy, will, I hope, induce them to make fuel) Returns of Loyalty and Gratitude as so strong an Obligation requires.

As this Parliament would necessarily determine in a short time, and as nothing will givefo much Weight and Credit to our Affairs abroad in the present Conjundure as to shew the Dependence 1 have upon the Affect ions of my People, 1 have judged it expedient lj>ecdi!y t* call a new Parliament i but 1 should think mylcli inexcusable,

4°9

if I parted with this without publickly returning you my Thanks for the ma^y eminent Instances you have given me of your inviolable Fidelity and Attachment to my Person and Government, and your unlhaken Adherence to the true Interestof your Country, and the Protestant Succession in my Family: By the divine Blessing, and your vigorous Assistance, I have been enabled to crulh and defeat the moil audacious Attempt that has ever been made to overturn the present Establishment, and at the same time to furnish that Support to our ancient and natural Allies which has already dilappointed some of the most dangerous V iews of Ambition with which our Enemies began the War: Such extraordinary Merit, as it will always be gratefully remembered by me, must endear the Memory of this Parliament to Posterity: From such Demonstrations of the Loyalty and Affection of my faithful Subjects, I do with the utmost Satisfaction repose myself upon them; and do not in the least doubt of receiving new Proofs of the same good Disposition in the Choice of their Representatives.

I have nothing so much at Heart as the Preservation of the Civil and Religious Rights of my People, and the Maintenance of the true Greatness and Prosperity of this Nation: From thel'e Principles I will never deviate; and in these Principles every true Briton will concur: Let this appear by your Conduct in the present Conjuncture; and let nofalfe Arts or Misrepresentations take place to interrupt or weaken that Confidence and Harmony between me and my People, which have been, and ever will be, productive of such happy Effects.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command, said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued until Thursday the Ninth Day of July next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued until Thursday die Ninth Day of July next.

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament, which we summoned to meet at Westminster, on the Thirteenth

Day of August lad, (lands prorogued to the Eighth

Day of this instant October-, we, by the Advice of our Privy-Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Eighth Day of this indant October, to the Tenth

Day of November next; and we have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Writ Patent, under our Great Seal, for proroguing the same accord-

4i5

ingly: And we do further hereby declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Tenth Day of November, be held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give their Attendance accordingly, at We, on the said Tenth Day of November next.

John Willes Esquire, Burgess for the Borough of Banbury, in the County of Oxon, addressing himself likewise to the Clerk (who, danding up, pointed to him, and then lat down) spake to the following Effect; viz.

I rife up to do myself the Honour of joining in this Motion, which, considering how well it has beenfpoken to already, I should have declined doing; but the very great Regard and Reverence I have for the Honourable Gentleman who has been proposed, will not differ me to be silent.

I am very glad to find, that all Persons are agreed to make choice of a Speaker, for this Parliament, who has already executed that Office so much to his own Honour, and the Satisfaction of the Nation; and there cannot be a more convincing Proof of his extraordinary Abilities, than that there seems to be no other Competition among us, but who shall be most forward to recommend him.

'Tis certainly a very great Pleasure to a generous Mind to meet with univerlal Applause and Approbation; but how solid a Satisfaction mud it be to that Honourable Gentleman, to be conscious to himself, that he has deserved it? That'tis not That Praise which mean-spirited Men sometimes give to Power, but That Reward which good Men always pay to Merit? That 'tis a Tribute judly due to that Candour and Impartiality which he has shewn to all Persons upon all Occasions

It would be necdlels for me to mention the great Talents necessary for this high Office, and how well the Hor nourable Gentleman is qualified for it: Of this, the greated Part of this House have been Witnesses, no Gentleman in the Nation can possibly be ignorant.

The great Difficulty in this'Question is not, Whether Mr. Onslow shall be chosen Speaker? bnt. Whether he will do this House the Honour to accept of it ? He has spent many Years, undergone great Fatigues, already it) the Service of the Publick; and might very well be allowed to take Advantage of that Excuse which even a Roman Writer thought l'ufficient: " The former Part of " ourLives we ought to give to our Country, the latter " to ourselves." Notwithstanding this, 1 hope the Honourable Gentleman will forgive me, if I edeem his own Ease and Happiness, as he himself has always done, of small Value, when compared to the general Good, and join with the united Voice of this House in giving my Vote for Mr. Onslow.

Your Majesty's dutiful Subjects, the Commons of this your Realm, in Parliament assembled, have, in pursuance of your Majesty's Direction, and of their ancient Right, elected One of their Members, to be their Speaker for this Parliament: And their Choice, Sir, having once more fallen upon me for this high and important Trud, they how present me to your Majesty, for your Judgment upon

their Election. Needled will it be in me, Sir, to mention on this Occasion, with regard to myself, what I fear can*-not but be too well known to your Majesty: It therefore bed becomes me with Silence and SubmiflJon to resign myself to your Royal Determination.

Then the L'rd Chancellor, after receiving Directions from his Majesty, said,

Mr. Onslow,

You have appealed to the King's own Experience and Knowlege for the Decision of the weighty Affair now under his Consideration; and it is from thence his Majesty has formed his Judgment.

After having had such dear Demondration of your Abilities, Zeal, and Application in the Service of himself and of your Country in Three successive Parliaments, his Majesty commands me to let you know', That he in-, tirely approves the Choice which his faithful'Commons have made, and allows and confirms you be their Speaker'.

Then Mr. Speaker said.

Since your Majesty has been pleased to confirm the Choice your Commons have made of me to be theif Speaker, it is my Duty, Sir, with all Humility, to conform myself to their Appointment, and your Royal Approbation of it, begging your Majesty's favourable Acceptance of my humbled Acknowdegements for this fresh Indance of your Majesty s Grace towards myself: and that your Majesty will vouchsafe to pardon my Failings and Infirmities, at lead not to impute them in any-wile to your faithful Commons. And that your Commons in Parliament, Sir, may be the better enabled to discharge their Duty to your Majesty and their Country, I do, in their Name, and on their behalf, by humble Petition to your Majesty, lay Claim to all their ancient Rights and Privileges, particularly that they, their Servants, and Estates, may be free from Arreds, and all other Molestation; that they may enjoy Freedom of Speech in their Debates, ard have Liberty of Access to your Royal Person when Occasion shall require it; and that all their Proceedings may receive from your Majesty the most favourable Interpretation.

Then the Lord Chancellor, after receiving further Directions from his Majesty, said,

Mr. Speaker,

The King has the utmod Confidence in the Duty and Affection of this House of Commons to his Person and Government, and a high Opinion of that Prudence and Temper which they will ule in all their Proceedings; and his Majesty does most readily grant and allow to them all their Privileges in as full and ample Manner as they have at any time heretofore been granted or allowed by his Majesty, or any of his Royal Predecessors.

There is one Suit, Sir, which you have 'made on your own Behalf: His Majesty has received the sured Pledge, that no Person in your Station ever dood less in need of it than yourself; but that you may want no Support in sustaining the Burthen of that important Trud which is repefed in you, his Majesty has directed me to assure you. That he will put the most "favourable Condruftion both on your Words and Actions.

And now I must beg Gentlemen to give me Leave once more to return my humble Thanks to the House; lor this great Honour they have again conferred upon me; and to allure Gentlemen of my Continuance of that Fidelity in their Service, which I am persuaded they believed I had ever practised before, or they would not have promoted me again to this important Trust. I can truly fav. That your Approbation of tny Service is with me the bell Reward I can have for it: Let me add this humble Request to it, that Gentlemen will be pleased to afford me those Allowances of Candour and Tenderness, which arc l'ometimes due to an old and faithful Servant, even in his Failings. After having said this for myl'clf, I am bound to exhort Gentlemen for their own Sakes, as well as for that of the Publick, to keep ftrtdfly to the Rules and Orders of the House, so wifely adapted by our Ancestors to the carrying on of Buftnefswith all necessary Deliberation, and yet with proper Dispatch; to prevent personal Altercations, and all other Indecorum, to which large Assemblies arc but too liable; and to preserve, in general, that Gravity and Dignity in our Proceedings and Deport ment here, which so much becomethe great Council of a Nation, and the high Office of Legislature: And that all this may be the better done, 1 am obliged also not only to recommend, but carncftly to cal I upon Gentlemen to rclblve to meet early in a Morning for the Bufi-nd's of the House: Tue Neglect of that must produce an Evil which will much affl-ft the Credit of our Proceedings, I mean an Over-haste in some Things, and too great Delay in others: If that has happened of late, I doubt not but Gentlemen will think it their Duty to reform this bad Praff ice; and the rather, because it may be leen in those printed Journals which are now in the Hands of many, and which, I hope, for various Re^fons, will be often and well perused, how very different the Attendance and Diligence of their Ancestors were here: They thought they were sent hither to do and to dispatch, as soon as they could, the great Business of their Country in Parliament; and that (to mention an Expression elsewhere used) the Top of an English Gentleman's Ambition was to become'an able Parliament-man, and to return to his Country with the Figure and Reputation which will always attend that useful and eminent Character.

Mr. Speaker rep irted to the House, That, when the House did attend his Majesty upon last in the

House of Peers, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both lloufesof Parliament j of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent M iftakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House) and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

As One of my principal Views in calling this Parliament was, that 1 might receive the most clear and certain Information of the Scnfc of my People on the present Pollute of Affairs, 1 was desirous to meet you as early as your own Convenience, as well as that of the Publick, would admit.

By the Advice of my Parliament I entered into the War against Spain, in order to vindicate and secure the

Trade and Commerce of my Subjects: By their Advice also, and in Conformity to my Engagements, 1 undertook the Support of the Kmprels Queen of , and

of the just Eights of the House of In Resent-

ment for this Conduct, so necessary for the Interests of my own Kingdoms, and of the ancient Allies of my Crown, France not only declared War against Me, but fomented and supported an unnatural Rebellion within this Kingdom. *ln carrying on this just and necessary War, I have found the most chearful and vigorous Support from my Parliament: And though the Success has not been answerable to our Wilhcs and just Expectations in the Low Countries, yet it must be allowed, to the Honour of this Nation, that no Part of the Misfortunes can be imputed to us.

The (ignal Successes which it has pleased God to grant us at Sea, have made the Enemy feel the Weight of our' naval Strength, to their great Loss, and the real and solid Advantage of this Nation: This has appeared most remarkably in the Operations of my Fleet this last Year, which have tended no less to the Honour of the Flag, than to the Reduction of the maritime Force and Commerce of France. The Government of the United Provinces has once more resumed that Conliftency which will give great Strength to the common Cause, cement more firmly the Friendship between this Kingdom and that Republick, and be a lading Security to our inseperable Interests. One great Effect of this happy Alteration' in Holland has already appeared, in the vigorous Declaration lately made by the States General to the Court of France, and the Orders given by them for committing Hostilities every where against the French King and his Subjects.

Some Overtures for a general Pacification have lately been made to me on the Part of France; and though iome of the 1'erms proposed were such as could not be approved, yet as I have had no other Aim, but to bring about a safe and honourable Peace, I have shewn the utmost Inclination to facilitate it, in Conjunction with- my Allies , and a Congress is actually agreed to be held at Aix./a Chape lie, whither the several Ministers will soon repair: I hope all the Powers concerned will bring with them the same Dispositions to effectuate this great Work, on just and reasonable Conditions, which 1 sincerely have.

In this Situation I am confident you will agree in Opinion with me, that it is necessary to be vigilant and attentive to every Event} and that there can be no Reason

YOX. 2£.

421

to expect a good Peace, but by being timely prepared to carry on a vigorous and effectual War. I therefore rely on your hearty and powerful Support, to enable me to ptefecute the War, in case the Obstinacy of our Enemies, in not agreeing to just and reasonable Terms of Accommodation, should render it unavoidable. For this Purpose I am now actually concerting the necessary Measures with my Allies, whose Interests I am determined to adhere to and support. Let us be in Readiness, in case the Negotiations should fail of the desired Effect, to convince our Enemies how much they are mistaken, if they vainly imagine, that Great Britain and her Allies, will submit to receive the Law from any Power whatsoever; and demonstrate to the World, that we will decline no Difficulty or Hazard for the Preservation of the common Liberty, and our own Independency, and essential Interests.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Necessity of adequate Supplies appears from what has been already mentioned. The proper Kftimates for the Services of the ensuing Year shall be laid before you,) and I desire you to grant me such Supplies, as your own Security and lifting Welfare, and the present critical and important Situation of Affairs, require. You may depend on their being applied only to the Purposes for which they shall be given; and if, by the falling out of Events, any Saving can be made, it shall be duly accounted for.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

If any farther Provisions shall be found expedient to render more effectual the good Laws lately made for the Security of the present Establishment, extinguishing the Spirit of Rebellion, and for the better civilizing, improving, and reducing into Order, any Part of the united Kingdom, I depend on your known Affection to me, and to your Country, seriously and early to set about to good a Work. I will only add. That there never was a Conjuncture in which Unanimity, Firmness, and Dispatch, were snore necessary for the Safety, Honour, and true Interest of Great Britain,

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House, for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to congratulate his Majesty on the signal Success of his Arms at Sea, which not only redounds so much to the Honour of the British Nation, but, by reducing the maritime Force of France, mani-fcllly tends to the Security of his Majesty's Government, and the Prosperity and Trade of these Kingdoms; to express our Satisfaction upon the happy Settlement of the Government of the United Provinces, in which a Prince, so nearly allied to his Majesty, has so great a Share; not doubting but the good Effects of that Settlement will be a thorough Union of Counsels between his Majesty and the Republick, especially as the vigorous Declaration, lately made by the States General to the Court of France, gives us the strongest Presumption, that in all Measures, whether of Peace or War, which shall be deemed for the Honour, Interest, and Security of these Kingdoms and that Republick, they will co-operate zealously and firmly with us; to express our Sense of his Majesty's paternal Care for the Good of his Subjects, in the sincere Disposition he has shewn for a general Pacification, by hearkening to the Overtures, lately made for that Purpose, and endeavouring, on his Part, to bring about a speedy, safe, and honourable Condufion, to this burthensome andex-pensive, though just and necessary, War: But if, contrary to our Withes and Expectations, the Enemies of Great Britain, by insisting on unreasonable and inadmissible Terms, make the Continuance of the War unavoidable, to assure his Majesty, that we will support him to the utmost: And, in order to convince our Enemies of this our stedfast Resolution, we will immediately ' grant such Supplies, as may, in Conjunction with his Allies, enable his Majesty to carry bn the War with Vigour, maintain the Honour and Dignity of the Cfown of Great

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne.

With Hearts full of the Cheered Joy wc congratulate your Majesty on the great and important Succelfes which it has pleased Almighty God to bellow on your Majesty's Arms at Sea, and which not only redound highly to the Honour of the British Nation, but, by reducing the maritime Force of France, manifestly tend to the Security of your Majesty's Government, and the Prolperity and Trade of these Kingdoms.

We beg Leave to express to your Majesty the great and just Satisfaction we have received from the happy Settlement of the Government of the United Provinces, in which a Pr ince, so nearly allied to your Majesty, has so great a Share; nor can we doubt, but that the good Effed resulting from that Settlement will be a thorough Union of Counsels between your Majesty and the Repub-lick; more especially as the vigorous Declaration, lately made by the States General to the Court of France, gives us the strongest Prelu nipt ion, that in all Measures, whether of Peace or War, which Hull be deemed for the Honour, interest, and Security of these Kingdoms, and that Uepub-lick, they will co-operate zealously and firmly with us.

With the deepest Sense of Gratitude we acknowlege your Majesty's paternal Care for the Welfare of your Sub-jeds, in the sincere Diposition your Majesty has shewn lor a general Pacification, by hearkening to the Overtures lately made for that Purpose, and endeavouring, on your Majesty's Part, to bring about a speedy, safe, and honourable Condition, to this burthensome and expen-five, though just and necessary, War.

A Petition of Arthur Anfty the younger, late Deputy-Bailiff of the Borough of Milbo in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; let-ring forth, That there are Nine capital Bailiwicks within the said Borough; and that, by ancient and immemorial Usage, Two of the capital Bailiffs of the said Bailiwicks ought, in each Year, according to a certain and known Rotation, as often as it comes to their Turn, at the Court -I eet held in the said Borough, at Michaelmas in every Year, severally to nominate and appoint a Deputy, to execute the said Office for them respectively, for the Year ensuing; which Deputy-Bailiffs, or One of them (in case Voi. *$.

there be but One appointed for that Year, or upon the Death or in the Absence of the other) is or are the Returning Officer or Officers of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, for the Time being; and that no other Person or Persons, except such Deputy or Deputies so nominated, have, according to the Usage and Custom of the said Borough, any Right to preside at the Election, or make a Return of Burgesses to lerve in Parliament for the said Borough: That the Petitioner was, at the Court-Leet held at Michaelmas 1746, appointed by One of the capital Bailiffs, whose Turn it was to nominate for the Year ensuing, to be his Deputy, and was accordingly, at the said Court-Leet, duly l'worn into the said Office, and had the Ensigns of his Office delivered to him; and that no other Deputy-Bailiff was, by any of the said capital Bailiffs, nominated or appointed for the said Year, besides the Petitioner: That an Election for Burgesses to lerve in this present Parliament for the said Borough was held on the 29th Day of June lad; and that, notwithstanding the Petitioner was the only legal Returning Officer at the said Election, one William Bishop senior, under a Pretence of his being One of the capital Bailiffs for that Year, contrary to the established Usage of the said Borough, took upon himself to act as Returning Officer at the said Election, and procured the Precept for making such Election from Thomas Coles Esquire, High-Sheriff of the said County, to be delivered him by Richard Ring the Under-Sheriff; and that the said Wm. Bishop absolutely refused to deliver such Precept to the Petitioner, notwithstanding the Petitioner often demanded the lame; and that the said William Bishop proceeded to act as Returning Officer at the said Election, and impowered some Persons to take a Poll there, and hath made a Return to the said Thomas Coles, High-Sheriff of the said County, of Michael Harvey and Jeffery French Esquires, to serve in this present Parliament, as Burgesses for the said Borough, although the said William Bishop had no Right or Authority to act in the said Election; That the Petitioner, who legally presided at the said Election, caused a Poll to be taken at the lame, of all the legal Voters of the said Borough, and returned lycott and Charles Churchill Esquires, who were duly elected to serve in this present Parliament, as Burgesses for the said Borough; but that the said Sheriff has annexed to his Writ the said Return made by the said William Bishop, of Michael Harvey and Jeffery French Esquires, as well as the Petitioner's Return of Thomas Medlycott and Charles Churchill Esquires; and alleging that the Return of the said William Bishop, is in Prejudice of the Petitioner's undoubted Right: And therefore praying the House, to take the same of the Petitioner into Consideration; and to do therein as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the Merits of the said Return be heard at the Bar of this House upon Tuesday the First Day of December next.

Anfiver to Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, upon Wed-Addrefr, nesday last, attended his Majesty with their Address: To which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

The early Marks of Trust and Confidence, which you repose in me by this Address, give me the greatest Satisfaction.

You may be allured, that I have nothing more at Heart than to put, as soon as possible, such an End to the present Troubles as may be confident with the Good of my People, the Security of my Allies, and the Honour and true Interests of my Kingdoms.

That, at the last general Election, Sir Edward Turner Baronet, William Scott, William Sloper, and Lafcells Metcalfe, Esquires, offered themselves as Candidates to represent the said Borough in this Parliament; and that the Petitioners voted for the said Sir Edward Turner and William Scott, who were duly elected by a Majority of legal Votes, and who only ought to have been returned as Burgesses for the said Borough: That several Persons were procured to vote for the said William Sloper and Lafcells Metcalfe by illegal and unwarrantable Practices; and that the Portreeve

and returning Officer, did admit several to poll at the said Election, without administering the Oath to them, which is directed to be taken by the Statute of the 2d of his present Majesty (though several of the Electors, that had taken such Oath, required and demanded that the same should be administered to them) and admitted several other Persons to poll, who had no Right to vote at the said Election; and, being intimidated by the Threats and Menaces of the said William Sloper, was induced thereby, and in pursuance of an illegal and unwarrantable Agreement of the said Four Candidates, to make a Double Return; whereby the Election duly made by the Petitioners, and such others who voted for the said Sir Edward Turner and William Scott is totally defeated, and rendered void, and the Petitioners at present deprived of being efle&ually represented in this Parliament: And Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard, at the Bar of this House, at the same time that the Matter of the Petition of Lafcells Metcalfe Esquire and William Sloper Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Double Return for the said Borough, and of the said Double Return, is appointed to be heard.
