Vol. 2$.

of Surrey, Esquire, being offered to be pfefented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives his Consent, that the House may do therein as they mall think fit:: 1

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; set-' ting forth, That King Charles the Second, by his Indenture bearing Date the 23d Day of February, in the 24th Year of his Reign, made between his said Majesty, of the.' One Part; and the Right Honourable George Viscount Grdndifan, Hemy Howard, of Little Walden, in the County of Essex, Esquire, and Edward Villiers, of Richmond, in the County of Surrey, Esquire, of the other Part; did demile, grant, and to Farm-lett, unto the said George Viscount Grandison, Henry Howard, and Edward Villiers, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, all that his Manor of Wookeing, in the County of Surtey, with all* its Rights, Members, and Appurtenances, and also divers other Manors, Hundreds, Advowsons, Lands, Tenements, Liberties, Privileges, Rents, Fines, and Hereditaments, in the said Indenture particularly mentioned and defctibed,: to bold to the said George Viscount Grandison, Henry Howard, and Edward Villiers, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, from the Feast Day of St. Michael the Archangel next ensuing the Date of the said Indenture, for the Terra of One thousand Years, fully to be complete and ended, without any Rent, or any other Thing, to be paid, rendered, or done, for the fame, to the (hid King, his Heirs or Successors: and that the several Manors, Hundreds, Advowsons, Lands, Tenements, Rents, Hereditaments, and Premises, in the said Indenture granted and demiled for the said Term of One thousand Years, are, by several mesne Alignments, and other Assurances in the Law, come unto and vested in the Petitioner, for the Residue of the said Term; and that there are above Nine hundred Years to come, and unexpired, of the said Term; and that, in regard there is no Rent or Service reserved or made payable upon the Grant or Demifetnade by the said Indenture, the Reversion expectant on the Determination of the (laid Term is consequently of no real Value or Consideration; but that foraftnuch as the Reversion and Inheritance in Fee-simple, expectant on the said Term, doth belong to his Majesty, in Right of his Crown, the said Abel Walter has thereupon made his most humble Suit to his Majesty, that he would be graciously pleased to give Leave, that a Bill may be brought into Parliament to enable his Majesty to grant the Inheritance of all and every the said Manors, Hundreds, Advowsons, Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, and Pre-miles, granted and demised, by the said recited Indenture, to the Petitioner, in Fee-simple; and that his Majesty hath been graciously pleased to signify his Consent thereto: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in for the Purpose aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Lieu-' tenant-General Oglethorpe and Mr. Taajfe do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

African A Petition of the Royal African Company of England Company, jjgjjg offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of -the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; letting forth, That the Trade to Africa is known and acknowledged to be highly beneficial to this Nation, as well on account of the many valuable Commodities which it naturally produces, as of the Supply of Negro Servants, fealooed to fudi Climates, with which it yearly fumilhes the British Colonies and Plantations in America; and that therefore former Parliaments have judged it necessary that the Forts and Settlements belonging to the Petitioners in Africa [hould be kept up, for the Protection and Benefit of all his Majesty's Subjects trading to , or interested in the Preservation of the same; and that the Petitioners having been at great Expence in erecting, enlarging, and maintaining, the said Forts and Settlements, former Parliament? have likewise granted sundry Sums of Money for better enabling the Petitioners to maintain and keep their said Forts and Settlements; but that the Petitioners have found by Experience, that such Aids have not proved sufficient for that Service; and that, according to the belt Information the Petitioners can procure, our most formidable Rivals in this beneficial Trade have granted such Privileges and Immunities, and established such large Funds, for the Support of their Forts and Settlements in Africa, and by that means have acquired such Influence and Power with the Natives, and such Advantages over the Petitioners, that it is become impracticable for the Petitioners to support and maintain their said Forts and Settlements, for the Protection and Benefit of all his Majesty's Subjects trading to, and interested in the Preservation of the Trade to, , without further Aid and Encouragement from Parliament: And therefore, in Consideration of the Premises, praying. That the House will be pleased to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and to enable them to keep up and maintain the said Forts and Settlements, for the Protection of all his Majesty's Subjects trading to the Coast of Africa; or to grant the Petitioners l'uch other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Customs in any Port of this Kingdom shall not have sufficient Money in his Hands, arising by the said additional Duty, to satisfy and pay such Reward as is or shall be due to any Exporter of British-ma.dc Sail-cloth or Sails, that then such Collector shall give to the Person intitled to such Reward, a Certificate, attested by the Comptroller, of what is due to such Person for such British Sailcloth or Sails so exported, certifying to the Commissioners of the Customs at London or Edinburgh respectively, that he hath not Money in his Hands, on the Branch aforesaid, sufficient to pay the same; and that the Amount of the Duty, on foreign-made Sail-cloth imported into England greatly exceeds the Amount of the Reward allowed on the Exportation of such Sailcloth as is manufactured there; and th&t very little or no foreign-made Sail-cloth or Sails is or are at this time imported into Scotland, for which Reason there is not any Fund in that Kingdom at present to pay the Reward which the Legislature intended to allow on the Exportation of British Sail-cloth from Scotland, as well as from England; and that although the Sail-cloth Manufacture in Scotland is now very considerable, and employs great Numbers of Poor, yet the same must inevitably decline, unlefe the Commissioners of the Customs at London are authorized to pay the same Reward to the Exporters in Scotland, as they are impowered to do by the last-recited Act with respect to the like Exportations from the Outports of England: And therefore pfaying the House to cake the Premises into Consideration; Weymouth A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, Bur-

WbaHa, tic. and Commonalty, of the Borough and Town of

Weymouth and Melcombe Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, Time out of mind, have received certain Duties called Petty Customs, or Wharfage, upon the Importation and Exportation of all Goods and Merchandizes into, and out of, the Harbour of Weymouth and Melcombe Regis aforesaid; and also certain other Duties there called Harbour Dues and Ballast Duty, which have been constantly under the Management of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and principal Burgesses, of the said Borough and Town, and by them applied towards repairing the Wharfs, and other publick Buildings and Works there; and that by the Variation of Prices of many Species of Goods at different Periods of Time, or other Accidents, the Petitioners apprehend there is a great Disproportion in the Duties; and that on some Species of Goods they are too high, or far above the Proportion of others; and that, of late Years, many Persons have refused to pay the said Duties; and that the Petitioners, in order to support their Right to the fame, have brought several Action^ and obtained Verdicts for Damages; but that,

- Vol. 25.

527

notwithstanding such their Right was thereby established the great Expence they were put to in carrying on such Suits hath greatly lessened that Fund; and the Wharfs, and other publick Buildings and Works, are in a ruinous Condition, and must be intirely destroyed, if not timely, prevented; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, jf the Duties were ascertained in better Proportion, and the Petitioners had Power to compel the Payment thereof in a summary Way, it would be sufficient to keep in Repair for the future what remains of their Wharfs, and other publick Buildings and Works; but that the Petitioners are advised That cannot be effected without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give Leave that a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes aforesaid; or to give such other Relief as to the House shall seem just.

A Petition of the principal Heretors and Freeholders of the Shire of Argyll, on behalf of themselves, and the other Heretors ana Freeholders of the said Shire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in order to the equal Approportioning of the Land Tax, and the Railing and Levying of the same the more effectually within that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, certain Quotas have Time immemorial been fixed and established both by Laws and Acts of Parliament, and constant uninterrupted Custom, to be paid out of each County; and, whether the Subsidy was higher or lower, the established Proportion has always been observed j and, to the End that the Quota put upon each Shire may be raised with Equality out of each Heretor's Lands, according to the Value of the same, Commissioners have, from tiiqe to time, been appointed before the Union, l'ome-times by the Privy-Council of Scotland, in consequence of a Remit from the Parliament, and in other Instances directly by the Parliament itself, in order, from proper Evidence, to establish a certain Value upon the Lands, which is called a Valuation, to be a Rule by which the Land Tax, and other public Burdens, were severally to be raised and levied from the same; and that by this Method all arbitrary Proceedings in the Commissioners, in making the Land Tax effectual, have in a great measure been prevented: That the Valuations within the several Shires serve not only for a Rule of levying and raising the Cess with Equality, but also are a Measure for determining the Qualification of a Freeholder to vote in an Election of a Member to serve in Parliament, as appears by the 21 ft Act, 3d Parliament, Charles arl. Anno 1681; and that, further, the several Valuations serve as a Rule for determining the Extent of Casualties payable to the Crown, as also to other Superiors; and is become still more necessary since the late Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for taking away the Tenure of Ward-holding in Scotland, and for converting the same to Blanch and Feu Holdings; and for regulating the Casualty of Nonentry in certain Cafes, iSc. which passed into a Law in the last Session of the lad Parliament, whereby, inter , it is flatuted, in order to ascertain the Quantum of the Nonentry Duty, That, from and after the 25th Day of March 1748, in all Services upon the Brieve of Mortanceftry of any Heir or Heirs in the Lands and Heritages therein referred to, the Retour, over and above the setting forth

A Petition of the charitable Corporation for Relief of Charitable industrious Poor, by assisting them with small Sums, upon Corporation. Pledges, at legal Interest, in General Court assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by virtue of a Chaiter from her late Majesty Queen Anne, and of Three Royal Licences since granted by his late and his present Majesty, the Petitioners were authorized to raise a Fund of £.600,000 for the Purpose of lending Money upon Pledges; and that the Petitioners, in consequence thereof, having actually raised several Hundred thousand Pounds, by the way of Shares of Five Pounds each, they carried on for several Years the said Business; and always supplied Persons, who make Pledges to them, at a moderate Rate; and carefully preserved such Pledges, and faithfully restored them, or the Surplusses due on them, to the Borrowers, without Imposition; until, by a most infamous Confederacy between some of their Directors and Servants, the Petitioners were defrauded of near their whole Capital; but that, in regard those Frauds were committed by particular Persons, the Dealings of the Corporation with Borrowers were no-ways impeached thereby, as they had been always carried on with strict Justice and Fidelity towards them: And the Court of Committee of the said Corporation, in Conjunction with many of the most considerable Proprietors, having deliberately considered of Means for raising a new Fund, whereby to pursue the Purposes of their Charter, find it wholly impracticable so to do, by reason that near Thirty thousand of the Corporation Shares are veiled in Trustees, Executors, Administrators, Infants, and Lenders, before the nth of October 1731; and several Thousand other Shares belong to Proprietors known to be dead, who have either no legal Representatives, or such as will not vest themselves with their Shares; and that several Hundred more Shares stand in the Names of Persons who are not known, nor do appear, but are supposed to be dead; all which Executors, Trustees, or Mortgagees (according to the Opinion of the most eminent Counsel) would not be j unified, if they obeyed a Call for the Payment of Money; which is of itself a Consideration sufficient to repel every Attempt to re-establish the Corporation without the Assistance of the Legislature; and that the Petitioners, labouring under this Difficulty, and being advised there is no Course at Law whereby to extricate themselves, mud inevitably fink, unless this House will be pleated to interpose so far towards their Relief, as to give all Proprietors in this Corporation, and their legal Representatives, their Option either to conform with such a Call as to a General Court shall seem expedient, or take their full distributi/e

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. John Butler was examined: Who said, That he is well acquainted with the Borough of and

knows moit of the Inhabitants: That great Numbers of Tradesmen in the said Borough are, from the Nature of their respective Trades, under a Necessityof giving Credit to their Customers for small Sums, particularly to Journeymen and Labourers, who receive their Wages Weekly; and 'tisvery usual for such Persons to refute to pay the Debts they have so contracted; being satisfied, that the Expence the Creditor must incur, in Purluitof his Demands, will be a sufficient Discouragement to him not to commence a Suit in the Borough, or Marshal's Court, where the Costs, before he can proceed to Judgment, amounts to about £. 4. for.; and, for Judgment; by way of Default, to £. 3. for.

Mr. John Symonds, Salesman and Taylor, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Butleras to the Necessity which Tradesmen arc under of giving Credit to the poor Inhabitants: And added, That himlcit has been a great Sufferer by it, his Debtors fettinghim at Defiance: and that he is obliged frequently to (it down with the Loss of jo or zo Shillings, there being no Method ot recovering it

at a less Expence than Four or Five Pounds.

Mr. George Pollard, D.Hiller, confirmed the Evidence of the foregoing Witnesses in every Particular.

Mr. IVilllm Steward, being examined, laid, The Sixpence of a Suit in the Borough or Marshal's Court, for a small Debt, amounts to Four or Five Pounds, though such Debt may be recovered in the City of London tot Five Shillings.

And all the Witnesses agreed. That a more easy and (peedy Method for Tradesmen to recover their just Debts at a small Expence, would tend to the promoting Industry and useful Credit, and be equally advantageous to the Debtor and Creditor.

And,

Mr. Crumpe, being examined, said. That the Rents of the settled Estate, in the Year 1725, being not fuiiicient to discharge the Annuities then claimed, the Company again took up Money upon their Seal, and continued lb to do till about Michaelmas 1745; during which Period the Company borrowed Money to the Amount of £. 84,700; and the Money so borrowed was, from time to time, for the most part, applied to pay the Annuitants and their other Charities.

That the Company reduced the Rate of their Annuities at several Periods from 30 to 25, to 20, and even to £' 5-

notwithstanding which, at Michaelmas 1745, they were indebted, by Bonds under their Seal, to the Amount of £.84,700, and Interest thereon to Michaelmas 1747, amounting to £.7,850 15 8, which makes the Principal and Interest, due on Bond at Michaelmas 1747, amount to the Sum of £.92,550 15 8; and that there is due, and in Arrear, to the Annuitants, at Michaelmas 1747, the Sum of £.9,628 2 6; and that the Money Legacies given by lundry Benefadlors, not inverted in Land, amount to £.21,099. 5 9; and the Arrears of such Charitities, at Michaelmas 1747, amounted to £. 1,434 13 4; that the Ample Contrail Debts of the said Company, on the 5th November 1745, amounted

And Mr. Crumpe, being further examined, said, That' it did not appear to him, by any of the Company's Books,* that the Account of Money Donations had been kept separate from the other Calli of the said Company; from whence he inferred, that the same had b^en exhausted in the Time of the civil Wars, and after the Fire of London: That he had carefully examined the Books, in order to collect the Particulars of the several Money Legacies which had been given either in Trull to purchase Land, or to pay and maintain the several Charities, and which had not been laid out in any Purchase; which Particular* was by him produced, and is annexed in the Appendix! And the Examinant further said. That, although tire Company had not inverted the several Donations in the Purchase of Lands, yet they bad paid and supported the fame, from time to time, till the Company llopt Payment in November 1745, except to some few Persons, who neglected to demand the lame.

And, in order to prove the annual Account of the Annuities the Company is liable to pay, and what they have to pay it with,

Mr. Crumpe was further examined, and produced Two Books, the First containing, as he informed your Committee, the Account of the Annuities payable at present; and the other an Account of the Subscribers for Annuities in Expectancy:

By the First of which Books it appears. That the present Annuities amount to £. 7,534; and the Reason the Sum varies from the Sum mentioned in the Petition, is the Death of Two Widows, since the Petition passed under the Company's Seal:

And by the other Book it appeared. That the Annuities in Expectancy, amount to £. 10,019.

And to shew the Income of the Company's Estate settled and secured to pay such Annuities,

A Book was produced, and proved, by the said Mr.

Crumpe, to contain a true Rental of all the Estates of the Company that were in Settlement to the Widows: And by the said Book, and the Examination of Mr. Crumpe, it appeared. That the Clear Income of the Estates so settled, amounted to £.4,148 17 a£ a Year.

And the said Mr. Crumpe being asked, what other Estates the Company had which were not in Settlement; he produced a Book, intituled, "A Rental of the House " Estate not in Settlement;" whereby it appears. That such Estate amounted to £.669 17 7 Annum, and the Outgoings to £.612 7 of; a Particular of which is contained in the Appendix N° 10.

And he said. That the several other Charges to which the Hall was liable, and which were not set down in the said Rental, made the Outgoings of the said Estate, called the House Estate, more than the Income.

And being asked, touching the Nature and Quality of the Estates in Settlement, and whether that Part that was in Houses or the IrijliEstate was of the greatest Value; he said the present Income of the Estate in Houses was £. 3,726 a Year, or thereabouts, within the Bills of Mortality; and the same are liable to Decay, and subject to daily Repairs, but yet of greater Value in tire whole than the Irish Estate.

That the Rent now reserved upon the Estate is £.420 a Year; of which several Companies have a small Part; and the Share of the Company of the said £.420 a Year is £-362 40^. That on letting the last Lease, in 1713 (which expires at Saints 1755) a Fine of£. 6,000 was given, and the Share thereof belonging to, and which came to, the Company, was £.5,120 u 4f.

APPENDIX, N'4.

The last Will and Testament of Sir 'Thomas Knight.

THIS is the last Will written, and Disposition of me Sir Thomas Grejkam, of the City of London, Knight,

concerning all my Manors, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, mentioned andconteyned in One Indenture Quadrupartite, made between me the said Sir Thomas Gresham, and Dame.^wr* my Wife, on the One Partie; and Philip Scuddamore Gent, and Thomas Celey, on the other Partie; dated the Twentieth Day of May, in the Seventeenth Year of the Iltign of our Sovereign Lady Queen Elizabeth.

First, concerning the Buildings in , called the

Royal Exchange, and all Pawns and Shops, Cellars, Vaults, Messuages, Tenements, and other whatsoever myne Hereditaments, Parcell or adjoyning to the said Royal Exchange, I will and dispose, That, after Expiration and Determination of the particular Uses, Estates, and Interest for Life, and Intayle thereof, limited in the said Indenture, bearing Date the Twentieth of May, I will and dispose. That One Moiety thereof shall remain, and the Use thereof shall be unto the Major, and the Commonalty, and Citizens of London, by whatsoever especial Name or Addition the same Corporation is made or known, and to their Successors, for Term of Fifty Years then next ensuing; upon Trust or Confidence, and to the Intent that they do perform the Payments and other Intents in these Presents hereafter limited, thereof by them to be done and performed: And the other Moiety of the said Buildings, called the Royal Exchange, Pawns, Shops, Cellars, Vaults, Messuages, Tenements, and other mine Hereditaments, with the Appurtenances thereto adjoyning, shall remain, and the Use thereof shall be to the Wardens and Commonalties of the Mysterie of the Mercers of the City of London; viz. to the corporate Body and Corporation of the Company of Mercers in London, by whatsoever especial Name or Addition the same Corporation is made or known, and to their Successors, for Term of Fifty Years next ensuing; upon Trust and Confidence, and to the Intent that they do perform the Payments and other Intents in these Presents hereafter lymited, thereof by them to be done and performed: And I will and dispose, That, after such Time as the One Moiety of the said Royal Exchange and other Premises, according to the Intent and Meaning of these Presents, shall conae to the said Major and Corporation of the said City, and from thence so long as they and their Successors shall, by any Means or Title, have, hold, or enjoy, the fame, they and their Successors, every Year, shall give and distribute, to and for the Sustenation, Maintenance, and Finding, Four Persons, from tyme to tyme to be chosen, nominated, and appointed, by the same Major, and Commonaltie, and Citizens, and their Successors, meete to read the Le(Shires of Divinity, Astronomy, Musick, and Geometry, within myne own Dwelling-house, in the Parish of St. Helen's, in Bish and in St. Peter's the Poor, in the City of London, (the Moiety whereof hereafter in this my last Will is by me lymited and disposed unto the said Major, and Commonaltie, and Citifons of the said City) the Summe of Two hundred Pounds, of lawful Money of England, in Manner and Form following; viz, To every of the said Readers for the Time being, the Sum of Fifty Pounds, of lawful Money of England, yearly, for their Sallaries and Stipends, meete fot* Four sufficiently learned to read the said Lectures: The same Stipends and Sallaries, and every of them, to be paid at Two usual Termes in the Year, yearly, that is to say, at the Feast of the Annunciation ot 0/. Mary the Virgin, and St. Michael the Archangel, by even Portions to be paid.

And farther. That the said Mayor, and Commonaltie, and Citizens, of the said City, and their Successors, from henceforth, and so long as they and their Successors shall, by any Means, have, hold, or enjoy, the ,said Moiety, before in these Presents to them disposed, shall give and

A. 1747.

distribute the Sum of Fifty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, of lawful Money of England, yearly, in Manner and Form following; viz. Unto Eight Almes-Folks, whom the said Mayor, and Commonalty, and Cittyzens, or their Successors, shall appoint to inhabit my Eight Almes-houses, in the said Parish of St. Peter's the Poor, to every of them the said Almes-Foiks the Summe of Six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, to be paid at Four usual Terms in the Year yearly, that is to say, at the Feast of St. Michael the Archangel, the Nativity of our Lord God, the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and Nativity of St. John Baptist, by even Portions;

And farther. That the said Mayor, and Commonaltie, and Cittizens, of the said City, and their Successors, from thenceforth, and so long as they and their Successors shall, by any Means, have, hold, and enjoy the said Moiety, before in these Presents to them disposed, shall give and distribute, at the Terms aforesaid, to the Relief of the poor Persons and Prisoners in the Prisons and Places called or known by the Names of Newgate, Ludgate, the King's-Benck, the Marshalsea, and Counter now kept in

Woodjlreet, and whereloever the same Prisons hereafter shall be kept, Fifty Pounds, of lawful Money of England, in Money, or other Provisions and Necessaries for them; viz. To every of the same Five Prisons or Places, Ten Pounds, at the Four usual Feasts or Terms of Payment of Rent within the same City of London most accustomed, or within Eight-and-twenty Days next after, by even Portions.

And as concerning the other Meietie, before in this my present last Will disposed, to the said Wardens and Commonaltie of the Corporation of the Mercers, I will and dispose, That, after such Time as the same Moietie, according to the Intent and Meaning of these Presents, shall come to the said Wardens and Corporation of the Mercers, and from thenceforth so long as they or their Successors shall, by any Means or Title, have, hold, and enjoy the fame, that they and their Successors, every Year yearly, shall give, and pay, and distribute, to and for the Finding, Sustenation, and Maintenance, of Three Persons, by them the said Wardens and Commonaltie, and their Successors, from time to time to be chosen and appointed, meete to read the Lectures of Law, Physick, and Rhetorick, within myne now Dwelling-house, in the Parish of St. Helens in Bishopf-gate-street, and St. the Poor, in the said City of L, (the Moyety whereof, hereafter in this my present last Will, is by me appointed and disposed unto the said Corporation of Mercers) the Summe of One hundred and Fifty Pounds, of lawful Money of England, in Manner and Form following;

To every of the said Readers, for the Time being, the Summe of Fifty Pounds, for their Sallaries and Stipends, meete for Three sufficiently learned to read the said Lectures, at Two usual Feasts in the Year, that is to say, at the Feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of St. Michael the Archangel, by even Portions to be paid: And that the said Wardens and Corporation of the Mercers, and their Successors, from henceforth, and so long as they and their Successors shall, by any Means, have, hold, or enjoy the said Moiety, before in these Presents to them disposed, shall yearly bestow and expend One hundred Pounds, of lawful Money of England, in Manner and Form following; that is to say, severally at Fower several Termes in the Year, in and about the Expencesand Charges of a Feast or Dynner for the whole Company of the same Corporation, to be had and made in the Mercers-Hall in the said City of London, at and in every their Quarter Day the Summe of Twenty-five Pounds: And farther that the said Wardens and Corporation of the Mercers, and their Successors, from thenceforth and so long as they and their Successors shall, by any Means, have, hold, or enjoy, the said Moiety, before in these Presents to them disposed, shall every Year give and distribute to the Relief of the poor Persons and Prisoners in the Hospitals, Prisons, and Places, called or known by the Names of the Hospitals of Christ, or Christ-

Collection of rl 1 HE House being informed, That some of the Duties on JL Commissioners for Taxes attended at the Door j House j, &c. They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the

House, pursuant to their Order, a Copy of the Report made by the Commissioners for Taxes, to the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury, relating to the Difficulties and Obstructions which have attended the Collodion of the Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights.

And then they withdrew.

And the Title of the said Copy was read.

The laid Copy is as followeth;

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury;

May it please your Lordships,

We have, in Obedience to your Lordships Commands, considered the present State of the Duties on Houses, Windows, and Lights, according to the Assessments returned to us by the several Surveyors throughout the Kingdom; and have hereunto subjoined an Account of the Manner of assessing, charging, and discharging, the fame, collected from the Letters and Accounts which have been transmitted to us by the Surveyors of these Duties.

We beg Leave to observe, it will appear by these Accounts, That many of the Windows or Lights in Dwelling-houses, and in some Place whole Houses, have been discharged or excused from paying to the said Rates and Duties chargeable by the present A.

And from our having been frequently acquainted by several of the Commissioners of the Land Tax, and many of our Officers, upon their attending the Commissioners, that they did not think themselves authorized by the Powers given by the Act:, as it now stands, to order the Assessments to be made according to the Instructions given by us to the Surveyors, as not thinking the Act sufficiently clear and explicit to justify them in the Execution of it, in consequence of such Interpretation; which, together with the Surveyors not being permitted in some Places to do their Duty, and the Methods which have been universally practised in Hopping up Windows or Lights, to evade the Payment of the Duties granted by the Act, have, in our humble Opinion, made it necessary to have the said Act explained.

We therefore humbly presume, that, in order to remedy these Inconveniencies, it will be proper to have a Regulation of the Act, as it now stands (which we are also advised to by his Majesty's Counsel, learned in the Law) and to add some further Clauses to enforce the Execution thereof, which have been prepared by us, and perused and amended by the Attorney and Solicitor-General, and are now put into the Form of a Bill, which we most humbly submit to your Lordships Consideration.

We further beg Leave to acquaint your Lordships, That upon the Representations made to us by the Receiver-General and the Surveyors-General of the Duties on Windows in Scotland (which have been laid before your Lordships) that many great Difficulties, Inconveniencies, and Obstructions, do attend the Execution of this Act, arising, among other Circumstances, from the Difference of the Law's and Customs of that Country and those of England, which make it impracticable to put the Law in Force as it now stands; we are humbly of Opinion, it will- be necessary that the Part of the Act relating to Scotland be also explained and amended.

We are also humbly of Opinion, That, if the Duty of Six Pence per Window or Light was laid upon all Houses having under Seven Windows or Lights, instead of under Ten, as it now stands, this Revenue would not only be increased, but the Tax would be more equal.

Upon the Whole, as this Duty is charged by former Acts of Parliament with the annual Sum of £.9,485 o 6| due to the Aggregate Fund; and as it appears to us, by the Returns of the Assessments made in the several Districts of this Kingdom, that the annual Amount of this Duty will not exceed the Sum of ,£.200,000, there will only remain the Sum of £.109,000 towards satisfying -the Interest- due upon the Annuities bearing £.4 per Cent. Interest, granted the last Session of Parliament upon the Sum of £.4,400,000, w'hich amounts to £.176,000.

The Manner of charging and discharging the Duties on Houses, &V. in the several Counties in England and Wales?

In general, throughout the Kingdom, all Offices and Outhouses whatsoever, adjoining, or not, to the Dwelling-house, either have not-been charged by the Assessors, or have been discharged by the Commissioners, upon Appeals; although there have been some Instances, where Offices that communicated with the Dwelling-house, or which had Lodging-rooms in them, were allowed to be charged.

In many Places, Window's in Stair-cases, Cellars, Garrets, or over Doors, though in the main or Dwelling-house, together with all Lights not glazed, have been discharged.

In some Places, Persons appealing as Poor, though they lived in their own Houses, or in other Houses which paid to the Church and Poor, as also if they rented under Forty Shillings per Annum, or would swear they were not worth Forty Pounds, have been discharged, at the Appeals.

Some Persons inhabiting Houses, which do not pay to Church and Poor, have been excused, though the said Persons have been reputed to be worth Two or Three hundred Pounds.

Rooms

C '

II

Geo. II.

Rooms in the Dwelling-house, where a few Sacks of Corn, or a little Lumber, has been laid, have been difo... charged, under the Name of Warehouses or Granaries.

In some Parts, Inhabitants of Freehold Houses, who rent small Parcels of Land (the Taxes of such Land being paid by the Landlord) have been exculed from paying these Duties, upon a Parish-Officer's alleging them to be poor.

Some Houses which arc built upon waste Ground, though inhabited by People of Ability, have been discharged.

Divers other Persons, though able to pay, have be^n excused, because their Names were not in the Church or: Poor's Books.

And in most Places, where the Surveyors have made Surcharges upon the Assessors Charge, the same have been (truck off by the Commissioners.

Some of the Surveyors have not been allowed to see the Assessors Books; and others not permitted to pals through the Houses, to number the Windows or Lights, as the Act empowers and enjoins them to do, but were threatened at the Peril of their Lives if they attempted it.

The- general Practice of (topping up Windows and Lights hath likewise been of the greatest Prejudice to this Revenue, as the same hath been done only with lool'c Bricks or Boards, which may be removed at Pleasure, or with Mud, Cow-dung, Mortar, and Reeds, on the Out-fide, which are soon washed off with a Shower of Rain, or with Paper or Pasteboard on the Inside, to evade the Payment of these Duties.

All which we most humbly submit to your Lordships.

Office for Taxes, '

T , n Jo. Ruharden,

Examining A Petition of Joshua Ward Esquire, was presented to Drugs,&c. the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, for about Fifteen Years last past, has almoll wholly been employed in relieving and curing poor Persons of divers grievous and loathsome Diseases, by certain chemical Preparations of his own Invention; during which Space of Time he has seldom had less than Two thousand Patients of this Sort conllantly under his Care, at his own Expence, many of which had been discharged from the Hospitals of London and Westminster as Incurables; and, of these, not left than Three hundred Soldiers at a time; the greatest Part of which Objects of Compassion has been perfectly Cured of their respective Maladies; and others recovered in such a manner, that they were made capable of following their Bufinest, so as to become useful Members of the Community; and that, as this Fad is most notorious, the Petitioner makes no Doubt but many Persons of high Rank, and the Officers of the several Regiments to which such Soldiers did belong, would readily attest the fame: That an Employment of this Kind, as it reflects the highest Pleasure and Satisfaction to the Petitioner, so it is of the greatest Benefit to the Publick, and the Petitioner makes no Doubt of his being intitled to the Protection and Encouragement of this House; but that it. is with the utmost Concern he finds himself under a Necessity to represent, that he is apprehensive, that, if the late Application of the Apothecaries of London to this House, in order to confine the making up and dispensing medicinal Preparations to Apothecaries only* should meet with Success, it would hinder the Petitioner from preparing those chemical Medicines which have been so very beneficial to Mankind, and deprive him of exercising that ipost excellent Gift of Charity which has lately appeared to be not only so much the Favourite of thele Days, by the EreCling of many Hospitals for Purposes of this Sort, but has always been protected and encouraged by the Legislature of Great Britain: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and make such Provision for the Publick and the Petitioner, as to the House shallfecm meet.

Ordered, That the said Pet ition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Co mmittee, to whom the Be-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Imposition of Six Pence per Chaldron on every Chaldron of Coals or Culm, and of Six Pence per Ton on every Ton of Coals usually sold by the Ton, which* was by an Act, of the 5th and 6th Years of the Reign of the late King William and QbeCn Mary, intituled, An Act for the Relief of the Orphans, and other Creditors, of the City of London, granted to the Mayor and Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, on all Sorts of Coals and Culm which should be imported into the Port of the City of London from and after the 29th Day of September in the Year of our Loud One thousand Seven hundred, for and during the Term of Fifty Years, shall be continued and paid, for and during the Term of Thirty-five Years, from the Expiration qi the said Term of Fifty Years, and no longer.

Resolved, That is the Opinion of this Committee, That, out of the Monies arising from the Imposition of Six Pence per Chaldron or Ton on every Chaldron or Ton of Coals or Culm, to be continued for Thirty-five Years, as aforiflaid, the yearly Sum of Three thousand Pounds Vol. 25.

be applied, for add. during the said Term of Thirty-five Years; towards paying the Annuities now payable, or which hereafter (Mil be payable, by the Company of . Mercers of London, to several Widows, and others, during their rdpe&ive Lives, in pursuance of Contracts heretofore entered into by the said Company, and to such other Creditors of the said Company as shall be deemed proper Gbjo&sof Relief; and that the Relidueoftbe Monies, which shall arise from the said Imposition, shall be applied towards paying the Interest which shall be due to the Orphans, and other Creditors, of the City of London, under the said Act of King William and Queen Mary.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, frohr and after the 29th Day of September which shall be in the Year of our Lord 1750, all and every the Manors, Messuages, Lands, Tenements, Markets, Fairs, and the Duties thereof and all other the Revenues of apd belonging to the City of London, in Possession or Rever-lion, mall stand and be charged with the full yearly Sum of Two thousand Pounds, over and above the yearly Sum of Eight thousand Pounds wherewith they now. stand charged, towards paying the Interest which shall be due to the Orphans, and other Creditors, of the City of London, under the said Act of King William and, Queen Mary.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Surpluses which have arisen from the Funds appropriated, by the said Act of King William and Queen Mary, for Payment of Interest, as it should become due, to the Orphans, and other Creditors, of the City of London, as also the Surplusses which shall arise from' the said Funds, and from, the Funds now appropriated for Payment-of such Interest, shall be applied by the Mayor, Commohalfy, and Citizens, of the said City of London, after reserving so much as will be sufficient to pay the Interest according to the said Act, to the Payment of and discharging the capital Debt due to the Creditors of the said City, under the said Act.

Upon the Petition of Chauncy Esquire, and

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The lad Determination of the House, made the First Day of June 1715, whereby it was resplved, That the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for this Borough is in every Tenant of any Burgage-Tenement in Fee, for Life, or Ninety-nine Years determinable on Lives; or by Copy of Court-Roll, paying a Burgage Rent of Four Pence or Two Pence yearly, being resident within the Borough, and not receiving Alms; was read:

As to Three of the said Ten Persons included in the Objection for Charity, and which the Counlcl for the Petitioners likewise objected to, as having voted lor Houses that were not Burgage-Houses, the Evidence given in Support of this Objection, and also by way of Answer thereto, was as follows:

With respect to Samuel Bigwood,

Solomon Hughes gave Evidence, That he was present at the lall Election, and at the Four preceding Elections: That he knows that the House for which Samuel Bigwood voted at the last Election, is Part of the House for which Christopher Read likewise gave his Vote; That the Two Parts were always reputed to be One Tenement, and to give a Right only to One Vote; which Vote was usually given for that Part which Read occupies.

That the same Part of the House for which Samuel Higiooood voted at the lad Election, was attempted to be voted for in the contelled Elections in 1723, 1734, and 1741, by Samuel Bigwood the cider, and his Vote was diiallowed: That he believes in 1727 his Vote was taken, though strongly objected to; but the then Mayor was in the Interest of the Candidates for whom it was given; and he believes that when his Vote was refused, the Mayors were in the opposite Interest to the Candidates for whom it was offered.

Richard Rendall being examined, laid. That the Two Parts of the House in which Read and Bigwood live, were reputed to be but One Tenement; and that the Vote offered for that Part, for which Bigwood voted at the lad Election, was refused at the contested Elections in the Years 1734 and 1741; and he said, That it is the general Reputation of old People in the Borough, that Bigwoocf s Part gave no Right of voting.

Being cross-examined, he said. That a Burgage-Tenement which pays a Rent of Four Pence is called a whole Burgage, and Two Pence a half Burgage: That an half Burgage has a Right to vote, but cannot be divided; nor did he ever hear that One whole Burgage paying Four Pence, could be divided into Two: That it is generally reputed that this Tenement pays only a Rent of Two Pence, which Two Pence is paid for that.Part for which Read voted.

In Answer to this Evidence,

James Mattjell was examined: Who laid. That he has known the Borough of Wefbury Fifty Years, during Vol. 25.

which Time the Tenement for which Samuel Bigwood voted was always reputed to give a Bight of voting; and that the Witness knows that Samuel Bigwood1 s Father voted for it Forty Years ago.

Being cross examined, he said. That the Vote for this Tenement was allowed in the Election in 1727; but whether or no it was allowed in the Elections in 1723, 1734, and 1741, he could not speak with Certainty.

John Mason, being examined, said. That he had been employed Three Years in collecting the Burgage-Rents; and that Samuel Bigwood's Tenement pays Two Pence a Year Rent, which the Witness himself collected last Year: That Read likewise pays Two Pence a Year: And the W itness does not remember that Read and Bigwood's Two Tenements were ever reputed to be One Tenement only.

Henry Barker said, That he was the Mayor's Serjeant in the Year 1732, and collected Two Pence Rent lor the Tenement for which Samuel Bigwood voted: That he has known the same 27 or 38 Years, and it was always reputed to give a Right to vote, and that he always understood io.

Edward Pear/e said, That at the last Election, Thomas Burgeft, William Aufton, Edward Thomas John Phipps, Richard Slug, Samuel Bayly, Robert

and Roger Cater, acknowledged they had resided within the Borough not longer than Three Weeks before the Election; John Gibbs, Thomas Naifli, and Thomas Green, a Fortnight; Robert Michell, Ten Days; Samuel -ridge, and Stephen Applegate, Nine Days.

He further said, That before the Time above-mentioned, William Aufton and John Phipps lived in the Town of Westbury, and Edward Phipps and Thomas Green at West bury-Leigh; which last mentioned Place the Petitioners Counsel admitted to be out of the Borough.

Henry Barker said. That before the Time they are said to have come into the Borough, the constant Residence of William Aufton and Richard Slug was in the Priory Tytk-ing; of Samuel Oatridge, Thomas Browne, and Robert Edwards, in the Town Tything; of Stephen Applegate, Samuel Bayly, and Roger Cater, in the Chauntry Tything:

That the Tythings called the Town and Priory Tythings are within the Town, and the Chauntry Tything very near the Town: That the Constables for those Tythings are chose at the Lord of the Manor's Court-Leet; and that they can execute no Warrant within the Borough; and that the Constables appointed by the Mayor's Court can execute no Warrant out of the Borough: That the Inhabitants of the said Tythings owe no Suit or Service to the Mayor's Court, but to the Hundred Court-Leet; and that the Land Tax for the Borough and Tythings are collected by different Collectors.

He further said. That by the Borough he does not mean any certain Number of Houses contiguous to each other, but such Houses as pay a Burgage-Rent, and which lie interspersed among the other Houses of the Town.

James Manfell said. That before the Time Thomas Naish came into the Borough he lived in the Town Tything, and John Phipps in the Priory Tything.

Being cross-examined, he said, That the Houses on each Side of Phipps's House are within the Borough; but that he is not able, as to all the Houses in the Town, to specify which are in the Borough, and which are not.

The Petitioners Counsel admitted, That before the Time they are said to have come within the Borough, Thomas Burgess lived out of the Borough, and John Gibbs and Robert Michell in London.

Translation. Refultat of the Conferences held between Messieurs the Earl of Chesterfield and Trevor, and Messieurs the Deputies of their High Mightinesse, March 30th, N.S. 1745.

I.

The Number of Troops which Great Britain shall furnish next Campaign, in the Auftr Netherlands, for the Service of the common Cause, shall not be left than Forty thousand Men; but may be greater, if Circumstances allow it: the King of Great Britain engaging, in all Events, for Forty thousand Men.

To make out this Number, there are already in the Netherlands Twenty-four thousand Six hundred and Fifty English; which will shortly be entirely completed by the Recruits which shall be sent thither immediately, and ace already embarked in part; viz.Cavalry, Three Squadrons

of 178 Horses; Dragoons, Eighteen Squadrons of 179 Horses; Infantry, Twenty-four Battalions' of 816 Men.

The Body of Hanoverians which- is there, consisting of Seven thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-four Men, viz. Sixteen Squadrons of Horse of 180 Horses, and Six Battalions of 814 Men, shall remain there till it be replaced by others, and till, without it, the Number of Forty thousand Men be still complete there; and what is wanting of this Number at present shall be supplied either by Subsidiary Troops, of which it is hoped the Number of Eight thousand will be there before the Month of May, or by new Levies to be made for the account of the King of Great Britain, by the Queen of Hungary, in the Netherlands, according to a Plan proposed for this Purpose, by which the Number cf Troops in the

Netherlands would be completed at the same time.

On the Part of the Republick, no less shall be employed than the Number of Thirty-nine thousand Seven hundred and Forty-six Men for the Service of the next Campaign, in so for as the Operations of the adverse Army, and the Necessities of the War, will permit; viz. Cavalry, Thirty-one Squadrons of 186 Horses; Dragoons, Fifteen Squadrons of 162 Horses; and Forty-two Battalions, One of Guards of 800, and the others of 750 Men.

Besides this, there shall be for the Garrisons at Namur, Tournay, and Dendermonde, Seven Battalions and some Detachments, making the Number of Seven thousand One hundred and Forty Men; and there shall be held in Readiness to serve in the Field, in order to replace others with them in case of Need, Seven Battalions in Reserve, making the Number of Five thousand Two hundred and Fifty Men; all this without including the Eight thousand One hundred and Fifty-four Men; viz. Cavalry, Eight

Great Britain and the Republick shall furnish, each to their own Troops, the necessary Field Pieces.

As to the heavy Artillery, it shall be furnished, Two-thirds by Great Britain, and One-third by the Repub-lick.

AH the Expences of the heavy Artillery shall be paid according to the same Proportion; and, in order to lessen them as much as possible, they shall jointly endeavour to effectuatethat the Government of the shall

charge itself with the Transporting of the said heavy Artillery, and its Train, by Land.

m.

In all the Expences of Sieges, with what thereunto be- . longs, Great Britain shall also bear Two-thirds, and the Repubhck One-third.

IV.

In all the other casual Charges of the War, not comprehended in the Two foregoing Articles, Great Britain shall pay Three-fourths, and the Republick One-fourth.

V

In case the Two Powers should think fit to promise, upon the Occasion of the present Troubles, new or farther Subsidies to any Courts or Princes, for the Advancement of the common Cause, Great Britain shall furnish thereto Three-fourths, and the Republick One-fourth.

VI.

None of the Proportions regulated above shall be alleged either on the one Part or on the other, nor drawn into Consequence hereafter, nor serve fora Precedent after that the present Troubles shall be ended.

Translation of the Convention between his Majesty and the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, signed and concluded at the Hague

the 5th May, N. S. 1745.

Whereas according to the Refultat of the Conferences held between Messieurs the Earl of Chesterfield Am-baflador Extraordinary, and T Envoy Extraordinary,

both Plenipotentiaries of his Britannick Majesty, and Messieurs the Deputies of their High Mightinesse for foreign Affairs, inserted in the secret Resolution of their High Mightinesse of the 30th of the Month of March last (which Refultat has been respectively approved by his Britannick Majesty, and the Lords the States General) the Council of State has been required to adjust farther, with those who should be authorized for that Purpose on the Part of his Britannick Majesty what concerns the heavy Artillery for a Siege, the Expences of a Siege, and all other casual Expences of the War which do not relate to a Siege, the Whole more fully mentioned in the ad, 3d, and 4th, Articles of the said Refultat; the abovesaid Messieurs the Earl of Chesterfield and , authorized to that End by his Britannick Majesty, on the one Part; and Messieurs the under-written Deputies of the Council of State, as specially authorized thereto, on the other Part; have agreed together on the following Points:

Art. I".

A complete Train of Artillery and warlike Stores shall be formed, pursuant to the Lift which has been exhibited and approved in the Conference which has been held; and such as this Lift is to be found annexed at the End of these Presents, quoted Letter A, agreeable to the Proportion settled by the 2d Article of the said Refultat.

Art. IId.

On the Part of his Britannick Majesty shall be furnished, for that Purpose, the Artillery and wartyke Stores which he has in the Low Countries.

Art. IIId.

If it should happen that what Great Britain shall furnish in the aforesaid Manner should exceed its Proportion as to certain Sorts, the Republick shall supply so much the

A 1747.

less of these Sortsj on the Other Side, it shall furnish what shall be wanting in the said British Artillery and warlike Stores, in order to form a complete Train, according to the Lift above-mentioned.

Art.IV">.

What One of the Two contracting Parties shall furnish, with respect to some Kinds, above its appointed Quota, shall bceftimated by Four Commissaries,o(whoni each of the Parties shall name and constitute Two.

Art. V"'.

Afterwards a Balance of what each Party shall have fumished above its Proportion shall be made; and, as this Balance cannot but be laid upon Great considering

that in examining the Lift of the Artillery and warlike Stores which it has in the Low Countries, it has been found that this Lift does not contain Two-thirds of the Total necessary to form a complete Train, his Britannick Majesty shall cause to be paid forthwith, or, at latest, in a Month after the Signature of these Presents here at the Hague, into the Comptoir of the United Provinces, what shall be found due to the Republick, agreeably to this Balance.

Art. VI«>.

Two of t'le said Commissaries shall assist at the Forming of the said Train, and shall have the Inspection that each Party shall furnish effectually its Quota: When in this manner a completeTrain shall once have been formed in common, whatever afterwards shall have been consumed or broken, or what shall come to be wanting therein by other Accidents, shall be repaired or supplied at common Cost, pursuant to the said Proportion; in such manner, however, that the Republick shall cause the said Reparation and Supplement to be made; but that Great Britain shall immediately reimburseits Part at the general Comptoir of the Union here at the Hague, upon the Foot that the fame shall be due to the State, including the Expences of Transportation towards the Places where the Train shall then be, inasmuch as these Expences ought to be borne by the Two contracting Parties, the Whole agreeable to the Certificate which the Council of State shall give;

Art. VII"*.

The common Train of Artillery shall be delivered up to the Custody, Management, and Direction, of Two Clerks, One of Artillery, and the other of warlike Stores, already established, or who shall be afterwards established by the Council of State; which Clerks shall have their Servants, according to the Usage of the Republick.

Art. VIII">.

The Clerks and their Servants shall be paid in the manner accustomed in the Repubhck; of which Expences Great Britain shall bear Two-thirds, and the Republick One-third.

Art. IX'h.

They shall be obliged to give an Account of the Artillery and warlike Stores, which they shall have received, to the Council of State, and to the Chamber of Accounts of the Generality, which shall examine and settle these Accounts pursuant to the Regulations of the State, which shall fuifice for the intire Dischar^e of these Clerks.

Art. X*.'

A Duplicate of these Accounts, settled, shall be delivered to the Mmiller of his Britannick Majesty, wholhall be here at the Hague, to serve for his Information.

Art. XI"1.

At the End of the present Troubles, all the common Train shall be divided between the Two contracting Par-

o

ties, according to the abovesaid Proportion; so that each shall have, pursuant to this Proportion, as near as can be, its Part of each Sort; and shall withdraw the individual Effects which it shall have fumished, as far as shall be possible.

Art. XII*.

the Republick shall furnish the Directors and Engineers, the Officers and Servants for the Artillery, and Miners, according to the Lifts hereto annexed, quoted letters B, C, D, as also in case of an apparent or actualSiege, the Officers, the Sappers, and the extraordinary Servants who

shall

2i Geo. II. 18" Mat tit.

shall be then necessary, who shall be paid, agreeably to the said Proportion, out of the common Chest which shall be formed for the Artillery and for a Siege, as shall be more ful;y mentioned hereafter, and that upon the Foot that the said Officers and Servants are paid by the State, and according to the Liquidation which shall be made by the Chamber of Finances.

Art. XIIIth.

In order to defray the Expences as well of the Artillery as of a Siege, with what depends thereon, a common Chest (h ill be formed, pursuant to the Proportion in the 3d Article of the said Refultat of the Conferences held.

Art. XIVth.

The Administration of this Chest shall be intruded to the Person who shall be appointed by the Council of State for this Purpose, in giving sufficient Caution to the Satisfaction of the said Council of State, and observing the Instructions at the End of this Convention; which CommilTary shall be treated, and have a Salary, upon the same Foot as the like Administrators have been heretofore treated, and paid } thereof by Great , and -J- by the

Republick.

Art. XVtt.

The General who commands the Troops of his Bri-tannick Majesty, as well as he who commands those of the State, shall each name a General Officer, who shall together have the Superintendency of the said Chest, observing the Instruction int'erted at the End of this Convention; and, upon an Order signed by the Two said Generals, the said Commissary shall make the necessary Payments: The laid General Officers, or either of them, shall have Liberty to inspect the Accounts and the Chest of the said Commissary, as often as they shall think proper, in order to be always informed of the State of Things, and to be able to judge, in time, of future Wants.

Art. XVIth.

The said Administrator shall render an Account to the Council of State, and to the Chamber of Accounts of the Generality; and this Account shall be examined and settled according to the Order established in this Country, which shall serve the said Commissary for an intire Discharge: A Duplicate of these Accounts, thus settled, shall be delivered to the Minister of his Majesty here at the Hague % for his Information.

Art. XVIIth.

In order to furnish this Chest, Great Britain shall furnish as soon as possible, to the said Commissary, a Sum of 20 Florins, and the Republick of toT; and, when there shall shall be Occasion for more Money, the said Commissary shall have it in his Power, on an Order in Writing of the Officers mentioned in Art. 15*, to draw for as much more Money as they shall judge necessary} Two-thirds upon the Person who fyall bo appointed in these Provinces, for that Purpose, by his Britanmck Majesty } and the other Third upon the Receiver-General of the Union here at the Hague;(or which Intent the Two aforesaid Officers shall certify, at the Bottom of the Bills of Exchange which the said Commissary shall flgn, that it is with their Knowledge that they have been drawn.

Instru<ftion for the Two Generals, the One on the Part of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and the other on the Part of the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, who shall have the Superintendence and Administration of the Money designed, on one Side, to defray the Expences of the Artillery, and other Expences which happen at a Siege; and, on the other Side, to supply the casual Expences of the War, not comprehending those of a Siege.

Art. Ift.

The Two aforesaid Generals shall give Orders in Writing to the Administrator or Cashier of the Laid Money, according to the Exigence of the Cafes, for the Payments which they shall judge necessary for the Service of the common Cause, so far as they may be brought to the Charge of the Two Powers above-mentioned.

Art. IP.

As there is a Difference between Great Britain and the Republick, in the Proportion according to which each of the Two Powers contributes to the Expences of the Artillery and of a Siege, and to the casual Expences of the War, Great Britain contributing to the Expences of the Artillery and of a Siege, -f, and the Republick -f; and to the casual Expences of the War 4, and the Republick i; and as the Cashier, on account of this Difference of Proportion, will be obliged to keep Two Accounts, the One on the Subject of the Expences of the Artillery and of a Siege, and the other concerning the casual Expences of the War, exclusive of those of a Siege, the Two Generals aforesaid, in ordering the Payments, shall have Regard to this Distihdlion, and shall nuke Mention thereof with a particular Word in their Orders, in Writing, to the Cashier, for his Information; for instance, they shall use the Expression of " Expences of the Artillery" for the Warrants of one Soft, and of " Casual Expences" for those of the other Sort.

Art. IIId.

Pursuant to this, the Two aforesaid Generals shall cause to be paid, out of the Money designed for the Expences of the Artillery and of a Siege, the Pay and Day-Wages of the Directors and Engineers, of the Officers of the Artillery and their Servants, of the Miners, of the Clerks and their Servants, for the Train of the heavy Artillery, according to the State which shall be formed of it in the Chamber of Accounts of the Generality: Item, the Expences for repairing or renewing the heavy Artillery, and the warlike Stores which relate thereto, in case that this Reparation or this Renewal can be done in the Field or in the Neighbourhood of the Army; as also the extraordinary Officers and the Servants who shall be engaged in case of a Siege, as well as the Costs of Labourers, Volun-tiers, Sappers, Gabions, Fafcines, and other such-iike Things which happen at a Siege; and that, upon a previous Order in Writing of the General who shall command the Siege, at the Bottom of which Order they shall signify, that these Payments have been made with their Privity; and shall take care that it be observed, with regard to the Payment of the Labourers and Voluntiers employed at a Siege, that the Money be delivered to the Majors of the Trenches; that these do pay the Labourers employed in the Trenches, in the Presence of the Majors of Brigade; the Labourers employed by the Directors and Engineers, in Presence either of a Director or Engineer; and the Workmen employed on the Batteries, in Presence of the chief Officer of the Artillery, under whose Orders they shall have served; and that the Officers above-mentioned, viz. Majors of Brigade, Directors or Engineers, Officers of the Artillery, and others, declare, at the Bottom of the Lift of the Labourers who shall have been employed each Day or Night, that they have been paid in their Presence.

Art. IVth.

They shall cause to be paid, out of the Money designed for the casual Expences of the War, those of Jour-nies of Officers who shall have received a formal Order

to take these journies, the Trumpets and Drums who shall also have been sent by Order, the extraordinary Guides employed to shew the Ways, the Labourers employed to make Intrenchments, a Head of a Bridge, and other casual Expences of the War, and of secret Intelligence, but upon an Order in Writing from the Field Marshal Count deKoningsegg.

Art. V*\

They shall take care that no other Payments be made out of the isaid Money, than those, which, according to the Nature of Things, ought to be paid out of it; and, to this Purpose, a Copy of the Convention shall be transmitted to them, which shall be made with the Government at Bru£eUs, concerning the Transportation of

the heavy Artillery.

Licensing a Petition of the trading Citizens of London, inhabit-

Pedlars*1 within the said City, and Parts adjacent, was presented

to the House, and read; Anting forth. That, in the 9th and 10th Year of the Reign of King William the Third, an Act passed for licensing of Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, to trade from Town to Town, or to other Men's Houses, travelling either on Foot, or with Horse, Horles, br otherwise, within the Kingdom of England, Dominion of Wales, or Town of Berwickupon Turned, except as therein is excepted; which said Act has, by Two subsequent additional Clauses, been continued for Ninety-fixand One Year, from the 23d Day of June 1710, thence next ensuing , and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the said Statute, however well intended, has proved of the highest Detriment imaginable to the fair Trader, by such as have been licensed practising illicit Dealing, and, under Cover of the said Statute, defrauding the Revenue, and abusing ignorant and unwary People with deceitful Wares and Merchandizes, to the great Scandal and Reproach of Trade: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation, and amend, or totally repeal, the said Act; and if it be the Pleasure of the Legislature to repeal the Act, that then, as an Equivalent for the fame, and to be appropriated to the like Uses, they would lay a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, on all Traders within the Limitation of the said recited Statute; and that the Act for that Purpose may be supported by such Clauses, on the behalf of the settled and fair Trader, and for the intire suppressing of Hawking and Pedling, as may appear most effectual to answer the laudable Intention of the said Equivalent5 or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Tabic.

Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting Peilars* forth, That by an Act of Parliament, made in the 9th and '

10th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for licensing Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, a Liberty is given them to trade from Town to Town, or to other Men's Hou!'e>, either on Foot, or with Horle or Horses, or otherwise, within the Kingdom of England, Lominion of Wales, or Town of Berwick upon;

which said Act, by subsequent additional Ciaules, has been continued from the 23d of June 1710, for Nmetv and Seven Yean; and that it is with great Concern the Pc-. 7 L tiuoners

D ized by

Licensing Hawkers and Pedlars.

Lingen's

Name.

59°

titioners find, that the Liberty given, in and by the said Act, for such Persons to trade from Place to Place as aforesaid, has proved destructive to Trade in general, and a great Discouragement to all fair Traders, who, in all the Cities and Towns in Great Britain, bear the Burden of Civil and other Offices, whilst those who have been licensed under the said Act bear no Office at all, but daily carry on an illicit Trade or Dealing, and, under Cover of the said Statute, defraud the Revenue, and impose upon and greatly abuse ignorant and unwary People, by felling them deceitful Wares, and often at double the real Value thereof, to the great Scandal and Reproach of Trade: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Confederation, and amend, dr totally repeal, the said Act; and if it be the Pleafore of the Legislature to repeal the Act, then, as an Equivalent for the fame, and to be appropriated to like Uses, they would be pleated to lay a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, on all Traders within the Limitation of the said recited Statute; and that the Act for that Purpose may be supported by such Clauses, on behalf of the settled and fair Trader, and for the intire suppressing of Hawking and Pedling, as may appear to the House most effectual to answer the laudable Intention of the said Equivalent; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved ks to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That by an Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for licensing Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, a Liberty is given to them to trade from Town to Town, or to other Men's Houses, either on Foot, or with Horse or Horses, or otherwise, within the Kingdom of England, Dominion of Wales, or Town or Berwick upon Tweed; which said Act, by subsequent additional Clauses, has been continued from the 23d of Juni 1710, for Ninety and Seven Years; and that it is with great Concern the Petitioners find, that the Liberty given in and by the said Act, for such Persons: to trade from Place to Place as aforesaid, has proved destructive to Trade in general, and a great Discouragement to all salt; Traders, who, in all the Cities and Towns in Great Britain, bear the Burden of Civil and other Offices, whilst fhofe who have been lidCrifed under the said Act bear no Office at all, but daily carry on an illicit Trade or Dealing, and, under Cover of the said Statute, defraud the Revenue, and impose upon and greatly abuse ignorant and unwaTy People, by felling them deceitful Wares, and often at double the real Value thereof, to the great Scandal and Reproach of Trade: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Corisideration, and amend, or totally repeal, the said Act; and if it be the Pleasure of the Legrcfature to repeal the Act, then, as an Equivalent for the fame, and to be appropriated to the like Uses, they would be pleased to lay a Tax, not exceeding Two ahillirigs a Year, on all Traders within the Limitation of the said recited Statute; and that the Act for that Purpose may be supported by such Cltufes, on behalf of the settled arid fair Trader, and for the intire suppressing of Hawking and Pedling, as may appear to the Horil'e most effectual to answer the laudable Intention of the said Equivalent; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved as to the House shall seem meet. Ordered, That the said' Petition do lie upon the Table.

Examining Sir William Calvert reported from the Committee, to

Drug*, Jcc. whom the Petition of several- Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, Apothecaries of the Cities of London and Westminster, on behalf of themselves, and all other the regular Apothecaries of the said Cities and Suburbs thereof; and also the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed. Apothecaries within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Seven Miles thereof, on behalf of themselves, and all other the Apothecaries within that Distance, not free of the Society of Apothecaries of the City of London; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions} and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Rc-solutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Letters Patent, granted by King James the First, on the Sixth of December, in the 15th Year of his Reign, were read; and recites, That the said King did, on the 9th of April, in the 4th Year of his Reign, by his Letters Patent, incorporate the Grocers and Apothecaries of the City of London; and lets forth. That it had been represented to him, on behalf of the Apothecaries of -dun, and also affirmed and appnved by Theodore de Mayerne and Henry Atkins, his Physicians, that in latter Years very many Empiricks, ignorant and unexperienced Men, inhabiting in the City and Suburbs of , did make and compound very many unwholsome, hurtful, false, corrupt, and pernicious Medicines, and fold and transmitted the same into many Parts of the Kingdom o( England, to the Reproach and Scandal, not only of the learned Physicians, and of the Apothecaries of the said City, educated and expert in the said Art, but also to the great Peril of his said Majesty's Subjects; and that, to prevent the Attempts of such wicked Persons for the future, his said Majesty, by the Advice of his Counsel learned in the Law, did think necessary to disunite and separate the Apothecaries from the Grocers, and to erect such Apothecaries into One Body Corporate and Politick, to whom, in all future Times, the Care and Amendment ofthofelnconveniencics should be committed: And therefore his said Majesty, being moved by the Petitions of the said Theodore de Mayerne and Henry , and also of the said Apothecaries, but chiefly out of his Regard for the publick Good, and to the end that the Ignorance and Ralhness of the aforesaid Empiricks, and ignorant and un-skilful Men, might be suppfeffed, from whence many Dangers daily arose to ignorant and credulous People, did, by those Letters Patent, disunite all Apothecaries, whether free of the Grocers or any other Company, from such Companies; and did constitute all Apothecaries, inhabiting within London and Seven Miles Distance of the lame, as had been brought up and were expert in the said Art, One Body Politick and Corporate, by the Name of the Master, Wardens, and Society, of the Art and Mystery of Apothecaries of the City of London: And in order to prevent, as much as possible, the Dangers and Inconveniences daily happening by unskilful, inexpert, deceitful, and wicked Men, praftlfing the said Art, it was declared, That no Person, free of the Mystery of Grocers, or any other Art or Mystery of the City of London, and brought up in such Arts or Mysteries, should keep any Apothecary's Shop, or make, compound, prepare, apply, or administer, any Medicines, or in any way fell any compound Medicines, or medicinable Compositions, or by any other Way whatsoever exercise the said Art of an Apothecary, within the said Limits, under the Pain of

Five Pounds for every Month such Person should exer-cile the said Mystery; which Penalty was to be levied by Di.lrels, or recovered by Action of Debt, or otherwise, in the Courts at ffestminster: And that no Person should kfeep an Apothecary's Shop or Warehouse, or exercise the said Art, or prepare, fell, or administer Medicines, but who had been Seven Years at least Apprentice to some Apothecary, free of the said Mystery; and which Apprentice, at the Expiration of his Time, should be by the said Mailer and Wardens (calling unto them the President of the College of Physicians, or any Physician or Physicians by him appointed, if, upon Warning, such Physician or Physicians would be present), examined and tried concerning his Knowledge of Simples, and preparing, dispensing, and compounding of Medicines; and by such Physician or Physicians, and Master and Wardens, approved, before he presume to keep an Apothecary's Shop, or in any Manner exercise that Art within the aforesaid Limits.

And full Power was given to the said Master and Wardens, from time to time, to survey, search, examine, govern, and correct all Persons, as well Freeman as others, exercising the said Art, or any Part thereof, within the said Limits, as often as they should think fit; and they, or One of them, or some Assistants by them to be appointed, at convenient Times and in convenient and lawful Manner, might enter into the Shop or House of any Person exercising the said Art, or any Part thereof, within the said Limits, where any Medicines, simple or compounded, Wares, Drugs, distilled Waters, chymical Oils, Syrups, Cohferves, Electuaries, Pills, Powders, Troches, Oils, Ointments, Emplaifters, or other Things whatsoever, which appertained to the Art of an Apothecary, should be probable to be found, and to inspect, search, and prove, whether such Medicines, Preparations, and Compositions, were wholsome, medicinable, and fit for the Cure, Health, and Relief of the People: And full Power was given to examine and try all Personsprofessing or exetcifing the said Art, or any Part thereof, within the said Limits, concerning their Skill and Understanding in such Art; and to prohibit all those from the Practice of the fame, whom they should find Impostors, unskilful, ignorant, or insufficient; or who should refuse to be examined; and also all such Medicines, Preparations, and Compositions, as they should find unlawful, deceitful, stale, unwholsome, corrupt, unmedicinable, or hurtful, to burn before the Offenders Doors; and might also im-pole and execute Punishments, and other Pains and Penalties, by Fines and Amerciaments, upon such Offenders, at their Discretion, and according to the Ordinances made by the said Society; but expert and approved Surgeons might exercise that Art, and.enjoy their proper Practice, as much as belonged to the Composition and Application of outward Salves or Medicines only, so that they did not vend to others such Salves or Medicines, according to the common Manner of Apothecaries.

As to that Part of the Petition which alleges the Impossibility of the said Company's answering the End of their Incorporation the Agent for the Petitioners informed the Committee, That as the said Charter had never been confirmed by the Legislature, the Corporation conceived that they were not vested with a legal Authority to execute all the Powers thereby granted; and therefore had not, for many Years past, attempted to destroy any bad Drugs or Medicines.

Mr. Hume reported from the Committee appointed to Assurances of consider of Heads of a Bill for better regulating of Af- Ships, &c. furances on Ships, and Goods laden thereon; and for preventing Frauds therein; That the Committee had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read: and are as followeth;
