Assurance* of Ship*, &c.

598

24 Mar

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in all A durances upon any Goods or Merchandizes, or Freight, where the Interest of the Assured is, by the Policy, valued at a Sum certain, or is valued at the Sum allured, or no particular Value is set thereupon, the Af-sured shall, in case of Loss or Damage, total or partial, recover only according to the true and real Value of the Goods and Merchandizes assured at the Place where the same were shipped, or the net Freight which would be due if the Ship had arrived safe, together with the Premium of such Assurance; but this shall not extend to prevent the Fixing of a particular Value in the Assurance upon the Weight, Measure, or Tale, or upon each Calk, Bale, or usual Parcel or Package, of each Sort of Goods or Merchandizes, which make up the interest of the Af-sured, or such Part thereof as shall be valued, as aforesaid, according to the Weight, Measure, Tale, or Calk, Bale, or usual Parcel or Package, by which such Goods or Merchandize are usually purchased or shipped at the Place where the said Goods or Merchandize, so valued, are purchased or shipped; provided that each Sort of Goods or Merchandize, so valued as aforesaid, be specified in the Assurance: and in case of Loss or Damage, total or partial, the Assured shall recover according to the Value fixed in the Assurance for the Goods the Assured hath loft, or which have been damaged, in proportion to the Value set upon the Goods, in manner before-mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Assurances upon any Ship or Vessel, or Share thereof, in which the said Ship, Vessel, or Share thereof, is valued at a Sum certain, or at the Sum assured, or no articular Value is set thereupon, the Assured shall, efore the Execution or Under-writing of such Assurance, specify in the Assurance the estimated Burthen of such Ship, and whether the Ship be of British Plantation, or foreign-built, and the Value of such Ship, and upon what Share of the Ship such Assurance is made; and, in case of total Lois, the Assurer shall, notwithstanding the Value is specified in the Assurance, as aforesaid, be at Liberty to controvert the Value of such Ship j and in case it shall appear, that the Assured has overvalued the said Ship, or Share thereof, Part, or more, in

such same the Assured shall recover only the true and real Value of the said Ship or Share; but in case the Value specified in the Assurance shall not exceed the true and real Value by Part, or more, then the

Assured shall recover according to the Value specified in the Assurance; and in all Actions to be brought upon such Assurances, the Assurer, if lie intends to controvert the Value of the Ship or Share specified in the Assurance, shall, together with his Plea to the Declaration, give notice to the Assured, that he intends, at the Trial of the said Action, to controvert the said Value; but in all Assurances upon any Ship, or Share thereof aforesaid, in which the Burthen and Built of such Ship is not specified in the Assurance, but the said Ship is valued at a Sum certain, or at the Sum assured, or no particular Value is set thereupon, the Assured shall prove what is the true and real Value of such Ship, or Share thereof; and shall recover such Value only, together with the Premium of Assurance in case of Lois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Assurances, where the Interest assured shall be Wages of the Master or Mariners of any Ship or Ships, the Amount of the Wages of the Assured, either per Month or for the Voyage, shall, at or before the Execution or Under-writing of such Assurance, be inserted in, or indorsed upon, the Policy; and in case of Loss, where the Time of such Lois appears, and the \\ages are by Agreement payable per Month, the Assured shall recover only a Satisfaction from the Assurer for of such Wages as accrued to him at the time of the Loss; but, where the Time of the Loss does not appear, in such case the Assured shall recover Satisfaction for Wages for of the Time that such Voyages are usually performed in; and where Wages are payable by

A. 1747-

the Voyage or the Run, in case of Loss, the Assured shall recover only of such Wages as would

have been due to him if the Ship had arrived safe.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in all Cases of Assurance against the Barratry' of the Master and Mariners, the Allured shall not recover upon account of such Barratry, unless it appears that the Master or Mariners run away with the Ship or Goods, or Hole, pilfered, or imbezzled the fame, or any Part thereof; and the Assured shall, in such Cases, only recover a Satisfaction for the true and just Value of the Ship and Goods, or such Part thereof as was so run away with, stolen, pilfered, cr imbezzled. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Assurances upon Goods or Merchandize from any Port or Place in Europe, there shall be, in or upon the Assurance, a Declaration, subscribed by the Assurer or respective Assurers for whose Account such Assurance is made; and on all Assurances upon Goods and Merchandizes from any Port or Place in A ft a, Africa, ox America, there shall be, in or upon the Assurance, a Declaration, subscribed by the Assurer or respective Assurers for whole Account such Assurance is made, or to whom such Goods hnd Merchandizes are actually consigned; and that all Other Declarations of Interest, not made as aforesaid, shall be and all Assurances, which have not

such Declarations, as aforesaid, shall he deemed, taken, and adjudged, to be made for the Account of the Person or Persons in whole Name the Assurance is made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Assurances, where the Assured, or the Broker or Agent employed by the Assured to make any Affur-ance, shall give Information or Intelligence to the Assurer, or shall undertake or warrant any Fact or Circumstance relative to the Ship, Merchandize, or Voyage assured, which may materially affect the Terms of the Assurance, such Information, Intelligence, Undertaking* or Warranty, shall be inserted in the AfluranCe before the Underwriting or Execution thereof; and no Evidence shall be admitted to prove, that any Information, Intelligence, Undertaking, or Warranty, was given or made, except what is inserted in the Assurance, as aforesaid; but this shall not be construed to extend to hinder the Assurer from giving Evidence to prove, that the Information, Intelligence, Undertaking, or Warranty aforesaid, was known to be false at the time of the making thereof; or that some material Information or Intelligence was known to the Assured, and concealed from the Assurer at the time of making the Assurance; and all Assurances, which have no such Information, Intelligence, Undertaking, or Warranty, inserted in the Assurance, shall be deemed and taken as if no Information, Intelligence, Undertaking, or Warranty, had ever been given or made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Cases, where the Interest of the Assured shall fall short of the Interest specified in the Assurance, the Assured shall be intitled to a Return of Premium, in proportion to the Deficiency of his Interest, allowing per Cent, to the Assurer; but, in all Cases where the Assurance shall be adjudged void, or of no Effect, by reason of any Fraud or Deceit, the Assured shall not recover any Part of the Premium paid for such Assurance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Actions to be brought upon Assurances in the Name or Names of any Person or Persons residing in Parts beyond the Seas, or not within the Reach of the Process of the Court where such Action shall be brought, such Court, in Term Time, or any Judge of that Court out of Term, may, upon Application or Motion in behalf of the Defendant or Defendants, and making it appear, to the Satisfaction of the Court or Judge, that the Plaintiff or Plaintiff) do relideor are without the Reach of the Process, as aforesaid, stay all Proceedings in such Action until the Plaintiff or Plaintiffs have given such. Security as the Court or udge shall deem sufficient to pay Colts to the Defendant, in case the Plaintiff or Plaintiffs

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Creditors of the Royal African Company of England,c n behalf of themselves, and the other Cre-

duois of the said Company, was presented to the House, and riad; setting forth. That the said Company are very conlitlerably indebted to the Petitioners, and a great many other Persons; which Debt, the Petitioners conceive, has been principally contracted by the said Company's In-▼eftments in divers Goods, Merchandizes, and Stores, by them exported to the Coast of Africa, for the necessary Support of their Settlements, and upon the Credit given to the said Company by the annual Aids granted to them by Parliament for that Purpose; and that, from the present melancholy Circumstances of the said Company, the Petitioners have but too much Real'on to consider their Forts, Castles, and Possessions, on the Coast of Africa, as the only remaining Property of the said Company, and consequently as the foie llefource and Security from which their unhappy Creditors can hope to obtain a Satisfaction for their just Demands; and that therefore the Petitioners and their Fellow-fuffcrers cannot bufbe alarmed at ever)* Proceeding which may tend to affect the lame; and that in this Light they consider a Petition, lately presented to this House by several Merchants of London, and others, setting forth the declining State of the British Trade to Africa from the Port of London, the Importance of the said Trade to Great Britain, and the Impossibility of preserving the same without maintaining the said Forts, Castles, and Possessions, in the Hands of a Company with a sufficient Joint-Stock: And therefore praying some effectual Provision in the Premises: and that, as the Petition presented this Session, by the said present Company, makes no Mention of thetr Creditors, contrary to their former constantPraftice the Pe-titioners think they should be wanting to themfekres and to their Fellow-sufferers, if they did not lay their same before the House; and that, from the known Justice and Humanity of a British Parliament, the Petitioners make

no doubt, but, in whatever Shape the House shall think Vol. 25.

it necessary for the publick Good to dispose of the said Company, or of their said Fort), Settlements, and Possessions, all due Regard will be had to, and effectual Care will be taken of, the just Claims and Demahds of the Creditors of the said Company; and the rather,.as many of them, if not all, have, by intruding the said Conjpany with Money, Goods, and stores, contributed to support the said Forts and Settlements, and thereby to protest his Majesty's Subjects trading to the Coast of Africa: And therefore praying the House to take the Prerrfife$ into Consideration; and grant them such Protection and Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the trading Citizens of the City of Durham, inhabiting within the said City, and Parts adjacent; and also,

A Petition of the trading Burgesses of the Borough of Stamford, inhabiting within the said Borough; and also,

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Traders of the Borough of Wool ton in the County of Wilts,

inhabiting within the said Borough; and also,

A Petition of the chief trading Inhabitants of the Pari fh of Woodbridge, in the County of Suffolk; and also,

A Petition of the trading Citizens of the City of Norwich, inhabiting within the said City, and Parts adjacent; and also,

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Capital Burgesses, and Inhabitants of the Borough of Banbury, in the County of Oxford; and also,

A Petition of the Traders of the Town and Corporation of Carnarvon, in the County of Carnarvon, inhabiting within the said Town, and Parts adjacent;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; severally alleging. That the Act, made in the 9th and 10th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for licensing Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, has proved detrimental to the fair Trader, and to the Revenue: And therefore praying, That the said Act may be amended or repealed; and if it be the Pleasure of the Legislature to repeal the said Act, that then, as an Equivalent, a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, may be laid upon all Traders within the Limitation of the said Statute; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and trading Inhabitants, of the Borough of Bridgwater, in the County of Somerset, was also presented to the House, and lead; alleging, That the said Act for licensing Hawkers, t Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, has proved of the greatest Prejudice to the fair and settled Traders; such licensed Persons not only, in the Course of their Dealings, imposing

*7

upon injudicious and unwary People, with deceitful Wares and Merchandizes, and Goods pretended to have been run, but being actual Promoters of Smuggling, by frequently carrying with them, and felling, uncustomed and prohibited Goods, whereby the Revenue is greatly defrauded: And therefore praying. That the said Act may be amended or repealed; and if it be the Pleasure of the Legislature to repeal the said Act, that then, as an Equivalent, a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, may be laid upon all Traders within the Limitation of the said Statute; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Freeholders and Traders of the Borough of Chipping Norton, in the County of Oxford, was also presented to the House, and read; complaining of the great Inconveniences and Loss that this Nation luftaihs, by reason of the great Number of Persons licensed to hawk and vend all manner of Goods they think proper, within this Kingdom; and setting forth, That fine Goods, and such as are charged with the highest Duty, are what belt answer their Purposes, and chiefly tend to promote the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, and render the Suppression thereof a Matter of the greatest Difficulty; and that, by their incessant Travelling about the Kingdom, they have an Opportunity of dealing with Persons who pay ready Money for their said Goods, and thereby prevent such Persons from dealing with the settled Traders, who are, by that means, in order to carry on their Trades, obliged to give large Credit for their Goods, which otherwise they would not have done, the bad Consequence of which is, as the Petitioners apprehend, that Multitudes of House-dwelling Tradesmen are rendered not only unable to contribute towards the necessary Expences of the Parishes where they dwell, but are reduced to such Poverty as obliges them to become chargeable to others; whereby the Burthen of the Poor is very much increased, and the Number of those who remain to support them is become almost incapable, in many Places, of doing it, or discharging the necessary Taxes and Payments: And therefore praying, That the Act for licensing Hawkers may be amended or repealed; and if it be the Pleasure of the Legislature to repeal the said Act, that then, as an Equivalent, a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, may be laid upon all Traders within the Limitation of the said Statute; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Traders, Freemen, and Inhabitants, of the City of Coventry, and County of the fame, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the present Act for licensing Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, is greatly evaded and abused, by such as have been licensed, and others, pretending to be Makers or Manufacturers of Goods, or to be their Servants or Agents; and others with Horses, Carts, and Carriages, with Goods for Sale, having only a Foot Licence; and that many, having none, travel from Town to Town, and House to House, defrauding the Revenue, and imposing on great Numbers of ignorant and unwary People, by felling faulty and deceitful Wares and Merchandizes, or bartering and exchanging such, using all manner of fallacious Dealing, to the great Scandal and Reproach of Trade; and as such kind of strolling Traders too frequently correspondwith Smugglers, and other clandcstine Dealers, and may, injure the Revenue in many Branches of the Duty on Goods and Merchandize, and do, by fore-itaHing Markets, and other illicit Practices, greatly injure all the settled fair Traders in general: Therefore praying. A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their common Seal, was pre-

22

fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a Petition of several Merchants of , and others, stiling

themselves interested in, and trading to, and the

BritiJ/iColonies and Plantations in America, hath been presented to the House; suggesting, among other Things, That the African Trade cannot be supported and pre-served against the powerful Competition of other foreign Joint-Stock Companies, without keeping, maintaining, and even increasing, the Number of our Forts, Castles, and Possessions, on that Coast, in the Hands of a Company, with a sufficient Joint-Stock: And representing to the House, That the Trade which is now carried on by the Merchants of tins City to the Coast of , and from thence to his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in rica, is the principal and most considerable Branch of Trade belonging to the said City; and that, since such Trade has been free and open, the same has been greatly increased, and his Majesty's Plantations thereby much better supplied with Negroes, and larger Quantities of the Manufactures of the Kingdom exported; and that the same is, at this time, in a very flourishing Condition: And therefore praying the House, That the Trade to Africa may remain free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchant Adventurers, within the City of Bristol, under their common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; reciting several Allegations contained in a Petition, presented to the House, of several Merchants of , and others, interested in, and trading to, Africa, and the British Colonies and Plantations in America:And representing to the House, That the principal and most valuable Trade of the said City depends, in a great measure, on the Commerce which is now carried on to the Coast of , and from thence to his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in America; and that since the Trade hath been free and open, the same is greatly increased and enlarged, our Plantations much better supplied with Negroes, vast Quantities of Woollen, Iron, Pewter, and other the Manufactures of this Kingdom, exported, many Families employed and supported, and his Majesty's Revenues greatly increased: And therefore praying, That the Trade to Africa may not be subjected to a Company or Joint-Stock; but that it may remain free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain.

And presented to the House a Petition of several of the Owners and Occupiers of certain Fen Lands, lying in the several Parishes of Downham, and Wentworth,

and in a certain extra-parochial Place called By all Fen, in the ljle of Ely and County of Cambridge, whose Names are thereunto subscribed:

Which Petition was read; letting forth. That the Petitioners Richard Houlditch Esquire, who is Owner of an hundred and Fifty Acres of Fen Land, lying in the said Parish of Downham, and Francis Longman, who is also Owner of Five hundred Acres of Fen Lands, commonly called Carter's Farm, lying in the said extra-parochial Place called Byall Fen (making, together, Six hundred and Fifty Acres of Fen Land) fie contiguous to each other; and that the said Petitioners, and the former Owners thereof, have already been at a great Charge, and expended several considerable Sums of Money in imbanking and draining the fame, and in erecting Water Engines thereupon, and for the Improvement and Maintenance thereof; and that the said Carter's Farm, and several other Acres of the other Petitioners Lands, included in the Bill depending in the House, for draining and preserving certain Fen Lands in the several Parishes of Money, Welney,

Downham, Witchford, and Wentworth, and in a certain extra-parochial Place called Byall Fen, being Adventurers Land, and for ever subjected to a large annual draining Tax, by an Act, passed in the 15th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, the Petitioners apprehend, That, after Payment of that Tax, and of the Tax intended by the said Bill to be laid on those Lands, very little (if anything) will remain from the said Lands for the Petitioners, the respective Owners thereof; and that all the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, that the same will be highly prejudicial to the several Estates of the said Petitioners, by reason that the said Fen Lands, lying in the said several Parishes of Downham, Witchford, Wentworth, and the said extraparochial Place called Byall Fen, being all low Grounds, and of very inconsiderable Value, and having only a Moor for making the greatest Part of the Banks, to keep out the Water, cannot be improved, drained, or preserved, or any greater, or more. Advantage made of the said low Grounds, to the respective Proprietors thereof, although the contrary is untruly suggested by the said Bill: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Pet itioners, That the said Bill will be rejected, or, at least, that all the Petitioners said Fen Lands may be left out of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and principal Traders, of the Town of Nottingham whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in the Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Tradesmen of the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Statute, now in Force, giving Liberty to licensed Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, to trade from Town to Town, and to other Men's Houses, however well intended, hath, for several Years past, been greatly prejudicial to the fair "Trader, by reafori such who have been so licensed, practice illicit Dealings, give great Encouragement to Smugglers and others, by vending and disposing Goods, which have not paid any Duty or Custom, and thereby not only defraud the Crown of the Revenue, but are enabled to fell Goods of equal Value, for less than the prime Cost to the fair Trader; and that, under Cover of the said Statute, such licensed Hawkers and Pedlars frequently impose upon People with deceitful and damaged Wares and Merchandizes, that are, in general, a Reproach and Scandal to Trade: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and repeal the said Statute; and that the Legislature will please, in lieu thereof, to lay a Tax, not exceeding Two Shillings a Year, on all Traders within the Limitation of the said recited Statute, as an Equivalent, and to be appropriated to the like Dfes; and that all Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, may be intirely suppressed; and the Petitioners otherwise -relieved in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet. The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the ingrossed Bill, from the Lords, intituled, An Act for the more effectual Trial and Punishment of High Treason, and Misprision of High Treason, in the Highlands of Scotland; and for abrogating the Practice of taking down the Evidence in Writing, in certain criminal Prosecutionsj and for making some further Regulations

relating to Sheriffs Depute; and Stewards Depute, and their Substitutes; and for other Purposes therein mentioned;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause or Clauses, for impowering the Court of Session in Scotland to regulate the Fees of the Clerks or Writers to the Signet there.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

The Lord Dupplin took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

The Lord Dupplin reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereunto Licensing subscri bed, Traders and Inhabitants of the Town of Shrew/-bury, in the County of Salop, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, who travel and trade about the Country, by virtue of an Act, made in the Ninth Year of Kiqs;

William the Third, are very prejudicial to the Petitioners,

and others the settled Traders and Inhabitants of England and Wales \and frequently fell Wares of various druids,

without Licences, with Impunity, most People-being ferq-pulous of becoming Informers; whe»fby hjjs MajestyS Revenues are diminished, and the Intention of the said Act of Parliament <vad«l; and that, notwithstanding the said itinerant petty Chapmen, who contribute nothing (except for their Licences, if taken out) to the Exigencies of the State, have mocha he Advantage of the Petitioners, who greatly, and with Chearfuinels, bear their Proportions in all public k Taxes, and may, consequently, afford to undersell the Petitioners; yet, taking Advantage of the weak and injudicious. Experience evinces. That they not only frequently vend damaged and unmerchantable Goods, but at higher Prices than settled and fair Traders commonly fell, to the great Detriment of the Petitioners and this Kingdom: And therefore praying. That, upon __

the Petitioners and others the lettled and lair Traders of this Kingdom railing and making good an annual Revenue, equal to the Money arising from the Licences granted as aforesaid, in such Manner as the House shall think proper, the said Act, or so much thereof as permits Hawkers,

Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, to travel and trade from House to House, may be repealed; or that the House will grant such Remedy in the Premises as the Nature of the Cale shall or may require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Court of Session in Scotland having, in pursuarree of an Act of the last Session of Parliament, ftnished the Examination thereby directed, touching the Titles and Values of the several Heretable Jurisdictions and Offices, 'claimed before that Court, and made a Certificate of *their Opinions thereupon to his Majesty, in his Privy-Council; and all the said Jurisdictions and Offices being actually extinguished, or resumed and annexed to the Crown respectively, from the 25th Day of March last, his Majesty has commanded a Copy of the said Cert ificate to be laid before this House; and recommends it to his faithful Commons, to make Provision for the Payment of such reasonable and just: Compensation and Satisfaction to the Proprietors of those Jurisdictions and Offices, as was by the said Act intended and directed.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow. Morning, take his Majesty's most gracious Message into Consideration.

Then the Title of the said Copy was read;

The laid Copy is as followeth;

Unto the King's most Excellent Majesty in Privy-

Council:

The humble Report and Certificate of the Lords of Council and Session in Scotland:

It appeared by an Account presented to the House, from the Commissioners of the Customs, and referred to your Committee, That there has been imported into this Kingdom, at a Medium for Ten Years last past, 693,404 Pounds of Indico in each Year.

And by an Account presented to your Committee, by the proper Officer of the Customs, it appears. That for Six Years of the said Term, immediately preceding the War with France, there was imported annually from France and French Flanders, 589,571 Pounds Weight of Indico, at an Average, in each Year.

By another Account, presented also by the proper Officer of the Customs to your Committee, of the Quantity of Indico exported from England {ox Ten Years last past, it appeared, That the Quantity exported to Ireland amounted, at an Average in each Year, to 65,822 Pounds Weight; and to foreign Parts for the same Time, at an Average for each Year, to 54,695 Pounds Weight.

So that the Consumption in England and Ireland appears to be, at an Average for the last Ten Years, 638,709 Pounds Weight.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine the folr lowing Witnesses:

Mr. Jennings: Who said. That in his Trade of a Linen Dyer they use nothing but French Indico; but that he had used about 300#. Weight of Carolina Indico, by way of Experiment; which, though it did not appear to the Eye equal to French, yet it opened kind, worked free, and gave as good a Colour as the French: That even the Dull proved as good in working as the Lumps; and that he apprehended the Indico's not appearing so well is to be attributed to the Want of Art in the Planters or Curers, to set it off.

And Mr. Chrutchley Cole, Woollen Dyer, said, That he had used Carolina Indico, which answered his Purpose as well as the French:

And he apprehended the Price of the French Indico would have been considerably augmented, had it not been for the Importation of the Carolina.

Mr. Olive, Callico Dyer, said. That he had used Carolina Indico, from 18 d.to 51. the Pound: That what he bought for 18 d.a Pound appeared, at the first Sight, to be unfit for any Use; but, upon Trial, he found, that by increasing the Quantity only, it answered the Purposes of the belt French; for 40 Pounds of the worst Carolina was equal to 30 Pounds of good French: That he had tried the very best Sort of Indico that could be bought for Money, both French and Spanish, and that the Carolina Indico stains as well and as deep as either: That the best Sort of Spanish Indico, called Flora, looks finer; but the Colour of the Carolina is as durable, and will answer all the Uses of the Flora in Callico Printing: That he apprehends, that there is a Possibility of fixing a Standard of Indico.

And all the aforesaid witnesses agreed, That there is an absolute Necessity for the Use of Indico in the Dyeing Trade; and that no good Blue can be dyed without it.

Mr. Daniel Valentine, Broker, said. That until the Year 1715, or 1716, great Quantities of Indico had been imported from Jamaica and Montserrat, which served for our Consumption when we had no French: That upon the first Importation of French it was not near so good as at present: That he has seen and fold Carolina Indico, which will answer all Purposes; and he never wanted a Market for it: That the last Ships which came in, viz. in March last, with about 30,000 Pound Weight, lowered the Price of Indico 3 d.per Pound: That the Spanish Indico is of different Sorts, from 3 6 to 6s. 6 per Pound; and at the same Time French Indico was at 5 per Pound: That before the Importation of French Indico the Jamaica Indico fold from 5 to 7 a Pound: And being shewn a Sample of Carolina Indico, he said, in his Opinion, it came near the best Spanish, called Flora, and r. juici answer the same Purposes.

a i Geos II. 19" Aprilis. 635

Mr. MatthrtvHud/on, Broker, confirmed the Accounts of the Quantities imported into Great Britain, and said. That Nine-tenths thereof is French Indico: That the Difference in the Sorts of French Indico is not more than in the Pound Value; but that he knows that the different Sorts of Carolina Indico is fold from 18 to 5J. and and Spanish from is. 6 dto 6s. per Pound: That the Price of French Indico, for Three or Four Years before the Commencement of the French War, was from 3 4J. to js. 6 d.at an Average: That he has seen as good

Carolina Indico as any he ever saw from France, and very near as good as the best Spanish, called Flora, which excels the French Indico.

That there are Three Species of Indico, called Copper, Purple, and Blue, which are applied to distinct Purposes; the Two last Sorts, giving the fined Gloss, are, for that Reason, made use of by the Cotton and Linen Dyers, and thehrft Sort by the Dyers of Woollen Cloth: That there is a visible Distinction between French and Carolina Indico: and that 'tis an cafy Matter to ascertain the Standard of Indico, since any Custom-house Officer, though he had never before been acquainted with that Commodity, would be made a competent Judge of it in aWeck'sTime as well as in Seven Years.

And Mr. Benjamin Vaughan, Broker, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Hud/on, in regard to the Easiness of fixing the Standard of Indico.

Mr. Michael Bland, Broker, said. That the Way to judge of the Standard or Value of Indico was by the Sight and the Touch: That there are Three different Species, the Copper, the Purple, and the Blue, which are all used fordiftinci Purposes; and that any Person, though he has never been acquainted with Indico, may learn to be a competent judge of it in Three Days Time.

Besides the Quantity of 30;oooo Pounds Weight, mentioned by Mr Valentine,

Mr. Arthur Gold, Matter of the Charming Nanney, from Charles-Town, South Carolina, being examined, informed your Committee, That he arrived in the River on Monday the 11 th of this Month; and that he has upwards of 30,000 Pounds Weight of made Indico on

board.

And Mr. Peter Bojlock, Matter of the Mary, from Carolina, said. He was taken by a French Privateer, and carried into Bayonne-, and that he had 27,000 Pounds Weight of Carolina-made Indico on board, which was fold

at Bayonne, while he was there, for Five Livres a Pound, and which was equal to what the French Indico fold for at that Port.

Mr. Watson, Clerk to Mr, Crockatt, produced to your Committee, an Account, which he said he knew to be the Hand-writing of Mr. Raper, Clerk to the Custom-house in Charles-Town, South Carolina, who transmitted the Accounts of the Expons of the Produce of that Province annually to Mr. Crockatt, by which Account it appeared, That 46,674 Pounds Weight of Indich, of the Crop of 1746, had been exported from Carolina: And the Witness said. He believed a much greater Quantity had been exported since, both from South and North Carolina.

Mr. Tuite, Merchant, being examined, said, That formerly ar Montserrat they made 30 or 40,000/^. Weight a Year, and now not a Fourth or Fifth Part of that Quantity: That the Reason that made them leave it off was, because it was inferior to the French: That Montserrat Indico is much inferior to the Carolina Indico, being worth little more than Half the Price.

Mr. Morrant, Mr. Pringle, Mr. Sacheverell, Planters in Carolina, informed your Committee, That they have all of them made Indico in that Province: That the Herb from whence Indico is made, grows in great Plenty in Carolina: That they could raise any Quantity of Seed in a Year or Two; but as People did not care to venture on an Uncertainty, none but the Rich attempted it: That if it was fixed to a Staple, and Encouragement given, the poor People wouldfcome into it; and that they think that Carolina will, in that Cafe, be able, in a few Years, to Vol. 15.

supply all the Indico Great Britain will want: They said. That the People of Carolina expected a Bounty for their Encouragement; and that the Healthiness of the Climate, and Cheapness of Provisions, and other Things, will, in Time, give them a great Advantage in this Manufacture.

In order to shew the Expence of erefling an Indico-Work to employ ao Negroes, they produced to your Committee, a Computation, amounting tojf. 96 x6r. o which they all agreed was a larger Sum than the Generality of Planters could be supposed to engage in, without some Certainty of having a Preference to Foreigners at this Market.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Gon-sideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upoo Morn-

ing next, resolve itself into a Committee: of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

A Petition of the Dyers of the City of was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Indico is absolutely necessary in their Trade; and that they cannot dye a good Blue without it: That the Importation of this useful Commodity has, for many Years, been mostly from France; and that some of the Petitioners have lately bought Indico, which they imagine to be the Produce and Growth of Carolina, and, on Trial, find it to be equally as good for dyeing as the French; and that as the Plant from which Indico is made grows there in great Plenty, so we may reasonably expect that we shall be supplied from thence with any Quantity, if proper Encouragement be given thereto but for a few Years; and that the Making of this beneficial Article in the British Plantations, will be of great Service to us, and be a Means not only of reducing the Price, but also of furnishing us with a more certain and constant Supply: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant such Assistance therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Crockatt

Esquire, on behalf of himself, and several other Merchants trading to his Majesty's Plantations in America, was referred.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred toconGder of the Report trom the Committee, to whom the Petition of fames Crokatt Esquire, on behalf of himself, and several other Merchants trading to h'S Majesty's Plantations in America, was referred, and of the several Petitions referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Encouraging of the Growth of Indico in his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in America, will be a great Advantage to the Trade of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty on all good and merchantable Indico, of the Growth of his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in America, will be a proper Encouragement for promoting the Growth and Making thereof in the said Colonies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of Six Pence in the Pound be allowed upon all good and merchantable Indico made to a certain Standard in the British Plantations in America, and imported under proper Regulations directly into Great Britain from the Place of its Growth, and where made; and that such Bounty be paid out of the Customs.

The Two First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Third Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

VOL. 2$.

The following Amendments were proposed to be made thereto; viz.

To leave out, after " Six Pence," the Words " in the," and insert, instead thereof! the Words " upon every;" and, after the Word " Pound," to insert the Word Weight:"

And the Question being put, That the Words " in " the," proposed to be left out, stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words, " upon " every" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And thcQuestion being put, That the Word "Weight" be inserted after the Word " Pound;"

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said llesolution, thus amended, That a Bounty of Six Pence upon every Pound Weight be allowed upon all good and merchantable Indico made to a certain Standard in the British Plantations in America, and imported under proper Regulations directly into Great Britain from the Place of its Growth, and where made; and that such Bounty be paid out of the Customs.

N. B. The Reason why these Amendments were made by the House to the said Resolution, is inserted in the Clerk's Minute-Book of this Day.

A Petition of several Clothiers, Dyers, and others, con- Encdunging cerned in the Woollen Manufacture at Trowbridge, its the County of Wilts, was presented to the House. and read; °

reciting some Allegations contained in a Petition of James Crokatt Esquire, presented to this House; and setting forth. That the Petitioners conceive the said Allegations to be true in general; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Subject of the said Petition, now under the Consideration of the House, is a Matter of great Importance to the Trade and Manufactures of this Kingdom: And therefore representing to the House, That Indico is indispensably necessary in many of our Manufactures; and that vast Quantities, to a very great Value, are annually consumed in this Kingdom; and that the chief Supply thereof, for many Years past, hath been from France; and that our being supplied with this valuable Commodity from the British Plantations, for which we now pay a same Sum annually to the French, will not only help to distress our Enemies, but at the same time be a considerable national Advantage, as well as a private one to the Petitioners, and all others concerned in the Manufactures of Wool, Flax, Silk, and Cotton, as they will thereby be capable of rendering their Goods cheaper at a foreign Market, and consequently of extending their private Trades; and that the Petitioners conceive the principal Reason why the Production and Manufacture of this valuable Commodity are reduced to almost nothing, is, the fraudulent and deceitful Methods made use of by the Planters in the Making and Packing of it, regarding only their own Emolument and immediate Private Advantage, which have brought Indico (the Produce of our Settlements) into such Disgrace, that no one cares to purchase or use it: And that the French, &c. take great Care, by Inspection, and Seals, before Exportation, to prevent Frauds; by which means they have brought the Commodity to the greatest Perfection, and into the highest Reputation; and that a national Assistance will avail little towards the Recovery and Extension of this valuable Branch of Commerce, without more Honour and Integrity arc exercised by the Planters; or such good and whol-some Laws constituted, and put in Execution, as may effectually prevent such gross Frauds, Abuses, and Adulterations for the future; and finally, that the Petitioners conceive it would be highly injurious to the Trade and Manufactures of this Kingdom in genera], to lay any Duty or Import on any foreign Indico, in order to encourage and promote the Consumption of our own Growth,

Clause A: " And be it Enacted by the Authority " aforesaid, That any Assignee or Assignees, to whom,

" by virtue of thi?, or any former, Act of Parliament,

" made for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, the Estate or " Effects of any Prisoner or Prisoners hath been, or shall be, assigned, is and are hereby impowered, by and with the Consent of the major Part, in Value, of such Prisoner or Prisoners Creditors, who shall be present at " a Meeting to be had for that Purpose, of which Twenty- one Dayspublick Notice shall be previously given, inTwo " London Gazettes, to make Composition with any Person or Persons, Debtors or Accountants to such Prison-" er or Prisoners, where the same shall appear necessary or " reasonable, and to take such reasonable Part, as can, " upon such Composition, be gotten, in full Discharge of " such Debts and Accounts; and-also to submit any Differenceor Dispute between such Assignee or Assignees,

" and any Person or Persons whatsoever, for, on account, " or by reason or means, of any Matter, Cause,.or Thing, " relating to such Prisoner or Prisoners Estates or Effects, " or to any Debtor Debts, due, or claimed to be due, to or from such Prisoner or Prisoners, to the final End and " Determination of Arbitrators, to be chosen by the said " Assignee or Assignees, and the major Part, in Value, " of such Creditors, and the Party or Parties with whom " they shall have such Difference, and to perform the " Award of such Abstrators, or otherwise to settle and agree the Matters in Difference and Dispute between " them, in such Manner as the said Assignee or Assignees, " with such Consent as aforesaid, shall think lit, and can " agree; and the same shall be binding to all the Credit " tors of such Prisoner or Prisoners; and the said Assignees are hereby indemnified for what they shall fairly " do, according to the Direction aforesaid."

Clause B: " Provided always. And be it Enacted, by " the Authority aforesaid, That no Person, who took the " Benefit of an Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year oflus " present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, shall have or receive any Benefit or Advantage of, or under, this Act, nor shall be deemed to be within the Meaning thereof; any thing " herein contained to the contrary notwithstanding."

The said Amendments, as far as Clause A, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

After which his Majesty was plealed to make a most gracious Speech, from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The King's At the Opening of this Session of Parliament, I inform-Speech. ed you. That a Congress had been agreed upon by the several Powers at War; and 1 have now the Satisfaction to acquaint you. That Preliminaries for restoring a general Peace have been signed between my Minister and those of the most Christian King and the States General of the United Provinces; the Balls of which isa general Restitution of Conquests made, during the War, on all Sides.

In consequence of these Preliminaries, which have been ratified by all the contracting Parties, a Cessation of Hof-tiiities has actually taken place in th Countries, and in the Channel; and certain Periods are fixed, according to former Practice, for its Commencement in other Parts of the World.

In this important Transaction, my great Views have been, ftcadily to adhere to the true Interests of Europe, to pursue and maintain those of my own Kingdoms in particular, and to procure for my Allies the belt Terms and Conditions that the Events of a War, in some Parts unsuccessful, did admit.

I have, in the Course of this Negotiation, acted with the most unreserved Confidence and Communication towards my Allies; and I hope, That when they shall have maturely weighed the Situation of Affairs, the Necessity from thence arising, and the Care and Attention which have been shewn for their Advantage and Security, they will not delay to accede to these preliminary Articles, but concur in effectuating the good Work of Peace.

The vigorous and powerful Support you have given me, during this Session, towards carrying on the War, has strengthened my Hands, in proceeding thus far in the Meal'ures of Peace. Nobody can suggest the lead Failure on the Part of Great Britain 1 which, not only for the fake of its own particular Interest, but of the common Caule, has taken on itself a Share of the Burthen unexam-3

pled in former Times. I hope soon to fee this necessary Work brought to Perfection, with the Concurrence of all my Allies, with whom it is my firm Intention to cultivate the most perfect Harmony, and to cement and strengthen, if possible, the Ties of our ancient Union and Friendship, in such a manner as may render the Peace secure and durable.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

My particular Thanks are due to you for the ample Provision you have made for the Service of the current Year. Nothing could have contributed so much to the putting an End to the Calamities of War, and reducing our future Expences, as these well judged Supplies. The most prudent Economy shall be made use of in the Application of them; and, you may be assured, nothing will give me more real Pleasure, than to take the First Opportunity of lessening the present Burthens of my People.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot sufficiently express my intire Satisfaction in your whole Conduct, during this Session; and I mutt recommend it to you, to promote in your several Countries a right Sense of those Measures which have been (o necessarily taken for the Security and Ease of my People As it is the earned Desire of my Heart to lee the Crown of Great Britain maintain that Figure, Strength, and Weight, in making War and Peace, which justly belong to it; it is equally so, to lee my good Subjects enjoy the Blessings of Tranquillity and Prolperity,

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command, said,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued until Thursday the 30th Day of June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued until Thursday the 30th Day of June next.

By the LORDS JUSTICES.

A PROCLAMATION.

Tho. Can/uar. Bedford,

Hardwicke, C. Pelham.

Gower, C. P. S.

WHEREAS this present Parliament stands prorogued to this Day, being the Thirteenth

of October, One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-eight,

We, with the Advice of his Majesty's Privy-Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, from thisThirteenth Day of October, to Tuesday the Twenty-ninth Day of next; and

that We have given Order that aCommission be prepared for the proroguing the same accordingly: And We do

hereby further declare his Majesty's Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Twenty-ninth Day of November, be held, and fit for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shires and Burghs of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance, accordingly, at on Tuesday

the Twenty-ninth Day of November next.

Given at Whitehall, the Thirteenth Day of October

1748, and in the Twenty-second Year of his Majesty's Reign.

GOD save the Kino.

MESSAGE from his Majesty, by the Honourable Mr. Bellenden, Gentleman-Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend his Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First time.

Refo/ved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I acquainted you at the Close of the last Session of Parliament, That Preliminary Articles fora general Pacification had been signed by my Minister, and those of

the most Christian King, and the States General of the United Provinces; to which the Empress Queen of Hungary, the Kings of Spain and Sardinia, and the other Powers engaged in the War, soon afterwards acceded.

I loft no Time in taking the proper Measures with my Allies for effedluating a General Peace, by a definitive Treaty, in which all Parties were to concur; and notwithstanding the Difficulties which must attend foexten-five a Work, wherein the respective Interests of so many Powers were to be finally adjusted by common Consent,

I have been able, by the Blessing of God, in the Course of the Summer, to complete it; and I have the Pleasure to acquaint you, that a definitive Treaty, previously concerted with my Allies, has been signed by my Ministers, and those of France, and the States General; to which all the other Powers concerned in the War have acceded, without Reserve.

It has been my chief Endeavour, in putting an End to the Calamities of War, to make the most effectual Provision for securing the Rights and Interests of my own Subjects, and to procure the best Terms and Conditions for my Allies, that the Situation of Affairs would admit: And I take much Satisfaction in being able to tell you, that I have found a general good Disposition in all the Parties engaged in the War, to bring this Negotiation to a happy Conclusion. From these Circumstances we may promise ourselves, under God, a long Enjoyment of the Blessings of Peace, provided we make the right Ule and Improvement of it. x

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

Mr. Oswald: And they are to meet upon Monday Sevennight, at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker's Chamber; and to fit every day, Friday, and Monday, in the Afternoon: And all that come are to have Voices: And they are to take into Confederation all such Matters as shall or may come in Question touching Returns, Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon double Returns in the First place; and

to report their Proceedings, with their Opinions thereupon, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question any Returns, are to do it within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are returned for Two or more Places, are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place:

And if any thing shall come inQuestion touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate:

And that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right Usual to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve Order*, in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured (b to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence-to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that ho Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker's Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

The Lord Barrington reported from the Committee, Address on appointed Yederday to draw up an Address to be pre- th* King's fented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn sP«ch. up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects* the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne, and to congratulate your Majesty on your safe and happy Return to these Kingdoms.

We acknowledge, with the utmod Gratitude, your Majesty's conllant Attention to the Good of your People; and beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on the Success of your Endeavours for restorin Peace to Europe, by the happy Conclusion of a Definitive Treaty, in which all your Allies have concurred without Reserve; and we cannot, on this Occasion, but admire your Majesty's Wisdom and Conduct by which you have, in so short a l'pace-of Time, reconciled and adjuded so many jarring Intereds, and completed this great and necessary Work.

Permit us, Sir, humbly to return your Majesty our Thanks for your tender Regard to your faithful Subjects, in taking the fird Opportunity to reduce the publick Ex-pences, which has been done with unusual Dispatch; and wc acknowledge equally your Majesty's Wisdom, in recommending to us Economy, and the Improvement of the Revenue, both absolutely necessary in our present Circumdances, in order tt> lessen the national Debt, eale your PeopleHand drengthen ourfolves against all future Events; and we allure your Majesty, That ve will omit nothing which may conduce to those important and salutary Ends.

It gives the highed Satisfaction to your faithful Commons, that your Majesty has beep graciously plealed to take Notice oif the Bravery of your Forces by Sea and Land, an Honour their Behaviour has modly justly deferred; and we do allure your Majesty, that all due Attention shall be paid, on our Part, to the Services of those gallant Men, who have signalized themselves so glorioudf in Defence of their Country. i

We arc truly sensible of the Importance of that signal'

Succcls which has attended your Majesty's Arms at Sea; through the Course of the War; and are fully convinced how necessary it is to maintain oUr Fleets in perfect Strength and Order, even in Times of the most profound Peace.

Your faithful Commons beg Leave humbly to assure your Majesty, That they will grant such Supplies, as are ne-. ceflary to secure effectually the Peace and Tranquillity of your Majesty's Government, and to preserv the Honour: of the Nation, by making good its Engagements; and that the chief Objedsof our Consideration shall be, what your Majesty has so graciously and wifely recommended to us, the Improvement of our Commerce, the Supporting and Strengthening of publick Credit, and the Culti* vation of the Arts of Peace, that your Majesty may be' enabled to gratify your Royal Inclinations, by making this Nation a flourishing and happy People, under your auspicious Government, and that of your Royal Family, to future Generations.

The said Address being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Anno 22° Georgii II*1 Regis, 1748. Prater*.

MR. Speaker reported. That the House, upon Thursday last, attended his Majesty with their Address: To which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I thank you most heartily for this very affectionate Address.

You may rely upon my ready Concurrence with you in the Execution of all such Measures as will relieve my People as soon as possible, from the Burthens which the Exigencies of War have laid upon them, and procure to them the Blessings of a safe and lasting Peace.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, t» consider of the Motion, made upon Thursday last, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty;

Ordered, That his Majesty's most gracious Speech toboth Houses of Parliament be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Fane took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Fane reported from the Committee, That they had

22

Come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Famborough Mr. Sydney Stafford reported from the Com-

Roadt. mittee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the County of Kent, living in and near the Road leading from Earn borough, in the said County of Kent, to a Place called Vot. 25.

Riverhill, in the Parish of SeveHoakes, in the same County,-whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the following Witm-ffes were examined; viz.

Mr. Francis Austen: Who said. That he is well acquainted with the Road described in the Petition, which is Eleven Miles in Length, and much frequented by Carriages and Hurfemen: That most Part of it is in a very ruinous Condition, and extremely inconvenient to Passengers; for in several Places the Road is so narrow, as not to admit Two Carriages to pals one another, nor even a Passenger on Horltback to pass by a Carriage:

That the Witness himlelt has been frequently obliged to get over into the Fields to avoid a Carriage: That at the bottom of Marmfcott llillis a deep hollow Way, which was absolutely impassable last Year for the Space of a Month, being filled i.p with Snow: That 'tis impossibla for the several Parishes, through which the said Road leacF,sufficiently to repair the same by the ordinary Course of Law; and that the Road is so narrow in many Places, that 'tis impracticable to render it commodious without a Power to compel the Owners of Lands on each Side to dispose of such Part of their Property as may be necessary for that Pu pole.

The Reverend Mr Thomas Curtis confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Austen in every Particular: And added.

That he (the Witness) had been often obliged to quit the Road at the Bottom of Marmfcott Hill, on account of the Snow last Winter, as well on Ilorfeback as in his Chaise.

The Witness added, That he had been Surveyor of such Part of the said Road as lies in the Parish of Seven -oak (which is about Three Miles) for Three Years lait past; during which time the Statute-work had been constantly done, and a Rate of 6 d. in the Pound had been levied on the Inhabitants, which had been applied towards the Repairing of the said Road: That the Witness had not yet settled his Accounts as Surveyor; but he believes he has laid out about Fifty Pounds of his own Money, besides the 6 d.in the Pound, as aforesaid, and yet the Roads are In a very ruinous Condition:

That great Part of the Road is worn yery hollow, and there are many Quicksands in it.

Mr. Peter IVinn, Mr. Robert Cockett, Mr. Ashton, Mr.

Know, and Mr. Infell, the several Surveyors of the Road for the Parishes of Famborough, Chevening, Otford, and Chelsfield, through which the said Road leads, being severally examined, all agreed. That though the Statute-work had been constantly performed, the Road was very bad; and that it was impossible to amend the same by the ordinary Course of Law: And Mr. Cockett, Surveyor fi r the Parish of Chevening, added, That a Rate even of Five Shillings in the Pounds would be insufficient to repair such Part or the Road as lies within the said Parish.

Importance of this Trade to his Majesty's Colonies in America is well known, and as the Preservation thereof is allowed principally to depend upon the Maintenance and Support of the Petitioners Forts and Settlements, therefore praying the House, on behalf of themselves, and their Creditors, to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant such lading Encouragement to the Petitioners, as may enable them to pay their Debts, and keep and maintain their said Forts and Cadies in a defensible Condition, for the Protection of a free and open Trade of all his Majesty's Subjects to the Coast of Africa; or to grant the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr.Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty'sCora-mand, acquainted the House, That his Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the Committee examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. John Low: Who said, That he was well acquainted with the Lands mentioned in the Petition, which have been always overflowed in wet Seasons, and are this Year more lb than ever: That these Lands cannot be drained by the common Tax of Bedford Level; but that a Fall might be made, sufficient for that Purpose, by the Help of Mills.

That the Lands are about io or 12,000 Acres, which, when drained, would be worth 8r. an Acre; but, in their present Condition, are worth little or nothing.

Mr. Thomas Johnson confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Low: And added, That he knew One Farm, confiding of 430 Acres, which had formerly been lett for 200 per Annum, but that the Rent was now reduced to £. 130 per Annum, the Lands being more liable to be overflowed of late, from the Defect of the Outfall for discharging the Land-water.

We Mary Therefia, (Be. make known by these Presents:

Whereas, in order to put an End to the fatal War, certain Preliminary Articles were agreed upon, the 30th of April of this Year, between the Ministers Plenipotentiaries of the mail Serene and most Potent Prince George lid. King of Great Britain, and the most Serene and most Potent Prince Lewis XV. the most Christian King, and their High MightinelTes the States General of the United Provinces, which have been since ratified by all the Powers concerned: The Tenor of the Fourth Article whereof is conceived in the following Manner:

The Duchies of Parma, Placentia, and Guaftalla, shall be yielded to the most Serene Infont Don to serve him as An Establ foment, with the Right of Reversion to the present Possessors, after that his Majesty the King of the Two Sici/iet shall have succeeded to the Crown of Spain, as also in case the said most Serene Infont Don Philip should happen to die without Children.

And whereas a Definitive Treaty of Peace having since been concluded, the several Points relating to this Afiair have been, by virtue of the Articles thereof, explained by the common Content of the Parties concerned, in the following Manner:

In consideration of the Restitutions that his most Christian Majesty and his Catholick Majesty make by the present Treaty, either to her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, or to his Majesty the King of Sardinia, the Duchies of Parma, Placentia, and Guaftalla, shall, for the future, belong to tire most Serene Infant Don Philip, to be possessed by1 him, and his Male Descendants, born in lawful Marriage, in the same Manner, and in the same Extent, as they have been, or ought to be, possessed by the present Possessors; and the said most Serene Infant, or his Male Descendants, foall enjoy the said Three Duchies, conformably and under the Conditions expressed in the Acts of Cession of die Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and of the King of Sardinia.

Theie Acts of Cession of the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and of the King of Sardinia, shall be delivered, together with their Ratifications of the present Treaty, tb the AmbafTador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Catholick King, in like manner as the AmbafLdors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiares of the most Christian King and Catholick King foall deliver, with the Ratifications of their Majesties, to the Ambafla-dor Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the King of Sardinia, the Orders to the Generals of the French and Spanish Troops, td restore Savoy and the County of Nice to the - Vol. 25.

Persons appointed by that Prince to receive them; so Treaty 6f that the Restitution of the said States, and the taking Peace with Possession of the Duchies of Parma, Placentia, and Guaf- France, &c. talla, by or in the Name of the most Serene Infant Don Philip, may be effected in the same Time, conformably to the said Acts of Cession.

Wherefore, in order to fulfil those Things to which we have bound-ourselves by the Articles before inserted, and in the firm Hope that the most Christian and Catholick Kings, and the future Possessor of the aforesaid Three Duchies, and his Male Descendants, will, on their Part, bond side and pundlually fulfil the Tenor of the Articles above-mentioned, and willlikewife restore to us, within the same Time, the States and Places which are to be restored to us, in consequence of the Second and Eighteenth Articles of the same Preliminaries, we do yield and renounce, for us and our Successors, under the Conditions expressed in the above-mentioned Articles, all Rights, Claims, and Pretensions, to us, under any Title or Cause whatsoever belonging, upon the aforesaid Three Duchies of Parma, Placentia, and Guaftalla, formerly possessed by us, and transfer the same Rights,

Claims, and Pretensions, in the bed and most solemn Manner possible, to the most Serene Don Philip, Infant of Spain, and his Male Descendants, to be born in lawful Marriage; abl'olving all the Inhabitants of the said Duchies from the Allegiance and Oath which they have taken to us, who shall be obliged, for the future, to pay the same Allegiance to those to whom we have yielded our Rights; all which, however, is to be understood only for that Space of Time that either the said most Serene Infont Don Philip, or One of his Defendants, shall not have ascended either the Throne of the Two Sicilies, or of Spain; for at that Time, and in case the aforefotd Infant should die without Male Defendants, we expressly reserve to ourselves, our Heirs and Successors, all Rights, Claims, and Pretensions, which have heretofore belonged to us; and consequently the Right of Reversion to the said Duchies.

In Witness whereof, (Be.

' Art. XV.

It has been settled and agreed upon, between the Eight High Contracting Parties, That for the Advantage and Maintenance of the Peace in general, and for the Tranquillity of Italy in particular, allThings shall remain there in the Condition they were in before the War, laving and after the Execution of the Dispositions made by the present Treaty.

Art. XVI.

The Treaty of the Alfiento for the Trade of Negroes signed at Madrid, on the 26th of March 1713, and the Article of the annual Ship, making Part of the feidTreaty, are particularly confirmed by the present Treaty, for the Four Years, during which the Enjoyment thereof has been interrupted, fir.ee the Commencement of the present War, and shall be executed on the same Footing, and under the same Conditions, as they have or ought to have been executed, before the said War.

Art. XVII.

Dunkirk shall remain fortified on the side of the Land, in the same Condition as it is at present; and as to the Side of the Sea, it shall remain on the Footing of former Treaties.

Art. XVIII.

The Demands of Money that his Majesty

has, as Elector of Hanover, upon the Crown of Spain, the Differences relating to the Abbey of St. Hubert, the Enclaves of Hainault, and the Bureaux, newly established

in the Low Countries, the Pretensions of the Elector Palatine, and the other Articles which could not be regulated, so as to enter into the present Treaty, shall be amicably adjusted immediately, by the Commissaries appointed for that Purpose on both Sides, or otherwise as shall be agreed on by the Powers concerned.

Art. XIX.

The Fifth Article of the Treaty of the Quadruple Alliance concluded at London, the ad of August 1718, containing the Guaranty of the Succession tot the Kingdom of Great Britain, in the House of his Britannuk Majesty now reigning, and by which every thing has been provided for

that can relate to the Person who has taken the Title of Treaty of King of Great Britain, and to his Defeendants of both j£*c*'"ic* Sexes, is expressly confirmed and renewed by the present *ra"ce' c* Article, as if it was here inserted, in its full Extent.

Art. XX.

His Britannick Majesty, as Elector of Ltt-

nebourg, as well for himself, as for his Heirs and Successors, and all the States and Possessions of his said Majesty in Germany, are included and guarantied by the present Treaty of Peace.

Art. XXI.

All the Powers interested in the present Treaty, who have guarantied the Pragmatick Sanction of the 19th of April 1713, for the whole Inheritance of the late Emperor Charles VI. in Favour of his Daughter the Empress Queen of Hungary and Bohemia now reigning, and of her Defeendants for ever, according to the Order established by the said Pragmatick Sanction, renew it in the bed Manner possible; except, however, the Ce(lions already made, either by the said Emperor or the said Princess, and those stipulated by the present Treaty.

Art. XXII.

The Duchy of Silesia and the County of Glatz, as his Prujftan Majesty now possesses them, are guarantied to that Prince, by all the Powers, Parties, and Contractors, of the present Treaty.

Art. XXIII.

All the Powers contracting and interested in the present Treaty, reciprocally and respectively guaranty the Execution thereof.

Art. XXIV.

The solemn Ratifications of the present Treaty, expedited in good and due Form, shall be exchanged in this City of Aix la Chapelle, between all the Eight Parties, within the Space of One Month, or sooner if possible. to be reckoned from the Day of its Signature.

In Witness whereof, We, the Under-written, their Am-baffadors Extraordinary and Ministers Plenipotentiaries, have signed with our Hands, in their Name, and by virtue of our full Powers, the present Treaty of Peace, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Aix la Chapelle, the 18th of October 1748.

Signed,

Separate Articles.

Some of the Titles made use of by the con trading Powers, either in the full Powers and other Acts during the course of the Negotiation, or in the Preamble of the present Treaty, not being generally acknowledged, it has been agreed. That no Prejudice shall, at any time, result therefrom, to any of the said contracting Parties; and that the Titles taken or omitted on either Side, on account of the said Negotiation, and of the present Treaty, shall not be cited, or any Consequence drawn therefrom.

II.

It has been concluded and agreed, That the French Language, made use of in all the Copies of the present Treaty, and which may be used in the Acts of Accession, shall not be made a Precedent, that may be alleged or drawn into Consequence, or in any Manner prejudice any

of the contracting Powers; and that they conform themselves, for the future, to what has been and ought to be observed, with regard to, and on the Part of Powers who are used and have a Right to give and receiveCopies of like Treaties and Acts, in another Language than the French.

The present Treaty, and the Accessions which shall intervene, having still the same Force and Effect as if the aforesaid Practice had been therein observed, and the present separate Articles shall have: fikewife the feme Force, as if they were inserted in the Treaty.

In Witness whereof. We, the Under-written, Ambaffactors Extraordinary and Ministers Plenpotedtiaries of his Britannick Majesty, of his moil Christian Majesty, and of the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, have signed the present Separate Articles, and caused the Seals of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Aix la Chapelle, the 18th of October 1748.

Whereas it has been my most earnest Desire, ever since Divine Providence has trofted me with the Government of the vast Dominions annexed to my Crown, to put an honourable End to the Troubles in which I found my Arms involved, and to concur in giving Peace to Europe, by all the just Means that should appear most conducive to that End: And whereas I knowing that several Ministers, particularly those of the Powers now at War, are meeting at la Chapelle, with the same View to a general Pacification: And it being the refore necessary that I should appoint One, to assist on my Part, endowed with that Fidelity, Zeal, and Understanding, requisite for such a Purpose, and finding in you, Don Jaime Mafones de Lima, Gentleman of my Bed-Chamber, and Major-General of my Armies, thele special and distinguished Qualifications, I do chuse and nominate you, to the end that, invested with the Character of my Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, you do repair, in my Name, to Aix la and repre-

To all, who flyll fee these Presents, Greeting. Whereas, after having acceded to the preliminary Articles of Peace, signed the Thirtieth of April last, at Aixla -pelle, we are sincerely desirous of concurring in the perfect Re-establishment of the general Peace in Europe, to which all the Powers that have signed and acceded, as we have done, to the abovesaid preliminary Articles, are disposed to give their Assistance, by reducing those same preliminary Articles, and other Acts depending thereon, into One definitive Treaty of general Peace. For those Reasons, and ether Confidemtions us thereunto moving, we, trailing in the Capacity, Experience, Zeal, and Fidelity for our Service, of our dear, well-beloved, and trusty, the Chevalier Oftbrio, Knight, Grand Croix, and Grand Conservator of our Military Order of the Saints Maurice and Lazarus, and our Envoy Extraordinary to the King of;
