APET IT IOjN of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Creditors of the Royal African Company of England, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Creditors of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners, and the rest of the Creditors of the said Company, are deeply interested in the Allegation contained in a Petition presented to this House, by the said Company, That they, the said Company, are indebted to the Amount of£.100,000: And representing to the House, That the said Company's Forts and Settlements, which, by Parliament, and sundry Resolutions of this House, have been declared necessary for the Protection of the Trade

to Africa, have, for many Years last past, been, in great measure, supported and secured by the Stores, Goods, and Merchandizes, supplied to the said Company by several of the Petitioners: That the repeated Aids, granted to the said Company by the Publick, have proved an Inducement, with most of the Petitioners, to trust them, which they would not otherwise have done: And that the Substance of the said Company being now reduced to the single Property they have in the said Forts and Settlements, the Petitioners, and the rest of the said Creditors, whose private Fortunes have been thus employed for the Publick Good, are in Danger of losing their just Demands,

A Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, as well for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highway or Road leading from the City of to the Bo-

rogh of Droitwich, in the County of Worcester, as for putting in Execution One other Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for enlarging the Term granted by the Lid first-mentioned Act, and for making the same morecffcftual; and for repairing other Roads therein mentioned, in the said County of Worcester-, was presented to t he House, and read; setting forth. That, by the said Acts, several Tolls and Duties were granted, continued, and made payable, to the Trustees therein respectively named for repairing the Roads in the said Acts described; and the Term granted by the Act of the 12th Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and the Tolls thereby granted, were to take place from the First Day of June 1714, and to continue for Twenty-one Years; which Term and Tolls were, by the Act of the Twelfth of his late Majesty, and the Articles, Rules, and Clauses, therein expressed (except such Clauses as are thereby explained, altered, or amended) and the Authorities and Powers for collecting and accounting for such Tolls, and for borrowing Money thereupon, and for putting the said Act of the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty in Execution.continued, and extended to the additional Roads and Streets in the Act of the Twelfth of his late Majesty mentioned, for the further Term of Twenty-one Years: That the Trustees, the better to put the said Acts in Execution, have, from time to time, taken up at Interest large Sums of Money, which, together with the Monies arising by the Tolls aforesaid, hath been applied according to the Directions of the several Acts; notwithstanding which, the Roads and Streets, so directed to be repaired, are, by means of many heavy Carriages passing through and over the fame, continually breaking up in several Parts, especially in the Winter Season; and such Parts thereof, as have been already amended, will in a short time become ruinous, if not constantly kept in Repair: That the Repairs of the Roads and Streets, by the said Acts directed to be amended and kept in Repair, cannot, withifi the Compass of the additional or continued Term, be effectually repaired, and Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, and now remaining due, be discharged, unless the subsequent Term of Twenty-one Years, granted and continued by the Act of the Twelfth of his late Majesty, be enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging and continuing the said subsequent Term of Twenty-one Years for such further Time or Term of Years, and with such additional or other Clauses, Powers, and Authorities, as the House shall fee meet.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Wm. Greig: Who being examined, said. That a great Trade had been formerly carried on in that Town, particularly of Fishery; and that a Custom-house had been built there for many Years, upon Account of the Commerce carried on at that Place.

And the same Witness also said. That there is a spacipus Harbour belonging to the said Town; and that it was the mofl commodious Harbour in that Part of the Country for the Preservation of Ships and Vessels.

And the same Witness gave Evidence, That for the better Improvement and Preservation of the said Harbour and Pier, and for facilitating the Sailing of Ships and Vessels into and out of the same with Safety, and to prevent the choaking up of the present Harbour, another Pier was directed to be built, which is begun, and some Progress made therein; but the same cannot be completed, in regard the Expence thereof will be much.

!greater than can be suppfied from the Revenues of the aid Town: And the said Mr. Wm. Greig added to his Evidence, That if some further Provision be not made for completing the said Works, and for the Preservation of the Harbour, the Trade of the said Town, which formerly was considerable, will be intirely loll.

That an Act of Parliament was made and passed, in the Sixteenth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for r pairing the High Road from the Town of Boroughbridge to Catherick, in the North-Riding of the County of York, and from thence to Pier/bridge, on the.River Tees, in the said Riding; whereby several Tolls were granted for repairing the said Road but that, in the said Act is contained a Pmviso, whereby all Carts and other Carriages, Horsesand other Cattle, laden with Coals, are exempted from the Payment of any of the Tolls by the said Act imposed, in respect of their passing or repassing on the said Road, at any Time between the First Day of May and the Thirtieth Day of October in each Year; and are only chargeable with the Payment of One fourth Part of the said Duties or Tolls, in reffed of their passing and repaying on the said Road, at any time from the Thirtieth Day of October to the First Day of May in each Year, during the Continuance of the said Act: And further setting forth, That the Trustees appointed to put the said Act in Execution, have made a considerable Progress in amending and repairing the said Road; but by realonof the great Number of Carts and other Carriages, Horses and other Cattle, passing and repassing on the said Road, laden with Coals, which do great Damage to the said Road, and by the said Afcl are exempt from paying the Tolls or Duties in Manner above-mentioned, the said Road cannot be effectually amended and made good, and kept in good and sufficient Repair, according to the Intent of the said Act, unless a further Duty or Toll be laid and imposed on all such Carts and other Carriages, Horses, and other Cattle, passing and repassing on the said Road, laden with Coals: That the Powers granted to the said Trustees, by the said Act, are, in many Instances, found insufficient, and several Difficulties have arisen in putting the said Act in Execution, whereby the good Purposes by the said Act intended are greatly obstruded; and that several great Sums of Money, to the Amount of Three thousand Four hundred Pounds, have been borrowed by the said Trustees, upon the Credit of the Tolls granted by the said Act; all which Sums have been laid out in amending the said Road, and cannot be repaid within the Time limited by the said Act, nor the said High Road kept in sufficient Repair, without afurther Term granted by Parliament: And therefore praying the House fogive Leave that a Bill be brought in for explaining, amending, and making more effectual, the above-mentioned Act of Parliament, in such Manner, and by such Means, as to the House shall ieem meet.

Wandsford A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Capital Bur-

Bridge. gefies, of the Town or Borough of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln, waspresented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Road leading from Wandsford, in the County of Northampton, to the said Town of Stamford, being Five measured Miles and an Half, is Part of the common High Road from London to Scotland, and greatly frequented by Travellers; and, by reason of the many heavy Carriages with excessive Burthens thereon, is become so very bad, deep, and ruinous, that it is inconvenient and dangerous to all Persons passing and repailing the fame; and that the said Road cannot be sufficiently amended, and kept in Repair, by the Performance of the Laws for repairing the Highways of this Kingdom, unless a Provision be made by Parliament for the railing Money for that Purpose: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the effectual amending and repairing the said Road, with the Monies anting by a Toll to be taken at a Turnpike to be erected on the said Road.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

That some Years ago there was erected in Edinburgh a large Fabrick, or Charity Work-house, for the Maintenance and Employment of the begging Poor, where above Five hundred poor Persons, besides Out-pensioners, are maintained; and such as are capable, employed in useful Labour: That the Funds for the Support of the Poor of the City arose chiefly from the voluntary Collections at the Church Doors; but although every Inhabitant was fenlible of the Advantage of usefully employing the Poor, and pleased with the Deliverance from the Nuifence of common Beggars, yet, Objects x>{ Companion being no more in Sight, the publick Charity of late Years has gradually declined, and, without some speedy Remedy, this large Fabrick, erected upon the -voluntary Contribution of the inhabitants, and other Donations, may, in place of being any longer ufefuMy employed, remain a spacious Monument of the Decline of

That the Petitioners, in the Course of their Dealings, are under a necessity of giving Credit to a great Number of Persons for small Sums, which, in the Whole, amounts to a great Sum of Money every Year; and, notwithstanding several of these Debtors are well able to pay the Petitioners, yet they frequently refuse lo to do, presuming on the Discouragements which the Petitioners lie under from the unavoidable Expence in suing for such Debts, and the Delays even after Judgment; and that the giving Tradesmen an easy and speedy Method of recovering their just Debts, and at a fmaft Expence, will, as the Petitioners conceive, greatly tend to the Promoting of lndufcry, and the Support of useful Credit: And therefore praying. grove, in the County of Worcester, whose Names are 5oad "j0."} thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and yCT* n read; setting forth. A Petition of several Merchants of the City of London,

Owners and Mailers of Ships, whose Names are there- our' unto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Ships bound to the Westward are frequently detained a long time, by contrary Winds, in

the Downs, which is an open Road, where they are exposed to the Danger of being wrecked in stormy Weather; and that on the 16th of December last there happened a violent Storm, which made all the Ships in the Downs drive, and forced many from their Anchors, some of which Ships fell foul of each other, and foundered; and some, attempting the Shore, were loft on the Sands:

And alleging, That these Mischiefs might be prevented, and the Lives of great Numbers of Seamen preforved, if a Harbour capable of receiving Ships was made on the Coast of Kent, between the North and South Forelands; and that the Petitioners apprehend, from several Ships in the late Storm having got Shelter in the Harbour of Ramsgate, that the said Harbour, though a dry Harbour, may be made capable of lately receiving a Number of full-built Ships, and Ships that will take the Ground, where they may lie secure whilst they wait foralair Wind to proceed either round the North or South Foreland:

scription, and on Calls on their Stock; and, wanting mote Money to complete their said Pure hales, and, if Opportunity should offer, to make other Purchases of other the said forfeited Estates, a Clause was inserted in the Malt Act, of the Year 1720, by which it was Rpafted, for the better enabling the Petitioners to raise, &tid pay to the Government, the Price, or Consideration Money, for the Purchase of the said Estates, That it should be lawful to and for the Petitioners, from time to time, to grant, felh and dispose of Rent Charges or Annuities, to the full Extent and Value of such of the said Estates as were, or should be, at any Time or Times, by them purchased in or by the way or method of Lottery, and for any Person or Persons, Bodies Politick or Corporate, in that Method to purchase such Annuities of the Petitioners; any Law, Statute, or Usage to the contrary in any-wise notwithstanding: And that, in pursuance of the said Power, the Petitioners have, by Three several Lotteries, granted Annuities, not according to the Value of the several Estates by them purchased, but to near the Extent of the yearly Income thereof; and the Sums thereby raised, and the Sums paid by the Stockholders on their Subscription and Calls, not being sufficient to pay the whole Purchase Money for the said Estates, the Petitioners were obliged to borrow great Sums of Money, upon Bonds, under their Common Seal, to make good the Residue of the Purchase-Money, till more Money could be raised by Sale of new Annuities, in the room of those that should be determined by the Death of the Annuitants: And that, on or about the Twenty-first Day of October 1728, a Licence, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, was granted by his present Majesty to the Petitioners, to carry on a Trade, by importing to England &\\ Wares, Goods, and Merchandizes, growing and arising in Scotland; and, by virtue thereof, the Petitioners did set up Manufactures of Iron Works and Timber, and brought great Quantities of Timber to the Port of London, but not having Liberty to export any Goods or Merchandizes to any foreign Market, the Petitioners could not apply themselves, with any Prospect of Success, to the most profitable Trade; viz. the Fisheries in Scotland, and upon the Coast thereof; the Profit of such Fisheries arising by Sales in foreign Markets: And that the Petitioners, having expended great Sums of Money in the said Timber and Iron Works, and being, on that and otherAccounts, entangled with a Multiplicity of Debts and Suits, were unable to carry on any Trade without a large Supply of Money j and therefore the Petitioners did, in the Year 1732, agree to a Subscription of Fifteen Pounds per Cent, on their Stock, to be paid by several Installments, in order to pay their Debts, and carry on Trade, but that very little of the said Call was complied with, and that only by some of the Stockholders: And that, by expending very great Sumsof Money in setting up and carrying on the said Manufactures, the Petitioners not only contrafted great Debts, butalfomade Default in Payment of their said Annuities; and the Stockholders refilling to comply with the said Call of Fifteen Pounds Cent, the Trustees for the Annuitants, in the Year 1733, took Possession of the Estates of the Petitioners in and other Creditors of the Petitioners took Possession of the Petitioners Estates in England -, and various Suits, both in England and Scotland, have been commenced and carried on with great Rigour against the Petitioners: And that, for want of a sufficient Fund, the Petitioners have, ever since the Year 1724, discontinued the Granting of Annuities, but that many of the Annuities formerly granted by the Petitioners, and all the Jointures on the Petitioners Estates, are fallen in, so that the Petitioners have now a sufficient Fund for making a new Grant of Annuities; A Petition of the justices. Grand Jury, Gentlemen, Suffolk Clergy, and other principal Inhabitants of the Body of the County of Suffolk, assembled at the Quarter-Sessions of the Peace, held at Beccles, in and for the said County, on Monday the Third Day of October 1748; and also,

A Petition of the Justices, Grand Jury, Gentlemen,

Clergy, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Body of the County of Suffolk, assembled at the Quarter-Sessions of the Peace, held, by Adjournment, at Woodbridge, in and for the said County, on Wednesday the cth Day of October 1748; and also,

A Petition of the Justices, Grand Jury, Gentlemen,

Clergy, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Body of the County of Suffolk, assembed at the Quarter-Session of the Peace, held by Adjournment, at Ipswich, in and for the said County, on Friday the 7th Day of October 1748;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; fcve-rally letting forth. That the Inhabitants of Three-fourths of the County of Suffolk, have, for several Yean, suffered great Inconveniencies and Hardships, and have been put to extraordinary and unnecessary Expences, by reason of the Assizes being generally holden, at both Times of the Year, at Bury, in the said County: And that they are forced to travel from feme Places Sixty, from others Fifty, and Forty Miles, to attend their Duty, either as Justices of the Peace, or to serve on Grand and Petty Juries, or to try such Causes as happen to be ready for Trial, most of which arise in the Northern and Eastern Parts of the County, as being most populous, and where the Trade of the County is chiefly carried on 5 And that Ipswich, being the County Town, the only

Gaol for the Body of the County is at that Town, and from thence the Pri Goners are carried to the Assizes at Bury, at the great Expence and Hazard of the Sheriffs; and the greater of late Years, Iince the infamous Practice of Smuggling has lb much prevailed on that Coast, where large Gangs of Smugglers are too desperate for a common Guard to withstand, as did appear in a late particular Instance, where a Smuggler was, by open Violence, taken from the Sheriffs Officers, who were conducting him from Ipswich to Bury Assizes: And alleging,

That this is a Mischief which, it is conceived, will often happen, if the Prisoners must continue to be carried from Ipswich Gaol to the Town of Bury for Trial: And that Ipswich is the only large and convenient Town near the Center of the County for holding the Assizes: And that there are Two very large and commodious Courts for the Judges to try Caules Civil and Criminal: And that this is no new Thing which the Petitioners pray for, Iince One of the annusd Assizes has been holden at Ipswich, by the late Lord Chief Justice Holt, and, within these Four Years, by another of the present learned Judges: And that, although the Petitioners thus aik for what will be a very great Convenience to much the largest Part of the County, yet it is a Pleasure to them to be able to represent, that it will also be rather a Convenience, as they apprehend than an Inconvenience to the Judges, if the Summer Assizes should be directed to be holden annually at Ipswich, inasmuch as they would save some Miles in travelling from Cambridge directly to Norwich, and thence to Ipswich, in their Road to London: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give Leave that a Bill may be brought in for fixing the Summer Assizes at Ipswich for the future; or to provide such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions do lie upon the Table,

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the Second Commissionu Reading of the ingrossed Bill, from the Lords, intituled, ers for An Act declaring the Authority of the Commissioners ap- *>nze c*uses' pointed by his Majesty, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, for receiving, hearing, and determining, Appeals jn Causes of Prizes, be now read:

That in order to the equal approportioning the Land Tax, and the railing and levying the same more effeflullly within that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; certain Quotas have, Time immemorial, been fixed and established, both by Laws and Acts of Parliament, and constant uninterrupted Custom, to be paid out of each County; and, whether the Subsidy was higher or lower, the established Proportion has always been observed: And to the end that the Quota put upon each Shire may be raised with Equality out of each Here-for's Land, according to the Value of the fame, Commissioners have from time to time been appointed before the Union, (ometimes by the Privy Council of,

in consequence of a Remit from Parliament, and, in other Instances, directly by the Parliament itself, in order, from proper Evidence, to establish a certain Value upon the Lands, which is called a Valuation, to be a Rule by which the Land Tax, and other public Burthens, were severally to be raised and levied from the same; and by this Method all arbitrary Proceedings in the Commissioners, in making the Land Tax effectual, have in a great measure been prevented: That the Valuations within the several Shires serve not only for a Rule for levying and railing the Cess with Equality, but also are a Measure for determining the Qualification of a Freeholder, to enable him to vote in an Elefrion of a Member to serve in Parliament, as appears by the 21st Act, 3d Par. Cha. II. Anno i 681: That, further, the several Valuations serve as a Rule for determining the Extent of the Casualties payable to the Crown, as also to other Superiors; and is become ft ill more necessary since the late Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for taking away the Tenure of Wardholding in Scotland, and for converting the same into Blench and Free Holdings; and for regulating the Casualty of Non-entry in certain Causes, tec. which passed into a Law in the last Session of the last Parliament, whereby, inter alia, it is

statuted, in orfter to ascertain the Quantum of the Nonentry Duty* That, from and after the 25th Day of March 1748, in all Services upon the Brieve of Mortanceftry of any Heir or Heirs in the Lands and Heretages therein referred to, the Retour, over and above the setting furth the old and new Extent of the Lands, in such manner as hath been heretofore practised, shall further set furth and express the Valuation of such Lands and Heretages: That there is not now extant any old Valuation of the united County of Argyll and Tar bat; nor indeed any, excepting One, which was made and finished in Anno 1688, immediately before the late happy Resolution, under the Direction and Management of Officers appointed by the Crown in these Times, which were iniquitous, and when that County was obnoxious to the r Government, which was unequal, neverfubmitted to, and so notoriously wrong and unjust, that immediately after the happy Resolution, by the Act imposing the Land Tax, in Anno 1690, being the 6th Act of the 2d Self. Bounty on A Petition of George Buchanan and John Crawford, Sail-cloth Agents for several Manufacturers of Sail-Cloth in

exported, that Part of Great Britain called Scotland: And the said Petition was read , setting forth. That, among the several Provisions, which, by divers Acts of Parliament, have from time to time been made for encouraging and extending the Manufacture of British Sail-Cloth, it is Enacted, That an additional Duty of One Peny per Ell be laid upon all foreign-made Sails or Sail-cloth imported into Great Britain by way of Merchandize, over and above all other Duties already chargeable thereon; and that out of the Monies arising by the said additional Duty, there be allowed a Reward of Two Pence for every Ell of British-made Sail-cloth or Canvas fit for or made into Sails, which shall be exported by way of Merchandize s That by a Clause, in an Act made in the Tenth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, reciting, That in many Ports of this Kingdom, from which British Sail-cloth is exported, there is not so much Money received, for the said additional Duty of One Peny per Ell, as is sufficient to pay the said Reward of Two Pence for every Ell of made Sail cloth or Canvas exported, as aforesaid, it is Enacted, That if the Collector of the Customs in any Port of this Kingdom shall not have sufficient Money in his Hands, arising by the said additional Duty, to satisfy and pay such Reward as is or shall be due to any Exporter of British-maAz Sail-cloth or Sails, that then such Collector shall give to the Person Intitled to such Reward a Certificate, attested by the Comptroller, of what is due to such Person for such British Sail-cloth or Sails fb exported, certifying to the Commissioners of the Customs at London or Edinburgh, respectively, that he hath not Money in his Hands, on the Branch aforesaid, sufficient to pay the same; which Certificate being produced to the said respective Commissioners, they are to cause the Monies thereby due to be paid in Three Months, by the respective Re-ceivers-General or Cashiers of the Customs, out of such Monies as are or shall be in their Hands, arising by the said additional Duty of One Peny per Ell on Sail-cloth imported, as aforesaid: That the Amount of the Duty on foreign-made Sail-cloth, imported into England, greatly exceeds the Amount of the Reward allowed on the Exportation of such Sail-cloth as is manufactured there: That very little or no foreign-made Sail-cloth or Sails is or are at this time imported into Scotland, for which rca-

l9

son there is' not any Fund in that Kingdom at present to pay the Reward which the Legislature intended to allow on the Exportation of British Sail-cloth from Scotland, as well as from England: And although the Sail-cloth Manufacture in Scotland is now very considerable, and employs great Numbers of Poor, yet the same mult inevitably decline, unless the Commissioners of the Customs at London are authorized to pay the same Reward to the Exporters in Scotland, as they are impowered to do by the last-recited Act with tespect to the like Exportations from the Out-ports of England: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that such Provision may be made for the Purpose before-mentioned; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Kinghorn Mr. Oswald reported from the Committee, to whom ar our, ttc the Petition of the Provost, Bailiffs, and Town-Council,

of Kinghorn, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition,

George Drummond Esquire was called: Who, being examined, laid, That there is a Ferry between Kinghorn and Leith, which is moll frequently used by Persons pairing between the North and South Parts of Scotland: And he said, That if the Harbour of Kinghorn was repaired, and made commodious, it would not only be of great Advantage to the Town, but to the Whole of that Part of the united Kingdom. Then,

Mr. John Dick, Master of a Ship, was called, and examined: Said, That he, having lived at Kinghorn 30 Years, was well acquainted with the Harbour there, which hath been several Years past in a ruinous Condition: That the Passage at the Ferry is attended with many Inconveniencies, by reason a small Quantity of Water flows into the Harbour, in regard there is a large Sand Bank in the Channel, which used to be Three Boats Length over, and now there is scarce Water enough for One; and frequently at Neap Tides, when the Wind blows Easterly, there is not, at High-Water, enough for the smallest Boats either to fail in or out.

Mr. John Ba/foure, being examined, confirmed the Evidence before given by Mr. Dick.

And the said Mr. Dick added to his Evidence, That the Harbour is now so bad, the whole Revenue -of the Town, applicable towards keeping the same in Repair, is not near sufficicent to put and keep the same in Repair.

That several Papers were produced, and laid before the Committee; wheteby it appeared, That the Magistrates and Inhabitants of the Town had made Application to a general Convention of the Royal Boroughs at whereupon Commissioners were appointed to inquire into the State and Revenue of the Town, and the Condition of the Piers and Harbour thereof} and they, after Inquiry, made a Report, That the Channel was much filled up with Sand.; that the Pier and Bulwark, which defended the Harbour from the Violence of Storms, were not only become ruinous, but several Parts thereof beat down.: And at another general Convention, held in 1743,agene-ral Contribution was recommended in the whole Boroughs, in order to repair the Pier and Harbour: But. it does not appear that any thing has been since done relating thereto.

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Adam Anderson, Agent for the Trustees, appointed by an Act of Parliament of the 17th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for raising and establishing a Fund for a Provision for the Widows and Children of the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, and of the Heads, Principals, and Mailers of the Universities of Andrews, and Edinburgh, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Cferk'sTable: Where the same was read; and is as folldweth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the Petition,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the 17th Year of his present Majesty, was produced; by which Act an annual Tax is imposed upon all Persons holding Benefices in the Church of Scotland, upon all Heads, Principals, and Mailers of the Universities of St. Andrews, and

Edinburgh, of cither £.1.Ilf 6, £. 3. 18. 9, £.5 .5.0,

or £.6. 11.3. Sterling, at the Option of the said Persons, and for which their Widows arc intitled to the respective Annuities of either £. 10, £.t 5, £. to, or £. 2$: And the Children of such as leave no Widow, to a Stock respectively of either £. 100, £. 150, £.200, or £. 250: And, in order to raise a Fund for securing the Payment of the said Annuities, it is, by the said Act, directed. That the Surpluses of the said annual Taxes, after the Payment of the Charges of Management, and of such Annuities as become due, shall be lent out in Sums of £. 30 to each of the said Contributors, at £.4 perC which Sums they are

obliged to accept, and to give Security for the Payment of the said Interest, and Repayment of the Principal, upon their ceafingto have a Right to the Benefices or Offices, in respect whereof they received the said Sams, by Promotion, Deprivation, Resignation, Death, or any other Manner: And that such Sum, so re-paid, shall be, in like manner, advanced to the Persons succeeding to such Benefices, or Offices: And that when the said Sums of £. 30 shall have been paid to Persons possessed of Benefices or the Offices aforesaid, the Surpluses of the said Taxes shall be lent out at Interest, in order to r&ifo a further Fund of £. 35,000: And that after this Fund is completed no further Increase shall be made, but the said Surplusses shall be annually divided amongst Children of the said Ministers and Officers of the said Universities.

1 ft. That to secure a reasonable Provision for the Widows and Children of younger Brethren, and future Intrants who will have paid an equal Value for it, a small Peduftion should 1 be made from the Provision allowed to the Families of those, who, at the Time of their Death, have paid only a few Years Tax for Support of the Fund.

adly. That to ascertain the Rife of the Capital, on which the Equity and very Being of the Scheme, depends, a certain Sum should be applied annually, for increasing the Stock.

MR. Southwell reported from the Committee, to Bristol

whom the Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Streets, kc. Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Sfeal, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition,

An Act, made in the 11 th and 12th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the 3d, for the better preserving the Navigation of the Rivers Avon and Froome; and for cleaning, paving, and enlightening, the Streets of the City of Bristol; was read.

Then the following Witnesses were called; viz.

John Foy, Edward Cooper, and Morgan Smith Esquires, who, being severally examined, said. That the Provision made in that Act for enlightening the Streets of the said City, hath, in many Instances, been found insufficient to answer the Purposes thereby intended, particularly for want of sufficient Power being vested in the Justices of the Peace, in their general Quarter-Sessions, to oblige the Inhabitants of the several Parishes and Precincts, within the City, to make use of publick Lamps in their respective Pari (lies, and to order the Number of such Lamps, and to ascertain the Length of Time such Lamps should be kept burning j whereby the Citizens and Inhabitants areexposed to the Danger of Murders, Burglaries, Robberies, and many other Outrages.

That the Enlightening of the said Streets, many of which are very narrow, is greatly obstructed by Signs, hung out before the Houses of several of the Inhabitants, which -obscure the publick Lights; and that in several of the Streets there is not one Lamp to be seen.

And they further laid. That the Clause in the said Act, by which the Owners of Houses are obliged to pitch or pave to the Middle of the Street, is an unreasonable Burthen on such Owners, where the Streets are very broad, great Numbers of such Houses being of small Value, and let at low Rents.

And the same Witnesses also said. That the Streets of the said City arc very much annoyed, and rendered very inconvenient for Passengers, in rainy Weather, by the great Number of Spouts which carry the Water off from many of the Houses to a considerable Distance into the Streets.

And they further gave Evidence, That the Pitching of the said Streets is daily worn away and torn up by the unreasonable Loads, which are carried in and through the fame, in Waggons, Carts, and other Wheel-Carriages, bound with Iron, and drawn by a large Number of Horses, whereby the E?pence of Pitching such Streets is not only rendered excessive, but the Streets ruinous and dangerous for Passengers.

And the same Witnesses testified, That the Number of Hackney-Coaches, used in the said City, is greatly increased; and the Halliers, Draymen, Carters, and other Persons driving Carriages in and through the lame, become very numerous, who often, commit great Difor-ders and Irregularities; for which no Remedy is at present provided i but if Power was given to the said Corporation to make Bye-Laws and Ordinances, from time to time, as Gccalion should require, those Inconveniencies would be soon removed, and the Offenders speedily brought to Justice.

Kilburn Sir Hugh Smithson reported from the Committee, to Roads* whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in ExecutionTwo Acts of Parliament, One passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and the other in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highway between a certain Place called Kilburn , in the County of

Middlesex, and Sparrows in the Coutity of Hert-

ford, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the Petition,

An Act, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highway between a certain Place called Kilburn Bridge, in the County ‘ of Middlesex, and Sparrows Hern, in the County of Hertford; and also, an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for continuing the Term granted by the first-mentioned Act, and for making the same more effectual; were read: And,

Joseph Taylor Esquire, laid before the Committee, an Account of the Money which had arisen by the Tollsgranted by the said Acts; and also, of the Expences attending the Repairs of the Road therein mentioned} whereby it appeared, That there is now due and owing, upon the Credit of the said Acts, the Sum of 2,700 and upwards.

Then the following Witness was called; viz.

Mr. Francis Page, Surveyor of the Highway, who, being examined, laid, That, although the Money arising by the Tolls, as also the Money borrowed on the Credit thereof, had been duly applied, as directed by the said Acts, yet many Parts of the said Road are out of Repair; and, as the Price of Materials for amending the same are increased, a large annual Expence will be required to be laid but thereon; therefore the Debt due and owing, together with the Interest, cannot be repaid, and the Highway effectually amended, unless the Term and Powers, granted by the said Acts, which expire the ift of May 1754, be further continued:

And he added. That the Toll now paid by Waggons, which travel that Way, is so small, the same is not diffident to repair the Damage done by them upon the said Road.

The Lord Deerhurst reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Bromsgrove, in the County of Worcester, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the Petition,

Mr. Edward Bearcroft laid. That the Road from Dyers Bridge, through the Town of Bromsgrove, to

Spadejbourne Brook, is in a very ruinous Condition, and very much broke up, occasioned by many heavy Carriages constantly passing thereon with Coals from Dudley to Droitwich, and other Places: That very great Quan-

tities of Coals are used in the Salt-works at Droitwich; and that sometimes Thirty Waggons pass the said Road in a Day, and return many of them loaded with Salt.

A Petition of the major Part of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, as well for the putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highway or Road leading from the City of Worcester to the Borough of Droitwich, in the County of Worcester, as for putting in Execution One other Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for enlarging the Term granted by the said first-mentioned Act, and for making the same more effectual, and for repairing other Roads, therein mentioned, in the said County of Worcester, assembled the 6th Day of February 1748, at the Dwelling-house of Anne Bedford, Innholder, situate in Droitwich, in the County of Worcester, pursuant to an Adjournment of the last Assembly of several of the Trustees assembled at the City of Worcester, for the Purposes aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that several of the Trustees for putting the said Acts in Execution have, in a clandestine and private Manner, and without any publick Assembly for that Pur-Voj., 25.

751

pose, and without previous Notice to the said Petitioners, or so much as asking their Consent or Concurrence thereunto, petitioned the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted and continued by the Acts aforesaid; but in regard the said Roads, mentioned in the said Acts, are now in good and fulfi-cient Repair; and for that the Money borrowed and secured, and now remaining due, on the Tolls thereof, will, by the same Tolls, be paid off long before the Expiration of the present subsisting Term; and as the ordinary Method prescribed by Law, will, for the future, amend and keep the same respective Roads in good and sufficient Repair; therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and not suffer the said Bill to pals into a Law, for the Realons aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Tradesmen, Worcester, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Droitwich, and of &c-the several Parishes of Salwarp and Hampton Lovett, in the County of Worcester, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Two Acts of Parliament passed, the One in the 1 zth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highway leading from the City of Worcester to the said Borough of Droitwich, and the other in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for enlarging the Term granted by the before-mentioned Act, for making the same more effectual, and for repairing other Roads therein mentioned; and that the Petitioners are informed. That Application has been made this Session of Parliament, to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted and continued by the Acts aforesaid: And further setting forth. That the Lanes called Baggbridge Lane and Frogg Lane, within the said Town of Droitwich, are in ruinous Conditions, occa-floned by the heavy Carriages of Salt and Coal to and from the Salt-works Handing and being at the End of each of the said Lanes; but the Money collected at the several Turnpikes, from the Waggons carrying such Salt and Coal up and down the said Lanes, has been always applied towards the repairing the said Highways in the said Two several Acts mentioned, and no Part thereof in repairing and keeping in Repair the said Two Lanes; and whereas also the common Highway leading from Hetherwich Bridge, within the said Town of Droitwich, to a Place called Ilarvington Village, in the Parish of Chadeftcy Corbett, in the direct Road to the Borough of Kidderminster, in the County of Worcester; the Highway leading from the lower End of the said Town of Droitwich, up a Hill called Harris's Hill, to a Brook called Boycot Brook, in the Parish of Salwarp, towards the Borough of Bewdley, in the same County; and the High-. way leading from the Bottom of the Hospital in the said Town of Droitwich, to a Place called Primflanes End, in the direct Road to the Borough of Evesham, in the said County; are, by the heavy Carriages of Salt, Coal, and other Commodities, become very ruinous, and out of Repair: And forasmuch as great Part of the Money collected at the said Turnpikes is paid by the Waggons carrying Salt and Coal to and from the said Salt-works at the End of the said Bagg Bridge and Frogg Lanes; and in regard the same Lanes, or the said other Roads or Highways cannot, by the ordinary Methods prescribed by Law in this respect, be repaired and amended, unless feme Provision be made by Parliament for railing Money for that Purpose: Therefore praying, That, in case Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, Provision may be made therein for amending, and keeping in Repair, the several and respective Lanes and Roads aforesaid, to the respective Places aforesaid, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House;

A PETITION of the Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, being Sufferers by Fire, in the Town and Borough of Houston, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, on Sunday the 19th Day of July 1747, a sudden and most dreadful Fire happened in the Town and Borough of Honiton aforesaid, by which more than One-half of the Houses of the said Town was burnt down j which unhappy Accident necesserily occasioned a considerable Deficiency in the Land Tax of the Houses so burnt, and Stock in Trade, from Midsummer 1747, to Midsummer 1748, amounting to the Sum of Sixty-four Pounds and Seven Shillings; and from Midsummer 1748, to Christmas 1748, the Sum of Thirty-two PoundsThree Shillings and Six Pence; in the Whole, the Sum of Ninety-six Pounds Ten Shillings and Six Pence j and in the Window Tax, and Tax on Houses, from Lady-day 1747, to Lady-day 1748, the Sum of Seventeen Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, as appears by the several Schedules, to the said Petition annexed; and that the Proprietors of the several Houses, and Owners of the said Stock in Trade, by reason of their feid Lois, and the Loss of their Goods and Stock, in Trade, are reduced to low Circumstances, and incapable to pay the said Arrears; and that, by means of the Poverty of the said Inhabitants, who were intirely unprovided in Materials for building, very few Houses, if any, have been built and finished; and at least Three Parts, or more, of the said Houses so burnt are not yet begun to be rebuilt: And therefore praying, That the House will- take the distressed Condition and Circumstances of the Petitioners into Consideration, and prevent any Process issuing out of his Majesty's Court of Exchequer against the acting Commissioners on the Land Tax of the said County and Division, and the Collectors of the Lind Tax, House and Window Tax, within the said Town and Parish, on account of such Arrears; and that the House will excuse them from paying the said Arrears, and exempt them from any Payment until the said burnt Houses shall be rebuilt, and fit for the Inhabitants to reside in, or for such Time as the House shall think fit; or that the Petitioners may have such further and other Relief in the Pre-miles as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for *3

Be/chier reported from the Committee to whom' the Petition of the several Tradesmen and Shop-' keepers within the Town and Borough of and the several Parishes of St. Saviour, St. Mary at Newington, St. Mary Magdalen BSt. Mary Lambeth, Christ-Church, late Part of St. Saviour, and St. Mary at Rot her hit h, in the County of Surry, and the several Precincts and Liberties of the fame, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, as well on behalf ot themselves, as of all others trading or inhabiting within the said Borough, Parishes, and Liberties, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition} and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. To prove the Allegations of the Petition,

Mr. John Symmonds was examined: Who said, That he is well acquainted with the Borough of,

and knows most of the Inhabitants: That great Numbers of Tradesmen in the said Borough are, from the Nature of their respective Trades, under a Necessity of giving Credit to their Customers for ImallSums, particularly to Journeymen and Labourers, who receive their Wages weekly; and 'tis very usual fir such Persons to refule to pay the Debts they have lb con traded, being satisfied, that the Expence the Creditor mull incur, in Pursuit of his Demands, will be a sufficient Discouragement to him not to commence a Suit in the Borough, or Marshal's Court; where the Colts, before he can proceed to Judgment, amounts to about £/l for. and for Judgment, by way of Default, to £3. ioj.

Mr. Richard Shaw confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Symmonds, as to the Necessity which Tradesmen are under of giving Credit to the poor Inhabitants: And added. That he has been a great Sufferer by it, his Debtors setting him at Defiance; and that he is obliged frequently to fit down with the Loss of ioj. or 20; there being no Method of recovering it at a less Expence than Four or Five Pounds.

Mr. William Steward, being examined, said, The Expence of a Suit in the Borough, or Marftial's Court, for a small Debt, amounts to Four or Five Pounds; though such Debt may be recovered in the City of London for Five Shillings.

And all the Witnesses agreed. That a more easy and speddy Method for Tradesmen to recover their just Debts at a small Expence, would tend to the promoting Industry and Uicful Credit, and be equally advantageous to Debtor and Creditor.

Upon the Evidence herestated, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Mr. Alderman Bethell reported from the Committee, ' Ranfeate to whom the Petition of several Merchants of the City of Harbour» London, Owners and Mailers of Ships, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, Common Council, Freemen, and Inhabitants, of the ancient Town and Port of in the County of Kent, One of the Cinque Ports; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee upon the first-mentioned Petition, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first Petition, the following Evidence was produced:

Captain Stephen Read, an Inhabitant of Ramsgate, said.

That in the Storm on the x 6th of December lait, moll of the Ships in the Downs were drove from their Anchors, and several run ashore near Ramsgate, some of which were afterwards got off, brought into the Pier, and there refitted: That he has known several Ships put into the said Pier in stormy Weather; and, on the said 16th of December last, a Ship, which was drove against the said Pier, might have got in during the Storm, if the Persons on board had cut away her Cable under her Bows, and run her a little further to the Southward: That the present Harbour at Ramsgate, which was only built by Fishermen of the Town, for their own Conveniency, may be greatly improved, and made capable of receiving Ships of 300 Tons Burthen:

That a great Number of Ships have been laved by putting into the said Harbour; and that, if it had been improved, a great Number of other Ships, which have been drove against the Rocks, might have been preserved.

Mr. Martin Brook, an Inhabitant also of Ramsgate, confirmed the aforesaid Evidence: And added, That if a Harbour was made, in which there was a Depth of Six Foot and an Half at Low-water, Ships of 200 Tons Burthen might with great Facility enter in a Gale of Wind.

Captain George Hooper, also an Inhabitant of Ramsgate, said, That, if a Harbour was made in the Downs, between the North and South Forelands, it would be of great Use and Advantage: And,

Captain George Haynes, a Pilot, and Inhabitant of London, confirmed the Evidence of Captain And add-

ed, That he never was in Ramsgate Harbour, nor onShore at the Town, since the Year 1737, but that he has frequently passed by the said Harbour to the Downs, and is of Opinion that it may be made capable of receiving a

South Forelands, for the Sheltering of Ships, which are waiting fora Wind to proceed Westward; for that the S-. and S. W. Wind?, which are the most dangerous to Ships riding in the Downs, blow directly into;

and that all such Ships as take Shelter there, may proceed to Sea to the Westward with any Wind that will carry Ships out of the Downs:

That the Soil there is Chalk and Sand, and that a Harbour may )oe made capable of receiving Ships drawing 14 Foot Water: That he apprehends all small Ships, waiting for a Wind to carry them to the Westward, would lie in this Harbour, and, by that means the large Ships would ride in the Downs with more Safety, as they would not be in Danger of the small Ships breaking loose, and driving against: and damaging the m.

Being further examined, he said, That Ships drawing 14 Foot Water, could not go into, or out of, the said Harbour until it was Three-fourths Flood; but that Ships of a smaller Burden might sooner: And that, in his Opinion the greater Number of Ships lying in the Downs, in Times of Peace, are under the Burden of aoo Tons.

And, being asked if he would lay a loaded Ship in a dry Harbour, he laid he would not chuse to lay her a-ground, if (he could float; but would sooner take that Method to secure her, than lay out at Sea in a Gale; and that at Bristol, where the Soil is, in some Places, Mud, and, in others, hard, all Ships are laid on the Ground, before they are unloaded: That it is very dangerous to lay (harp-built Ships on the Ground; bust a Bason might be made in the said Harbour, in which they might float.

Captain Adam Spencer, formerly Master of a Ship, and a Merchant in London, laid, That the properest Place, for a. Harbour, between the North and South , is

Ramsgate: That he apprehends it is practicable to make a Harbour there: That the Soil, which is a hard Chalk, will hold Water.

But, being aflted the Question, he said, That he had never bored the Ground.

That Sullage, or Seaweed, is frequently brought into the Harbour with the Tide, and is constantly conveyed away by the Farmers for Manure: And that, if a South

Pier was erected, it would prevent Sullage driving into the Harbour:

That he has founded at about 11 or 1,300 Feet South from the Pier Head, and found 6f Foot Water, at Low Water: That the Low Water Mark is about 600 Feet South from the Pier: And that the Shoals near the Harbour are sufficiently covered with Water every Tide: Thatfull built Ships, loaded, may be laid on the Ground without any Damage (which he the Witness has often padifed, and would again, rather than lie in the Doztms, in a Storm;) and that (harp-built Ships might lie against the Pier Head, without any Detriment:

Captain Martin Brook, an Inhabitant of Ramsgate, and who has been Matter of a Ship in the Virginia Trade about Thirty Years, said. That is the most convenient Place fora Harbour between the Two and is the best situated forlheltering Ships in hard Gales, from S. S. E. to S. S. W.; and that Ships may go out of that Harbour with any Winds that will carry rhem out of the Downs to the Westward; and frequently with greater Expedition, particularly with E. and E. N. E. Winds, when Ships in the Downs cannot-purchase their Anchors; and that, when the Wind (hists fair on Lee Tides, Ships in the Downs cannot get up their Lee Anchors in less than Six Hours;.and, if the Wind blows hard, it will take

Three Hours more topqrchafe the other Anchors; and* in Winter Time, the Winds frequently blow so hard that Ships cannot get up their Anchors before Flood.

Being further examined, he said. That, at some Times, Ships may fail out of the Downs while Ships in the Harbour are waiting for a Tide to carry them out, whereby such Ships may possibly, at that Time, Jose their Passage; for those which draw Ten or Eleven Foot Water mult wait Two or Three Hours between the Ebbing and Flowing of the Tide; and those which draw Thirteen Feet must wait Four or Five Hours; but that, in general. Ships in this Harbour would sooner get to Sea, when a fair Wind offers, than Ships anchoring in the Downs'.

That, as the small Ships would be in this Harbour, the King'sShips, East India Ships, and otherlacge Ships in the Downs, would not only avoid the Damages that are fre-questlycaufed by suchfmallShipsbreaking loose but, would likewise lie in a much safer Part of the Downs, and gain better Anchorage; whereas they now ride near the -win and otherdangerous Stations, where the Sand is loofo in order to be as much aspofiible out of the Way of the small Ships; and that, in particular. Captain George Hooper, an Inhabitant or,

said. That the most convenient Situation for a Harbour between the North and South Forelands, is near and that it is more practicable, in his Opinion, to make one there than at any other Place, for that there is a very good Bottom of Sand and Chalk, in which a Ship may, by her Motion make a Dock, without damaging herK.ee!: And that he wmuld prefer grounding a Ship on Chalk to lying in the Downs: And that the Soil, if a Bason is made, will hold Water:

That the Damage done in the Downs is most commonly caused by the Winds from S. S. E. to S. S. W. That when Ships are broke loose by those Winds, Ramsgate lies aknoft right to the Leeward, and is at such a convenient Distance that there is Time to make proper Sail to get in; which they may do with great Eale and Security, as they generally break loose at the First of the Flood, when there may be 14 or 16 Foot Water in the Harbour; for that it is full half Flood on the Shore, cr rather more, before the Flood makes to the Northward in the Offing:

That Ships may fail out of this Harbour with any Wind that will carry Ships out of the to the Westward,

and even with a N. E. Wind: which Ships in the Downs cannot take the Benefit of, if it blows hard; and also at other Times, when Ships cannot purchase their Anchors; and that it is commonly, in moderate Weather, Two or Three Hours, and in stormy Weather longer, before Ships can purchase their Anchors, when a (air Wind offers to proceed to Sea to the Westward:

And he confirmed the Evidence of the last mentioned Witness, with regard to the Advantages the King's Ships' and other large Ships in the Doivns would receive from the making such a Harbour for small Ships: And he added, That small Ships, by taking Shelter in the Harbour, would avoid the Danger they are very liable to of foundering:

That, in the late Storm, on the 16 th of December, Two or Three Coasting Vessels took Shelter in the said Pier; and that, about Forty Years ago, a Dutch Ship of 700 Tons, with Jury Mate, came in there; and^since that Time, a Ship called the Gtddfo of about 400 Tons, which in attempting to go round the North Foreland, had (truck, also put into the said Pier, and was there repaired, and afterwards proceeded to London: And he added, That there has been little Alteration in the said Pier since the said Ship of 700 Tons took Shelter there:

Captain Michael Wilkins Conway, an elder Brother of the Trinity House, and an Inhabitant of London, said. That

he has been Matter of a Ship, and Twenty-one Years a Pilot; when he patted his Examination for a Pilot he was particularly examined as to the Downs, which he is well acquainted with, and has often piloted his own Ships through the Downs, and has been even desired so to do by a Captain of a Man of War:

That the most dangerous Winds in the which

are from S. , S. E. to S. S. W. sufficiently point out Ramsgate, or thereabouts, as the most natural and convenient Situation for a Harbour: And that, if a Harbour, was there erected, Ships might fail out of it, to the Westward, with any Wind that would carry Ships out of the Downs, and even with a ftropgN. E. Wind, as also with afcantWind at S. E. and by E. with the Assistance of a Flood Tide under their Lee, when Ships in the Downs cannot purchase their Anchors: And that Ships in the Downs, drove from their Anchors, in stormy Weather, might, with a little Seamen's Skill, be directed into this Harbour: And that, for want of such a Harbour, Numbers of Lives, Ships, and Cargoes, have perished.

That Ships bound from London to the Westward are obliged to wait in the Downs for a fair Wind: And that-the same Tide which brings them from the North Foreland, would carry them into the said Harbour, where they would ride with Safety, without Wear and Tear of Anchors and Cables: And that small Craft might be a-float there, and be able to carry out Pilots, Anchors, Cables, and other Assistance and Necessaries to Men of War and large Ships in Distress in the Downs: And that, at all Times, Boats might go out, either from or Ramsgate, to such Ships in Distress.

And being asked if Ships could enter the said Harbour when it blew a Storm from N. W. to N. E. he said they could not; but that, when the Wind was at N. E. he apprehends, the Ships, instead of making for a Harbour, would proceed to Sea:

That the great Ships are obliged to ride in bad Road, to be out of the Way of the small Vessels, which commonly lie in the Small Downs, and are generally ill fur-niftred with Anchors and Cables, and frequently break loose, and drive Ships foul of each other, whereby sometimes a whole Fleet is set adrift: And that, if a Harbour was only made for the Reception of Ships of under 200 Tons, it would prevent 9-ioths of the Damage that happens in tire Downs: That he apprehends, that if a Harbour was made at Ramsgate, all Ships under 200 Tons, waiting for a Wind to proceed to the Westward, would take Shelter therein.

And, being asked, whether he would lie in the Downs with a loaded Ship in moderate Weather, or go into Ramsgate Harbour, he said. That if the Ship was of Two hundred Tons Burthen, and full built, and would take the Ground, he would carry her in: And added. That in Time of War, the Merchants Ships are commonly built (harp, and in Time of Peace, full: And that he believed there are now more Ships, belonging to the Merchants of London, that will take the Ground, than that will not:

That, when the Wind is at S. E. the small Ships cannot drive against the large ones; but that in Storms, the Wind is very variable, and frequently (hists to all Points of the Compass:

That he apprehends the Shoals near Ramsgate would greatly protect the said Harbour, for that upon deep Shores the Sea runs heavy; whereas the said Shoals would break the Weight of the Sea, and in (hallow Water, when the Wind is down, the Sea is still: That Ships attempting to get into the Harbour in a Storm, would not be in any Danger of running upon the said Shoals, if directed by a Pilot, or even a fltilful Seaman: And that, in Ptocefs of Time, the said Harbour might by degrees jbe extended <HVof» the Quern and Whitt Dike to the

And being asked the Question, he said, That, if he was drove from his Anchors in the , and a proper Harbour was made at Ramsgate he would endeavour to take Shelter there; but that if there was no Harbour or Pier there, and he could not keepout at Sea, he would run his Shipafhore to the Westward of Ramsgate upon the Chalk Rocks, where (he would make a Dock for her-self, and all Parts of her Body would bear equally: That there was more Danger in running a Ship upon Sand, by reason that the Sea will walh away the Sand in several Places; and as some Parts of the Ship are thereby left without Support, (he is in Danger of breaking; but that hard Chalk, and even Sand, in a Harbour which is well (heltered, is proper Ground to lay a Ship upon; for that the Shipwrights in the River Thames bed their Docks with Gravel:

That he had often viewed- the Harbour at Ramsgate from the Shore and had rode round the Coast from Margate to Ramsgate, but never was in Ramsgate Harbour in a Vessel at Low Water; nor did he ever goon a particular Survey, or thiak it necessary (b to do, to judge of the Utility of this Harbour, which was evident to all Persons navigating Vessels in the Downs:

That the Soil at Ramsgate is Chalk, covered, in some Places, Two or Three Feet with Sand, which Soil, he apprehends, is a proper Foundation for a Harbour; but that he has never bored it:

That a great deal of Seaweed, or Sullage, is frequently brought into the present Pier, which the Farmers constantly take away for manuring their Land i And that he apprehends such Suliage, or Seaweed, will not cause any Obstruction in, or be of any Inconvenience to, this Harbour.

And being asked, whether if a Pier was extended from Ramsgate a Quarter of a Mile into the Sea, it would not, in Process of Time, flop the Suliage, so as to swerve up the Mouth of Sandwich Haven, he said. That he did not believe any Impediment would be caused thereby, for the Course of the Waters would not be altered; buc that, if such an Inconvenience was apprehended, the Harbour might be constructed in such a manner, as that Arches might be turned on each Side, through which the Suliage might be carried away with the Tides.

Captain George Stevens, an elder Brother of the Trinity House, said, That he had been employed at Sea from the Year 1712 to 1741, and was now concerned in a Ship trading to the East-Indies: That the Opinion of the Corporation of the Trinity House had been desired upon Two Plans of different Dimensions, which were laid before them, for the erecting a Harbour at Ramsgate, and that they were unanimously of Opinion, That the Execution of the smallerPlan would be very useful and convenient for the Reception of small Ships out of the Dozens, and thereby afford the larger Ships, which now lie off the Goodwin, an Opportunity of riding more safely.

Being further examined, he said, That the Corporation did not examine any Witnesses as to the Practicability of building such Harbour; but that the Manner in which the said Plans were to be executed, was explained to them by Captain Elliot, who was that Day made a youngef Brother; and, upon such Explanation, they consideredi the Plans, and did all agree, that if a Harbour could be made at that Place, it would be very convenient.

That, in Time of War, Ships are built sharp; and in Time of Peace, full; and that most Ships are now built in such it Manner as to take the Ground loaded:

That when the Wind blows hard, there is a great Surfs on the Deal and Sandwich Coast, which renders it very inconvenient for Boats to put off to the Assistance of Ships in Distress in the Downs; and that when Assistance is given, an extravagant Price is infilled on; but that, if Two Pier Heads were erected at Ramsgate, small Craft might lay afloat there, and carry Assistance to such Ships in Distress; and though such small Craft could not put to Sea from Ramsgate, with the Wind from S, E. to S.W. they might tide it out, and Relief might, in that Cafe, be sooner given from Ramsgate, than from Deal, by reason that the great Surfs there renders it impossible to ship large Anchors there, when the Wind blows hard; and that, at all other Times, there is a greater Probability of Ships being assisted from a small Harbour at Ramsgate, than from the Beach at Deal.

And being asked, if he was drove from his Anchors in a Ship drawing 14 Foot Water, with a S. or S, W. Wind, at half Tide, whether he would pursue the Advice of his Pilot in running his Ship alhore, or attempt, against the Opinion of such Pilot, to make for the said Harbour; he said. That, if he was in great Distress, he would not pursue such Advice, but would make for the Harbour i or if he was in a large Ship, he would keep the Sea as long as possible: And that he has not a particular Knowledge of the Rocks to the Westward of Ramsgate, but, from what he has heard, has always dreaded them.

Captain Richard Straton, Deputy Master of the Corporation of the 'Trinity House, said. That they heard no Evidence upon those Plans, excepting an Explanation given thereof, by the said Captain Elliott-, but that the elder Brothers are themselves, from their own Experience, proper Judges of the belt Situation for a Harbour in the Downs.

And the said Witness, being examined as to his own Opinion, said, That he thought that, if a Harbour could be made, at Ramsgate, it is the properest Situation between the North and South Forelands for Iheltering small Craft, and the most convenient for their Proceeding to Sea.

And he added, That, in his Opinion, it would be fiercely possibly for Ships of 200 Tons to enter the said Harbour i but there is no other Place in the Downs capable

Captain John Sibfon, an Inhabitant near Radc/iff-Cross, said. That he was Owner of a Ship of 3 20 Tons, which had 1,700 Quarters of Corn, and other Goods, on Boards and was drove from her Anchors in the in the late

Storm: That the Master on Board set Ramsgate Pier by . his Compass, and attempted to enter it, but afterwards the Night coming on, he loft Sight of it, and run ashore about 200 Yards to the Northward of it, where the Lives of the Persons on Board, and all the Materials of the Ship, were saved: That if the said Ship had run ashore as much to the Westward of the said Pier as she did to the Northward, all the Freight might have been laved, by reason that Waggons might have been loaded there, which they could not be at the other Place:

Tha % upon this Occasion he went down to Ramsgate, and law within the Pier there, Ten Ships which had been drove ashore in the late Storm: That, during his Stay there, he took a Survey of the Place, and is of Opinion, That there is not any other Place between the North and South Forelands; capable of being made a Harbour for

That Ships which are intended to enter this Harbour, might anchor in a parallel Line between the Harbour and the South Foreland; and that, as there is a Tide comes from the Northward Two Hours and an Half before Low Water, such Ships, if they were in any Danger, might put back into Ramsgate Road.

And, being asked, he said, That if he wasdrove from his Anchors in the Dozvns, he would endeavour to get into this Harbour rather than keep out at Sea: And that, in High Water, a Ship drawing 14 Foot might enter the said Harbour:

That the Soil at Ramsgate is Chalk mixed with a few small Flints, and covered with about a Foot and an Half of loft Sand: That this Sand is brought in with the Sea, and is foloofe, that it crumbles away when a Ship beats upon it; and that the Chalk is of so soft a Nature, that the Keels of Ships grounding thereon are immediately buried: And that In's Ship did, in three Weeks Time, by her Motion, make a Dock for herfelfof Nine Feet deep; whereas if it had been hard Ground, she must have been beat to Pieces when Ihe run ashore in the Storm, or by her Movement afterwards: And that' the said Ship lay upon thevery Place, where, according to the best Judgment the Witness is able to form from the Plan of the Harbour, the North Pier is intended to be e reified.

And being asked, he said, That it is not eligible to lay a sharp Ship on the Ground, except in same of Necessity; but that, he apprehends, a sharp Ship might safely take that Ground; and that, if a Harbour was made, he himself would sooner lay a Ship a-ground there, than anchor in the Downs:

That he believes the said Pier was never cleaned: And that when he was at Ramsgate, he went down to the Shore every Morning; and, though there was then a strong Southerly Wind, hefaw nothing drive into the said Harbour but a little Seaweed, which was conveyed away by the Farmers as it came in.
