Translation of the Convention between his Majesty and the Empress of Russia, signed at St. Peterfbourg, 9th December 1747.

In the Name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity.

ALTHOUGH his Majesty the King of Great Britain

and her Imperial Majesty of all the by virtue of

the Treaty of defensive Alliance concluded the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-two, and happily fub-lifting hitherto, have reciprocally promised each other to use their Endeavours and Efforts principally to the end that a general Tranquillity may be maintained in nevertheless his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, in order to give each other reiterated Proofs of their mutual Friendship, and of their sincere Delire to proceed always with one Accord for the Safety of their common Allies, and to secure themselves from certain Events which might happen in the next Year One thousand Seven hundred Forty-eight, and to put themselves in a Condition against them, they have furnished with their full Powers; to wit. His Majesty the King of Great Britain, John Earl of Hynd-ford, Viscount lnglesbury and Nemphler, Lord Carmichael of Carmichael, Peer of Great Britain, the King's Lieutenant in the Shire of Lauerk, and Knight of the most ancient and illustrious Order of the Thijtle, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of his laid Britannick Majesty to her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias: And her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, her Chancellor, actual Privy-Counsellor, Senator, and Knight of the Orders of St. Andrew, of the White Eagle, and of St. Alexander Newjky Alexei, Count de Rumin,

and her Vice-Chancellor, actual Privy-Counsellor, Lieutenant of the Company of Body Guards, actual Chamberlain, and Knight of the Orders of the White Eagle, of the Black Eagle, of St. Alexander Newjky, and of St. Anne, Michael Count de Woronzow: Which Ministers, after some previous Conferences, and after having communicated to each other their respective full Powers, are agreed on the following Articles:

Art. I.

Her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, without attending to some Hopes which might be entertained of the Renewal of the Conferences of Pacification between the belligerent Powers, engages nevertheless, in order to second the Views of his Britannick Majesty, to forward a speedy Peace for the Good and Safety of the common Allies, to hold in Readiness, during the Course of the Year One thousand Seven hundred Forty-eight, to be Vol. 25.

computed from the First Day of January inclusively, tint'll the First Day of January One thousand Seven hundred Forty-nine, making, in the Whole, a Year of Twelve Months; upon the Frontiers of Livonia, adjoining to Lithuania, a Body of Thirty thousand Men, Infantry; and, besides that. Forty or Fifty Gallies, with the necessary Crews, upon the Coasts; so that they may be able to act upon the first Requifltion to be made by his Britannick Majesty, and express, at the Place where Necessity shall require it, in order to assist his Majesty as well as the common Ally her Majesty the Empress of the Romans, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia.

Art. II.

His Britannick Majesty engages, on his Part, in order to supply the Expences which the Maintenance of the said Troops and Gallies shall cause to the Empress of all the Ruffias, to pay to her, once for all, for the Year 1748, One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, as soon as the Ratification of this Convention shall have been exchanged.

Art. III.

In case his Britannick Majesty should please to retain the said Body further, during the Year, 1749, under the Conditions settled by the present Convention, his Majesty engages to notify it betimes; namely, in the Month of November of the Year 1748, to the end that, if his Britannick Majesty should not have further Occasion to keep the said Body in that Country, it may go back again, as shall be judged convenient, into the Heart of this Empire.

Art. IV.

As the Conditions for the March and for the Subsistence of the aforesaid Troops, in case they should be; required by his Britannick Majesty to pass the Frontiers of Russia, have not been settled in the Convention of the Twelfth June of the current Year One thousand Seven hundred Forty-seven, his Britannick Majesty, to obviate eventually all Sort of Difficulties, and to reap the good Effect of this Convention in case of Need, as well as to defray the Expences and Subsistence of the aforesaid T roops and Gallies, engages to pay to her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias, besides the Hundred thousand Pounds Sterling above stipulated for the Maintenance of the Troops upon the Frontiers of Livonia and Courland, the Sum of Three hundred thousand Pounds Sterling a Year, without the Hundred thousand Pounds Sterling above-mentioned being deducted in any Manner loever; and to cause to be paid regularly, for every Four Months, beforehand, the Sum of One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling; so that the Payment for the First Four Months shall be made as soon as the said Troops, at the Requisition of his Britannick Majesty, shall have put themselves in Motion, and: shall quit the Frontiers of Livonia: And these Subsidles shall be continued, till, by his Britannick Majesty's own Pleasure, the aforesaid Troops be returned to the Frontiers of Livonia: Her Imperial Majesty of all the Ruffias engages, on her Side, to join to the aforesaid Body, and so fend. Six thousand Men, Coffiacks and Calmucks, in order to a ft at the first Requisition on thp Part of his Britannick Majesty, from the same Frontiers of Livonia or Courland, against such neighbouring Power of the Empire of Russia who may think of attacking the States of his Britannick Majesty, or those of her Majesty the Em-' press of the Romans, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, in the following Manner; to wit. That a necessary Number of the Troops shall be employed on board the Gallies and Kantfchebaffes, and the^ft in Conjunction with the Cof-Jacks and Calmucks by Land.

Art.' V.

Although her Imperial Majesty' of all the Ruffias charges herself, by virtue of the preceding Fourth Article, with the Maintainince of the Troops, it is however agreed. That in case that, by the common, Consent of the Two high Parties, the Reason of the War should require that these Troops, being in Pursuit of the Enemy,' or otherwise, should depart from the Enemy's Countries, and should enter into the Territories of some allied or neutral Power, his Britannick Majesty obliges himself, in

Treaty ith Russia.

9° Martii.

A. 1748.

Treaty with that Cafe, to provide the aforesaid Body of Troops as well with Provisions and Forage, as with other Necessaries, according to the Tenor or the Convention lately concluded the Nineteenth of November of the present Year 1747, with regard to a Body of Imperial Troops of granted to the Two Maritime Powers*

Art. YY

But howsoever difkant thele Troops may be in pursuing the Enemy, be it either in the Enemy's Countries, or in allied or neutral Countries* her Majesty the Empress of all the Ruffles shall be at any time and always at Liberty to make them return, in case that her Empire be attacked by any Power, Christian or not Christian; and his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages not only to conX tinue the Payment of t be Subsidies above (lipulated till the aforesaid Troops be returned upon the Frontiers of Livonia, but to furnish at the same time her Imperial Majesty of all the Rufflast without Obstacle, and in the Whole* during all the time that the War shall last, the Succour stipulated by the Treaty of defensive Alliance concluded between the Two high contracting Parties in 1742, in Ships or in Money, according as it shall be found most convenient, or most useful for her Defence, on the Part of her Majesty the Emprefi of all the Ruffles,

Art. VII.

His Btitartniek Majesty engages likewise not to entef into any Negotiation of Peace or Armistice, without having concerted with her Majesty the Empreft of all the Ruffles, and much iefs to conclude any thing which should relate to the Peace, but to invite in time to the Conferences, which shall be held, One or more Imperial Ministers of Russia; and not to favour without him, or without them, any Proportion of Peace made on the Part of the Enemy; but to take care, in Conjunction with him or with them, that her Majesty the Emprcfe of all the Rufflasbe comprehended in this Peace, without which his Britamdck Majesty engages not to consent thereto; to the end that her Majesty the Empress of all the Raffias, as a Power which, in truth, does not directly take Part in the War, but which co-operates so effectually to the Re-establishment of the Peace, may not be exposed, in Resentment of the Succour to be granted, to any Prejudice or Inconvenience.

Art. VIII.

The Ratifications of the present Convention ftutll be exchanged here at St. in the space of Two

Months, or sooner, if it can be done.

In Testimony whereof, we the aforesaid Ministers hav caused Two Parts of the present Convention to be made of the same Tenor, containing the Eight preceding Articles, and have signed them by virtue of our Full Powers, and have set thereto the Seals of our Arms.

Done at St. Petersburgh, the 9th of December One thousand Seven hundred Forty-seven.

(L. S.)

Translation of the Additional Convention for the Campaign of 1748.

THE allied Powers having found that the great Augmentation of Infantry, settled by the Convention of the 26th of January of the present Year, required also a Proportion of Cavalry;

Article ift

Her Majesty the Empress Queen hereby engages to cause Four Regiments of Horse to march, each Regiment confiding of One thousand efie&ra Men; which shall be put in Motion as soon as poflime, even without waiting for the Arrival of the Russian Troops, if by any unforc-seen Delay of the Russianstheir March can take place before the arrival of the said Body of Troops.

Article II4.

The better to enable the Empress Queen to defray the Expences of the March and of the Subsistence of the said Four thousand Men, his Majesty the King of Great tain, oi the Lords the States General of the United Provinces and the Low Countries, engage themselves to pay to her Imperial Majesty, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, an *4

additional Subsidy of £. too,000 Sterling; to wit

£. 75,000 on account of his Majesty, and 25,000 on account of the States General: Which Sums shall he paid at Two Payments; to wit,£. 50,000 on the ill of the Month of June, and £. 50,000 on the lit of the Month of July next.

Article IIId.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, having (that he might not let (lip any Opportunity of augmenting the Forces of the Allies) by this Disposition, made an Addition to his Contingent of 3,000 Horle, the Lords the States General engage, by the present Convention, to augment their Contingent, already fixed at 66,000 Men, by the Addition of 1,000 Horse and 2,000 Foot, over and above what has been stipulated in the ad Article ;and the Specification of the Corps, of which the said Addition shall becomposed, shall be made immediately after the Signature of the present Convention. Concluded and signed by the under-written Ministers Plenipotentiaries and Deputies respectively authorized for that Purpose on the Part of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, her Imperial Majesty the Queen of Hungary and , and

their High Mightinesses the States General of the United Provinces, at the Hague, the 3d, of May 1748.

A PETIT IO N of the Merchants, and others, in- African iV terested in the Trade to Africa, from the Port of Trade. Liverpoole, was presented to the House, and read; alleging.

That the Petitioners are of Opinion, That the bell Security and Protection of our Trade to the Coast of , from Pirates, or other Enemies, mull always principally depend upon his Majesty's Ships of War frequently visiting, properly stationed, and timely relieved, on the Coast:

And that whereas Forts and Settlements on that Coast: are generally esteemed necessary, as Marks of Sovereignty and Possession, to prevent our Rivals from the Pretence or Claim of any exclusive Right of Trade, by reason of the Forts and Settlements they now have, or hereafter may be possessed of, such Forts and Settlements, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, would prove a Burden and Nuisance in the Hands of any Joint-Stock Company, whose private.Interest has, and ever will be, found incompatible with the Interest of the separate and open Traders:

And therefore praying. That our present Forts and Settlements on the African Coast may be taken into his Majesty's immediate Possession, and supported by the Publick, for the general Good of the British Trade j or, if this cannot be obtained, that the Care of them may be committed to the Merchants trading to that Coast, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet; not thereby to acquire any other Advantage or Right in the said Trade, but what shall be in common with all his Majesty's Subjects.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the State of the Trade to Africa.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

Mr. John Bernard said, That the Road from the Eall End of a Lane called Maningate Lane, near the Town of Kingston upon Thames, to the Beginning of the Pavement in the said Town, and from the End of the Pavement of the said Town to the South End of the said Town, is in general very narrow, and much out of Repair.

And it appeared to the Committee, That the last mentioned Road is very much out of Repair, and very jaarrow: That the same might be made a good Road at a small Expence, provided proper Powers were given "by Parliament; and would have been made so long ago, but for want of such Powers.

Mr. Horatio Walpole of King's Lynn reported from the Committee, to whom the.. Petition of the Merchants, Navigation. Owners and Mailers of Ship's, Lighters, and Vessels, and others, concerned in the Trade and Navigation of the Town and Port of King's Lynn, and upon the River called the Great Ouze, in the County of Norfolk, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the II )uL; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and , is as followeth; viz.

To/prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Committee examined,

Mr. William Elftobb: Who said, That the several navigable Rivers which serve the Counties of Suffolk, Cambridge, Huntingdon, and Northampton, fall into the River Ouze, near Denver Sluice, above Downham Bridge, which River runs to the Port of Lynn, through the several Parishes mentioned in the Petition; and that the Owners of Lands lying within those several Parishes are bound to repair the Banks of the said River.

Mr. same said, That he has had frequent Conversion and Transactions with several of the Land-owners in the Parishes described in the Petition, and has often attended Sessions of Sewers: That the Witness is satisfied the Land-owners in those several Parishes are obliged to repair and maintain the Banks of the Riverin the rel'peftive Parishes; and that he has beard most of them declare themselves to that Purpose: That the Method of repairing the said Banks is let down in an Adjoill Book kept for the several Parishes; by which Book it appears, what Part of the said Banks the Owners of particular Parcels of Land are bound to repair and maintain; and the rest of the said Banks are repaired by what is called a common Charge, that is to lay, by an Acre-lhot of all the Lands in the said Parish or Level.

Mr. Elftobb, being examined in regard to the Rapidity of the Current of the said River, informed your Committee, That he has been conversant in the Navigation of the said River about 25 Years, in which Period of Time the Rapidity of the Tides is greatly increased; and that the Tides have been observed to rile Two Feet higher in that Period:

For the Cause of such Increase, as well in the Height as Rapidity of the said Tide and Current, the Witness assigned the following Keafons:

That a great many Points of Land, which formerly projected into the River for about the Space of a Mile above, and as far below, the Town of , are now, by the continued Action of the Water, walked away; and the Inlet is worn much wider than formerly, by which means a greater Quantity of Tide-water is received: That several of the Forelands, which were formerly left for defending the Banks, are likewise scoured away; and many of the Banks, are now defended by Faggots and "Wood, commonly called Counter Shores, which greatly enhances the Charge of repairing the fame.

That the Trade and Navigation of the said River is very much increased within these 25 Years, which thft Witness apprehends to arise from the following Causes:

The Increase of the Burden of the-Ships and Lighters used in the said Navigation, by which means the Country is supplied at a cheaper. Rate with such Commodities as they take from the Port of Lynn:

That

i % "Geo. II. 14* Ma. 757

That the Navigation of fotne of the find Rivers has been extended, particularly from Yaxley to Thrapfitn; and another Reason of the Increase of the said Navigation is the Decay of the Outfall at Wi/bech.

Being acted if it was not possible to carry on the Navigation without Horses, he said, That it is absolutely impracticable: That the River, between Lynn and Germans is, in fbme Places, near a Mile wide; and many Sands are lodged in that Part of it; and the Channel is very crooked: That the Tide is very rapid, and the Waters are sometimes greatly agitited by Wind, so that the Strength of Horses is absolutely necessary, to prevent the Dangers the Vessels mud otherwise inevitably be exposed to: That feme of the Sands extend themselves to a great Distance from the Shore, which obliges the Navigators to use !o great a Length of Line, that it is impracticable to manage it by Men.

And the Witness said farther, That if it was practicable to navigate the said ltiver without Horses, which he does not apprehend it is, it mud be attended with such extraordinary Expence, as must be a great Burden on the Commodities with which the Country is served, and consequently diminith the Trade:

That l'mallLighters are much more exposed to Danger than the large ones; for that the large Lighters can often go from Lynn, when the small ones are confined by the Weather: That the narrow Part of the River, betwixt Germans and Stowbridge, is so crooked that the large Gangs of Lighters cannot be managed with Safety without Horses.

Mr. John Paine said, That he had been acquainted with the Navigation of the River Ouze about 30 Years: That he had served Mr. Bonning, a Coal-Merchant, in the Office of Crimp; and, after his Decease, managed the Bufi-nels for his Widow: That the Current of the River is more violent, and there is a greater Flux of Water, than formerly, occasioned, as the Witness apprehends, by the Mouth of the River being wide*-: That when he first was concerned in the said Navigation the largest Ships then used carried no more than aoo Chaldron of Coals, but that they now carry from 200 to 250 Chaldron: That the Lighters, used to unload the Ships Thirty Years ago, carried no more than 30 Chaldrons; but that the Lighters now used carry upwards of 100:

That the Country could not be served without using larger Lighters than formerly; for the Ships being increased in Tonnage, and consequently more lofty, it is impossible to unload them into a small Lighter without losing Half a Cnaldron of Coals in Ten:

That the Navigation of large Lighters is so much safer than small, that the Merchants at Cambridge refusecl to trust their Goods in small Lighten; and the Witness knew One Person, who was, on that account, obliged to buy large Lighters, to prevent the total Loss of his Business; forthat a great Number of small Lighters have been loft, and but few large ones: That there are several other Conveniencies in the Use of large Lighters; for that the (mailer Boats used to go with no other Covering than a Haircloth or Tilt; but that several of the large ones have Decks, which are very necessary for preserving several Sorts of Goods, particularly Salt, Flour, and Corn: That it is impossible to navigate large Vessels without Horses, they being lo heavy, and the Obstruction of the Ebbs and Currents lo great, that no Force of Men could manage them: That there are Places in the River so broad, as to require Fouri'core Fathom of Line, which the Strength of Men could never draw tight:

That the Navigation f the River has been extended within thele late Years, particularly front Yaxley to fion, and likewise from Lynn to Northampton, as also from Temsford to Bedford.- And that the C -amerce his been much increased in all its Branches, tlpecialiy in the Com and Coal Trade.

Charles Benton informed your Committee, That he was by Profession a Bridgeman , with h tjc exnlaineni t > be a Person whose Business it is to puot Boats up the River from Lynn:

VOL.25.

That he had known the River abotrt 24 Yeats; and that the Currents and Tides are now more rapid thart formerly: That it is impossible to carry on the Navigation without Horses, the River being so broad as to make it »le‘-cessary to vrfe a Line Fourfccrre Fathom long, which is fixed to a Pole Five or Six and Thirty Foot high; so that it would be impracticable for Men to prevent the Line from dragging in the Water:

That Boats often come from Germans loaded; and if the Wind should turn in their Passage, without the Assistance of Horses, the Loading must infallibly be loft, and the Boats beaten full of Water: That the small Craft, used heretofore, which lay not above Six Inches above the Water, was much more dangerous than Lighters now used, which lie 13 or 14 Inches above the Water; and that not a Tenth Part so many Vessels have been loft since the large Ones were used as formerly: And the Witness confirmed the Evidence of Mr. in regard to the Loss that muftattend the Unloading of Coals into fmaH Lighters; and the Necessity there was of having some Lighters built with Decks, for the Preservation of such Goods as would suffer Damage by Water.

Mr. John Kent said, That hewasa Bridgeman, and had been acquainted with the Navigation of the Rivers about 40 Years; and he confirmed the Evidence of the Two foregoing Witnesses, in regard to the Rapidity of the Tides, the Necessity of the Use of Hories, and the Utility of large Lighters; and also of the Loss that would attend the Unloading of Coals into small Craft: And added, That the Coals so loft would be the very best of the Coals.

Mr. Elftobb being examined, as to the Prejudice accruing to the respective Land-owners, by haling on the Banks, informed your Committee, That the Damage occasioned thereby, was, in the Opinion of the Witness, very inconsiderable: That the Banks are much injured by the Action of the Waters, particularly between Germans and Lynn; and he thinks it would cost the Land Owners near as much to repair them without haling upon them, as it does at present: And this he is the better enabled to assert, as he was employed, about Two Years ago, to survey the said Banks, on Occasion of a Dispute between the Inhabitants about haling.

And being required to inform your Committee of what he knew, with respect to the Demands made by the said Land-owners on the Navigators, for the Liberty of haling, he laid, That about Twelve Years ago, he, the Witness, was concerned in the Navigation; and that one Benjamin Barrett, who lived at Dozvnham\nNort hamptonshire, brought a Paper from Sir Thomas Hare, One of the said Land-owners, to the Witness, which Paper was ligned by several Owners of Gangs, who had agreed to pay Sir Thomas certain annual Sums, for the Liberty of haling on his Banks: That the Witness ligned the said Paper, and, to the best of his Remembrance did thereby agree to pay to the said Sir Thomas 5 s.a Year for his own Gang; though he said he never paid any Money in consequence of signing the said Paper.

Mr. Benton being examined, as to the Interruption given to the Navigation by the Land-owners, said. That he him-ft-lf had paid Money for Liberty of haling: That there was a Demand made on one Jonathan Rawlins, who, on his refuting to pay it, was iued for it, and obliged to pay:

ticut, in New England, in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That his Majesty King Charles the Second, by his Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of England, in the 14th Year of his Reign, in Gonfi-deration that the said Colony of Connecticut was, as to Part thereof, purchased for, valuable Considerations, and as to other Part thereof, gained by Conquest, and with much Difficulty, and at the foie Endeavours and Charges of John fVinthropp, and others therein named, and thereby become a considerable Addition to his Majesty's Dominions: And, in regard the said Colony was remote from the other English Plantations, and to the end the Affairs and Business which should, from time to time, arise concerning the same, might be duly ordered and managed, did incorporate the said John Winthropp, and other the Persons therein named, as such other Persons as should be thereafter admitted of the Company of the said Colony, by the Name of Governor and Company of the English Colony of Connecticut, in New England in , with

perpetual Succession; and for the better ordering the Business of the said Company, there were to be One Governor, One Deputy Governor, and Twelve Assistants, to be, from time to time, elected out of the Freemen of the said Company, who were to apply themselves to take care for the bell ordering the general Affairs concerning the Lands and Hereditaments thereby granted, and the Plantation thereof, and the Government of the People thereof: And the Charter appointed General Assemblies to be had twice in every Year, by Two Persons to be elected by the Majority of the Freemen for every Town or City in the said Colony, to advise of the Business of the said Company, and the Governor, Deputy Governor, and Assistants, in General Court assembled, were impowered, from time to time, to make, ordain, and establiflj, all manner of wholesome and reasonable Laws,. Statutes, Orders, Directions, and Instructions, not contrary to the Laws of this Realm of England, as well for the settling the Forms and Ceremonies of Government and Magistracy, fit and necessary for the said Plantation and the Inhabitants there, as for the Erecting of Offices, and the Ordering of Elections, according to the Course of Corporations in England, and the same Laws to revoke, under their Common Seal; and for the Directing, Regulating, and Disposing of, all, other Matters and Things, whereby the People might be religiously, peaceably, and civilly governed; which Laws, Statutes Ordinances, Instructions, Impositions, and Directions, to be made by the Governor, Deputy Governor, and Assistants, as aforesaid, and published in Writing, under their Common Seal, were to be duly observed and put in Execution, according to the true Intent and Meaning thereof: And the said Charter was at all Times to be a sufficient Warrant and Discharge against his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, to the Officers putting such Laws, Statutes, and Orders, into Execution: And that the Crown having, by the said Charter, intruded to the Governor and Company of the said Colony the foie and absolute Power of making Laws, Statutes, and Ordinances, for the Government and Civil Ordering of the fame, they have ever since continued in the full Exercise and Enjoymmt of such Power, without the Intervention of the Crown; and the Laws and Ordinances winch they have, from time to time, made and establi filed, have been so wholesome and reasonable, and agreeabx to the Laws of this Realm, asjuftly to merit the Confidence in them reposed; nor has the lead Exception,

That as their Charter has invested the Governor and Company of Connecticut with the full Powers of Government, and as they have never yet abused any of the Privih ge# granted by their Charter, and as the most valuable of them, should this Bill pass into a Law, will be irretrievably torn from them, in Violation of the Security and Sanction of the Charter; and as they have, on all Occasions, acted with the greatest and most affettionate Duty and Zeal toward* his Majesty's Person and Government, and largely contributed, during the late 'War, both with their Lives and Fortunes, in the Service of their King and Country, the Petitioner in Behalf of the said Colony of Connecticut may be heard, by his Counsel, against; the said Bill; and that the same may not be passed into a Law.

Deputy Comptroller of the Cuf-toros at the Port of Waymouth, said, That he has lived at the said Port above Twenty Years; and that he apprehends the said Corporation have a Right to demand and receive the Duties called Petty Customs, or Wharfage, as well as the Harbour Dues and Ballast Duty; and that they have been constantly under the Management of the said Corporation, and by them applied towards the repairing the Wharfs and other Works there: Then, . 1

Mr. Herbert, being again examined, informed your rCommittee, That he had been Collector of the said Harbour Dues and Ballast Duty for Seven Years; during which time he has known several Instances of Persons refusing to pay the said Duties; el'pecially for the last Fife Year great Numbers have refilled to pay the said Duties: of Petty Customs, or Wharfage, as well as the Harbour Dues, which has caused a great Diminution of the said Revenues; and that several Actions have been brought for the Refusal of such Payment, and Verdicts obtained . thereupon; but that the Expence of carrying on such Spits hath considerably lessened the said Fund; And,

Difficulties as to th* Payment of the Troops raised: That the above-mentioned £. iQOjQOp are destined for the Payment of the Arrears of the Generals and Officers who served in the Low Countries, as Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Persons who shall be interested in, or intitled unto, any Bill or Bills payable in Course out of his Majesty's Offices of the Navy or Victualling, or for Transports, which were made out on or before the 31st Day of December 1748, and who shall, on or before the 20th Day of April next, carry the same to the Treasurer of his Majesty's Navy, to be marked and certified by him to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, shall be intitled unto, and have, an Annuity for the Principal and Interest due on the said Bills, after the Rate of jf. 4 per Cent, per Annum, to commence from the 25th Day of this Instant March, payable half-yearly, in lieu of all other Interest; the said Annuity to be charged upon the Sinking Fund, transferable at the Bank of England, until redeemed by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Persons who shall be interested in, or intitled unto, any Debentures payable out of his Majesty's Office of Ordnance, which were dated on or before the 31st of December 1748, who shall* on or before the 20th Day of April next, carry the same to the Treasurer of his Majesty's Office of Ordnance, to be certified by him to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, shall be intitled unto, and have, an Annuity for the Principal and Interest due on the said Debentures, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 25th Day of this instant March, payable half-yearly; the said Annuity to be charged upon the Sinking Fund, and to be transferrable at the Bank of England, until redeemed by Parliament.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question feverafty put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe reported from the CoO> Wfcftmiaflp mittee, appointed to const Jer of, and report to the House, Flfc Market, the State of the British Fishery, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Petition of the Inhabitants of the City and Libert}' of Westminster, whose Names are

ai Geo. II. 1? Marti.809

Westminster thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the Fish Market. Qf (he Inhabitant* of the said City and Liberty, to them referred; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth:

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

Capta: n Michael Wilkins Conzoay, 'Thomas Smith Esquire, and David ColumbclT, who proved, That the City and Liberties of Westminster had been greatly increased in the Number of Buildings and Inhabitants since the Year 1699, when the Act for making a Free Market

paised: And that the Price of Fish hath continued to advance, even since the Conclusion of the War '

And that Turbuts are sold by the Hollanders for One Shilling, which in London are fold for Twenty Shillings, by reason that the Persons who buy them of the Dutch Fishermen, keep them, even till they are considerably wasted, in order to supply the Town with such small Proportions as may keep up the Price: And that in other Fish thete are also Arts used to raise the Price exceedingly, though not in so higfr a Degree as in the Article of T urbuts:

That Salmon was fold in the Fish mongers Shops for double the Price they paid for it to the Fishermen.

They further proved, That Lobsters, and many other Kinds of Fish, particularly Fresh-Water Fish, were brought over Land to , and from thence down

the Thames to billingsgate, which increased the Prices to the Inhabitants of Westm who were obliged to buy them at Second Hand from those who bought them at Billingsgate:

That the Profits made by the middle Man, or Factor, deprived the Fishermen of that Gain which would encourage more Men to follow the Business, and consequently increal'e the Number of Seamen.

They further proved, That the Price of Flesh Meat had been advanced.

They proved. That the Fishermen had refused at Billingsgate to fell Fish, out of their Boats, to private Persons, alleging as the Heafon for such Refusal, That the Fish in the Boats belonged to Fishmongers:

And that the Fish landed at Billingsgate was surrounded by the Dealers, in such a manner, as to prevent private Persons buying for their Ule at that Market.

And your Committee was informed, by a Member present, That most of the Smacks that go from

end 10 the North Portlands, to buy Fish, carry Nets and Tackle with them, on Pretence of Fishing, belong to Fishmongers.

1 And the Witnesses further said. That there was Room

for a convenient Fish Market near the new Bridge at Westminster, the Landing of Boats at which Place would save the Carriage of Fish down to Billingsgate, and back; and, in their Opinion, would prevent the great Profits of the middle Men, above Specified, and thereby much abate the Price of Fish, and increase the Number of Fishermen, and tend to destroy the Monopoly of Fish.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions: Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a tree and open Fish Market in the City of Westminster, would greatly tend to increase the Number F Fishermen, and improve and encourage the Fishery of this Kingdom

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a free Market for the Sale of Fish in the City of Westminftei-.

The First Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was agreed toby the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Shrewsbury, was presented to the House, and read; sett ing forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, an Application made by the trading Part of the Nation, to have that Branch of Commerce, carried on to Hudson's Bay, which has been confined long in the Hands of a few, to the great Detriment of the British Trade and Navigation in general, to be rendered open and free henceforward to every British Subject: And alleging. That the Petitioners are convinced that such a Step would greatly conduce to the Benefit of this Kingdom, and, in a large measure, promote the Consumption of our Woollen, Iron, and other Manufactures: And therefore praying the Content of the House thereto.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

American said Province, to be appointed by their- Majesties, their Paper Credit. Hejrs and Successors, and Twenty-eight Assistants, ot Counsellors, to be advising and assisting to the Governor, to be elected in such manner as is therein directed; and that it should be lawful for the Governor, with the Advice and Consent of the said Council or Assistants, from time to time, to appoint Judges, Commissioners of Oyer and Terminer, Sheriffs, Justices of the Peace, and other Officers, to their Majesties Council and Courts of Justice belonging: That their Majesties did thereby also ordain. That there should be convened and held, by the Governor, upon every last Wednesday in the Month of May, every Year, forever, and at all such other Times as the Governor should appoint, a Great and General Court or Assembly, which should consist of the Governor and Council, or Assistants, for the Time being, and of certain Freeholders of the said Province, to be, from time to time.elected by the major Part of the Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, qualified as therein mentioned: And their Majesties did thereby, for themselves, their Heirs and Successors, grant to the said Governor and to the Great and General Court or Assembly, for the Time being, full Power and Authority, from time to time, to make, ordain, and establish, all manner of reasonable Orders, Laws, and Statutes, not repugnant to the Laws of the Realm of England, as they should judge to be for the Welfare of the said Province, and the Government thereof: And that the said General Court, or Assembly, should have full Power to name and settle annually all Civil Officers within the said Province, such Officers excepted, the constituting of whom was reserved to their Majesties, their Heirs and Successors, or to the Governor; and to impose 'and levy proportionable and reasonable Assessments and Taxes upon the Estates and Persons of the Proprietors and Inhabitants of the said Province, to be issued and disposed of by Warrant, under the Hand of the Governor, with the Advice and Consent of the Council, for their Majesties Service, in the necessary Defence and Support of the Government of their said Province, and the Protection and Preservation of the Inhabitants, according to such Acts as were, or should be, in Force therein; and to dispose of all Matters and Things, whereby their Subjects, Inhabitants of the said Province, might be religiously, peaceably, and civilly governed, protected, and defended; provided always. That in the framing and passing of all such Orders, Laws, and Statutes, and in all Elections and Acts of Government whatsoever, the Governor should have the Negative Voice; and it is thereby ordained. That the said Orders, Laws, and Statutes, should be, by the First Opportunity after the making thereof, transmitted unto their Majesties, their Heirs and Successors, for their Approbation or Disallowance: And their Majesties . did thereby also grant unto the said Inhabitants divers other Privileges, Liberties, and Immunities: And that King William and Queen Mary did, on the Twelfth Day of December next alter granting their Royal Charter aforesaid, by their Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of England, constitute Sir lVilliam Phipps Knight, to be their Captain-General and Governor in Chief over their said Province of the Massachusetts Bay; and thereby required him to execute all Things in due manner that should belong unto that Trust, according to the several Powers and Authorities mentioned in their said Charter, and in the said Commission, or such further Powers, Instructions, and Authorities, as he should then receive, or which should, at any Time thereafter, be granted or appointed him under their Majesties Sign Manual and Signet, by Order, in their Privy-Council, in pursuance of their said Charter, and according to such reasonable Laws and Statutes as then were in Force, or which thereafter should be made and qgreed upon, in such Manner and Form, as by their said Charter was directed: And the Inhabitants of the said Province have been since governed by the Laws, according to their Constitutiun, in pursuance of the aforesaid Commission, and other like lawful Commissions, in Form aforesaid, issued under the Great Seal of the Kingdom: . And that a Colony, being the Progeny of a State, hath, Vot. *5.

as the Petitioner conceives; by the Laws Nature; an undoubted Right to the Liberties of its Mother Country:

And that, by the Act of Parliament, made in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled;

An Act for the Encouragement of Trade, it is expressly declared, That his Majesty's Plantations beyond the Seas were inhabited and peopled by his Majesty's Subjects of his Kingdom of England: And the Petitionerapprehends;

That those Inhabitants, being English Subjects, had, and their Successors, the present Inhabitants, now have, a clear and certain Title to the Benefit of the Common LaW, and to the common Liberties of Englishmen; and that the Laws are, and ever ought to be, the foie Measure of their Subjection, and the Rule of the King's Government' over them: And alleging, That the Petitioner apprehends, if the Bill, now depending before the House, " To " regulate and restrain Paper Bills of Credit, in the " Colonies and Plantations in America, and to prevent th'fe " same being legal Tenders in Payment for Money; and " for the better enforcing his Majesty's Orders and Instructions throughout the said Colonies and Plantations;" should be carried into a Law, by the Matter therein contained, for enforcing the Royal Orders and Iri-flruftions throughout the Colonies, all future Orders given by all future Princes, or by or under their Authority, to the Governors of the Colonies, however reougnant they may be to the present Constitution of Great Britain, and her Colonies, will be virtually contained in it, and receive the Sanction of Parliament from it; and that the Orders to those Governors, being in their Nature relative to the People under their Government, however illegal they would have been before making such Law, when they come to be ratified and enforced by it, they will thereby themselves become Laws, and necessarily bind the People j and that this' Bill, passed into a Law, by its natural Operation and Effects, will take from the Inhabitants of the Massachusetts Bay, not only the special Powers and Privileges they enjoy by their Charter, but likewise all the Liberties they hold in common with other Subjects:

And the Petitioner also conceives. That although a Remedy for the JBviis attending Paper Credit in the Colonies is much to be desired, yet the present Bill is not only dif-proportionate in its Parts relative thereto, but insufficient in the Frame of it to cure those Evils; and is moreover liable to a Construction very prejudicial to the Interests of the Constituents of the Petitioner: And therefore, ih

Behalf of the said Province of the Massachusetts Bay, praying. That the Petitioner may be heard, by IiisCounfel, against the said Bill; and that the same be not palfed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of Peregrine Furye Esquire, Agent for his Majesty's Province of South Cain , was pre-

fented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Province of South Carolina has been, forfeveral Years past, under his Majesty's Government, which has been exercised by Governors appointed by his Majesty's immediate Commission, who, in Concurrence with the Council and Assembly, enadl Laws; which Laws, in the ordinary Course of the Legislature, continue in Force till repealed by his Majesty; but, in Cafes of an extraordinary Nature, byexprefsClauses being inserted therein, the Execution of such Laws is suspended until his Majesty's Royal Pleasure be known thereupon: And that under thisConstitution it is conceived, That the said Province have not trans-grefled any Bounds prescribed to them, but have proceeded with a due Regard to the Authority of the Crown: And that the Want of a sufficient Quantity of Gold and Silver in his Majesty's Plantations in , to circulate

in Trade and Commerce, has from Necessity, occasioned an Emillion of Paper Bills of Credit, to answer as a Medium- of Trade: And that such Emissions, in the Province of South Carolina, as they were founded in true Policy,

respecting the Circumstances of the Country, have been, from time to time, made by the Authority of the Legislature there, with the Royal Approbation, for carrying on the annual Services of Government, and for the daily Circulation of Trade amongst the Inhabitants; but that the Bill now depending in the House, to regulate and restrain Paper Bills of Credit, in the Colonies and Plantations in America, and to prevent the same being legal Ten-

ders in Payments for Money; and for the better enforcing his Majesty's Orders and Inllrudlions throughout the said Colonies and Plantations; is made to extend generally to all the British Colonies and Plantations in as well

those under his Majesty's immediate Commission and Government, as under Proprietors and Charters, which must be founded on a suppol'ed Misbehaviour, in all the said Colonies and Plantations alike: And that the Bill adapts One uniform Remedy to the Whole, though each is composed of various Constitutions; in some of which, particularly in the said Province of South ,the Authority of the Crown has always had its due Weight and Influence: And that, under the Appearance of a Regulation onty, the Bill works a total Suppression of all Paper Bills of Credit, of what Denomination soever, without substituting any other Medium of Trade, the Want whereof will necessarily occasion a much greater Confusion in Dealings than ever would proceed from the Excesses of a Paper Currency, and can produce no other Effect in this Province than a total Stagnation of Trade: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioner, That the Paper Currency of South Carolina will not become the Subject of this Bill; and, with respect to such Parts of the said Bill as relate to the enforcing all the Royal Orders and Instructions throughout the British American Colonies and Plantations generally, without restraining them even to the Paper Currencies, which appear to be the primary Object of this Bill, further expressing the Hope of the Petitioner, That a Bill which may so materially affect the Constitution of the British Subjects in Ame, will not be passed into a Law, especially when the Instructions of the Crown are obligatory upon all Governors, whose Commissions are during his Majesty's Will and Pleasure: And therefore, <uid as the Tendency of this . Bill is of the highest Concern and Importance to the Welfare and good Government of the said Province, to its commercial Interest in particular, and to that of all other Countries who have any Intercourse or Connection therewith, praying, in Behalf of the said Province, That the Petitioner may have Liberty to be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, before the same do pals into a Law; or that the House will be pleased to grant such further and other Relief to the said Province, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, if he thinks fit.

American A Petition of Robert Charles Esquire, Agent for his PaperCredit. Majesty's Colony of New York, in America, was present-cd to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said Colony is under his Majesty's immediate Commission and Government, where the Governor, Council, and Assembly, form Three distinct Branches of the Legislature: And that, under this Constitution, they have, for many Years past, exercised, and do still exercise, their Right of making Laws for the Publick Utility, and good Government, of the said Colony; which Laws are constantly transmitted to England, to be laid before his Majesty, for his Royal Approbation: And that, from the Want of Gold and Silver in the said Colony, sufficient for a Medium of Trade, they have been laid under the Neccfiity of issuing Paper Bills of Credit, to avoid Confusion in their Dealings with each other; and, as the utmost Care has been taken in the Appointment of proper Funds for redeeming the said Bills, and for sinking them duly, according to their respective Periods, the Petitioner does not apprehend that any Complaints are made by the Britishi Merchants trading thither, that such Emission of Paper Credit, thus guarded in that Colony, has been any Discouragement to the Commerce of this Kingdom: And that nothing can more effect ually evince the upright Intentions of the said Colony, with respect to their Paper Currency, and demonstrate the publick Attention for supporting the Honour and Credit of their Government, than Two Acts Vol. 25.

prevent the same being legal Tenders in Payments for Money; and for the better enforcing his Majesty's Orders and Instructions throughout the said Colonies and Plantations; extends generally to all his Majesty's Colonies, and thereby brings the said Colony of New York under the Censure of a Behaviour that the Petitioner hopes they will not be found to deserve: And that a total Suppression Suppression of Paper Credit, in the Manner aimed at by the said Bill, will lay his Majesty's faithful Subjects in the said Colony under great Inconvenlencics, and prove a heavy Discouragement to them in carrying on their Commerce: And that those Parts of the said Bill, calculated for enforcingtlie Execution of all the Royal Orders and Instructions (not confined to the Subject of Paper Currency only) will very materially and moll sensiblyaffed the Constitution of all the Britishi Colonies in America, particularly that of the said Colony of New York: And therefore, as the Bill is, in its N iture and Tendency, of high Concern and Importance to the Welfare of the said Colony, praying, That the Petitioner, in Bdialf of the said Colony, may have Liberty to be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, before the same do pals into a Law; or that the said Colony may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants and other Inhabitants of the Town of Liverpoole, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend all Monopolies or exclusive Companies in Trade, are greatly prejudicial to the true interest of any trading Nation, and have always been found a Bar to the Improvement and Extension of those Branches of Commerce, which have been so confined; and that, in particular, the Petitioners are fully persuaded, that the long Continuance of the Hudson's Bay Trade in the Hands of a Company, whose interest has plainly been to do little in it, and who accordingly have put in Motion only Two or Three Ships yearly to such a vast Tract of Country, must necessarily appear to have been a Detriment to the British Trade in general, a considerable Hindrance to the Consumption of our Woollen, Iron, and other Manufactures, and has given the French, our worst Rivals, a fair Opportunity of extending their Trade, from the Canada Side, into a large Compass of that Continent, and even close up to the Company's Settlements, the Benefit of which would otherwise have been the Property of the British Subjects:

And therefore (as the Petitioners presume that the Company's Charter cannot legally support their pretended exclusive Right to the foie Exercise of it) praying. That this Branch of Commerce, now under the Consideration of the House, may be declared free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects; whereby the Rival Projections of a Number of different Adventurers will beetnployed to extend and enlarge it, our Manufacturers will be served, and the most effectual Means furnished for finding out a Passage, this Way, into the South Seas -, the Importance of whichDiscovery sufficiently appears from the Sense of the Legislature of Great Britain, fully expressed in the Large-ness of the Reward they have thought fit to offer for it.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Ditto. A Petition of the Merchants Of as presented

to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Hudson's Bay Company have, for many Years past, monopolized the Trade to Hu Bay, and the Countries adjacent, under Pretence of a boundlcfs and uncon-troulable Charter, and foie Right of the Trade of all the Seas, in whatever Latitude, within the Entrance of Hudson's Strahs, and of all lands on the Confines thereof, with the whole and inrjrfc Liberty of Trade and Traffick there, in Exclusion of 'all'other his Majesty's Subjects, without the Company's LipeAce: And alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend','ihat any Encouragement from, the Crown to the Company was originally meant to favour and afljft the effectual rcojecution of Attempts to discover a new Passage into the South , and to find a Trade for Furs, Minerals and other Commodities; and to settle, and improve the Country; whereas the Company have never made any real Attemp't to discover such new Passage; nor have prosecuted the Fur'Trade further than to answer their own private Ends, though capable of being carried to the greatest Extent; and have neglected the rich Minerals of which this Country is productive in the greatest Degree; and have not opened a Trade in any other Commodities, but suffered the Trade of so considerable a Part of the World to languish in so narrow a Channel, as only to employ some Years Two, other Years Four, Ships with Cargoes of incon-flderable Value; and, though Matters of so great a'Tract of Land, have made very few Settlements thereon, and those supplied, from time to time, by a small Number of hired Servants sent over from England; and that the Trade of this Country is capable of being greatly extended; and that great Quantities of rich Copper and Lead Ore may easily be obtained, and Whalebone and Oil had in great Plenty, to a considerable Increal'e of our Navigation, and great additional Exportation of the briti/k Manufactures; and that the extending of the Trade into the Country will be the most effectual Means to attain the wished-for Discovery of the Western Passage: And therefore, as it has been found from so many Years Experience, that every Benefit and Advantage that might have been naturally and justly expected to arile 22

to the Publick from such an Indulgence of the Company, exclusive of all other Subjects, has been totally overlouked and neglected; and a rich and far-extended Country, abounding with the Means of a profitable Trade, so far loft to this Kingdom, so that the Exertion of this Right pretended by the Company seems only to have been, to conceal the very being of this valuable Country, and its Advantages, from the rest of the World; and as the Petitioners apprehend, that were the Trade laid open to this Country, witha full Liberty to all his Majesty's British Subjects to settle there, the greatest

and most extensive Benefits would be derived to this Nation from such a Latitude; praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and that they will make such Order and Provision therein as to the House

shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the' said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Interest of these Kingdoms} and that it doth not appear to the Petitioners, that the great Ends designed by granting the said Charter were ever effectually prosecutedby the said Company, further than toierve their own private Views, though capable of being pursued and extended to ar.fiver the greatest National Advantages, as well in respect to Trade, and the Discovery of a new Passage, as aforesaid, as to the vast Number of Inhabitants that by this time might have settled there, by whom Dif-coveries would in all Probability have been promoted } and that valuable Branch of Commerce, now enjoyed by our Rivals the French, by means of their Settlements on Canada, in a great measure prevented; from whence the additional Consumption of the Manufactures of Great Britain must naturally have proceeded } a Consequence highly conducive to the Welfare of the Nation; and that in case the House should declare illegal this Monopoly, so long carried on by the said Hudson's Bay Company, and authority be given to all his Majesty's Subjects to trade in Hudson's Bay, and the extensive Countries adjoining, the Trade to those Parts, it is conceived, may be more effectually carried on by private Adventurers than by any Company, as the Expence of Forts feetr.s absolutely unnecessary, from the humane and*peaceable Deportment of the Natives, and their* Disposition to cultivate a good Understanding with the English, who use them well: And therefore, and as it is presumed that the Charter of the Hudson's Bay Company is void, both in respect to the unlimited Grant of the Lands, and the exclusive Trade; and as the great Ends of the Charter have not been pursued, but the Trade intothofe remote Parts discouraged i and as, among other national Advantages which result from laying that Trade open, the so much-wished-for Discovery of a new Passage, by means of the Extension thereof, may soon be effectually found out} praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, that the Trade to Hudson's Bay may be free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects; and that such Order and Provision may be made therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; felting forth, That the Inhabitants of the City of Glasgow have at all times distinguished themselves for the Pro-teflant Cause, and the true Interest of their Country; and that, in the Year 1688, they shewed the greatest and most early Zeal for the Support of their great Deliverer King William, after having suffered the most grievous Periecutrons under the former Government j and that in the Year 1715, when a Rebellion was raised against his late Majesty, the City of Glasgow levied and maintained, at their own Expence, a Regiment, which marched to Stirling, and joined his Majesty's Army; and that in the Year 1745, when the restless Spirit of the disaffected FaClion again broke out into the late detestable Rebellion, this City, by his Majesty's Authority, raised and subsisted Two Battalions of Six hundred Men each, One of which, by his Majesty's Appointment, was commanded by the Earl of Home, which, within Nine Days, joined his Majesty's Troops at Stirling, where they remained for the Defence of that Pass, till the Rebels returned from England; and that they then marched to Edinburgh, andjoined his Majesty's Army under the Command of General Hawley 1 and fdon after served and suffered in the Action near Falkirk, and had the Honour to receive Thanks in his Majesty's Name for their Behaviour on that Occasion; and that the said City had not only, by all their Actions, supported zealously his Majesty's Government, when, under the Protection of the Laws, they could perform their Duty with Safety, but ventured to shew their Constancy, and inviolable Attachment, to his Majesty, even during the time that the Pretenders Son, with his Rebel Army, was in Possession of, and lived at free Quarters, in the City, the Terrors of which could not draw from the Inhabitants the lead Respect or Regard to that flagitious Assembly of Rebels, or to their Chief; and that this Behaviourof the City rendered them so obnoxious to the Rebels, that they felt the Effects of their Rage in Two heavy Fines which the Pretender imposed on, and forcibly extorted from them, amounting to a Sum of £.9,056 lor. 9 \d.which said Sum the Petitioners being under a Necessity of borrowing, though at the lowed Rate of Interest for which they could procure the fame, they have since likewise been obliged to grant Securities for the further Sum of £. 1,036 8j. 7 as Part of the growing Interest due upon the said Sum; and that the publick Stock of the said City did further pay,

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe, from the Committee ' appointed to consider of, and report to the House, the State of the British Fishery, acquainted the House, That the Committee had agreed upon a further Report; which they had directed him to make to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth: viz.

In relation to the Whale-fishery, the Committee have examined the following Witnesses:

Mr. Elias Bird, Shipbuilder:

Captain Alexander (lay, who has been in Greenland, and in the Whale-fishery above Forty Years:

V

Mr. Henry Bird, formerly Owner of several Ships then employed in the GreenlandWbale-fishery:

Mr. Rickard Baker, now concerned in Vessels employed in the said Fishery:

John Adamson, Mailer of a Vessel employed in the said Fishery: And,

Mr. John Powell, Owner of Ships trading to North America:

From whose Evidence your Committee have drawn the following State of the Whale-fishery:

That the Whale-fishery to Greenland and Davis's Straits is a very advantageous Branch of Trade: That for the last Three Years the Dutch and Germans made of that Trade alone, at an Average, each Year, £. 277,699; and that they bad in each of the said Years also, at an Average, 216 Ships employed; which mull, according to the usual Management of that Trade, employ above 8,oooo Seamen:

That the Whale-fishery to Greenland and Davis's Straits was originally carried on by the and

was greatly encouraged by Queen Elizabeth, who allowed a Bounty of 20 s. a Ton on all Shipping employed therein; which, comparing the Value of Money then with the present Time, may be deemed equal to 50

By this Encouragement the English not only acquired the Wale-fishery to Greenland, but also to the Straits discovered by Captain Davis, in the said Queen's Reign, the Whales of which Place being esteemed, one with another, worth £. 500 a Fish.

That the chief Reason the English have loll this Trade, is, the Want of Men skilful therein: That in the Civil War of 1641, moll of the Men skilled in the Whale-fishery, being bold, hardy, and dexterous, were taken from that Trade, and employed in the War, and also in the ensuing War against the Dutch; insomuch that, after the Restoration, there were few or no Englishmen that knew how to carry on that Fishery; for that, when the South~Sea Company attempted to regain this Fishery in the Year they were, at a great Charge, forced to hire men from abroad

The Manner of carrying on this Fishery is as follows: Every Vessel hath Six Boats; and ineach Boat must be Three skilful Men, viz. One dexterous in throwing the Harpoon, a Dart which hath a lliarp barbed Iron Head, which is fallened to a Line of a great Length; this they mutt fix in the Whale, and, when fixed, the Fish draws the Boat after it with great Swiftness, and Danger to the Men: when the Fish begins to tire, and the Boat comes near, they kill it with their Lances; to perform which, Vol. 25.

they mull also be bold and dexterous: There must also be One Man thoroughly skilled in managing the Line, and One other /killed in fleering; the leall NegltCl in either of which mull overset the Boat, or break it to Pieces, to the Loss of the Mens Lives, as it is carried on with vast Impetuosity by the Whale into narrow Channels, amongst Fields and Islands of Ice.

In each Ship of 300 Tons, but of 42 Meh, which U the necessary Crew, there must be Eighteen of them Har-pooneers, Steerfmcn, and Line-coilers, which Arts cannot be learned without many Years Practice.

The aforesaid Evidences declared, That it was necessary to have several Years Encouragement, in order tb train a sufficient Number of Harpooneers, Line-coilers, and Steerfmcn; and that at present the Charge Of Wages, the Risque through the Ignorance of our Men, the Difficulty of hiring proper Persons, the Expence of building new Ships, and many other Inconveniencies attending the Attempt of recovering a lollTrade, had not only prevented the Increasing of this Fishery, but rendered it in Dangtf of being entirely loft, their being only at present Two Ships employed therein.

And, among the many Discouragements, they mentioned Two Acts of Parliament, the One of the Sixth of his present Majesty's Reign, which grants a Bounty of 20 s.a Ton on Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery; and the other of the Thirteenth of his laid present Majesty, which grants a further Bounty of ior.; the last of which Acts is already expired, and the other will expire in the Year 1750.

And the Witnesses added. That if a Bounty of 40/. per Ton was allowed for Seven Years of Ships employed in the Whale-fishery, it would encourage the building such a Number of Ships, and the breeding such a Number of Men ikilful in the several Arts before-mentioned; that, at the Expiration of such Bounty, his Majesty's Subjects would be enabled to carry on the said Fishery with any further Encouragement.

And your Committee was informed, That there are now several Merchants, and others, ready to employ con-lid erable Sums of Money in attempting to regain the said Fishery, in case such Encouragement was given.

And your Committee was further informed. That the Whalebone used in the British Manufactures amount yearly toaconsiderable Value; which at present is molily-imported from abroad.

And it likewise appeared to your Committee, That Harpooneers may be had from his Majesty's Dominions in America; which will be of great Service towards retrieving this Fishery: And,

Mr. John Powell, before-mentioned, acquainted your Committee, That, if the aforesaid, Bounty was extended to Ships fitted out from America, there are Numbers of Merchants who will immediately build Ships to be employed in the said Fishery, and get Indian and other Harpooneers; and did not in the leall doubt, but to carry on the said Fishery with£ucccfs: That the Situation of his Majesty's Plantations in North America being nearer to Davis's Straits than that of Holland, will giv.e them si great Advantage over the Dutch.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Cop-sideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day SevcnJ night, relblve itself intoa Committee of the whole House; to consider of the said Report.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trade to Africa ought never to be taxed with any Duties whatsoever, for the Support and Maintenance of any Forts or Settlements there.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, Tnde t® and others, concerned in the WoollenManufactures, in the Hudson* Town of IVakefeld, in the County of York, was presented a^‘ to the House, and read; representing to the House, That t hcHudfons Bay Company have, for many Years passed, monopolized that Trade, under Pretence of a boundlef. Charter from King Charles the Second; but haveprosecuted the same no further than to answer their own private Ends, their Exports not exceeding Two to Four thousand Pounds per Annum, and their Ships not more than Two, and of late Years Four, employed at a Time; though the Trade is capable of being carried to a vast Extent, to the great Benefit of this Kingdom, from the large Quantities of our Woollen, Iron, and other Manufactures, that may be exported thither; and that to attain so great a National Advantage, nothing else is wanting than the Authority of the Legislature to lay the Trade open, and make it free for all his Majesty's Subjects; and, as the Charter of the Company is void, both in respect of their Boundaries, and exclusive Trade; and as the most National Advantages must undoubtedly result from theTrade being made free; Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to make such Provision therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Commonalty Ramsgate of the Town and Port of Dover, in the County of Kent, Harbour, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That by a Clause in an Act of Parliament, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act for the Repair of Dover Harbour, it is provided and enacted,

That all Ships and Vessels belonging to the Port of Ramsgate, in the Isle of Thanet and County of , having a Pier of their own, which, by reason of their Poverty, they are not able to maintain, shall be exempted from contributing and paying any thing towards Dover Harbour aforesaid; and that as all Ships and Vessels belonging to the Port of Ramsgate, have, ever since the Palling of the said Act, enjoyed the Benefit of the Exemption therein contained, it is equally reasonable, that Ships and Vessels belonging to the said Town and Port of Dover should likewise be free from the Payment of the Duties to be imposed by the Bill, depending in the House, for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate; and for cleansing, amending, and preserving, the Haven of Sandwich: And therefore praying. That a Clause may be inserted, in the said Bill, whereby such Ships and Vessels may be exempted from the said Duties; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A PETITION of the several Persons, whole Names Ouze are thereunder written, being Proprietors of the Navigation. Banks, or Sea-walls, adjoining to the River , between a certain Bridge at Stowbardolph, and the Borough of King's Lynn, on behalf of themselves and the other Proprietors of the said Banks; viz. Sir Thomas Hare, Sir Robert Brown, James Vernon, Martin Fowlkes, John Davis, John Spelman, Henry Bell, Edmund Harwich, Esquires, John Green, jar. Patrick, Patrick Docking, Robert Hayes, John Hall, Jonathan Jones, Thomas Field, Robert Abraham, William Chadd, Gentlemen, was presented to the House, and

read; setting forth. That the said Banks, or Sea-walls, are ablblutely necessary to be maintained, and kept in good Repair, to preserve many thousand Acres of valuable Land against the Inundations of the said River, and of the Salt Waters; and that the said Banks are generally raised from Seven toTen Foot above the adjoining Lands, that Height being required to defend the Country against the Spring Tides, and which Banks are, for the moll part, very narrow at the Top, and composed of Brulhwood, and in Ibme Places only of Reed and Sea-sand, which are very improper Materials to support the Weight and Strength of Horses, haling upon the same; and yet, if any Breach should be made in any Part of the said Banks, the said whole Level of Land mull inevitably be drowned: And that the Navigation upon that Part of the said River, lying near the Mouth of the River, where the Tide flows in its full Strength, was formerly carried on without any haling, as it is in other Rivers, where the Tide ebbs and flows; but if, at any time, it was found necessary to hale upon the said Banks, it was always done by Men, and not by Horses; and that when any such Attempt of haling with Horses was made, it was constantly opposed by the Land-owners; but that, of late Years, the Size of the Vessels, or Lighters, has been much enlarged, and NineorTen large Lightersare frequently fastened together in One Gang, thereby to carry on a more gainful Trade:

And that this Increase of the Number and Size of the Lighters hath brought upon the Lightermen and Bargemen the pretended Necessity, which they allege, of haling with Horses, to the great Damage and Impoverishment of the Proprietors of the said Banks, or Sea-walls, and Danger of drowning the Country: And that the Advantages hereby accruing to the Lightermen and Bargemen induced them to set up a pretended Right or Claim to hale with Horses on the said Banks; and an Action being brought for determining the fame, upon a full Hearing of the Merits of the said Cause, last Summer Assizes at Norwich, for the said County, before a special Jury, it was determined there was no such Right; and that thereupon the Lightermen, Bargemen, and Traders, are now applying to this House, but without having the Consent or Concurrence of the Bank-owners, for a Bill to impower them to hale with Horses on the said Banks, which mull greatly

10 D assess

afieft and endanger the Property of the Petitioners, and all other the Land-owners within the said Levels: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may have Liberty to be heard by Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against any such Bill.

Edinburgh, and of the Minutes of general Meeting of the % Contributors to that Charity, on the 04th of July 1739, it is let forth:

" That though the Funds in the City of Edinburgh, tt which were yearly distributed for maintaining the Poor, " were very considerable, yet, from Experience, and a " strict Examination, the Manner of distributing weekly " and quarterly Pensions to that Time used, neither answered the Purpose of subsisting them comfortably, or " employing them usefully, in regard they can be under no Controul, either how they dispose of their Pensions, " or how they employ their Time, in both which, it was too evident, there was a very gross Abuse, and which, " it was hoped, might be prevented, were they so lodged " as to be under the Inspection of proper Overseers: And " that, beside. One great Article of Expence would be " much diminished in their Lodging, since, at that time, " every One or Two had their own Beds to provide separately, the yearly gross Charge whereof was, at least, computed at£.800 Sterling: And that, as the Method " of maintaining and employing the Poor in a Workhouse, " had succeeded so extremely well, in many Instances, in " England, and in the Town of that it gave the

" greatest Encouragement to attempt something of " that Nature in the City of Edinburgh, where there were such large Funds for endowing of it: And that " it was then agreed, Thai a large Hospital, or Workhouse, " should be built for the regular Maintenance and Employment of the whole Poor of the City, and for taking proper Care of Orphans and Foundlings, to be " endowed with the Poor's Funds, that were then under " the Cclleftion of the Kirk Treasurer, and were distributed, partly by the Magistrates and Town-Council, " and partly by the particular Kirk Sessions; whereof " the neat annual Amount would come out to above " £.1,700 Sterling, and with £.200 Sterling, yearly, out " of the City's Revenue, and by such Contributions as should be thereto made by the several Societies or Corporations within the City, and other piously disposed " Persons: And that the Management of the said Workhouse should be in Eighteen, to be chosen by the '* Magistrates and Town-Council, ordinary and extraordinary} Eighteen by the Kirk Sessions, whereof Two " by each Session; Eighteen Merchants, to be chosen by Ballot} eighteen Tradesmen, whereof each of Fourteen Corporations to chufeOne, the Barbers and Wig-' makers to chufc One} and the Candlemakers to chuse

George Drummond Esquire, laid, That he has been a Manager of the said Charity, and that above 500 Persons have been annually maintained within the said House} and that Stipends have been allowed to a considerable Number of Out-pensioners} and that the Persons relieved were such as were decayed Burgcflis of, or Housekeepers in, the said City.

Mr. James Stuart confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Drummond: And added. That Ire had been also a Manager of the said Charity; and that the Persons whom the Managers consider as proper Objects of Relief, are such as have lived Three Years in the City, and been employed in useful Labour, and brought a Certificate thereof from some reputable Inhabitant; That the Managers have not admitted or relieved common Beggars} and that, since the Workhouse was erected, common Beggars were very rarely seen in the said City, for that the Managers obliged them to enact themselves to leave the City under the Penalty of going to the House of Correction.

Then the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That since the Workhouse hath been erected in the City of Edinburgh, a considerable Number of indigent Persons

have been annually fed and cloathed; and such of them as were capable have been employed in useful Labour, by which Means the said City has been kept free from Beggars.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the necessary Charge of fopporting the said Work-house amounts annually to a large Sum, Part whereof hath arisen from voluntary Collections at the Church Doors, and other Places of Divine Worship; that other Part of the ford Sum arising from Donations, Legacies, and the Charity Boxes, fixed at the Doors of the said House, has decreased gradually, and such Deficiency has, from time to time, been supplied by extraordinary voluntary Collections.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Workhouse is proper and useful for the Maintenance and Employment of tire Poor; has been hitherto managed with Care and Economy, and ought to be supporled; and, in order to make an equal, just, and effectual, Provision for the Support thereof, the Aid of Parliament is requisite,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill to make an equal, just, and effectual, Provision for the Support of the Charity Workhouse erected in the City of Edinburgh.
