A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, and principal In- preveqtin£ habitants, of the Corporation of Gr and Milton, in Mischiefii the County of Kent, was presented to the House. and read; ,rotn Gu«-setting forth, That the Petitioners observing in the Votes Pow<kr-of the House, a Bill depending to prevent Mischiefs that may happen by keeping in any One Place too great a Quantity of Gunpowder, beg Leave to lay before the House their very great Fears and Uneasiness, concerning the prodigious Quantity of Gunpowder at this Time deposited in the Magazines and otherHouses at Til amounting to upwards of Twenty thousand Barrels, and being within little more than half a Mile distant from the Towns of Gravesend and Milton: And they further represent, That besides the excessive Quantity at Tilbuty , there are moreover several hundred Barrels of Gunpowder in the Magazine in the Town of Gravesend: And that since the Peace with France and Spain, whereby lb many Men of War have been paid off, such large Quantities of Gunpowder, from on board the Men of War, have been lent to 'Tilbury Fort; that the Magazines there cannot contain them, whereby the Governor's House is filled with Gunpowder, that being common tiled Buildings: That the Buildings of the Garrison, where Fire is usually kept, is no more than Ten Yards distant from the said Buildings:

That the Mischiefs to be apprehended from Accidents common to Gunpowder, either by casual Fire, Lightning, or Treachery, are too vastand astonishing for human Reason to calculate, for the Force and Effects of such a dreadful Quantity: And that those which seem most obvious are, besides the Loss of One of the most considerable military Stores in the Kingdom, the utter Destruction of the Petitioners and their Properties, the Merchant Ships in the River, and, in great Probability, infinite Mischief to the City of London; since it is known, by Experience, that the blowing up of One single Powder-mill has done /

Damage Ten Miles Distance: It is further apprehended, as an Evil consequent to any terrible Accident from the Gunpowder at Tilbury, That the Navigation of the River Thames would be absolutely ruined, the Sea-Wall, for several Miles, by any such excessive Explosion, must be torn up in such a manner, and such Breaches made in it, as would be the Work of Ages to repair: And therefore praying, That, in passing the said Bill into a Law, Provision may be made against these prodigious Evils, in such manner as the House shall think fit.

A Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others. Inhabitants of Eafi Greenwich, and other Places adjacent, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants thereof, and adjoining thereto, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That in the Parish of Eafi Greenwich, and within a Quarter of a Mile, or thereabout, of the Town in which a Market is held, and in which there is a Royal Palace, and that well known luperb Building the Royal Hospital for Seamen, there is a Storehouse or Magazine, wherein are frequently kept Twelve thousand Barrels of Gunpowder, and sometimes to the Amount of Fifteen thousand j and that, besides the great Danger which mud attend all Places of this Kind, this Storehouse (lands in an open Field, not inclosed with any Fortification whatever, whereby it is exposed to Treachery, and every Accident; and, from its being situate so close to the Uiver , it is conceived

great Mischief may happen from the firing the Ships Guns, as they pal's and repafsat lb fma!l a Ditlance hom it', especially :f, through Negligence or Accident, a Ball should be left in any One of the Guns, an instance of which has lately happened; and that the said Storehouse (lands so near to the River, on the Banks whereof grow

Vol. 25.

a great Quantity of Reeds, that if any df these should be set bn fire, as they have been* the Gunpowder contained in the said Storehouse would be in great Danger of being fired; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if, through Treachery, or by Lightening* or any other Accident, so great a Quantity as Six or.Seven hundred Tons fb^uld take Fire, atnong many great Mischiefs which would'fol low, not only the LiVes and Properties of the Petitioners, but the said Palace and Hospital* the Ring's Yards and Stores at Deptford, and W and the Banks and Navigation of the River Thames, and the Ships failing and at Anchor therein, would be inevitably destroy-fdi and almost inconceivable Damage accrue to the Cities, of London and /V^flminster: And therefore praying. That tire said Storehouse may be repsoved to such a DistanCe from the Habitations of the Petitioners* as that the Petitioners Lives and Properties may be preferred* and the several other Mischiefs beforertneotioned may be prevented, in such manner as the House shall think fit.

Trade to ‘ A ^TlTfON of the underwritten Merchants and Iiudson'sBay, XV Traders of the City of London, was prerented to the House, and read; alleging, That tlfe Petitioners apprehend they have an undoubted Right to Traffick with all Countries belonging to the British Crown, and with all other Countries- in Amity with his Majesty, unless deprived by Act: of Parliament: That all Monopolies and exclusive Companies are prejudicial to the Trade of this Nation:'That the raft Countries around and adjoining Hudson's Bay, claimed by that Company as their exclusive Property, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, may be much improved, and the Trade greatly Wreased, if the House think proper to lay the Trade open to all his Majesty's Suttyefts: That most of the neighbouring Nations in Europe!, by prohibiting or discouragrng our Manufactures,

' make it necessary that All proper Encouragement should be given towards the increasing our Colonies, and Exten-. fionofotirTraiddand Navigation: That the House having always been ready to retrieve, extend, and protest, the -British Trade froma.ll illegalexclufiveGrants and Mo-' " ttopohes; and expressing the Hope of the Petitioners,

That the House will think it of publick Benefit to opeh :the Trade in Hudson's Bay to all his Majesty's Subjects, that they may have Liberty'to land, build, and trade :there, Withoht-having their ShipsOr Eflfefts seized; which Will not only tend to the enlarging the Sale of Manufactures, but the finding out the North-weft Passage; or to give the Petitioners such other Relief and Encouragement to extend Trade into those Parts of America, 8cc. as to the House shall seem meet.

Ditto. A Petition of the Merchants of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, was allb presented to the House, and ' read; alleging, That in case the House should declare to

be'illegal that Monopoly so long exercised by the "Bay Company (greatly to the Advantage of a few People, but little to that of the Publick) and should resolve to give a ftee Permission to all his Majesty's Subjects, as well as the Company, to trade into Hudson's Bay, and the extensive Countries adjacent, that it would be greatly conducive to the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, particularly the Woollen and Iron Manufactures, with the Advancement and Prosperity of which the Welfare of this Nation is so'inseparably coanefted; and that the Inhabitants of that vast Country have been found to be a 07,

humane People, and always inclined to promote an amicable Intercourse with such as treat them kindly,

which makes the Keeping of expensive Forts there quite unnecessary; so that the Trade to those Parts may be carried on to much better Purpose by private Adventurers than by a Company; and that industrious Inhabitants might make very convenient Settlements in many Parts of those vast Countries, by which means the Natives, by a more frequent and intimate Intercourse with them, would soon be instructed and induced to promote aTraffick with the other Natives remotely distant: and, by supplying them with British Commodities, would bring down into our Hands a great Part of the Furs and other valuable Produce of that vast Country, which now fall into the Hands of our great Rivals the French, whose Strength and Commerce mud always increase in proportion as ours decay; which rauft, the Petitioners are afraid, inevitably be the Cafe, unless some new Channels inTrade are opened to us; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion the present Trade into Hudson's Bay is of trifling Advantage to the Nation (the Company, as the Petitioners are informed, not exporting above the Value of 3 or Annum) in

companion of what it would soon be, were the Trade laid open, whereby the Publick might enjoy the Benefit of an immense Treasure, now almost buried, and sacrificed only to the confined and avaricious Views of a few: And therefore, and as the Charter of the Bay Company

is, as the Petitioners apprehend, absolutely inconsistent with the Welfare of this Nation, and void, by their never having fulfilled the principal Condition of their obtaining so extensive a Grant, viz. the endeavouring properly and vigoroufty to find out aNorth-weft Passage, and in settling Colonies, as in other Parts of the Continent of America; and as the Petitioners apprehend the British Fishery in particular is a most valuable Branch to this Nation, which they have always been, and still are, particularly felicitous to cultivate in the belt Manner, may thereby be greatly improved and extended; praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make such Order and Provision therein as the House shall think fitting.

A Petition of the principal Traders and Inhabitants of the Town of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Opening of the Commerce carried on to Hudson's Bay, which has for many Years been confined in the Hands of a few Persons, to the great Detriment of the Trade of this Kingdom, and the Navigation in general made free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects, will be very advantageous to the Kingdom in general, and greatly promote the Consumption of the Iron and Woollen Manufactures: And therefore praying the House to act therein as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be taken into Consideration at the same time that the Report from the Committee who were appointed to inquire into ,the State and Condition of the Countries adjoining to Hudson's Bay, and of the Trade carried on there; and to consider how those Countries may be settled and ..improved, and the Trade and Fisheries there extended and increased; and also to inquire into the Right the Compary of Adventurers trading into Hudson's Bay pretend to have, by Charter, to the Property of the Lands and exclusive Trade to those Countries; is taken into Consideration.

the Second, his said Majesty, in Confederation of the great Cost and Expences the said Undei takers had been at, and of the Discoveries they lead then nude, and in order tocncourage them to go on with their Undertakings, was graciously pTeased, by his Letters Patent, Or Charter, bearing Date the Second Day of May, in the Twenty-second Year of his then Majesty's Reign, to incorporate, create, and make, the said Prince Rupert, the said Duke of Albemarle, the said Earl of Craven, and others the Lords and Persons named in the said Letters Patent, or Charter, One Body Corporate and Politick, by the Name of the Governors and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay; and, by that Name, to have perpetual Succession, tsc. giving and granting the reby, to the said Governor and Company, the foie Trade and Commerce of all those Seas, Straits, Bays, within the Entrance of the Straits called,

which were not then actually possessed by, or granted to, any of his said Majesty's Subjects, or possessed by the Subjects of any other Christian Prince or State, with divers and fiindry Privileges as in the said Letters Patent, or Charter, now lying before this House, will appear: That the Petitioners apprehend the said Letters Patent, or Charter, to be both reasonableand legal; and that it doth not contain further Privileges than what were absolutely necessary to induce the Adventurers to begin and carry on a Trade, attended with great Charge and Difficulties at first, and without any Probability of yielding any Profit to the Adventurers for a considerable time; and that, if a Charter had not been granted, there is no Reason to think that any Trade would have been carried on th-'re from this Country, any more than there had been for the Space of upwards of Fifty Years next after the said Discovery; and that by means of these Letters Patent, or Charter, this Nation hath not only received great Advantage in its Revenues, by the Trade carried on by the said Governor and Company, but hath the foie Trade into Hudson's Bay, no other Nation interfering with the Company therein -, and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Tcade into the said Bay cannot be carried on or managed so advantageously, either to the Honour or Interest of this Nation, as in a Company, and in a Joint-Stocki which they formerly made appear to the Satisfaction of the- whole Legislature; and that the Legislature hath always expressed this to be their Sense, by the Encouragement they have given this Company whenever the Trade into Hudson's Bay hath been under the Consideration of Parliament; and the Petitioners are not conscious that they have done any thing to lessen that favourable Opinion which this House had of them: That the Petitioners conceive, that they have fully answered the Ends of Iheir Charter, by carrying on the Trade to the Advantage of this Nation, by establishingFadlories, and building Forts, at a very great Expence, for the Conveniency of their Trade with the Indians. and protecting it from the Attacks of any European Natives, or of the Indians', and also by using their Endeavours to find out a Passage into the South Seas, in all Places where a Passage would have been of any Use, to the great Lois and Damage of the Company, as well as of the Lives of several of his Majesty's Subjects: That the Petitioners hope, that it Hull not be imputed to them as a Crime, that, after having a certain Knowlege, by their Settlements in the South and South-weft Parts of that Bay, and as far as the Latitude of 59' North, that there is no Passage in all that Part of the Bay; and, after having made fruitless and expen live Attempts to find out a Passage in more Northern Parts, as-far as Latitude 66*, they have not persisted townlle their Capiia] in looking for a Passage, which they have no Reason to think exist?; and in case it doth exist, and cap be found, will not be of any manner of Use; and, moll probably, if dilbovered, the Discoverers will never be able to get back, to give any Account thereof: And they also hope tl»ey. are nor blameable on account of there being mi Colony established within the Limits of their Charter, (ince. it is not what they had in View when the Charter

A Petition as well of the Mayor, Capital Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Borough of in the Counties

of Norfolk and Suffolk, as of the Land-owners, Farmers* principal Inhabitants, Merchants, and Navigators, living in and near Thetford aforesaid, and trading upon the River Brandon, commonly called ‘the Ouze, between

Thetfordand a Place called the , near Brandon

Forty, in the said Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, was present ed to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for making navigable 'commonly called the Rivers Brandon and divers

' Persons therein named were conllituted Commissioners for determiningallControversies, which mightarife, in relation to the Making of the said Rivers navigable, in maintaining the Navigation thereof, for settling the Rates of Carriage of Goods on the said Rivers, and for ascertaining the Satisfaction for Damages done to the Banks of the said Rivers, by haling and drawing of Vessels, navigated thereupon; and Power was given to the said Commissioners, or any Five of them, to chule other Persons, residing in the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, to be Commissioners,

in the Head of such Commissioners, as should, from time to time, die: And that all the Commissioners, appointed by the said Act, have been long since dead, and that no new Commissioners have been appointed in their Head: And that some Disputes have of late arisen between the Own*, ers of Lands and Banks, adjoining to the said River, commonly called The Lesser Ouze, from Thetford to Brandon, and from Brandon to a Place called The White House, near Brandon Ferry, relating to the Haling-ways there, and other Matters concerning the said Navigation: And that the said Differences cannot be adjusted and settled by any other Means than by expensive and tedious Law Suits, un-lefsfome further Provision be made by Parliament for appointing new Commissioners, and inverting them with Power to determine all Disputes relating to, or occasioned by, the Navigation of the said River: And that the said River and Navigation go into the great River Ouze, in the County of Norfolk: And therefore praying, That Ibme Provision may be made in the Bill now depending in the House, for preserving and improving the Navigation of the River Ouze, in the said County of Norfolk, by impowering the Lightermen and Bargemen, navigating thereon, to hale with Horses, on the Banks of the said River; and for providing a reasonable Satisfaction to the Owners of the said Banks; for appointing new Commissioners for putting in Execution the Purposes of the said recited Act, so far as the same relates to the Navigation of the said River commonly called The Lefjer Ouze, from Thetford to Brandon, and from Brandon to a Place called The White House, near Brandon Ferry; or that such other Relief may be granted as to the House shall leem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are African thereunto subscribed, Creditors of the Royal 0,nPan>i

pany, on behalf of themselves and the rest of the Creditors of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That, although by a Bill depending in the House, for extending and improving the Trade to Africa, all and every the British Forts, Settlements, and Fastorics, on the Coast of , from Cape Blanco to the Cape of Good Hope, inclusive, and all the Territories within those Limits, and the Islands thereunto adjoining, (all which now are in the Possession of the Royal African Company of England) are intended to be absolutely verted in a new Company, without any express Provision for the just Demands, or any Saving of the just Rights, of the Creditors of the said present Company, whose foie Security they are, yet such is the Reliance of the Petitioners upon the Justice, Honour, and Companion, of Parliament, that they will not attempt, by any Application for their private Interefb, anywise to retard the Progress of a Bill which the House has judged and declared necessary for the publick Good; but that, on the contrary, the Petitioners are content to refer their Dcmands to the Consideration of the House, whenever they shall think fit to enter thereupon: And that the Petitioners are, in the mean time, ready and desirous to do every Act in their Power for immediately vesting their said Security in whatever Hands the Wifclom of Parliament shall judge fit: And lotting forth. That the Petitioners, fb long since as Mayi748,represented to the said Company, in Writ- ing. That the ruinous Condition of their Forts and Settlements, their notorious Inability to support and defend them, without the Aid of Parliament, and the Indifpofi-tion of the Legislature to intrust them'with those Aids* did most evidently point out the Necessity of surrender* ing their said Possessionsto the Crown, which could alone preserve them from falling into the Hands of the Rivals of Great Britain; and therefore the Petitioners required the

laid Company immediately to make a dutiful Tender thereof to his Majesty, to whom the Petitioners, who claimed a prior Interest therein, were ready to submit and refer their Demands: And that the Petitioners, finding that the said Company, far from paying a proper Regard to such their Application, were about to fend new Officers to their Settlements in Africa, which* in the Apprehension of the Petitioners, might be attended with dangerous Consequences, not only to their Interests, but also that of the Publick, the Petitioners, in or about the Month df

June following, remonstrated to the said Company, in Writing, the Impropriety of their taking such a Step at that Time, and under their then Circumstances, without the Consent of their Creditors, or Approbation of his Ma-

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the further Report from the Committee appointed to consider of, and report to the House, the State of the British Fishery, the Resolutions which the said Committee of the whole House had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, -That the enlarging the Whale Fishery will be of great Advantage to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom.

j Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Act of the Sixth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the further Encouragement of the Whale Fishery carried on by his Majesty's British Subjects, and continued by an Act of the 13th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, granting a Bounty of 20 per Ton on all Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery, be further continued for the Space of Seven Years, to commence from the Time of the Expiration of the said ,last mentioned Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Sum of Twenty Shillings per Ton, to be 'paid out of the Customs in like manner as is directed by the former Act, be granted as an additional Bounty on Shipping employed as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Bounties of 20 and ao be granted and paid in like manner to Ships fitted out in his Majesty's Dominions in America, and discharging in Great Britain under the like Regulations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Act, of the 5th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Greenland Fishery, and continued by an Act of the Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, be likewise further continued for the Space of Seven Years, to commence from the Time of the Expiration of the said last mentioned Act.

The Three First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time*was, upon the Question put thereupon, with an Amendment thereunto, agreed to by the House; and is as followeth; viz.

' Resolved, That the said Bounties of 20/. and 20 s, be

granted and paid in like manner to Ships fitted out in his Majesty's Dominions in America, and discharging in Great Britain under proper Regulations.

The last Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

BountittYc ^>ct*t‘on Manufacturers of Linen Cloth in the

' ' Town of Warrington, in the County of Lemcaster, whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and of many others concerned in the said Manufacture, waspresented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Irish Linen Manufacture hath such very great Encouragements given to it by the Parliament of Ireland, over and above what is given in this Kingdom, that by means thereof the Irish do undersell the Petitioners; and that if the Bounties given by the British Parliament are continued to the Irish, without putting the Petitioners upon a Par with them, with regard to Bounties (which the Petitioners apprehend cannot be done without laying before the House a true State of both the British and Irish Linen Manufactures) the Petitioners mud be obliged to quit their Trade, to the utter Ruin of themselves, and of many Thousands of People depending upon the same: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of those whose Names are subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, Inhabitants of the Borough of Wigan, and other Places adjacent, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, who are Dealers in the Linen Manufactures of this Kingdom, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by an Act made in the 15th and 16th Years of his present Majesty's Reign, for granting to his Majesty an additional Duty on foreign Cambricks imported into Great Britain, and for allowing the reout a Bounty upon certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported, a Bounty is given of One Peny for every Yard of British and Irish Linens made of Hemp or Flax, of the Value of Six Pence per Yard, and not exceeding 12 d. per Yard, and of One Half-peny for every Yard of such British and Irish Linens under the Value of 6d. per Yard, which, within the Term of Seven Years, from the 25th Day of March 1743, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, should be exported out of Great Britain to Africa, America, or Portugal; and that the said Bounty was by a subsequent Act made in the 18th Year of his present Majesty, enlarged One Half-peny for every Yard of such Linens of the Value of 5 d.per Yard, and notex- ceeding 12 d. per Yard; and Three Half-penies/vr Yard for every Yard of above the Value of Yard,

and not exceeding 18 d Yard; the same to have Continuance to the End of the said Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament: And that the Petitioners are informed, that Application is making to Parliament for a Continuance of the said Bounty after the Expiration of the said Term of Seven Years; And therefore representing to the House, That if the same be granted, it will tend to the Ruin of many Branches of the Linen Manufactures in the said County, and other Northern Counties in that Part of Great Britain called England, and to the Impoverishment of several Thousand Families which have been supported thereby; for that the Manufacturers in the Linen and Cotton Trade in those Parts have, for many Years last past, wrought up large Quantities of British and Irish (but mostly of Irish) Linen Yarn into Cheques, and other Goods, aconsiderable Part whereof have been exported to the British Plantations, and other foreign Markets, without the Aid of such Bounties as have been granted to other Branchesof the Linen Manufactory; and have still carried on the Trade, although under great Disadvantage and Discouragement, in hope that, at the End of the said Term, those Bounties would cease; but that, if the same be continued, the Manufacturers in Ireland, who have their Yarn free from the Duty of from Five to Fifteen Pounds per Cent, (in proportion to the Fineness and Value of the

Yarn) which is paid to the Crown upon the Importation thereof into this Kingdom, with the Advantage of the said Bounties, and the Enqciiragements given to them in Ireland, are enabled to give greater Prices for their Yarn than the Petitioners can afford to give, and to underfcll them so much in all foreign Markets, as in time to suppress the Trade of the Petitioners; whereby (besides the Mischiefs and inconveniencies above-mentioned) that Branch of his Majesty's Revenue arising from the Importation of Irish Yarn, will be greatly impaired, if not totally loft; and Foreigners will also gain the Opportunity of sup-plyinghis Majesty's Plantations with Cheques, and other coloured Goods, as they have formerly done; all which may be prevented, if the Linen Trade in his Majesty's Dominions may be set upon such a Footing, as to give all his Majesty's Subjects equal Advantage and Encouragement therein: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and give such Relief therein as to the House shall seem fit.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Cheque, and other Linen Goods, and the Traders and Dealers in the Linea, Manufactory, within the Town and Parish of Mane lifter, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and the Parts adjacent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others the Manufacturers.Traders, and Dealers in the Linen Manufacture, within the said Town and Parish, and Parts adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; reciting Part of the said Act made in the 15th and 16th Years of his present Majesty's Reign; and letting forth, That the Manufacturers of Manchester Goods have, for many Years last past, worked up large Quantities of British and Yarn intoCheques,

and other Goods, a considerable Part whereof hath been exported to the British Plantations in America, and other foreign Parts, without the Aid of those Bounties which have been given to the Exporters of other Branches of the Linen Manufactory; and that by the Encouragement now given, by the Parliaments of Great Britain and Ireland, to the Manufacturers of coarle Linen in Ireland, they are enabled to give greater Prices for Yarn than can be afforded by the Linen Manufacturers of this Kingdom; the Price of Yarn imported from Ireland being, since the passing the said Act, very greatly advanced; and ail Yarn exported out of Ireland being charged by the Parliament there with a Duty of One Half peny per Pound at an Average, amounting to about J. 6 Cent.: And alleging, That unless some Method is taken by Parliament to bring the Manufactures of Linen Yarn in Great Britain and Ireland upon a more equal Footing, many very considerable Branches of Trade in the Manchester way will be greatly lessened, if not entirely loft to this Nation; and that Foreigners will consequently find out Opportunities of supplying his Majesty's Colonies abroad with Cheques, and other coloured Linen Goods, as they formerly did, to the Ruin of many Thousand Families in this County, employed in such Manufactures, and who are wholly supported thereby: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give such Relief therein as the Nature of the same requires, and as to the House shall seem meet.

To the Honourable the Commons ®f Great Britain, ' in Parliament assembled:

The humble Proposel of the Royal African Company of England.

The Company being indebted to furidry Persons in the Sum of One hundred and Seven thousand Two hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Eight Shillings and Five Pence, as appears by an Account, delivered in to this Honourable House the Twenty-second of this Instant, pursuant to their Order; and having been heard, by their Counsel, against the Bill for extending and improving t he Trade to Africa, with respect to their Property, humbly hope and rely. That they have made it appear that they have an undoubted Right to the Lands granted by their Charter, and to the Forts and Castles by them purchased and built thereon.

But the said Company, being willing and desirous to do and contribute all in their Powerto facilitate such Measures as this Honourable House, in their great Wisdom, shall judge most proper to be taken, for extending and improving the said Trade, and for preserving the same to Posterity, do, in the most humble and dutiful Manner, beg Leave to

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there be laid before this House, in the next Session of Parliament, an Account of the Tenor and Amount of all the Bills of Credit which have been created and issued in the several British Colonies and Plantations in America, as well those under. Proprietors and Charters, as under his Majesty's immediate Commission and Government, that shall be then outstanding, distin* guishing the Amount of the same in each Colony or Plantation, and the respective Times when such Bills so outstanding were issued, with the Amount of the said Bills in Money of Great Britain, both at the time when such Bills were issued, and at the time of preparing the said Account; and also the Times fixed for the calling in, sinking, and discharging, such Bills, and the Funds appropriated for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy-Council.

The House, according to Order, refoved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider lurther of the Report, which, upon liles the 23d Day of this instant May, was made from the Committee who were appointed to consider of, and report to the House, the State of the British Fishery, and the Appendix to the said Report.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed t)ie Chair.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the Iioute will pleaseto receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe accordingly reported, from the said Committee, the Resolution which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the carrying on the British Herring and Cod Fisheries will be of eminent Advantage to the Trade and Navigation of thele Kingdoms, and is highly worthy the Consideration of Parliament, and deserves proper Encouragement.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolution: And that Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe, Mr. Alderman Janffen, Sir James Lowther, Admiral Vernon, and Sir Richard Lloyd, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for the further Encouragement and Enlargement of the Whale Fishery; and for continuing such Laws as are therein mentioned; and for the Naturalization of such foreign Protestants as shall serve for a certain Time on board such Ships as shall be fitted out for the said Fishery.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Lieutenant-General Oglethorpe took the Chair of the Committee.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

1 come now to put an End to this Session of Parliament; which is become the more necessary, by reason of the advanced Season of the Year.

The definitive Treaty of Aix la ChapeUe having been, by my Order, laid belore you several Months ago, you have all been fully informed of the Terms and Conditions on which it was made; and have already had the Satife-fastion to fee them carried into Execution, by the several contracting Parties, with great Punctuality and good Faith, so far as the 'fime and Distance ot Place would admit: Nothing now remains, but to preserve and improve the Peace lo happily re-established; all the Powers concerned have declared therriselves in lo clear and friendly a Manner on this Subject, as leaves no room to doubt of their sincere Disposition to render the Peace lading in all Parts: My earned Desire to promote the Welfare of my own Subjects, and the general Tranquillity of Europe, will make me exert my Endeavours for the same good End, by steadily adhering to the Engagements 1 have entered into, and cultivating the most perfect Union and Harmony with my Allies, upon whole ready Concurrence in all proper Measures for that Purpose I have the greatest Reason to depend.

It is with great Satisfaction I have seen Part of this Session employed in Considerations for advancing the Trade and Navigation of my Kingdoms: I hope, at your next Meeting, you will be able to perfect what has now been begun, particularly by taking the proper Methods to render our nava Force the most ulefuland serviceable, which is so eh ntiai to the Protection of our Commerce, and to our Security in all Times.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

1 return you my Thanks for the Supplies you have granted me, and for the Attention you have shewn to maintain the public Credit, which I rejoice to fee in so flourishingaCondition at the End of an expensive, though necessary War: The Readiness with which you have enabled me to satisfy the Demands ofmy Allies isvery agreeable to me, and cannot fail to produce the belt Effects.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is with particular Pleasure that I now meet you in Parliament at a Time when the complete Re-establish-‘ ilient of a general Peace has restored to my People the Blessings of Quiet and Tranquillity, the good Effects re-fulting from hence do already appear in the flourishing Condition of our Commerce, and the Rife of the publick. Credit, which naturally lay the surest Foundations of an Increase of Strength, and of lading Prosperity, to my Kingdoms. I have not failed, this Summer, to make use of every Opportunity of cementing and securing the Peace; and it is my firm Uesolution to do every thing in my Power for the Preservation of if, and religioully to adhere to the Engagements I have entered into.

I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, That 1 have found all the contracting Powers in the definitive Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, as well as the rest of my Allies, in the

lame good Disposition; and have no Keaton to doubt of their Concurrence in the same desirable End: It Is unnecessary forme to tell you, That nothing can contribute lb much to the Continuance and Improvement of this happy Situation of Affairs, as the effectual Supporting of that Weight and Influence which properly belong to the Crown of Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Officers to prepare, and Iky before you, the Estimates for the.Service of the entiling Year. I desire such Supplies only as shall be found necessary for the Security and Welfare of the Nation; and in that View, I must earnestly recommend to you the Maintaining of my Fleet in its full Strength; and that you would-be watchful to improve any Opportunity of putting the National Debt in a Method of being reduced with a ftrnft Regard to pobhek Faith, and private Property.

Mv Lords and Gentlemen*

I have nothing to desire of you, but that you would, with Unanimity and Dispatch, pursue such Measurrs as imy'be n:oft conducive to your own real and lifting Interest: Whatever good Laws you shall propose for the Advancement of our Trade and Navigation, and for encouraging a Spirit of Industry in all Parts of the Kingdom, will be extremely acceptable to me: And you may rest allured, That I shall always look upon the true Great-ness of my Crown, and the Stability of my Government, as inseparably united with the Happiness and Prosperity of my People.

Usual Order*. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be cleded or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured l'o to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, This House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Re/o/ved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour: and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Re/o/ved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given faste Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Re/o/ved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, (b taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the speciial Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker's Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Eleven

of the Clock in the Morning, to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar, and Westminster shall be kept free and open 1 and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending thi9*House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in -

fier hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be. no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or (hereabouts.

Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same putin Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen, attending the Members of this House, to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be dicharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the Intercepting or Losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post-Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster-General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning, till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the lead immediately after the Riling of the House; and also on every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members, to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away; lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be font to the Postmaster-General.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the Printing thereof; and that no Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Mr. Charles Townshend reported from the Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which he read in his Place; alnd afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our fin cere and hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg leave to congratulate your Majesty on the complete Re-establishment of a general Peace, whereby the Blessings of Tranquillity are restored to your People; and to express our Satisfaction at the good Disposition which your Majesty has found in all your Allies, as well as in the contracting Powers in the definitive Treaty of aft la Ckapelle, to continue and preserve so desirable a Situation, from whence we have not only the comfortable prof-pest of future Ease, but may likewise promise ourselves, through the flourishing Condition of our Commerce, and natural Rife of publick Credit, a gradual Increase of our national Strength.

With a Zeal and Gratitude indispensably due to the many Instances of your Majesty's paternal Affection for your People, we acknowledge your great Wisdom in recommending to us the Reduction of the national Debt, as an Object worthy of our most serious Attention; and we assure your Majesty we will apply ourselves, with all possible Diligence, to find out the properest Means to ac-complilhfo greatandneceffarya Work, with the strictest Regard to publick Faith and private Property.

This House, earnestly desirous effectually to promote the mutual and inseparable Interest of your Majesty and your People, w'li grant such Supplies to your Majesty as shall be found necessary for the Security and Welfare of the Nation, which cannot be better provided for than by maintaining the Fleet in such a Condition as may enable your Majesty to preserve that Weight and Influence which properly belong to the Crown of Great Britain: And we will do all that in us lies to encourage a general Spirit of Industry, and advance our Trade and Navigation, the Two great Sources of the Wealth and Strength of this Kingdom.

Your faithful Commons assure your Majesty they are fully sensible. That their present and future Prosperity and Happiness depend, under Gdd, upon the Stability of your Majesty's Government, and the Succession established in your Royal Family.

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by' the House.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of his Majesty'smost Honourable Privy-Council, do humbly know his Majesty's Pleasure, when be will be attended by this House.

Yarmouth A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and

Haven, tee.Commonalty, of the Town and Borough of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common-Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Haven and Piers belonging to the said Town have, for many Years, been repaired and maintained by a Duty imposed by several successive Acts of Parliament upon Coals, and other Goods and Merchandizes imported into the said Haven; and that by an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act to revive, continue, and amend, an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for clearing, depthening, repairing, extending, maintaining, and improving, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth; and for depthening, and making more navigable, the several Rivers emptying themselves at the said Town; and also for preserving Ships wintering in the fai.l Haven from Accidents by Fire: the several Duties granted by the said Act of the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty's Reign, for the Purposes therein mentioned, were revived, and made payable, for the'Perm of Two Yeare, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament:

That the said Haven and Piers were, at the Commencement of the said Act of the Twentieth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, and still continue, in a very ruinous Condition; and will be in Danger of falling in a short time into utter and irreparab e Decay, unlessiome further and more effectual Provision be mad: by Parliament for the Preservation thereof; the Money directed to be applied in repairing, improving, and maintaining the fame, not having been near sufficient for that Purpose; and that the Navigation of the said Rivers will be subject to great Obstructions and Annoyances; and not only Ships wintering in the said Haven, but also the said Town, be exposed to frequent and terrible Accidents by Fire, if the Provisions and Regulations contained in the said Act of the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty's Reign, for preventing such Obstructions, Annoyances, and Accidents, are not continued and enforced: And therefore praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A PETITIONof the Reverend Roger Pettiward^ Dr.Mort-Doctor in Divinity, heretofore called Roger Mart- lock'* Name. lock, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That Walter Pettiward, late of Enfield, in the County of

Middlesex, Esquire, deceased, the Petitioner's Uncle, made his last Will and Testament, bearing Date on or about the 13th Day of April 174c; and thereby, after giving several pecuniary Legacies ana Annuities, gave, devised, and bequeathed, all the Rest and Residue of his Estate real and personal to the Petitioner his Nephew, his Heirs, Executors, and Administrators respectively for ever, subject to the Payment of Two Annuities in the said Will particularly mentioned, upon Condition that the Petitioner took upon himself the Surname of, and wrote himself by the Name of, Pettiward; and, in that Cafe, the Testator made

That there arc Four chief Streets within that City, commonly called East, West, North, and South Gate Streets, which meet and crolseach other in the Centre of the same City: That in the Middle of the Upper Part of the West Gate Street are several old decayed Houses or Tenements, One Shed called The King's Board, and a ruinous old Tower called Trinity Tower, which not only llraiten the Room for the Markets; but stand so near to the Buildings on each Side of the Street, that on one Side of the said Street there is not Room for a Carriage to pass, and on the other Side thereof there is only Room for a Carriage; so that Foot Passengers cannot go by a Carriage so -passing, without great Danger, several Persons having been hurt, and some have lost their Lives, by Carriages passing through the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Committee examined several Witnesses thereupon: And

Thomas Smith Esquire, being examined, relating to the" Ground for the Holding of a free Market for the Sale of Fish in the City of Westminsteron the Piece of Ground near Cation Row, allotted by Act of Parliament for that Purpose, said, That, by the Act, intituled, An Act for making a free Market for the Sale of Fish in the City of

Westminster, which Act was to take Place at Michaelmas last, the Commissioners of the Bridge are authorized and impowered to make a Grant of a Piece of Ground they are possessed of, near Canon Row, to be made use of for holding a Fish-Markef, for the Grant of which Ground the Trustees of the said Market were to pay to the Commissioners of the Bridge Five Pounds, as the Consideration or Purchase Money for the fame, which Ground is as followeth:

East Front to the Thames 71 Feet 3 Inches: From the North Side, next to Manchester Court, from East to West, 265 Feet 6 Inches: The West Side, next Can:n Row, 87 Feet 6 Inches: South Side, next Bridge Street, to the Two new Houses already granted by the Commis*

He further said. And it appeared to your Committee, by the Minutes of the Trustees of the said Market, That, at a Meeting of the said Trustees, on Monday the 27 th Day of November 1749, it was resolved, " That George Harrison, William " Lowndes, Thomas Smith, Harman Henry Cheere,

Mr. Smith bein£ further examined, in relation to the Reasons why the said Fish Market was not opened by the Trustees, he shewed their having taken all Measures for (o doing.

And further laid. That they had also borrowed the Sum of£. 400, upon the Credit of the said Act, at £ 5 per Cent, for carrying the same into Execution, of which they had expended about £. 200 for the Palling the said Act, and other Expences, and that about^.200 remains now in Hand for the Carrying the Act for the said Market into Execution.

And to the same Point why the said Market was not opened:

The Reverend Doctor Wilson, one of the Trustees of the said Market, said, That Application had been made to the Commissioners of the Bridge by the said Trustees:

That they were told by the said Commissioners, That they could not lett the Ground go out of their Hands, nor any Part of it, till the said Bridge was finished, nor even then, left some Accident should happen, as the Sinking of a Pier, or any other Difaiter: And that the said Commissioners have had no Board since the First Monday In July last, till the 28th of November last, when a Committee of the Trustees waited upon them.

And it appeared by the Examination of

Mr. Walter Taylor, Mr. Arnold ThompfonMr. Augustine Styles, Mr. John Deale, and Mr. Joseph Oliver, being a Committee on behalf of the whole Body of the Cod and other Fisheries, for Harwich, London, and Gravesend,

That the Fishermen are desirous to furnish the Cities of London and Westminster with Fi lb, at reasonable Rates, provided the said Market could be immediately opened upon the Ground allotted for that Purpose: And they further laid. That if this Market was opened, it would give more Encouragement to the Fishery, and the Cities of London and Westminster would lie thereby furnished at a better and a cheaper Rate, and the Benefit arising by opening this Market would give such Encouragement, as to enable several Fishermen to enter into an Agreement and subscribe a Sum of Money, in order to try for the Turbot Fishery, which happeneth in the Summer Season, when the Fishermen have little else to do in other Fisheries: The said Turbot Fishery is now all in the Hands of Foreigners: And that they believe the English can carry on that Fishery: And they unanimously declared.

That the Success of the said Market depends upon its being immediately opened: And if it was Hopped for One Year, it would come to nothing.

Tney further said, That they had viewed the Ground intended for the Market; and the whole Ground would be a very commodious Place; but at present the adjoining Stairs, and Landing Place, and the Head of the Stairs on the North Side the Bridge, with the Slip, would serve to make a hard Shift, till the whole Ground could be had; and if that Place was opened, they would bring Fish to the Market directly; That this will only lerve for the Use of small Craft, but when the whole Ground is given it will be convenient for large Craft.

And being asked if the Building of the Bridge can be carried on if the Market should be opened on the Stairs and Slip? They answered, Yes: For they can move the Boats immediately: And they apprehend it would not hinder the carrying on the Works of the Bridge, because it is very inconvenient to move the Timber over the Stairs, as the left Side of the Wharf is more convenient.

And your Committee further inquired whether the Market could be immediately opened upon the Ground allotted for that Purpose; and examined.

Mr. James Stedman, Surveyor and Carpenter: Who said. That he had surveyed the Ground, and taken the several Dimensions, which are set down upon a Plan; which he delivered in, and is hereunto annexed.

And being aiked, if there was Room to open a Fish Market, and carry on the Works of the Bridge at the same time? he said, Yes;* as there is 71 Feet 3 Inches in Front next the Thames, on the Wharf, East-ward; and there is Feet 6 Inches Return at the North Side, adjoining to the Houses at the End of Court: That, at the West End of the Two Houses which are built from the North End of the Yards to the North Side of the Ground next is 43

Feet 5 Inches; so that making a parallel Line, by the North Side down the River, will leave about a8 Feet for the Use of the Market at present: That, on the West End of the Ground, there are Two Centres almost finished, which, when taken away, will leave Room enough to frame Four Centres, if wanted: That there is an. old Building, which is about 76 Feet by 33, and some Sheds adjoining, which are 61 Feet by 13, or thereabout, which are of no present Use to the Bridge; and, if taken down, would make Room enough to frame Two Centres more, or, at least, to remove the Timbers which lie next the Water Side, which will give more Room to remove the Frame of the Centres to the Water Side: That Two Centres are already finished, and Two others almost finished; and that Six more will be wanted: That Four more may be finished at one time, after the Two which are in Hand are taken away: That the Centres are the largest Timber that will be wanted for the Bridge; and that, when any Centres are finished, they are removed upon the Wharf, near the Water Side, to make Room to frame others; and that the Centres may be finished and taken away, and the Fish Market held at the same time, as there is 43 Feet between the North Wall of the Ground between Manchester , and the present Wall of the Yard already built: That there is a large Quantity of Stone, which the Witness apprehends to be of no Use to the Bridge; and, as to the Chequc-house, it may stand as it does, and there is Room enough to open a Fish Market, and to come to the same without any Hindrance to the Works of the Bridge:

That there is Room enough to frame Two Centres more, and for all the necessary Works of the Bridge, without pulling dowh the Sheds; which Sheds, as the Witness is informed, are filled with Deals, and other Materials, which are the Property of private Persons, and not intended for the Use of the Bridge; and that there is no other Place in Westminster so convenient for the said intended Market.

Thomas Smith Esquire being aiked if any Part of the Ground allotted for the said Market is lett by the Commissioners of the Bridge? he said, That a Carpenter lays a great many Materials upon the Ground, which he don't apprehend belongs to the Bridge, but does not know that the Commissioners draw any Advantage therefrom; and if the said Commissioners would make a Conveyance of the Ground allotted by Parliament immediately to the Trustees, they could make a Shift with the Stairs, the Landing-place, the Head of the Stairs, with such Part of the North Side of Bridge Street as should be convenient for the said Market.

Mr. Henry Cor dwell and Mr. Thomas Radcliffe, Surveyors and Carpenters, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Stedman in every Particular.

Mr. John Snow, Builder, who a (lifted Mr. Stedman in taking the aforesaid Plan, laid. That there is sufficient Room for a temporary Market, without obstructing the Works of the Bridge; and that a great deal more Room might be made, by pulling down the old Building and Sheds; and that there is likewise a great Quantity of 'Stone on the Premises, which the Witness apprehends to 15

be the Property of private Peluns, and not designed for the Use of the Bridge.

11 having been moved t o your Committee, That Charles Labelye Esquire should be examined, on the bthalfof the Commissioners of the Bridge, in relation to the Inconveniencies that might arise to the Building of the Bridge, by giving immediate Possession of the Ground allotted by Parliament to the Trustees for the Fish -Market: And the said

Charles Labelye Esquire being called, and Mr. Sted~ man's Evidence being read, he said, The Dimensions of the Ground laid down by Mr. Stedman were right; but that That Part of the Ground next the Stairs, together with the said Stairs, is, of all other Ground in the Power of the Commissioners, the most wanted, and will be the longest wanted: And he delivered in a Plan of the said Ground, which he explained to your Committee:

That the Commissioners now pay jf. 158 a Year for Ground on the other Side of the Water; and that, for want of Room, the whole Bridge is now incumbered with Materials: That the Commissioners had indeed fold some Ground before the Sinking of the Pier, when they imagined they should have no further Occasion for it; but that the Witness is not in a Situation to know any thing of the Commissioners letting Ground, Mr. being the proper Person to apply to for Information on that Head.

Being aiked if Timbers are carried down the Stairs? he answered. That the large Timbers are carried by the Wharf; but small Materials are carried down the Stairs: That several of the Piles which are used have been carried through the Water Gate, and down the Stairs; and several others must be carried the same Way: That Three or Four of them are carried in a Day, which are for immediate Use: and, if such Piles were to be carried off the Wharf, they must necessarily stay for High Water, and lose Half their Time; and, in the Opinion of the Witness, those Piles could not be carried down the Stairs, if the Market was held there.

Mr. Walter Taylor, being'further required to inform your Committee, whether it would be inconvenient for Fishermen to go through Bridge with their Boats ? he laid, It would, lor the following Reasons — There is some Difficulty in/hooting the Bridge; and, after the Boats are through, it would be very inconvenient for them to lay at the Landing-place above Bridge in bad Weather, being more exposed to South-eastdrly Winds than below Bridge; but he knows of no Accident that ever happened to any Boat there: That the Witness has founded the Water, and has found it much shallower, being not Half so deep at the Stairs above as at the Stairs below Bridge: That it is uncertain how long Vessels may be obliged to lie at the Market; but that Boats may come to the lower Stairs at Low-water, when they cannot come to the upper Stairs: That, at the Off-Side of the upper Stairs, there is a Shelf or Sand Bank which runs towards the Bridge; and at (ometimes you may comean Hour, sometimes an Hour and an Half, sooner to the lower Stairs than to the upper.

And being aiked, whether those Inconveniencies might not be dispensed with for'Three or Four Months ? he answered, I cannot say.

And being a/ked, whether Vessels laden with other Materials had not lain at the upper Stairs? he said. He could not tell.

Mr. Styles, being examined as to the Difference between the landing at the lower Stairs and the upper, laid. It is very considerable; since the short Tide that goes through the Bridge would often oblige the Boats to go beyond the Stairs, for Fear of Damage, which would prevent their being at Market, and occasion the spoiling the Fish.

Mr. Labelye, being further examined, said, That there

is the same Depth of Water at the Stairs above Bridge as below 5 and that he does not know of any Inconve-niency which would occur to the Wbrks of the Bridge,

from

from holding the Market at the Place proposed, except the Expence of making a Pair of temporary Stairs, and another Cheque: That he cannot say what the Expence of another Cheque would amount unto; but the Stairs would cost between 50 and £. 100.

Mr. James SteJman being asked the same Question, he laid, That the Expence of such a Pair of Stairs would be about £. 10; and that he, the Witness himself, would undertake to make such Stairs for £.:

That Boats lying at such Stairs would be Ibrne Obstruction t but if the Stairs were made at the lower Side of the Wharf, the Obstruction would be less.

Mr. Labelye further informed your Committee, That 40 Foot along Bridge St, from the Corner of the House, upwards, making a Triangle within; and 40 Foot from the Corner of Canon , downwards, making a Triangle inward; may be allowed, though with some Inconveniency; and that the Witness should not be against the immediate conveying the Land,- under a Reservation of the Use thereof for the Bridge for One Year.

Thomas Ledtard Esquire, Surveyor to the said Commissioners, being aiked, whether all the Materials, which liein the Sheds on the (aid Ground, belong to the Bridge? he said, That great Part of them do; but that a private Person has the Occupation of the said Sheds and Ground; and he believes some of the Materials are his own.

Then the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the forthwithOpening of a FreeMarket for the Sale of Fish, in the City oi upon the Piece of Ground allotted by Act of Parliament, will be of Utility to the Publick, and conduce to the lowering the Price of Fish, and the Encouraging of the Fishery,

which is a great Nursery for Seamen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all that Piece of Ground near Canon Row, which was in the Possession of the Commissioners of the Bridge when the Act passed for making a free Market for the Sale of FHh within the City of Westmitjler, &c. ought immediately to be conveyed to the Trustees for the said Market, upon their paying the Consideration Money in the said Act mentioned; but that, for the better carrying on and finishing the Works of the said Bridge, there ought to be a Clause in the said Conveyance, reserving to the Commissioners of the Bridge the Use of Part thereof for a Wharf and Working Yard for one Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the opening forthwith of a free Market for Fish, until the said Land can be entirely surrendered to the Use of the Fish Market, it will be necessary that the Ground 40 Foot in Front, along the North Side of Bridge Street, from the Corner of the House upwards, making a Triangle within, and 40 Foot from the Corner of Canon Row, downwards, making a Triangle inwards with a Communication between the said Two Pieces of Ground, being Part of the said Ground for the said Fish Market, be immediately put into the Possession of the said Trustees, that a temporary Market may be forthwith erected thereupon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trustees for the said Market shall forthwith have free Liberty of the Stairs and Landing-places of the said Stairs on the North Side of the Bridge for the Use of the said Market.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of James Clarke, of East Moullfey, in the Country of Surry, Esquire, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives his Consent, as far as his Majesty's Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read j setting forth. That King Charles the Second, by Letters Patent under his Great Seal, bearing Date the Twelfth Day of March, in the 29th Year of his Reign, granted and

demised to Sir James Clarke, the Petitioner's Grandfather,

since deceased? amongst other Things, all the Manor'of East Moullfey, with the Appurtenances, in the County of

Surry j and also all those Passages of Water upon the River Thames, called Hampton Court , between East Moullfey and Hampton Court; and Hampton Ferry, between Moullfey and Hampton Town, and the Boats thereto belonging; and all Customs, Tolls, and Profits, whatsoever, thereunto appertaining, being Part of the Manor of East Moullfey, in the County of Surry aforesaid, and Parcel of the Pof-sessions of the Honour of Hampton Court aforesaid; to hold the said Manory Passages, and Ferries, with the Appurtenances, unto the said ‘Sir James Clarke, his Executors, Ad-fiaTnistrators, and Assigns, from the Expiration of a certain Term of Years before granted, unto the said Sir James Clarke, which expired in the Year 1698, for and during a long Term of Years, at and under certain yearly Rents

in the said Letters Patent reserved; and that the said Sir James Clarke, the Petitioner's Grandfather, held and enjoyed the said Manor, Ferries, and Premises, under the said Letters Patent, to the Time of his Death, which happened on or about the 31 ft Day of March 1703; and that, upon the Death of the said Sir James Clarke his Son, Sir James Clarke, the Petitioner's Father, since also deceased, entered upon and enjoyed the said Manor, Ferries, and Premises, to the time of his Death, which happened on or about the 16th Day of April 1^28; and that, upon the Death of the Petitioner's said bather, the Petitioner became intitled to the said Manor, Ferries, and Premises, for the Remainder of the said Term of Years granted, and demised by his late Majesty, as aforesaid: That the Two said Ferries now are, and for many Years last part have been, lett to Persons who have, or ought to have, made it their constant Business to attend, and carry over Persons, Cattle, and Carriages, passing and repassing at the said Ferries: And that passing of Rivers by Ferries being at bed very tedious, and, in time of Floods and high Winds, exceedingly troublesome, and sometimes very dangerous, many Applications have been made to the Petitioner, for building a Bridge at Hampton Court, as a Matter that would be of general Use and Advantage to the Publick, and particularly to all Persons having Occasion frequently to pass and repass the said River; and that, upon such Application, and in order to contribute every thing in the Petitioner's Power for effecting so de-firable a Work, the Petitioner caused a View to be taken of the Place'proposed for building the said Bridge, and finds the same every Way proper for the Purpose, as well in respect to the Navigation, as to the Bed and Banks of the said River, such Bed and Banks being a very strong and firm Gravel; and at East Moullfey, where One Foot of the intended Bridge is proposed to stand, all Barges and other Vessels going up the River, and requiring Cattle to draw them, always take fresh Horses; and that the Petitioner therefore is advised, and apprehends, that a Bridge built from Hampton Court to East Moullfey will not be the least Obstruction to the Navigation of the said River; and that the Petitioner, in order to promote to the utmost-of his Power every thing that may be advantageous

23 Geo. II.

geous to the Publick, upon a reasonable Satisfaction being made for the Loss of the Profits arising by the said Ferries, is willing, on his Part, to erect, or cause or permit to be erected, a Bridge over the River of Thames, from Hampton Court to ' East Moullfey aforesaid; but as the Place where the said Bridge is to be built is not only very near One of the Royal Palaces, but also is Part of the Inheritance of the Crown; and such Bridge cannot be erected without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: Therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration; and give Leave that a Bill may be brought in lor the Purpose aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Ordered, That a List of the Widows of such reduced Officers of his Majesty's Land Forces and Marines who died upon the Establishment of Half-pay in Great Britain, and who were married to them before the 25th December 1716; with an Estimate of the Charge thereof for the Year 1750; be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the Deficiency, at Christmas 1749, of the Income of the additional Rates and Duties on Glals Wares and spirituous Liquors, for satisfying the several Annuities chargeable thereupon by an Act ol Parliament of the 19th Year of his Majesty's Reign, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That Surplusses dated at Lady-day 1749, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That Surplusses ftaced at Michaelmas 1749, he referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Fane took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Fane reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next.

Mr Fane also acquainted the House, That he waa directed by the Committee to move. That they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morn-next, Nine of the Clock.

A Pet ition of the Bailiffs, C hamberlains, Commonalty, Ditto,

and Fishermen, of the Town and Corporation of wold, in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of South-wold hath, for Time out of Mind, been an ancient Filliing Town for Herrings and Sprats, which are redded by the Merchants, Fishermen, and others, residing in and near the said Town; and also for catching Cods, Skates, and other Line Fish, which has been the only Support of a great Number of Families, forfeveral Years iad pall: And that, to the Surprize of the Petitioners, the Dutch have, for better than Eight Years pad, lished in their Schuytes lb near the Shore, that their Nets have iv.ept upon the Ground; which not only sweeps the Herring Fish out of the Bay, but also hinders the Petitioners in laying Lines for Cod, Skates, and other Fish, as there have been One hundred Dutch Schuytes at a Time anchoring and driving in the said Bay, in Two or Three Fathom Water; so that the Petitioners, to their great Loss, cannot fish by Night or by Day: And that, if at any time the Petitioners inform them thereof, or give them the lead Umbrage for their foul Fishing, they threaten torun over them, and fink their Boats, or tear their Nets with their Lee Boards; which Proceedings, the Petitioners are informed, are contrary to Treaties, and, if not prevented, in future will be the intire Ruin of a great Number of Families: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration; and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet:

Water-Car- A Petition of sundry Bargemasters and Navijzators of the viage on die River Thames, whose Names are t hereunto subscribed, on Thames. behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House and read; setting forth. That several Acts of Parliament have been made, and several Powers have been granted, from time to time, for settling tile Rate of Locks, for ascertaining the Price of Freight, and for making certain Rules and Orders to regulate the Navigation of the River Thames; and though these have not answered all the good Purposes they were intended to procure, yet it is undeniably true, that they have prevented a great Number of Evils, which must have otherwise accrued; but that as thefeAdf sand Orders will all be expired in a few Months, the Petitioners are under very alarming Apprehensions of the mischievous Consequences which must ensue; for that when the Rates of the Locks shall be subject to no Limitations, and the Barges in their Navigation regulated by " no Rules or Orders, great Obstructions must attend the Commerce, carried on by Water, between the City of London and the several Counties bordering upon the River Thames', which cannot but be exceedingly detrimental to Trade m general, and absolutely ruinous to the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying. That, the Premises being taken into Consideration, the Evils the Petitioners point out may be guarded against by such Methods as the Parliament shall lee meet.
