Tower Sir Hugh Smithson reported from the Committee, to Hamlets whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Trades-Small Debts. men> Housholders, and Shopkeepers, within the Tower Hamlets, in the County of , and in the Liberty

of his Majesty's lower of whose Names are

thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, Liberties, Precincts, and Places, within the said Hamlets, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition { and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Robert Day said. That several large Manufactories are carried on within the Tower Hamlets: That in the Parish of Christ-Church Spittlcfields, where he has lived 26 Years, there are 2,400 Houses, 1,000 of which are not rated to the Poor, being inhabited by Journeymen Weavers and other Artificers and Labourers, who cannot support themselves and their Families, without Credit for small Sums:

That the Petitioners lay under great Discouragements from giving Credit to such Persons, who frequently refuse to pay their Creditors, presuming on the Difficulties they labour under, from the Charge infuing for such small Debts, the Charge in suing a Person to Execution in the Marshalsea Court, or the Court, the only

effectual Courts they have resort to, to recover such small Debts, being from Three to Four Pounds.

Mr. William Hollier, Sailcloth-maker, said. That in the Tower Hamlets several Manufactories are carried on; That in his Business sometimes near a,oooo Persons are employed, who cannot support themselves and their Families without Credit for small Sums: That he has loft, in the Three Years past. Twenty Pounds, by lending small Sums from Five Shillings to Twenty Shillings, not thinking them worth his suing for, by reason of the great Expence attending the suing for them: That when he has applied to some of his Debtors to pay him in small Sums weekly, they have refuted him, and defied him to sue them.

Mr. William Carter, and Mr. Joshua Wood, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence of the aforesaid Witnesses, with regard to the Difficulty in suing Persons for Sums under Forty Shillings.

Mr. William Carter further said, That after Judgment obtained, in either of the aforesaid Courts, a Writ of Error may be brought in the Court of King's Bench, by which Means the Debtor has an Opportunity of getting off; which has been practised.

All the aforesaid Witnesses severally said, That a more ealy and speedy Method of recovering small Debts will greatly tend to the Promoting of Industry, and support useful Credit, within the said Hamlets.

Upon the whole, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a BiH for the more ea(y and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the Tower Hamlets, and in the Liberty of his Majesty's Tower of London, and in the several Parishes, Liberties, Precincts, and Places, within the said Hamlets.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Vol. 25.

more easy and speedy Recovery ot small Debts within the Tower Hamlets, and in the Liberty of his Majesty's Tower of London, and in the several Parishes, Liberties, Precincts, and Places, within the said Hamlets: And that Sir Hugh Smithson, Mr. Brookfbank, and Sir William Beauchamp ProElor, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Merchants, Weavers, Throwfters, Growth of Dyers, and other Manufacturers of raw and thrown Silks, s>lk jn in behalf of themselves and many Thousand labouring Amer, ca* People, depending on the Silk Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have, within these few Years, improved the Manufacture of raw Silk into thrown, and afterwards into plain and wrought Silks and Velvets, so as not only to supply our home Consumption, but to export great Quantities, whereby several Thousands of Persons have been employed:

And that the Supply of fine short raw Silk has been heretofore from Italy and Spain, (except a small precarious Portion thereof from China) the Throwing of which gave Employment to great Numbers of young and infirm People: And that the Spaniards are vigorously attempting the Increase and Improvement of the Manufacture of wrought Silks and Velvets in that Kingdom; for the Encouragement whereof, the Exportation of raw Silk thence is absolutely prohibited t, and the raw short Silk of Italy, which has been always freely exported, except from Piedmont, has this Year been also prohibited to be exported from any of those Territories; where great Encouragement is given to promote the Manufacture of wrought Silks and Velvets, having now a favourable Opportunity by great Numbers of Weavers, late Inhabitants of Genoa, who, during the intestine Troubles there, ftieltered themselves in many other Towns through the Italian Dominions: And that the Price of thrown Silk, the only Species now allowed to be exported from Italy, is lately risen from 30 to 40 per Cent, which has already occasioned the putting down a great many Looms, and will soon occasion the putting down many more, to the great Prejudice of the Silk Manufacture, and the Ruin of great Numbers of poor Families, who, for want of Employ, must become burthensome to their respective Parishes:

And that the Petit ioners apprehend it to be of the utmost Importance to secure to these Kingdoms so valuable a Branch of Business as the Silk Manufacture is; which, nothing can more certainlyeffect, than producing a Supply of raw Silk in fomfe of his Majesty's Dominions; and which, the Petitioners are informed, from undoubted Authority, may be done in the Southern Colonies of America, where the Soil and Climate are as favourable as in any Part of Italy, for the quick Growth of Mulberry Trees, and the Breeding and Nurture of Silk Worms; and from whence Five hundred Pounds Weight of raw Silk has been imported into London, from Carolina and Georgia since the late general Peace, which, upon Trial, has been found to answer, in the several Operations, all the Purposes of the best Italian Organzine: And that the Petitioners conceive if proper Encouragement was given to the Production of raw Silk in his Majesty's Colonies in America, it would be a Means, in a few Years, of securing a constant and considerable Supply thereof for the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, and be a Saving to the Nation of some hundred thousand Pounds, annually t

paid to Italy and Spain, for their thrown and raw Silks, besides many other great and national Advantages which would accrue by the Returns thereof in Goods to America:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give such Relief therein as the Nature of the same shall require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers, and In- Sr. Georg* habitants, of Saint George the Martyr, in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Storey, was presented to the Maintenance House, and read; letting forth. That a proper Maintenance and a Support of Parish Ministers, who have large Cures of Souls, and an amicable Settlement and Adjustment <Jf all Differences and Disputes with respect to their Tythes, Dues, and Demands, tend greatly to promote and establish a Parochial Unity, Peace, and Harmony, and to prevent the Odium which arises from vexatious and litigious Suits and Controvedies; and that the said Parish of Saint George is a Rectory in the Gift of the Crown, and is very populous and extensive; and the Minister's Duty so very great and laborious, as to require a Curate or Assistant for the due and regular Performance thereof; and that there is not a suitable and effectual Provision for the Rector, nor any P&rfonage-house erected or to be found within the said Parish; and that no Rector hath for many Years resided in the said Parish, except One Rector about Ten Years since, forafmall time; and that the Reverend Doctor LeonasdHoward, the present Rector, being now

resident in the said Parish, the Petitioners, on the Twenty-sixth Day of December last, did, in publick Vestry, appoint a Committee to examine into the Nature, Custom, and Manner, of paying Tythes to the said Rector; but could find no legal Modus, or any certain or unvaried Custom, of paying such Tythes, but the same to be very unequal and uncertain, some few paying largely, others very little, and others nothing at all, to the said Rector; and that the said Tythes or Payments scarcely amount to the annual Sum of Seventy Pounds, having greatly diminished in a few Years; and are likely to fall much lower, being almost grown a voluntary Payment, at the Pleasure of the Parish-toners; and no visible Right appears to the Petitioners, in the Rector, to demand any certain Tythes or Stipend for his large Duty, as aforesaid, but that he is intirely remediless, except by commencing a long, expensive, and disagreeable Law-Suit, with his Parishoners; and that the Parish Church of Saint George aforesaid was rebuilt, by Act of Parliament, about the Year 1733, as One of the Fifty new Churches; but there being at that time no resident Minister, the Consideration of his Income or Support was neglected, and no Clause for that Purpose was inierted, as in other Bills of the like Nature; and that the Petitioners are much affected with the present bad State and Condition of the said Rectory, and are most willing and desirous to do what in them lies towards the Maintenance and Support of their Re Cl or and his Successors, and to encourage his and their llclidence in the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be

fiven to bring in a Bill for the settling some Stipend or laintenance for the said Rector and his Successors, to be raised within the said Parish, and in such Manner as the House shall think proper; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

for cleansing and making navigable the Channel from the Rithe, at Colchester, to Wivenh whereby several other Duties were laid on, and made payable for. Channel; but as the Power and Authority of the Mayor and Commonalty of Colchester hath ceased for several Years last past (in whose Names the said Duties could be recovered and received, and legal Discharges given for the same by and under the Authorities of the said several Acts) the said Lock cannot be now supported, nor the Channel kept cleansed, and fit for Navigation, unfefs some further Provision be made by the Aid of Parliament: And that, for several Years last past, the Pavements of the Streets and Lanes in the said Town, and the Liberties thereof, have been decaying; and are now in so bad and ruinous a Condition, and so covered with Dirt and Filth, that it is dangerous to Persons passing and repalling in and through the said Town (a Mile of which Pavement is in the direct Road from London to Harwich) and the Power and Authority of the said Mayor and Commonalty having ceased, as aforesaid, the same must remain in such Condition, unless some further Power is given to compel the Repair and Cleansing thereof, there not being sufficient Power in the Law now in being effectually to remedy the lame: And therefore praying. A PETITION of Philemon Pownoll,

Jacob Pickering, and Elizabeth his Wife, which laid Philemon Pownoll, israel Pownoll, and Elizabeth are all the surviving Children of israel Pownoll, deceased, late Ship-Builder of his Majesty's Yard at Plymouth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners said Father, by many Years Labour, and at a very great Expence, invented an Engine for raising Ballad, Sullage, and Sand, and removing Banks, Shelves, and Shoals, in Rivers and Harbours, and thereby cleaning, deepening, and opening, the fame, and for performing other Works of that Kind, for which he obtained a Patent in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; but died before he could put the same in Execution, leaving several young Children, of which the Petitioners are the only surviving; and

Januarii . 1749.

the Time for which the said Patent was granted expiring before any of the.Petitioners came of Age, the said Invention, or any Part thereof, hath never been yet put in Practice; and that the said Engine exceeds all others hitherto made use of for such Purposes, in the following Particulars, among many others; viz: That it can work at the Depth of Twenty-one Feet under Water, and raises Sixty Ton an Hour, which it discharges with equal Expedition, at the Edge of High-water Mark, by Boats of a new Invention for that Purpose; and that the said Engine does not leave Holes or Depths, but levels the Ground where it has wrought; and may be applied in tearing up and dispersing Banks and Shoals at Sea at the Didance of several Leagues from the Shore; and that the Petitioners Father greatly lessencd his Fortune by carrying on the said Invention; and the fame, though completed, cannot be carried into Practice without a further Expence of feme Thousand Pounds; and there is no Probability that the Petitioners can ever be reimbursed the feme, or what has been already expended by their said,

Glasgow, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, on the WesternCoaft of Scotland, the most populous Part of that Kingdom, great Quantities of Salt are used in the Herring and other Fisheries, as well as for Home Consumption; which Salt being at present clandestinely run in from Ireland, to avoid paying the Duty, and the fame, by reason of its Mixture with Rock-Salt, being not only preferable in Quality to what is made in Scotland at the Salt-works along the Forth, but also cheaper, for the Reason before-mentioned, as well as others.

the same greatly discourages the erecting of Salt-pans upon the said Western Coast, for making white Salt for the aforesaid Purposes; and that the Petitioners, notwithstanding these Difficulties, are willing to erect Saltpans at Port Glasgow, provided Liberty was given them to bring Rock Salt from England to be refined there, chargeable with the same Duties as are now paid, and under such Restrictions and Regulations, for securing the Payment thereof, as shall be thought necessary; by which means not only his Majesty's Revenue will be much increased, but great Advantages accrue to the Publick; but that, by the Laws now in being, Rock-Salt cannot be carried above Ten Miles Distance from the Pit: And. therefore praying the House to grant the Petitioners the Liberty of carrying Rock-Salt to Port Glasgow -, or such Relief in the Premises as to che House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Persons who lately served on board the Prince Frederick and the Duke private Ships of War, in bchdf of themselves, and of all the other Mariners who served onboard the said Ships, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That in the Year 1745 the Ships the Prince Frederick and Duke were fitted out by the Subscription of private Adventurers tocruife on the Enemy; and that, in order to man the said Ships, certain Articles and Proposals were printed and dispersed, whereby it was expressly stipulated, that One Moiety of all the Prizes taken in the said Cruile should be allowed Vol. 25.

in lieu of Wages to the Officers and Seamen who should embark and be employed in that Service, in such Shares and Proportions as in the said printed Articles and Proposals were particularly expressed; and that the Petitioners, and several other Mariners, did, upon the Faith of the said printed Articles and Proposals, engage in the said Undertaking; but that, after the said Ships had failed from the Places where they were fitted out, and immediately before they proceeded to Sea, other Articles, ready prepared and mgrofled, were produced, and impoftd upon the Petitioners, and the relt of the said Mariners, by which Articles teveral of the Owners were appointed Attornies and Agents for the Management and Sale of such Prizes as should be taken, and Five per Cent, reserved to the Commander in Chief of the said Ships, out of the Shares which the Petitioners were to be intithd to; and that the said Ships, in their Cruise, made Capture of the Lezvis Erasmus and the Marquis Two French Merchant Ships, laden with Money and Elfects to a very great Value; which Captures were carried in in the

Kingdom of Ireland, and there condemned, though they might with equal Eafeand Safety have been brought into England; and that the Petitioners have Ileaion to apprehend, that, during the Stay of the Captures at K.injale % great Part of their Cargoes were embezzled; and untrue Accounts, lessening their real Value, were at that time industricully propagated; and several of the Mariners, being thereby imposed upon and deceived, were induced, to part with their Shares for One Quarter of their Value , and that the said Captures were brought to England in the Month of September 1745, and consigned to the said Agents, who delayed the Making of any Dividend until January following, when £. 400 was issued upon each Share, as was also another Dividend of £. ,00 in August 1746; and that aConted having arisen touching the Legality of the Sentence of Condemnation in Ireland, the fame, after very great Delays on the Part of the Managers, was, upon the pressing Applications of the Petitioners, brought to an Issue, and determined, in July 1748, in favour of the said Sentence; and in September following another Dividend o{£. 60 upon each Share was obtained;

since which the said Agents have not made any further Oi-vidend; and that the said Agents, upon the Payment of all the said Dividends, not only took and deduced the Five perCent. which wasreferved by the Articles imposed upon the Petitioners, and the other Mariner^, in Manner before-mentioned; but have also, by various Artifices and Pretences, oppressed and taken from the Petitioners, and the said other Mariners, large Sums of Money; and that the said Agents, having dill a very great Balance in their Hands, refule to come toa fair Account for the lame, and bid the Petitioners Defiance, well knowing the lnabiuty of most of the Petit ioners to go through t he burthensome and expenfivcChanccrySuits that are necessary for each of their obtaining Justice: and alleging, That by reason of the Variety of the Claims, and the great Number of Persons interested therein, and the Extenlivencfs of the Accounts of the said Agents, it will be utterly impracticable for the Petitioners to obtain any final Determination of this Matter, in the ordinary Course of Proceedings; and therefore, as the Legislature has thought proper to grant Relief in finular Cates, expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the House will think this Cate a proper Object of their Justice and Compassion; and that they will not suffer a Body of Men who have added Riches to the Nation by the Spoils of its Enemies, to lofc the Property they have so acquired and w'on at the Hazard of their Lives; the Petitioners hereby offering to allow, out of the Monies in the said Managers Hands, the necessary Charges ofexecuting any Commission for the Petitioners Relief, in a summary Way: Ami therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for determining the Petitioners Demands on the said Managers, and intered in the said Prizes, in a summary Way; or that furh other Relief may be given the Petitioners in the Pren:i*es, as to the House shall lcem meet.

African A Petition of the Royal African Company of England,

Company, offered to be presented to the House.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House, to do therein as they shall think fit:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the great and heavy Charges of maintaining the Forts belonging to the Petitioners, since the Trade to Africa has been free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects, have not only been the principal Means of ex-haufting the Capitals that have been, from time to time, paid in and subscribed by the Petitioners, but the Petitioners have also been obliged to contract many and great Debts to the Amount of about One hundred and Thirty thousand Pounds, which they are unable to Pay and fe-tisfy, or make any Agreement for the fame, without the Aid of this House: And that the many Dangers to which the African Trade, especially that of the Gold Coast, is now exposed, is too well known: And that the Preservation thereof intirely depends upon the speedy Aid of Parliament, in makingan effectualProvision for the Maintenance and Support of the British Forts and Castles belonging to the Petitioners: And that the Trade for Negroes on the Gold Coast, which are the best and most valuable Negroes for the British Colonies, and which are now greatly wanted; and also the Inland Trade for Gold, Ivory, Bees-wax, Dying-woods, Gums and other Commodities, is capable of being greatly extended and im-

proved, by a Joint-stock Company: And, if the House shall think fit to make a sufficient and effectual Provision for the Maintenance of the Petitioners Forrs and Castles, so that the Burthen thereof may not lie on the Trade, the Petitioners are ready and able, and offer, to procure a Subscription of a sufficient Joint-stock, to be employed in the said Trade, under, and subject to, all reasonable Regulations; and also to take upon themselves the Satisfying of the Debts owing by the Petitioners, and submitting it to the Consideration of the House, whether such ajoint-stock to be actually employed in the said Trade is not, in the Nature of Things, the best and most effectual Security that can be given to the Nation, for the due Application of the Money to be granted for the Maintenance of the said Forts: And further setting forth, That the Petitioners are also ready to submit to all such Regulations on behalf of the separate Traders, as the House shall think fit:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and make such effectual Provision for the Maintenance of the said Forts and Castles as the House shall think most conducive to the Retrieving, Extending, and Preferring, of the said Trade; and to grant the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Merchants in London, trading [mportatta to his Majesty's Colonies in Americawas presented to the °> Salt from House, and read; letting forth, That the Inhabitants of those Colonies are frequently under great Difficulties for want of Salt proper to cure and preserve Fish aftd other Provisions, which useful and necessary Commodity is often so scarce, andat such exorbitant Prices, that the Petitioners are thereby prevented from improving the AdvantagesNa-ture has so liberally bestowed on them of Fish and other Kinds of Provisions in great Plenty: And that thebeftSalt for such Uses in those Climates is found by Experience to be that made in the South Parts of Euro, which, by the Act, 15 Car. 1. Chap. 7 several of the Colonies are deprived of t he Liberty of importing, without being first landed in Great Britain: And as it is a bulky, coarse, and perishable Commodity, will, by no means bear the Charges attending the Transportation to different Countries: And that as the Freight and Charges of transportingSa.lt ic often more than the first Cost, so, in the Course of our Trade to America, most of that Expence would be saved; for that many Ships fail from England annually, laden with C^rn to several Ports in Europe, where the best Salt is made, and from thence proceed, in Ballast, to North America, in order to return to Great Britain laden with the Produce of those Colonies: And that, were they allowed to carry Salt in Place of Ballast, it would not only lave the whole Freight of such Salt, but also the Expence of purchasing Ballast, which they are now obliged to load in those Parts:

And that the Necessity of such Salt in America does evidently appear by the said Act 15 Car. 1. wherein Liberty is granted to carry Salt from any Part of Europe, directly, to New England and Newfoundland:And that by the Act

13 Geo. 1. Chap 5. it is given to; and also

Sir Hugh Smithson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Grand Jury, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the County of Middlesex, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee there* upon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followetii; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

William Witaker Esquire, informed your Committee, That the Courts of Westminster-haH have no Jurisdiction

in personal Actions under 40 j.: That the common Method of recovering small Debts within the County of dlesex is in the County Court: That the Proceedings in the said Court being according to the Strict Rules of the Common Law, and reduced into Writing, and subject to Removal both before and after Judgment, are necessari-ly expensive and dilatory; the Charges of recovering a Debt of 2 s: amounting to£. 3, and Judgment not to be obtained in less than Four Months: That the Court can issue out no ededual Execution, which is the Cause of great Oppression to the Defendant, but of no Advantage to the Plaintiff; and often obliges Plaintiffs to bring Actions in the superior Courts to recover the Debt and Costs on the Judgment he has obtained in the County Court; by which Circuity it is possible from an Action commenced in the County Court, for Five Shillings, to accumulate the Costs to Fifty Pounds.

Upon which Evidence the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for preventing Delays and Expence; in the Proceedings in the County Court of Middlesex; and for the more easy and speedy Recovery of smallDcbts in the said County Court.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preventing Delays and Expences in the Proceedings in the County Court of Middlesex; and for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts in the said County Court: And that Sir Hugh Smithson, Mr. Hardinge, Mr. Hay, and Mx.Talbott, do prepare, and bring in the fame.

fore this House, an Account of the Quantity of Iron imported for Ten Years last past, from the British Colonies in America, distinguishing each Year, and the Quantity imported from each Colony, and distinguishing also how much in Pig, and how much in Bar.

And he produced an Agreement which was executed by Doctor Fenton, Vicar of Lancaster, and several Persons on the Behalf of the Merchants of that Town, whereby the said Doctor Fenton, in Consideration of an annual Sum to be paid him during the Time he should continue the Incumbent of that Vicarage, did consent, That a Piece of the Glebe Lind of the said Vicarage should be vetted in Trustees, by Act of Parliament, for the Making of a Quay, or Wharf; and to which Agreement the Approbation of the Bishop of Chester, as Diocesan, is subscribed.

Edward Mar ton Esquire, Patron of the said Vicarage, being present, informed your Committee, That he had not any Objection to the vetting the said Land in Trustees for the above-mentioned Purpose.

Mr. Samuel Touchil confirmed the Evidence of Mr.

Fenton: And added. That the present Wharf at Lancaster is (0 (mail, that it is impossible to land more than One Hogshead at a Time; and when Four or Five Ships are in the River together, some of them are under the Necessity of waiting a Fortnight or Three Weeks before they can be unladed; and that this Delay is attended with great Danger both to the Ships and Cargoes, by reason of the bad Anchorage and precarious Mooring upon the uneven Ground in the said River.

A Petition of the Merchants and others concerned in the Herring Fishery of LoweJioff,.\n the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of Lowefloff abovesaid, hath, for timeout

of Mind, been an ancient Fishing Town for Herrings, which are caught and made Red Herrings of by the Merchants and others residing in and near the said Town; but that, to the very great Surprize and Damage of the Petitioners, the Dutch and French Fishermen come upon our Coasts and Fishing Grounds to fish for Herrings; whereas the Petitioners apprehend they have no manner of Right whatsoever; having heard that neither of them ought to fish for Herrings within Sight of our Land; notwithstanding which, both of them do, in great Numbers, fish amongst us, in our Fishing Grounds, and very near our Shore: And that their Boats, being twice as big as those of the Petitioners, and carrying double the Quantity of Men, and their Crafts, or Nets that they fish with being much stronger than those of the Petitioners, their Fishing Boats dare not fish amongst them, for fear of being cut from their Nets, or otherwise destroyed by them; which has often been the same with many of the Petitioners, to the Lossof many Hundreds of Pounds, and even for many Fishing Seasons last past (but more particularly for the Two last) by reason they kept fishing upon our Coasts and Fishing Grounds, and got Plenty of Fish, and the Petitioners few or none; so that it made that little Fish they did get excessive dear, as well for our Consumption at t Home, as also the several foreign Markets they went to; which tends greatly to discourage not only the Fishery in general, (which is a great Nursery for Sailors) but also Trade and Navigation, to the very great Loss of the Vol. 25.

Merchants, as well at home as abroad, and more particularly. to the Petitioners, many of whose only Support is Fishing; which, if not timely prevented, will be the Ruin of the said Fishery, as well as many of the Petitioners and others concerned in the said Fishery: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration; and grant them such Relief as to the House shall meet meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to coHfider of the State of the British Fishery.

Boroughbridge, in the County of York, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Innholders, and other principal Inhabitants, of Newport-Pagnel, in the County of Bucks, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Town, was presented to the House, and rend; letting forth, That there is an ancient Road, leading from the Northern Part of England, through the Towns of Leicester, Harborough, Northampton, Newport-Pagnel, IVo-burn, and Dunstable, and so to London; for the better Repairing of several Parts of which laid Road, several Acts of Parliament have been made and passed, and the Terms and Powers thereby granted have been enlarged by subsequent Acts, and several Turnpikes have been erected thereon, in pursuance of the said Acts, and large Sums of Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, which still remain unpaid: And that, it being apprehended, that, for the better Repairing of the said Road, and for securing the Sums of Money borrowed thereon, some longer Time, and other Provisions, are necessary to be added to some of the said Acts, the Petitioners, with many Gentlemen and other principal Inhabitants of the Counties of Nottingham, Derby, Leicester, Northampton, Bucks, and other Counties, did sign a Petition to be presented to this House, to obtain such Amendments therein as the House should judge meet and convenient; but that, to the great Surprize of the Petitioners, they are informed that, before such their Petition bad been presented to the House, another Petition has been already presented, for Leave to bring in a Bill to repair the Roads between the Town of Bedford and Market Harborough aforesaid, and to erect Turnpikes thereon: And that the Petitioners are apprehensive, if such a Bill should pass into a Law, it will be extremely detrimental to

Lunce, 2 90 die Januarii;

Anno 23* Georgii IIdl Regis, 1749. Prayers.

A PETITION of several of the principal Inhabitants, Tradesmen, Manufacturers of Cutlery Wares, and common Carriers, of the Town of Sheffield, in the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was pre-

lected to the House, and read; setting forth, That the moll common Road from the said Town to London has hitherto been through Harborough aforesaid, to Northampton; betwixt which Towns the Road has been so extremely bad and ruinous, for many Years pall, and is at present so difficult and dangerous, notwithstanding the Tolls, that the Petitioners despair of its being made better; and that the Petitioners are informed, and have great Reason to believe, that if the Bill, depending in the House, for repairing the Road leading from Knotting Westwood Gate, in the County of Bedford, over Bridge,

through Kettering and Rothwell, in the County of Northampton, to Market Harborough, in the County of Lei-ctfter, should take effect, it will be a Means of opening a shorter and better Road from Market Harborough to London, of expediting the Carriage, and Ibortening the Journies, of the Petitioners, and the rest of the Inhabi-

Januarii. ^.1749.

tants of the said Town, and the Neighbourhood thereof, and of other trading Towns in the North: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Rotherham, in the County of York: And also,

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Che/lerfeld, in the County of Derby, and the principal Inhabitants and Tradesmen of the same Place: And also,

A Petition of the Manufacturers, and others, of the Town of Leicester, in the County of Leicester: And also.

A Petition of some of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Market Harborough, in the County of Leicester;

Werealfo severallypresented to the House, and read; severally setting forth. That the Road now leading from.

Market Harborough to London, through Northampton, has for many Years past been exceeding bad and ruinous, and in Winter-time has been, and now is, almost impassable; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Bill, now depending in the House, for repairing the Road leading from Knotting West-wood Gate, in the County of Bedford, over Ditchford Bridge, through Kettering and Rothwell, in the County of Northampton, to Market Harborough, in the County of Leicester, should take effect, it may be the Means of opening a shorter and better Road to London, and will be of greater Service and Advantage to the said Towns, and all other Places in the ' North using the said Road; And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

The House being informed, That Mr. Bowen, from Dispositk* the Treasury, attended at the Door; of Grama.

He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursumt to their Address to his Majesty, an Account shewing how the Money, given for the Service of the Year 1749, hath been disposed of, distinguished under the several Heads, until the 24th Day of this instant Januan 1749, and the Sums remaining unsatisfied, with the Deficiency thereof.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Account was read.

Mr. George Fox reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Landholders, and others the principal Inhabitants, of the North-Riding of the County of Yorkr; and also the Petition of several Gentlemen, and others, usually travelling the Road from the City of Fork to Northallerton, through Boroughbridge, in the County of York; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the lame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the Committee examined,

Mr. John Batchelor, an Inhabitant of Who said. That he has viewed the Road mentioned in the Petition; and that the lame, or the greatest Part thereof, is in so bad a Condition, that it is impracticable to repair it by the ordinary Course of Law, nor is it possible for Carriages to pass: That the said Road is the nearest between York to Northallerton, being Five Miles nearer than the Road by Boroughbridge, and about Two Miles Vot. 25.

nearer than the Road by Helperby: That many Persons travel the said Road, the Witness having met several Wheel Carriages in Summer, but they cannot pass in Winter; but he cannot lay what the Tolls would amount to, in case a Turnpike was erected upon it: That Materials proper for repairing Highways are to be found near to great Part of the said Road, especially between Eajingwould and Northallerton; but cannot say whether It is the fame

from Northallerton to Boroughbridge: That there is a Turnpike Road from Northallerton to Boroughbridge.

And being asked the Question, whether, if there were Three Turnpike Roads from Northallerton to York, viz. the present one by Boroughbridge, the other by Helperby, and the last through Eajingwould and Yhirjk (which last is

the Road mentioned in the Petition) which of the Three would be of moil Advantage, or repaired at the least Expence ? he laid. He could not tell: And the Question as to Utility, being repeated to him, he laid. He thought the Road through Yhirjk would be the raoft useful; and, if both Roads were good, it would be the most frequented: That there is little or no Manufacture carried on at Northalierton, YhirJk, or Boroughbridg; but there is Watu-

carriage from Boroughbridge to York: That the chief Trade from Yhirjk to York consists of Butter brought from the former to the latter Place; but that such Butter might be sent to Boroughbridge, whence he apprehends it might be carried cheaper to York by Water-carriage; but he believes that the Navigation has been sometimes interrupted by the River being froze:

That if this Road was mended, it would induce Travellers coming from Newcastle to York to pass on it, arid would be of Use to Trade: That many Travellers pass through this Road in Summer, particularly that Part between Northallerton and Malton; and, if it was made good, would ipduce Gentlemen to go that Way to Scarborough, instead of going over Black Hamiltonbut he could not pretend to say what the Tolls might amount to:

That the Persons at Eajingwould and Yhirjk are but indifferently supplied with Coals; but, if this Road was made good. Carriages would go in Winter for Coals: That he does not know of any Person that has gone from Northallerton to the Coal-pits in Winter; but the People lay by Magazines of Coals, which they bring over the bad Road in Summer, in order to fetch them over the good Road in Winter:

That he does not know how far it is from Eajingwould to the nearest Part of the Navigation of the River Ouze, but it is Six computed Miles from Eajingwould to Boroughbridge: That they use Coals at Eastngwould which are brought up the River Ouze, but more of the Ryley Fell, though those are double the Price of the other; but he believes no People beyond Eajingwould fetch any Western Coals'.

Richard Lane after confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Batchellor, in regard to the Roads through Eajingwould and Yhirjk being the nearest Way from Northallerton to York, it being Five Miles nearer than the Boroughbridge Road, and Two Miles nearer than the Road through Helperby-, and as to the Road mentioned in the Petition being very ruinous:

But, being asked the Question, he said, That the Road from York to Boroughbridge might be repaired at less Expence than that through Yhirjk and; but

that he does not know whether the Boroughbridge Road has a Communication with the Two great Northern Roads which lead, one to Darlington, and,

and the other to Richmond and Catherick.

That the only Trade carried on betwixt would, and York, consists of Butter and Bacon, which they carry from Yhirsk to Eastngwould, and from thence to York-, and that if this Road was repaired, it would be of great Advantage to People dealing in those Commodities.

Being asked whether it would not be cheaper to carry the Butter from Thirsk to Boroughbridge, from whence it might be sent by Water-carriage to York, than to carry it along the Road, in case the same was mended ? or whether

That there are likewise several Markets and Fairs held upon this Road, there being Three Markets Weekly at York, One at Thirsk, One at Northallerton, and One at Eafingwould; and that there are Sixteen Fairs annually held at the aforesaid Towns, viz. That many People go to Market through the other Road; but, if this Road were mended, it would take off many Travellers from the other Road, the Road mentioned in the Petition being nearer.

And the Witness said, He was of Opinion, that, if the Road were mended, the Judges, and Persons on the Circuit, would make use of it.

Being asked the Question, he said. He believes the Persons who have the greatest Property on the said Road desire it should be repaired; and that he believes it to be the Desire of the Majority of the Gentlemen of Yorkskhrc, and even of those that live on the Boroughbridge Road:

That this Petition was not signed by the Justices of the Quarter-Sessions, nor the Grand Jury; but there was Notice given, in the Newspapers, of a Meeting to be held, to consult of Measures for repairing the Road; in consequence whereof, Fifteen Gentlemen, who were possessed of great Property adjoining to the said Road, mer, and resolved on this Petition.

And being asked if this Petition was signecUat that Meeting, or whether any Three Subscribers signed it in the Presence of one another ? he said, He believed the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of York signed it in that manner; and that the Gentlemen, in his Opinion, would have had no Objection to signing it altogether.

That, among the Fifteen Gentlemen present at the aforesaid Meeting, there were all the afling Justices of the Division, and they all agreed for a Petition; but it was not drawn up then; and that Notice was given of the Meeting in the Newspapers, and the Intention of the Meeting was publickly known.

As to the Performance of the Statute-work, the Witness said, That he has been Surveyor of the Highways for the Parish of Eafingwould: That several of the Parishioners

performed their Six Days Labour; but the Witness cannot take upon him to say, that Half the Parishioners did it:

That the Parish of Woodford have performed their . Statute-labour, and paid Nine Pence in the Pound in the

present Year.

And being asked, whether any Persons in the Parish of Woodford, not keeping a Team, have performed the Duty the Law requires of them as Labourers? he said, He believed they had; but that the Statute-work is insufficient to repair the said Road.

And being asked, if he had ever known Six Pence in the Pound levied? he produced an Assessment, to prove, that it had been raised and laid out: That he had known the said Sum raised heretofore in Woodford, but could not take upon him to say it had ever been raised in -would', but, in case it had, it would be insufficient to repair the Roads in that Parish, as the Witness believes, though it should be raised and laid out for Seven Years together; and he cannot say whether even a Crown in the Pound would do it: That Six Pence in the Pound in the Parish of Eafinrivouldwould amount to 36 Pounds, and they have Ten Miles in the Whole to repair; and that Six Pence in the Pound would be insufficient for the Repair of this Road alone: That, when he was Surveyor, £. 20 had been laid out in Eafingwould Parish:

That he cannot speak to the Statute-work in any other Parishes save Eafingwould and Woodford; only he knows *4

that Rafial, Thirsk, and some other Towns on the same Road, have been indicted; and that when he mentions Six Pence in the Pound, he means, that the Statute-work has been performed besides:

That there are other Roads to repair in the several Parishes, besides the Road mentioned in the Petition; but he does not know what Proportion they bear to the High Road, but believes it to be about One-third to the Whole:

That if the Statute-wofk had been done for Four or Five Yean, the Roads would have been in a better Condition than at present, but would not have been sufficiently repaired.

Being asked what the Expence of repairing the said Road would amount to He said, That in his Opinion it mi^ht be repaired, on a Medium, at 150 a Mile; That he undemands the Nature of this Work, not by Experience, but from Information of Persons who have been employed in the like Works: That he had made a Calculation of the Expence of throwing up the Road, and leading Gravel, and would be wilting to undertake it at £. 150 a Mile: That he would proceed to amend the said Road by throwing up with a Plough where the Road would admit, otherwise with a Spade, and would then cover it with Gravel: That he proposed to make the Road at least Five Yards broad at the Top, and Eleven or Twelve between Ditch and Ditch: That the Gravel would cofl about Twelve Pence a Load, including Carriage; but he cannot say what Quantity of Gravel would be necessary to cover a Mile.

Being asked if he had no Hopes of being employed in making this Road ? he said. He had not; but that he had considered the Expence, and calculated it: That he shewed this Calculation to some Gentlemen concerned; but had it not with him at the Time of his Examination.

Being asked what was his Reason for fixing the Expence at £. 1 50 a Mile ? and what Method he pursued in making his Calculation ? he said. He could not tell or describe what Method he took.

Being further examined as to the same Particular, he said. He was by Profession a Gardener, and, as such, had been used to guess at Levels by Sight; and that his Reason for fixing this Calculation at 150 a Mile, was, that though some Parts of the Road require more Gravel than others, he thought between Thirty and Forty Loads of Gravel would, upon a Medium, repair Two-and-twenty Yards of this Road, which is a Chain, and that Eighty Chains are a Mile: That in some Places, where the Materials He contiguous to the Road, it might be repaired for less; but that he forms his Calculation at what the Road would cost repairing, at a Medium, from one End to the other; and that he made his Calculation upon View.

Being asked what Tolls would be necessary to be laid for repairing the said Road ? he said. That he apprehended Four Pence Half-peny a Horse would raise£.35a annually upon Horses only: That some Persons have calculated it at that Rate, a Man having been set to observe what Passengers passed and repassed at the Places where the Toll-bars were proposed to be set up; but he does not speak this of his own Knowledge.

He then offered to produce to your Committee a Calculation of the said Tolls; and, being required to inform your Committee whence he had such Paper, he said, He had it from Mr. Jackson i And,

Mr. Jackson, being examined, informed your Committee, That he received the Original from the Witness himself, and had only made a Copy of it for the Witness; which Copy was the Paper he had offered to your Committee: Whereupon,

Mr. Lancaster, being further examined from whence he had the original Calculation; he said, He had it from Mr. Goulton, who delivered it to him, by Order of the Gentlemen, at the Meeting aforesaid: That Mr. Goulton was an Attorney employed by the Gentlemen to draw up-such Things: That he was at the Meeting, and acted as

Whitby A Petition of the Coal-owners, Fitters, and Owners of

Harbour. Ships, redding in and near the Town of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That whereas a Bill for the more effectual repairing and preserving the Piers and Harbour of Whitby-, in the County of York, is now depending in this House, for the laying on an additional Duty of One Half-peny a Chaldron on all Coals vended from Sun-

derland, and Blyth, the Petitioners conceive, that the granting an additional Duty on all Coals exported from the said Port and Haven will be highly prejudicial to the Trade thereof, and a very great Hardship to the Petitioners; in Confederation that an Act of Parliament was made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for the Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, wherein it was Enacted, That, from and after the 24th Day of June 1717, and for the Space of Twenty-one Years then next following, a Sum, not exceeding Four Pence perChalder, should be paid by the respective Coal-owners and Fitters, for all Coals and Cinders brought down the said River, from below a Place called The New Bridge, and put on board any Ship or Vessel, the Duties arising by such Coals and Cinders to be applied to the Improvement of the said River, Port, Haven, and Harbour; which said Act of Parliament was accordingly complied with, and the Duties arising by virtue thereof expended in erecting a Pier on the South Side of the said Port, and other Works, agreeable to the Purport of the said Act, amounting toupwards of Twenty-seven thousand Pounds; which very great Sum the Petitioners have paid, not having the least Aid from any other Port, Place, or Person, whatsoever: And that whereas after the Expiration of the above in Part recited Act, the Works done were found insufficient to make the said Harbour safe and commodious, another Act was granted in the 20th Year of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation and Improvement of the River IV ear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland aforesaid, wherein it is Enacted, That from and after the 24th Day of June 1747, for and during the Term of Twenty-one Years, a Sum, not exceeding Two Pence per Chalder on al l Coals and Cinders brought and carried down the said River, and put on board any Ship or Vessel, shall be paid by the respective Coal-owners and Fitters, for the building a North Pier, and other Works, in order to make it a safe and commodious Harbour for Ships of a considerable Burthen to fail into and out of at all Tides; which Duty, according to a reasonable and moderate Computation, will amount to Twenty thousand Pounds, and upwards, during the Term granted by the said Act j and that the Petitioners have hitherto borne, and are now willing to bear, these heavy Expences, for the Improvement of their Port and Haven, without requiring any other Aid j and that they have Reason to believe other Ports have been exempt upon the same Considerations: And therefore graying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration; and grant the said Port an Exemption from the said Duty of a Half-peny per Chalder, or such other Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, Tha.t the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the more effectual repairing and preserving the Piers and Harbour of Whitby, in the County of York, is committed.

PownolPs Mr. Wilkinson reported from the Committee, to whom Ballad En- the Petition of Philemon , Israel Jacob

gwt. Pickering, and Elizabeth his Wife (which said Philemon Pownoll, Israel Pownoll, and Elizabeth , are

all the surviving Children of Israel Pownoll, deceased) late Ship-builder, of his Majesty's Yard at Plymouth, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it ip at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Letters Patent of the Eleventh Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for veiling the Property of an Engine, invented by Israel Pownoll, for removing Banks, Shelves, and Shoals, in Rivers and Harbours, and thereby cleansing, depthening, and opening the fame, and for performing other Works of the like Nature, was read: And,

Colonel John Lewis produced to your Committee Two Certificates, the One extracted from the Register of Stoke Damerell, in the County of Devon-, and the other from that of Chatham, in the County of Kent, to shew the Time of the Death of the said Israel Pownoll, and the respective Times of the Birth of his Children: Then,

Mr. John Cockburn and Colonel Lewis informed your Committee, That the said Israel Pownoll never made any Engine in pursuance of the said Letters Patent, having hurt his Fortune lo much in the Invention, that he was unable to carry the same into Execution: And,

Colonel Lewis said. That he had been acquainted with the said Israel Pownoll ever since the Year 1715: That if he had carried his Project into Execution, the Witness must have known it; but that he has frequently heard, and verily believes, that the said Mr. Pownoll greatly impaired his Fortune by the Invention, and that he had not Money sufficient to carry it into Execution:

That the Witness had been conversant in Engines of this Nature, and, in his Opinion, this fer excels any which has been hitherto used, but that it cannot be made for less than £.1,000; and, if other Persons were suffered to , make the like Engines, it would be impossible for the

Heirs of the original Inventor to reimburse themselves \ that Expence: And,

Mr. Cockburn confirmed the Evidence of Colonel Lewis, as to the Utility of the Engine.

And, to prove the Necessity Of an Act of Parliament ' for veiling the Property of the said Engine in the Heirs

of the Inventor, the Act of the lift of the First,

Chapter 3d, was read, which limits all Grants by Letters Patent to the Term of 14 Years, and to the foie Ule of the Inventor.

Thomas Martin, being examined, said. That he knew the said Sir James Clarke, called in the said Letters Patent James Clarke Gentleman, and also his Son Sir James Clarke, the Petitioner's Father, who both enjoyed the Rents and Profits of the said Manor, Passages, and Ferries; and that Mr. Clarke, the Petitioner, upon the Death

'i 3 Geo. II. 31°

of his said Father, which happened about 20 Years agoj became intided to the Premises, and is now in Possession of the fame.

Then, in order to prove the Petitioners Title to the Premises, a Settlement, made upon the Marriage of the Petitioner, was produced; whereby, after Recital of the said Letters Patent, the said Manor of , and

all the other Premises mentioned in the said Letters Patent, were, amongst other Things, veiled in Trustees, foi the Use of the said Sir James , the Petitioner's Father, during his Life, if the said several Terms of 78 and 77 Years should so long continue; and, after his Decease,

for the Payment of the Jointure of Dame Mary his Wife, during her Life, in case Ihe should survive him, and the said Terms should so long continue; and, after the Decease of the Petitioner's laid Father and Mother, then to the Use of the Petitioner, and his Assigns, during the Remainder of the said respective Terms.

Then, in order to prove the Utility of building a Bridge crols the Thames, from Hampton-Court, to East Moulsey, as proposed by the Petitioner,

The laid Thomas Martin was again examined: Who said, That a Bridge would be much piore convenient than the Ferries are, inasmuch as the latter are very indifferently taken care of, and Passengers are obliged to wait a considerable time before they can be carried over: That the Place where the Petitioner proposes to erect a Bridge, is as proper for that Purpose as any Part of the Thames, the Stream being the re very gentle, and the River strait, and the Bed and Banks being a strong and firm Gravel; and that it can be no Detriment or Obstruction to the Navigation, as all Barges, and other Vessels, going up the River, are obliged to take fresh Horses at East Moulsey, where One Foot of the intended Bridge is proposed to Hand.

With regard to the Loss which the Petitioner will sustain by this Undertaking,

Thomas Taylor, Lessee of the Petitioner, said. That he pays the Petitioner an annual Rent of f. 40 for the Profits arising by the said Ferries.

Westminster Sir Peter Warren reported from the Committee, to Small Debt*, whom the Petition of several Persons, whose , Names are thereunto subscribed, being Traders inhabiting within the City of Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and such Part of the Duchy of Lancaster as adjoineth to the Liberty of Westminster ;and also the Petition of the Inhabitants of

the several Parishes of St. Margaret and gelift, St. George Hanover-Square, St. James, St. Martin in the Fields, St. Paul Covent-Garden, St. Anne, St. Clement Danes, St. Mary le Strand, within the City and Liberties of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster

which lies within the said Parish of St. Clement Danes, and adjoins to the said City and Liberties, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberties, and Duchy; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place -, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Henry Scott, Mr. Wm. Lucas, and Mr. Howell Powell, were examined: And said. That the Traders within the said City and Liberties are obliged to give Credit for small Sums of Money to poor People, who frequently refuse to pay such Debts; and that the Creditors are often discouraged from attempting the Recovery thereof, by reason of the great Expence attending the lame.

And Mr. Powell also said. That the Court which has been established in the City of for Recovery of

small Debts in a summary Way, has been of great Advantage to the Inhabitants of that City.

Mr. Christopher Pinchbeck laid, That he had tried Causes in the Court of Conscience in London, and that the Process therein is extremely easy; and the Expence upon each Suit sometimes Six Pence, and never more than Eighteen Pence.

And in Support of the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition,

John Scott Esquire, Mr. Tho Paulin, and Mr. Dobson, were examined: And said. That the trading Inhabitants of the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Duchy of Lancaster, are under the Necessity of giving very extensive Credit for small Sums of Money; and that the Recovery thereof is frequently attended with great Inconvenience, Difficulty, and Expence; and that they apprehend a summary Way of determining such Debts would encourage Industry, and support useful Credit.

Then the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

proved the Allegations of their Petition; except only the Allegation, therein contained, which relates to the Recovery of small Debts in the Kingdom of Ireland.

A Petition of the Clothiers of Trowbridge, in the Seduction of County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; Anifken to

setting forth. That the Legislature, for a long Series of foreign Parti. Years past, has regarded Manufacture as being of the gre&test Importance to the Welfare of this Nation, for-as much as it fumilhes Employments for the Poor, raises the Value of Lands, and increases the Navigation, Wealth, and Strength, of this Kingdom; and that, upon thele Accounts, the Parliament, from time to time, by many Laws, have given it great Encouragement, and also endeavoured to prevent the Seduftion of our Artificers into foreign Parts, and to preserve our Manufactures as much as possible to ourselves; but that, notwithstanding these Precautions, of late several evil-minded Persons, being Enemies to the Profoerity of their Country, or from private Views, in open Violation of the Laws, have actually seduced into foreign Parts many of our Artificers and Workmen in our Staple Manufacturethe Woollen Trade, as well as in other Branches of the Manufactures of this Kingdom; as also have been aiding, assisting, or abetting, in conveying into foreign Parts Tools and Engines uled in our Manufactures, or Draughts, Models, and, Descriptions of Tools and Engines used in the said Manufactures, which have a great Tendency to deprive us of the Benefit of them } whereby it appears, that the Laws already in being are not sufficient to restrain and deter such evil-minded Persons from being guilty of such unnatural and pernicious Practices: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to inflict such Pain9 and Penalties as may be thought mostconducive to rcltrai* all such evil-minded Persons from being guilty of such de-struftiveand unnatural Practices for the future, and to oblige all present Delinquents to return to their nativeCoun-try; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in tl'.e Premises as to the House shall i'eem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants of the City of London African trading to Africa, and the British Plantations in America, Trade, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth,

That the Trade to the Coast of Africa is of the utmost Consequence to this Nation, and to the British Plantations; and that past Experience has incontestably proved, that this Trade has declined or flourished in proportion as it has been restrained or left free and open; that the British Forts and Settlements on that Coast might be rendered greatly serviceable to the Trade in general, if put under such Regulations, as that all his Majesty's Subjects might equally enjoy the Benefit of trading with the Negro Merchants; which the Petitioners apprehend they would be debarred of, if placed under the Direction of a trading Joint-Stock Company; and that some of his Majesty's Ships of War, properly Rationed on that Coast, are the greatest Security against the Incroachments of Rival Nations, the Insults of an Enemy, and the Ravages of Pirates: And therefore praying, That this Trade may continue free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects; and that the said Forts and Settlements may be put under such Management, as will be most conducive to this End; and that such Provision may be made for their Support and Maintenance as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Trade tb the Coast of Africa is of very confi-

African

derable Consequence to the general Interest of the Kingdom, and peculiarly affects the Merchants, and other trading Inhabitants of the said City, who have largely adventured their Properties therein, and carry on the same in a very extensive Manner; and the Petitioners are well satisfied they will continue so to do whilst that Trade remains free and open; and that the Petitioners conceive, that by supporting the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, under such Regulations as shall be for the common Benefit of his Majesty's Subjects, his Majesty's Rights of Sovereignty and Possession will be preserved, and the Forts and Settlements made serviceable to Trade t but that they will become highly prejudicial to it, if placed in the Hands of any Joint-Stock Company: And therefore praying the House, That the Trade to Africa may remain free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects; and that the Forts and Settlements may not be placed in the Hands of any Joint-Sto'ck Company.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Adventurers within the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read j setting forth. That the Trade to the Coast of , and more especially to the Gold Coast, is of very great and considerable Consequence to the Interest of the Kingdom in general, and to that of the said City in particular, from whence the same is carried on in a very extensive Manner} and that the rendering the said Trade truly beneficial to all his Majesty's Subjects, will intirely depend on keeping it still free and open: That the Petitioners apprehend, that the British Forts and Settlements on the said Coast are proper to be supported upon a respectable Foot, for preserving his Majesty's Right of Sovereignty, and, under due Regulations, may be made serviceable to Trade; but will become a great Burthen, and highly prejudicial to it, if placed in the Hands of any Joint-Stock Company; and that a sufficient Number of his Majesty's Ships of War, properly stationed on the said Coast, will tend greatly to the Security and Protection of the said Trade: And therefore praying, That the said Trade may still be preserved free and open } and that the said Forts and Settlements may be taken under his Majesty's immediate Protection, and the Care thereof committed to Merchants, who shall have no other Advantage from the said Trade than in common with all his Majesty'sSubjects; or that such Provision may be made for the Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants, and others, concerned in the African Trade, from the Town of , was also

presented to the House, and read; setting fofth, That the Petitioners for a great many Years past, have had, and now hold, a principal Share in the Trade to the different Parts of the Ajrican Coast; and can say, that they have done as much, at lead, as any other Part of the British Subjects, in bringing it to that flourishing State which the Nation at present enjoys the Benefits of: That it appears plain to the Petitioners, from Reason, long Experience, and various Trials, that this Branch of foreign Commerce can never be preserved and supported in Britain by any Joint-Stock trading Company whatsoever, but only by a free and open exercise of it on One equal Foot allowed to every Adventurer: That the Forts and Settlements on the African Coast have hitherto been, and will always remain while in a Company's Hands, a Prejudice and Discouragement to the Trade; but might probably be rendered very serviceable thereto, if either taken immediately into the Hands of the Government, and supported at a national Expence, for the impartial Benefit of every one concerned in it, or put into the Hands of a regulated Company of all the African Merchants in Great Britain, on some such Plan as was proposed in the Bill which passed in the House the last Session of Parliament} and in such manner, as no Part of the British Subjects should obtain superior Benefits from them above their Fellows, nor any distinguishing Advantages in the Prosecuting of any Part of this Trade: That the Petitioners

A. 1749.

think this, with the Countenance of a. Man of War or Two stationed on the Coast, is the only effectual Way to enable the Subjects of this Kingdom to contend with all their foreign Rivals, and to perpetuate to the Nation a principal Share in the valuable Advantages of an African Trade: And therefore praying to be continued in the same free and open Exercise of this Branch of Commerce, which for many Years the Petitioners have enjoyed, and the Nation in general has found so greatly beneficial; and that the bold Attempts, groundless Insinuations, and false Suggestions, of a few, who seem to have little Acquaintance with either iheAfrican Trade or Coast, and not the least Merit on which to ground their Expectations of those peculiar Advantages above their Fellow-Subjects, which they are so strenuously contending for, may not prevail to deprive the Petitioners of any of their valuable trading Rights, or to cramp them in any degree in the Exercise of them: And further praying. That the Forts and Settlements on the Coast may be for the future put under such a Management and Regulation as to the House shall seem meet, in order to give the Petitioners, and every British Adventurer without Distinction, an equal Share in the Benefit of them.

And the said Petitions w'ere severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Matters of Ships uling the Coal Uncancetled Trade, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf Booth for of themselves, and of many others using the said Trade: ulKi'

And the said Petition was read j setting forth. That the Manner of carrying on the said Trade, is, that when Ships arrive in the Port of London, the Matters employ Crimps or Factors to dispose of their Coals, who, with the Masters, enter into Bonds to his Majesty, payable within Three Months, for the Duties of the Coals; and the Matters are allowed Two and a Half per Cent. Discount, if the said Duties are paid within Sixteen Working Days after the Entry of the Ships; and the Crimps or Factors, for their Pains and Trouble, are allowed from the Matters a Commission of a Half per Cent, upon the Amount of the whole Cargo; and the Matters make up an Account with their Factors every Voyage, in which the Factors always charge all the Duties, and their Commission; and that the Petitioners having for many Years, according to this Method, employed Sir Malthus Ryal, William Williford,

John Gibson, and others, as their Crimps or Factors,

aid, from time to time, along with them, enter into Bonds for the Payment of the said Duties, and always left in their Factors Hands sufficient Value to pay those Bonds, and which they, the Petitioners, had the strongest Reason to believe the Collector of the Customs regularly received from their Factors, because otherwise he would have demanded Payment thereof when due, as the Duty of his Office required of him; which he never did: And the Petitioners, thinking the y might safely rely on the Care and Integrity of the said Collector and their Crimps (the latter being jointly liable to the Penalty of the Bonds) and the Nature of their Trade obliging them to return to their Loading Ports with their Ships, with the utmost Expedition, neglected to take up several of their Bonds; and that Williford dying insolvent, and the Collector of the said Duties, being also dead, greatly in Arrear to his Majesty for the said Duties, as the Petitioners are informed; and the said Gibson having, since the Death of the said Collector, likewise become insolvent; and an Extent having issued against the said Gibson and Sir Malthus Ryal, for Non-payment of the said Duties, the Sollicitor of the Customs did write several Letters to the Petitioners, in which he demanded, to their great Surprise, Payment of Bonds, some of them due above Twenty Years ago, upon Pretence that the said Duties are Hill unpaid: And further alleging. That the Petitioners apprehend, that, had not the said Bonds (though still remaining in the Collectors Office) been regularly paid, the Collector could not have annually made up his Accounts; nor would he have delivered up to the Petitioners, as he has done, great Numbers of Bonds entered into since the Date of these Bonds, for which they are now threatened to be lued, without taking the least Notice of any former Bonds; nor would he, upon Application made to him by several of the Petitioners, to know whether they had any Bonds Handing out against them, have replied, as he did, that there were none (although, since his Decease, many Bonds, entered into by

33 Geo. II.

7* — 8* Februariu

981

the Petitioners who thus applied, were found Uncancelled ip his Office) had he not been conscious of the Certainty of the Fad, that these Bonds were paid: And further letting forth, That although, on the Death of Williford, the Collector demanded no more of his Executrix than Eighteen hundred Pounds for Coal Duties due by the said Williford, yet now the Commissioners of the Customsdo demand Ten thousand Pounds, alleging, that there are Bonds to that Amount (landing out against him; and that it appears by attested Copies of the Crimps original Bills, and attested Copies taken out of their Books, delivered to the Sollicitor of the Customs, and by the constant Practice of this Trade, that the Petitioners regularly paid to the Crimps their Duties of every Voyage before they left the Port of London; which Duties the Crimps must have paid to the Collector, and the Collector must have received the feme, had he pursued his Instructions, which were, as the Petitioners are informed, not to permit any Ships to enter which had any Bonds (landing out against them that were due; and to put in Suit, against the Matters and Crimps, all Bonds within Fourteen Days after they became due; and therefore whatever Loss the Crown may suffer, the same must intirely proceed from the wilful Neglect or Contrivance between the said Collector and Crimps, to which the Petitioners were, no-ways privy, neither could they propose any Advantage therefrom, having regularly paid these Duties to the Crimps, in Manner before dated: And what makes it dill more hard upon the Petitioners, is, that they are now deprived of all Redress against the said Crimps, through their Insolvency; which they might otherwise have had, had their Bonds been put in Suit in due time, or had they had Notice of frheir remaining unpaid; and that in some Instances, as the Petitioners are informed, the said Col-.lector has charged Crimps, in his Books, with Duties owing to the Amount of large Sums; when, upon Examination, it appeared, that these Duties are paid, and the Bonds taken up; and that as the Collector has been guilty of such unjust Practices, it may reasonably be presumed he has charged the Petitioners with Bonds which have been regularly paid by their Crimps, notwithstanding the Bonds are now remaining in his Office; and that this Fraud could not have been carried on, had the Collector's Books been truly kept, and properly inspected and chequed by the Comptroller, or other Officers appointed for that Purpose; and that, should the Bonds be now put in Suit against the Petitioners, they and their Families must be inevitably ruined, and forced to seek their Livelihood in foreign Countries: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

The Lord Robert Manners reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull; and also the Petition of the Burgesses and principal Inhabitants of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, whoseNames are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Guild or Brotherhood of Masters and Pilots, Seamen of the Trinity-house in Kingston upon Hullwere referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Robert Taylor was examined: And feid, That he was born in the Town of Hull; and that it has been the constant Practice, during his Time, when the Streets of the said Town have wanted repairing, for the Corporation to find the Gravel, Cobles, Sand, and other Materials; and the Inhabitants, before whose Houses such Reparations were wanting, to pay the Wages of the Workmen and PaviOrs; but that lately some of the Inhabitants have refuled to pay the Workmen and Paviors for the said Reparations; and that, by reason of the Narrownels of the Wheels of the Carriages, and of the excessive Weights carried thereon, and also by the Use of Trucks, the said Streets are frequently very much damaged, and . are now in several' Places in very bad Repair.

Being asked if certain Tolls, which are col led ed by the Corporation, are not particularly applicable to the Repair‘ot the said Streets ? he laid. That the Corporation receive of Persons, who are not free of the Town, a Toll upon every Load of Corn that is carried into the Town, and a Rent for the Standing of every Stall; but never understood that such Tolls or Rents were applicable to the Repair of the Streets; nor ever knew it disputed, till lately, that the Inhabitants were liable to pay the Workmen for repairing the Streets in the said Town.

Mr. Henry Musgrave was examined: And said, That ho^bts lived in the said Town Seventeen Years, and been a Httafekeeper therein about Fourteen or Fifteen Years; and that during that Period the Materials made use of in ' repairing the said Streets have been found by the Corporation; and the Expences of repairing and paving the lime have been paid by the Inhabitants.

Mr. Taylor was further examined: And said, That te-veral of the Inhabitants of the said Town neglect to sweep the Streets before their Houses; and that Dirt, and ether Annoyances, are frequently laid in the said Streets in the Night-time; and in such a private Manner, as renders it extremely difficult to doted the Offenders:

That in the last Winter several Houses were broke open and robbed, and Attempts made to break open several others, notwithstandinga military Guard is polled in the Market-place, and Centinels are placed at every Gate of the said Town.

That the Ships in the Haven, which are loading or unloading, lay full against the Merchants Staithes, where there is no Quay; and that about Two Years ago a Ship wasfet on Fire; and the Town would have been burnt, if very great Care and Industry had not been uled to extinguish the Fire: That all the Ships in the Haven lay close to each other; and that if a Fire hapipens in any One of:

them, it may communicate to the rest, and greatly endanger the Town; and that there is no Provision to oblige the Persons on board such Ships to put out their Lights at a certain Time.

Mr. Musgrave was further examined: And said, that the Trinity-houseappoint an Officer called a Haven-master,

but his Power only extends to the Moorings of the Ships in the said Haven:
