To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Darnel Gill, Clerk to the Dean and Chapter of Westminster, said. That the Right of holding a Market in the City of Westminster is a Franchise or Privilege belonging to the Dean and Chapter of St. Peter, -minster; and that the same Franchise did formerly belong to the Abbot and Convent: Ar.d,

Mr. John Lock, who had been an Inhabitant of minster near 40 Years, said, He had bought Provisions of different Sorts at a Market called The Round Wool-Jlaple; which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Atkinson.

And a Release was produced from the Dean and Chapter of Westminster, to Sir Joseph Ayloff ami Daniel Gel!;

whereby it appeared. That the Ground whereon the said Market, called The Round Woo, had been held, was formerly the Property of the Dean and Chapter of minster; and had been by the said Dean and Chapter conveyed to the Use of the Commissioners for building minster Bridge, in pursuance of the Powers granted by an Act of the 1 at h Year of his present Majesty; the Execution of which Deed was proved by the Reverend Doctor Wiff on and the Reverend Mr. Ingram, Prebendaries of the said Collegiate Church.

Then Mr. Lock further informed your Committee, That, in pursuance of such Conveyance, the said Ground had been appropriated to the Purposes of widening and rendering more commodious the Streets and Passages to the new Bridge, and, in consequence, the Market discontinued; and it has been a great Inconvenience to the Inhabitants of Westminster, who have been obliged to buy their Meat dearer, and go to other Markets, since the fliutting up the Market as aforesaid; and that the Wit-nels, in particular, has been obliged to go to other Markets.

Mr. Atkinson said. That, when the said Market was held, many Country People ufod to bring Provisions to it.

Mr. Daniel Gell, being examined, laid. That the Dean and Chapter of Westminster haJ appointed a Committee of Three of their own Body to consider of making a Flesh Market, together with the Person who is Lessee, for a Term, of the Office cf Keeper and Sweeper of the Market lately held in The Round Woolstaple: That the Chapter has agreed with the said Lessee, and that the Agreement is entered in the Chapter Book: And,

Mr. Richard Combes, the said Lessee, informed your Committee, That he had agreed with the Committee appointed by the Dean and Chapter, that, if the said Dean and Chapter would lay out the Money arising by the Sale of The Round Woolstaple Market in the Purchase of some other convenient Place, he was ready to build and let up such Conveniences as might be necessary for the holding a Market; which the said Dean and Chapter agreed to do, as soon as they were sufficiemly impowered, and could find a Place proper for that Purpose:

That the Witness has endeavoured to find out such a Vol. 25.

Witness informed the Committee, contained a sufficient Part of the said Leasehold Ground for the said intended Market: And,

Mr. Henry Keen, Surveyor to the said Dean and Chapter, produced and explained to your Committee, a Plan of the said intended Market; and Mr. Combes also produced a Plan of the Ground in its present Situation; which he likewise explained.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the holding the publick Market within the City of Westminster hath, from ancient Times, been held imme-cl.ately from and under the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter, Westminster, by their Lessee of the Office of Keeper and Sweeper of the said Market.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That as the old and usual Place of holding the said Market, which was in The Round Woolstaple in King Street, in the said City, hath been converted to the publick Use of widening the Streets to and from the new Bridge, it is necessary, for the Accommodation and Benefit of the Inhabitants, and others, resorting thereto, that the said Market be held in some other convenient Place of the said City.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the most proper Place for the new holding the said Market is between the Broad SanEluary and Bow , which Place is now in the Possession of several Tenants, under Lease from the said Dean and Chapter, for Terms of Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary a Power be given to enable the said Dean and Chapter to hold the Market in such new Place; and, for this Purpose, that they be at Liberty to treat with, and purchase from, any of their said Tenants, their Interest in the said Premises, and invest in such Purchase such Money as hath arose from the Sale of the old Market place; notwithstanding any Restraint they maybe under, as Trustees for the Church, in disposing of the said Money, from or by any Acts of Parliament which have passed for building the new Bridge, as such Interests are not Freehold.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That when the new Place hath been purchased, and the Buildings and other necessary Conveniencics provided there for holding the said Market, that the said Market be preserved from Encroachment; and, in order to prevent the fame, that it will be necessary and expedient to forbid the vending and exposing to Sale any Flesh Meat, Poultry, or other Provisions, in any House or Shop, or on any Stall, within One hundred Feet of Assize from any the Bounds of the said Market, without the Licence of the Keeper and Sweeper of the said Market; and that a reasonable Penalty be inflicted on such Persons as shall act to the contrary.

The Lord Vupplin, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred toconsider of the State of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow-cth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That thfe Encouraging of the Importation of China raw Silk, to be manufactured in this Kingdom, will be a publick- Benefit, and greatly contribute to the Increase and Improvement of the Silk Manufactures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Encouragement of the Importation of China raw Silk^the several and respective Duties, now payable thereupon by virtue of several Acts of Parliament now in Force, shall, from and after the 24th Day of June 1750, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the Duties so determined, there shall be payable and paid, from and after the said 24th Day of "June, the same Rates and Duties, upon all China raw Silk imported into this Kingdom, as are now by Lavy payable for raw Silk of the Growth of Italy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion , of this Committee, That, from and after the said 24th Day of June, the like Drawback shall be allowed, upon the Expectation of China raw Silk, as is now allowed upon the Exportation of raw Silk of the Growth of Italy.

Part of it under an apparent Dii'couragement, and con-iining and limiting this Branch of the African Trade, which many Years Experience has shewn can be the most successfully carried on when free and open to every trading Subject: And praying the House to take' the Premises into Consideration; and to protect, and continue' all the Subjects of Great Britain, without Distinction, in the full Enjoyment of the free and open Exercise of their Trade and Commerce to all the different Parts of the African Coast, which they have long enjoyed, and which has been-found in the highefr Degree beneficial to this Kingdom.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called.

Captain Robert Martyn: Who laid. That a Lock had been erected upon the said River, which was of great Advantage to the Navigation thereof;, for, when the upper Gate of the said Lock is (hut, the Back-water is sufficient to carry Hoys and Lighters from one Quay to another; and, when the lower Gates of the said Lock are opened, the Rapidity of the Stream clears the River, and makes a great Depth of Water.

That he cannot exactly say what the present Condition of the Lock is, not having seen it very lately, but it was much out of Repair when he law it lad; but he believes something has been done to it since; and, if the Lock was to continue out of Repair, it would greatly endanger the choaking up the River.

That there are other Expences which attend the preserving the said Navigation; viz. a Lighter with a Harrow, which ought condantly to be employed to remove Shoals, which is attended with a considerable Expence; but the Witness cannot ascertain how much: Then,

Mr. John Aicfounder confirmed the Evidence of Captain Martyn, in regard to the Necessity of keeping up the Lock, in order to prevent the River being choaked up.

And he further informed your Committee, That he, together with Four other Persons, had surveyed the said Lock and Gates, and also the Sluice-head at the Hythe Bridge in Colchester, on the 29th and 30th of January

last: and he delivered in to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of the necessary Repairs thereof, signed by himself and Four other Persons, who a Hi (led him in taking the said Survey; which Estimate the Witness said was an exact and fair one, to the bed of his Judgment; and by the said Estimate it appeared, That £.536 16s. id. was necessary for the immediate Repair of the Lock and Gates, and £.19 14*. for Repair of the Sluice-head.

Mr. William Stinger, Collector of the said Duties, being

examined as to the Arrears of the Duties, said, That the Arrears of the Duties under the Act of the 9th and 10th of his late Majesty amount to£.204 it id: That these Arrears are due from several 'Traders in the Borough of Colchester, who refused to pay the said Duties, from the Year 1749, because the Chanel was so bud, as to (lop their Craft; and that the Merchants took Advantage of the Dissolution of the Corporation, after which there was no legal Power to compel the Payment of the said Duties.

That there had been^. 65 remaining in the Hands of the Witness ever since the Year 1740; and that he had heard there was about £.170 in the Hands of the late Receiver.

And, being asked the Question, he said, He was ready to pay this Arrear into the (lands of the Commissioners for the Navigation, though the Mayor and Corporation did not exist; and that, in his Opinion, the said Commissioners had a Power to compel the Payment of the said Arrear, and to give him a sufficient Discharge for the fame; but that the Opinion of Counsel had been taken as to that Point, which was, That, as the Mayor and Corporation did not Cub lift, there was no Power of recovering the said Duties.

That the new Duty had been condantly paid: That a Collier some time ago refused to pay it; but, upon threatening him, he paid it; and that the net Produce of the said new Duty has been, communi £.90 a Year.

That there are other Expences attending the Preserving of the said Navigation, such as Digging, the Working of Lighters, Harrows, &c. which, in the Opinion of the Vox,. 25.

Witness, would amount to £. 106 a Year, besides the ' repairing the said Lock; but, as the Witness is not p}avigai>>i« perfectly acquainted with those Affairs, he cannot pretend &Ci to form an exact Estimate of the Expence.

Mr. Alefounder said. That, when the Lock and Sluices were put in Order, the Expence of keeping them so, and Salaries to Persons to attend the fame, would amount to 40 or 50 Pounds a Year; besides the Expence of* ' keeping the Chanel clean, the Amount whereof the Witness cannot pretend to compute: And,

Mr. Freshfield informed the Committee, That it would cost 80 Pounds to provide a new Barge and Harrow; and £.70 or £. 80 a Year to keep the said Chanel open, exclusive of the Expence of the Lock and Sluices,

Mr. John Box, a Sea Waller, informed your Committee, That he had viewed the said Chanel for the Length of a Mile: That in One Place the Side is decayed for about 40 Rods, which mutt be repaired with Stakes or Piles, and Land Ties or Bullies: That there will be 1,009 Piles wanted, which will cost at lead 1,000 Shillings, besides the Expence of Land Ties and Worknianftlip:

That the Bankshavegone to Decay of late Years; and that there is anabfolute Necessity for repairing that Part of the Bank he speaks of in the manner before described: That the River must likewise be made deeper about 18 Inches, and Two Points taken off, which will cost aoo more:

That he speaks of a Place about a Mile below the Lock; but is not sufficiently acquainted with the River to give Evidence to any other Place, having never surveyed it.

Mr. Henry Bevan informed your Committee, That he had a Draught on Mr. Blatch, late Receiver of the Duties, for 150; which he, the said Blatch, paid: That the Witness had another Draught of £.170, for Work done about the said Navigation, which Mr.

Ejfecutor of the said Mr. Blatch, refused to pay, though he had Money in his Hands, because he said the Commissioners Power did not signify a Farthing; but that he would pay the Witness, if he would give him a Bond to indemnify him, if any future Demand should be made* for that the Commissioners had no Power to give a Discharge, since the Dissolution of the Corporation.

That the Lock and Chanel cannot be supported without (bme further Provision, the present Duty of 3 per Chalder upon Coals not being more than Half sufficient for that Purpose; and that the Witness believes 6 in the Chalder would be sufficient, and not less; for that the Repairs of the said Lock and Sluices, together with working the Harrow, and repairing the Banks, would amount to £.100 a Year, exclusive of the prime Cost of putting the before-mentioned Particulars into Repair, and of Salaries to Persons employed therein.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. James Williams said. That the said Parish is very, extensive, very, populous, and a great Number of poor Persons to be taken care of.

That in the said Parish there are Nine Wards, and, by t&e Laws in being, only Four Overseers can be appointed; which, by Experience, have been found to be too few to make, the Collections within the Time allowed, and to do the other Duties incumbent on Overseers of die Poor, without totally neglecting their own Business.

That the Scavengers in the said Parish are generally very young Inhabitants, who contract with Rakers to clean the Streets for what Money they can coiled j and are imposed upon by the Rakers, and the Streets left in a very dirty Condition; oftentimes great Heaps of Dirt. are left in the Streets.

A Petition of Samuel Plumm George and

William Monk, Attornies of the Court of the King's Palace of Westminster, was presented to the House, and

read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, by virtue of and under Letters Patent granted by his late Majesty King Charles the Second, bearing Date the Fourth Day of October, in the Sixteenth Year of his Reign, have been severally admitted to their Office of an Attorney of the said Court (the Jurisdiction whereof extends Twelve Miles round Westminster-hall, the City of London excepted)}'and, as such, have Freeholds in their said Offices, and, in respect thereof, are severally charged and pay to the Land Tax, after the Rate of One hundred and Twenty-five Pounds a Year; and that the Duty of such Attornies is to sue out all Writs, and prosecute and defend all Suits, in the said Court; and, by means of the Business transacted there, a large Revenue arises to his Majesty from the Stamp-Duties; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Bill, now depending before the House, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts within the 'Tower Hamlets, and in the Liberty of his Majesty's Tower of London, and in the several Parishes, Liberties, Precincts, and Places, within the same Hamlets, should pass into a Law, the Right, and Interest of the Petitioners in their respect iveOfficts will necessarily be' greatly impaired; and inasmuch as this House has, on ajl Occasions, shewn the tendered: Regard to the Freeholds and Properties of the Subject; and that the Petitioners have, for several Years last past, made the Business of such Offices their principal Study and Employ-, ment: Therefore praying, That they may be permitted, by their Counsel, to submit their same to the Considera-. tion of the House; or that, by the said Bill, if the same shall pass into a Law, such Relief may be provided for the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee,-upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Creditors A Petition of the several Creditors of the Royal mf African Can Company of England, whole Names are thereunto Company. subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the just and bona fide Creditors of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Petitioners are surprifcdand alarmed to find the Royal African Company (after such solemn and repeated Declarations of their utter Inability) now receding from the Proposal by them made to this House last Year; and offering, by their present Petition, to take upon themselves the satisfying of their Debts, though alleged to amount to about One hundred and Thirty thousand Pounds; and that, from the Company's present distressful Situation, the Petitioners conceive but little Likelihood of their being able in a great Number of Years, if ever, to satisfy and discharge so large a Sum; and the fatal Experience they have had of the Company's Treatment of their Creditors, the Delire insinuated in their said Petition, of being enabled to make some Agreement for their Debts, and the Suspicions of late endeavoured to be raised against the trading Part of the Creditors, as if they had taken unjust Advantages of the Company's Necessitics, afford but too much Reason to suspect, that the Company's Intentions are (how flourishing soever their Circumstances may hereafter prove) to force their Creditors into a Composition, by litigating their most just Demands; And that, to obviate lo false and injurious an Aspersion, and to give the House the strongest Afl'urance and Satisfaction of the Fair-nefsof these Demands, the Petitioners, and others of their Fellow-Sufferers (whose Claims amount to about Fifty thousand Pounds) have voluntarily verified the same by Affidavits, whereby it will appear, that most of the Debts which have accrued for Goods, Work, and Materials, were contracted upon express Promises on the Part of the Com-pany;and in full Expectation, on the Part of the Creditors, of immediate Payment out of the Aids from time to time granted by Parliament for the Support of the said Company's Forts and Castles on the Coast of; and that this House having, last Session, in tender Compassion of the ill Treatment and Distrelfes of the said Creditors, been generously pleased to take them under their Protection, the Petitioners trust they shall not be again left at the Mercy of the Company, or to the Hazard of a precarious Undertaking: And therefore praying the House, That they may continue under the Protection of Parliament, which, as they esteem to be their highest Honour and Security, they shall ever with the utmost and most rc-spectful Gratitude remember and acknowlege.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

African A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, the principal Trade. Tradesmen, and Inhabitants, of the ancient Corporation of Rippon, &c. was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That a pernicious Scheme has been formed, and offered to Parliament, by some West-India Planters in London, to deprive the Out-ports of this Kingdom, and all the rest of the British Subjects, of that Liberty and Trade to the African Coasts which they now enjoy, and to have this Branch of foreign Commmerce confined solely to themselves, as an exclusive Joint-Stock Company; and that the Petitoners conceive, to discourage Trade in Voi. 25.

the Out ports, and to confine it so London', tfiuft be attended with many mischievous Consequences to the Nation in general; and that all Monopolies, oi1 exclusive Companies, in Trade, must be certainly a great Hindrance to the Extensionand Improvement of it: And therefore praying. That the House will take it into Consideration i and that all the British Subjects, without Distinctioti, may be continued in their full Enjoyment of that Trade to all the different Parts of the African Coast which they have long possessed, and which for many Years past has been by Experience found in the highest Degree beneficial to this Nation j and that no Part of the Inhabitants of this Kingdom may be put under any distinguishing Dif-couragements in the Prosecution of any Branch of it.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Pres African ton, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the Trade. House, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners apprehend the Scheme which is offered in Parliament, by a few in the City of London, to confine the Trade to the Coast of Africa, in Part or in Whole, to a Joint-Stock trading Company, will, if carried into Execution, be greatly prejudicial to the general Good of this Kingdom, and particularly to the Out-ports of it, this being the principal Branch of foreign Commerce they have to be concerned in: And therefore praying, That the Trade to Africa, in all its Parts, may dill continue open and free to every British Subject, which, by long Experience, hath been found the only effectual Way to support, improve, and extend it; and that the lelfilh Views of a few may not prevail to deprive the rest of their Fellow-Subjects of any of their Rights of Trade, or to put them under any distinguishing Disad vantages in the Exercise of them.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

hi°f S'r William Calvert reported from the Committee, to America w^otn l^e Petition of the Merchants, Weavers, Throw-fters, Dyers, and other Manufacturers of raw, and thrown Silks, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousand labouring People depending upon the Silk Trade was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appeared by several Accounts presented to the House from the Commissioners of the Customs, and reterred to your Committee, together with the Evidence of several Witnesses examined thereon, that the Exportation of wrought Silk has of late Years very much increased, and the Importation of wrought Silk has very much decreased: For,

Mr . Daniel Gobbi, who has been a Silk Weaver 45

Years, said. That great Quantities of raw Silk have of late Years been manufactured into thrown Silks, and afterwards into Silks and Velvets: That this Manufacture has been increasing, from Year to Year, even since the Witness began Business, and is now more than sufficient for Home Consumption: That great Quantities of the said Manufacture had been exported to foreign Parts, particularly Tabbies to France, and flowered Silks to Germany; and that he has exported of late several Thousand Pounds worth of wrought Silk from Chester to Ireland.

Mr. John Sabatier said, That, for Two or Three Years 24

last past, he has exported wrought Silk from Chester for Ireland, to the Amount of Two or Three thousand Pounds per Annum.

Mr. Lewis Chauvet, who has been a Silk Weaver 17 Years, said. That he has exported great Quantities of wrought Silks to France, and other foreign Parts; and that the Manufacturers of England could make double the Quantity sufficient for Home Copfumption, if a necessary Supply of raw Silk could be obtained.

Mr. James Crockatt, Merchant, said, That, for Ten Years last past, he has exported, One Year with another. Silks of English Manufacture, to the Amount of£. 2,000 per Annum, to the Colonies of Jamaica and South Carolina', and that he don't export a Tenth Part of the -lish manufactured Silk that is lent to Jamaica only:

That the Silk which he has exported has been of various Species, from Fifteen Pence to Thirty Shillings a Yard; and he has likewise exported some Velvets:

That he is certain this Silk is English Manufacture, having bought it of the Weavers of Canterbury and Spittle-fields-, and the Witness has likewise heard, that we export Silk Stockings to Italy and Spain, which are esteemed better than those made in those Countries.

Mr. Samuel Lloyd, Merchant in the Silk Trade, informed the Committee, That he had resided a considerable time in Italy:

That the Supply of fine short raw Silk, proper to be worked by Engines, has been chiefly from Italy, some from Spain, and a small Quantity from China, likewise a small Quantity from the Southern Parts of France:

That he cannot say what Quantities have been imported from China; but that the Supply from thence is precarious, the East India Company not knowing what Species of Goods they shall import: That sometimesthey import more, sometimes less, and sometimes none at all; which last Circumstances has been the same for Five Years together:

That the Price of Italian and China Silk has been of late Years nearly the same; but there is some Difference in the Quality, and, if we could receive a certain Supply from China, the Witness is of Opinion, that it would not answer all Purposes:

That the Throwing ofSilk employs Children and infirm Persons.

Mr. Nathanael Pattison, a Merchant in the Silk Trade, said, That our Manufacturers are supplied with raw short Silk chiefly from Italy: That the China Silk is not fine enough in common for the Warp, but that he has had some as fine as any Italian: That the Turkey Silk is in general too coarle to be used for the Warp; and that China Silk, some Years, was imported as bad as the Turkey-, and that if a sufficient Quantity was imported from China, it would not serve all the Purposes; for the Manufacturers can depend on the Goodnels of the Italian Silk, but not upon that of China.

Mr. Samuel Lloyd, being further examined, said, That Prohibitions have been laid on the Exportation of all short raw Silk throughout all the Italian Principalities and States, as well as in Spain, inso much that his Correspondents in those Countries have found it impracticable to export such Quantities of raw Silk as have been already contracted and paid for; and he produced a Letter, dated Rome, 23 August 1749, to shew, that a Silk Manufacture had been set up in that City, and great Encouragement given thereto.

Mr. John Delamare produced several Letters from his Correspondents in Spain and Italy, several Paragraphs whereof were read; by which it appeared, That the said Prohibitions have been rigorously put in Execution in the respective Countries; and he also produced an Edict, dated July 2d, 1749, prohibiting the Exportation of short raw Silk throughout the Papal Dominions: And he informed your Committee, That the like Prohibition had been enforced and rigorously executed in Piedmont for Twenty Years last past; (o that what raw Silk has been exported from the other Parts of Italy for Six Months past has been by Stealth.

Mr. Twin Lloyd, who came from Italy last June, being examined, said, Several Manufactures for wrought Silks are erected at Parma, Pisa, and other Parts of Italy, to which all possible Encouragement has been given; and that the Troubles at Genoa has greatly contributed to the estab!idling those Manufactures, great Number of Artificers having been driven from thence to seek Shelter in other Parts of Italy.

To prove the Increase of the Price of thrown Silk, the only Species now allowed to be exported from Italy, Mr. John Delamare laid before your Committee several In-

voices; by which it appeared, That, on the 9th May 1749, he paid for a Bale of Bolonia Silk /. 254; and that, on the 28th November in the same Year, he paid for a Bale of the fame. Species and Quantity /. 340: That, on the 5th of March 1749, a Bale of Piedmont Silk cost him/. 189; and that, on the 8th of October in the same Year, a Bale of the same Species and Quantity cost him £.244, fb that the Price is advanced about 30 to 36 per Cent.-, the Reasonof which Advance, his Correspondents informed him, was from the great Demand: That the Silk Manufacture is so considerable, as to employ, in the Manufacture of Broad Silks only in 20,000

Persons.

Mr. Leivis Chauvet, being further examined, said. That he has been obliged to discharge 150 Persons, which was One-third of the Persons he uled to employ, and to put down several Looms, which was the same of the Weavers in general; and that this arose from the Scarcity and advanced Price of raw Silk.

To shew that a Supply of short raw Silk may be had from our Southern Colonies in

Mr. Job Rothmalher said. That he is well acquainted with the Province of South Carolina, which abounds with Mulberry-trees: That the Red Mulberry-tree is the natural Produce of the Country, and the White may be easily propagated: That the Growth of the Mulberry-tree is so quick, as to produce Fruit in Four or Five Years; and there being many Silk-worms there, they would make more Silk, if properly encouraged.

And it appeared to your Committee, by the Eyidence of Two Members present, That the Mulberry-tree proper for the Nature of Siik-worms soon grows to Perfection in the Southern Colonies, where there now are a great Number of Trees of that Sort, and some very large; and that they had known wrought Silks manufactured from the Silk produced from South Carolina.

Mr. Philip Lee said. That he is acquainted with the

Soil and Climate of Virginia, which abounds with Red and White Mulberry-trees, which are the natural Produce of the Country: That he has seen Silk-worms there, which have been destroyed for want of Care in the Winter.

That he likewise. knows the Province of North Carolina, and has been in a House there where they made a great Quantity of Silk.

Harman Vereljt Esquire said, That he received last Year Six Boxes of raw Silk from Georgia, consigned to him as Accomptant to the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America, containing, in the Whole, aoo Weight; and that he had received before, at different Times, 133 Pounds Weight, and upwards: And Mr. James Crockatt said, That he received last Year Four different Parcels of raw Silk from South , amount-

ing, in the Whole, to 226 Pounds Weight: And Mr. John Nicholson said. That he has received, within these Two Years last, about 100 Weight; and his Broker told him, it answered all the Purposes of Piedmont Silk.

Then Mr. John Batchelor, a Weaver, produced to your Committee Two Pieces of flowered Velvet, which he said he himself had made from Carolina and Georgia Silk: That this Species of the Silk Manufacture is the most difficult to work of any, and required the belt Silk; and that the Carolina and Georgia Slik answered the Purpose as well as any he had ever worked.

African A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and principal Trade. Tradesmen, of the City of , was presented to the

/ House, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners have been informed, That there is an Attempt made by the Royal African Company of England, which may tend to monopolize the Trade to the African Coast, which the Petitioners apprehend will greatly injure the Out-ports of this Kingdom, and prove hurtful to the Trade of the said City in particular; and that all his Majesty'sSubjects do now and have long enjoyed' the Benefit of that Trade, and that many of them have at this time the greatest Part of their Fortunes embarked in it: And therefore praying the House, That none of his Majesty's Subjects may be put under such distinguishingDiscouragements as must naturally arise from any. Monopoly of a. Branch of Trade, which, upon its present Footing has proved of such general Benefit to the Trade of this Kingdom.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common-Council, free Burghers, and Freemen, of the Burgh of Appleby, in the County of Westmoreland, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have observed, that a Proposal is offered to Parliament to confine the Trade of the African Coast to the Port of Lon* don, and to deprive the Out-ports of these Kingdoms and all the rest of the British Subjects, of that Liberty of Trade which they now enjoy to the said Coast\ and that

the Petitioners are apprehctrfrve of the Danger that may arise to a Community from a Monopoly of any Kind:; And therefore praying. That all the British Subjects may be continued in the full Enjoyment of that free Trade to any Part of the African Coast, which they have long poffefted, and which has by Experience been found for many Years so beneficial to these Kindoms.

A Petition of the Merchants of the Town of Plymouth, trading to Africa and the British Plantations, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Trade to the Coast of Africa is of the utmost Consequence to this Nation, and to our British Plantations; and that past Experience has inconteftabiy proved, that this Trade has declined or flourished in proportion as it has been restrained, or left free and open; and that the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast might be rendered greatly serviceable to the Trade in general, if put under' such Regulations, as that all his Majesty's Subjects might equally enjoy the Benefit of trading with the Negro Merchants that live under the Protection of those Forts and Settlements; which the Petitioners apprehend they will be debarred of, if placed under the Direction of a trading Joint-Stock Company» and that some of his Majesty's Ships of War, properly stationed on that Coast, are and will be the greatest Security against the Encroachments of Rival Nations, the Insults ot Enemies, and the Ravages of Pirates: And therefore praying. That the Trade to the Coast of Africa may continue free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects (the Merchants of the said Town having sent Three Sail of Ships to the Gold Coast this lafi! Year); and that the said Forts and Settlements majrbe put under such Management as will be most conducive to this End; and that such Provision may be made for their Support and Maintenance as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Coosideration of the Committee of the wholo House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Papers presented to the House upon the Sixth Day of this instant February, from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, relating to the Trade to Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seventy-one thousand One hundred Sixteen Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Sixpence, being the Surplus Monies remaining in the Exchequer, at Michaelmas last, 1749, of the Subsidy of Poundage on Goods and Merchandizes imported, after satisfying all Payments due thereupon, be applied towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty for the Service of the Year 175b.

A Petition Of the several Merchants arid Traders of the City of London, and also of the Mailers and Owners

of Ships, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, in fitting out Ships and Vessels from the River Thames to foreign Parts, find great Advantage in employing such Ship-builders, Rope-makers* Mail-makers, Block-makers, Sail-makers, Ship-chandlers, and others, who inhabit upon the Banks of the River Thames, below London Bridge; and that great Numbers of the moll useful Artificers and, Tradesmen of that Sort retide, and carry on their federal Trades and Occupation* between London Bridge and the Parish of Saint Mary Rq~ t her hit h, on the Surry Side of the River Thames; and are obliged to rife at all Hours in the Night, as Accidents happen to Ships in the River , or otherwise* where their Assistance is necessary; and that by virtue of an Act made in the Iaft Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for opening and making a new Road from the bast End of New Street, in the Parish of St. *John , to

and through the several Places therein mentioned, and for keeping the said Road In Repair for the future* a new Road is now opened through the Parishes of St. Mary Magdalen Bermondsey, St. Mary Rotherhith, and St. Nicholas and St. Pauls Deptford, whereby the Communica-

tion by Land between London and his Majesty's Dockyard at Deptford, and also the East India Warehouse at

Rotherhith, and his Majesty's Victualfing-Office* is less* by near Three Miles, than the old Road heretofore made use of: and that a Passage from London Bridge to Rotherhith, to enter upon such new Road* leads through the Parish of St. John Southwark, in which there are many narrow and inconvenient Streets and Lanes* now very dangerous to pals in the Night-time, for want of propetf Lights, and a weil-regulaled Watch; and will be much more so when the aforesaid new Road is perfectly finished and completed; whereas were an effectual Provision made for a Nightly Watch, arid proper Lights, it would not only be a great Security to the Persons and Properties of all his Majesties Subjects passing to Deptford Dock, and the other Places before-mentioned, in the Night-time; but also such regular Watch would be a great Safeguard against Fire's, that might dellroy great Quantities of naval Stores always reposited in Warehouseson the Banks of the River Thames, in those Parts, as also a great Help in case of Accidents by Fire amongst the Shipping in the River Thames; and that the Petitioners, being convinced so

freat a Good cannot be obtained without establishing a und for carrying the same into Execution, have applied to the Minister, Churchwardens, and other principal Inhabitants, of the said Parish of St. John who

from Ireland. County of Lancaster, and in the City of , for and

on behalf of themselves, and the several other Soap-boilers and Tallow-chandlers residing in the adjacent Parts of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the pernicious Practice of running Soap and Candles from Dublin, and other Parts in eipe-

cially the former, all along upon the West Coast of South Britain, hath beers carried on for many Years last past, and daily increases, to the great Hurt and Diminution of his Majesty's Revenue upon that of Soap and Candles, and to the great Decay of the Trade of Soap-boiling and Candlemaking. and to the manifest Lois of the Petitioners, and their Fellow-Sufferers, employed therein; and that, be-

tides the present unavoidable Difference of the Market Prices of Soap and Candles betwixt this Kingdom and Ireland, occasioned by the very great :Di(proportion of Duties upon them, and their Materials laid in the former more than in the latter Kingdom, another very material Thing happens to contribute to this Practice of running Soap and Candles by Sailors, Passengers, and other Traders betwixt Ireland and England, being very numerous, which is, that they bring the same from Ireland lapr up in Paper, and in small Parcels, concealed in the Cielings and other Parts of the Ships or Vessels, convenient for that Purpose; which easily escapes in the Search of the Officers, and affords an Opportunity as easy, being so portable, for the Runner to convey and fell the same on Shore; and if the Officers be so lucky as to findTuch ParceU on board the Yame, they are admissible to an Entry in the'Custom-house; and the pretent Duties upon the Import of such Soap or Candles ncJt near equalling the Value of it here, the' Owners rather chuse to entcVand pay the Duty for thelaffie, than to'forfeit it; and, as the worst same that! can befall these Runners, is but the Forfeiture of the Soap or Candles, and nothing else, they become the more emboldened in this Practice to so great an Excess, that the Petitioners doubt not to make appear that at least Two thousand Tons of Soap, or upwards, in-a clandestine manner, by these Kind of Smugglers, are conveyed Worn. Ireland to Great Britain every Year, without paying any Duty for the fame; by which

Britain, in its Revenue, according to the present Duty of Soap, and its Materials only, which are therein manufactured here, fuftairts a Loss of Forty-one thousand Six hundred Pounds pet- Annum, or upwards, one Year with aflother; and that the Petitioners are ready to make the Truth of the Premifts satisfactorily to appear, upon Leave being given them;-and hope they have done so to the Satisfaction of the Commissioners of Excise; a Petition of tH* time Import with this, which1 was presented to the Lords of the Treasury last Year, being by them referred to the said Commissioners; who made a strict.Inquiry, in all or most of the' Ports of this Kingdom, into the Nature and Extent of the Abuse; and made their Report thereon- to the said Lords of the Treasury, to whose Report the Petitioners refer: And expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that proper Provisions may pass into a Law for restraining and preventing the like evil Practice for the future.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the subscribing Planters and Merchants African interested in, and trading to, the British Sugar Settlements Trade, in America, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the very' Existeoce and Preservatiomot the Sugar Colonies depend upon the BritiJJt Trade to Africa; and as the settling and fixing the Manner of carrying on this Trade for the future is now under the Conlidpration of this House, and as the Fortunes of most of the Petitioners are in the Sugar Colonies, begging Leave to fub-mit and lay before this House those Methods, by which, as the Petitionersconceive, that valuable Branch ot Commerce, in which the general Trade and Navigation of this Nation isfo essentially interested can only be retrieved, preserved, and extended: And setting forth. That the dangerous Rivals to this Nation, the , carry' on

successfully this Branch of Trade to the Coast of by which they are enabled to improve and extent* to an incredible Height their Commerce to and ftom Colonies; and that notwithstanding the Crown,

Britain has been in Possession of that Trade, particularly on the Gold Coast and Whydah, ahove Fourscore *‘rays»

yet the French are daily encroaching on the Rights.° e British Subjects there; and are continuing such their Endeavours to that Degree, that, unless immediate Care is taken to preserve the Forts and Fortifications on that Coast, the French will soon become Matters thereof, and consequently of the most valuable Branches of Trade on the Coast of Africa, and thereby soon exclude the Subjects of Great Britain from every Part of that Coast, as they have already done from the G um Coast: And, as the proper Methods to preserve and secure this Trade to the British Subjects, and to render it beneficial to the British Sugar Colonies, further alleging. That the Forts

and Fortifications there ought to be put into and constantly kept, not only in a defensible, but in a respeestable Condition; and that as the Aid of Parliament is absolutely necessary for that Purpose, the Ends of granting such Aid will be much better answered by committing that Trust, and Application of the Money the House shall think proper to grant, to an incorporated Body of Men, with a Joint-Stock made answerable, under Penalties, for the due Execution thereof, than to any temporary', mutable, and transient Set of Men whatsoever, who might renounce it at pleasure, anti who would be answerable each for his own Acts only, and not One for the Acts of another; and that the Trade to that Part of the Coast of Africa called Guinea will, as the Petitioners conceive, be carried on more beneficially to the British Nation and its Colonies, if, besides leaving it free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects, a Company with a joint trading Stock be likewise permitted to trade thither, than it can poflibJy be by private Traders only', without such a Company; lb as such a Company are inverted with no Rights or Privileges to exclude, obstrud, or hinder, any other of

A Petition and Representation of the Magistrates and Town Council of Ayr, and of the Merchant Traders at the Port of Ayr, in North Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by the Sixth Article of the Union of England and Scotland, all Parts of the united Kingdom are to have the same Privileges of Trade; notwithstanding whereof, the Planters,

and same other-', in London, as the Petitioners are informed, have formed a Schenv*, and offered the same in Parliament, to deprive the Out-ports of this Kingdom, and other Bri-if;Subjei is, of their Liberty of Trade to the

African Coast. a:ui c!:e where, which they now enjoy; and to have this Branch of foreign Trade confined iolely to themselves and the Port of London, as One exclusive joint Company, to the great Discouragement of Trade in the Out-pmts, and the Lcfs of the King's Revenue, and which must be attended with many mischievous Consequences to the Nation in general, seeing all Monopolies, Or exclusive Companies in Trade, are certainly a great Hindrance to i!v Extension and Improvement of Trade, on which the Welfare and Happineisof these Kingdoms much depend: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into l'crious Consideration, and not to grant any such exclusive Privileges; but all the Subjects,

without Distinction, to continue in the full Enjoyment of that free and open Exercise of Trade to all the different Parts of the African Coast, and cllewhere, which for many Years past have been by Experience found in the highest Degree beneficial to this Kingdom; and That none of the Inhabitants of any Part of the Nation may be put under any distinguisiiing Discouragements in the Prosecution of any Branch of it.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Owners of Ships, and others, of the City of Chester, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have lately heard with much Concern of a pernicious Scheme being formed, and offered to Parliament, fending to deprive the Out-ports of this Kingdom, and all the rest of the British Subjects, of that Liberty of Trade

Vol. 25.

to the African Coast that they now enjoy; and to have this Branch of Commerce confined Iolely to a particular Company in London, as an exclusive Joint-Stock Company: And as the Petitioners lately have made a Beginning in the African Trade from the said City, and hope to extend and prosecute the fame, alleging, That confining the said Trade in such a manner must be attended with many pernicious Consequences to the Nation in general, and to the Out-ports in particular; and that the Petitioners conceive, that all Monopolies or exclusive Companies in Trade must be a great Hindrance to the Extension and Improvement of it: And therefore praying the House to take the said Trade into their Protection, the Plantation Trade also depending upon it, and not to suffer the present pernicious Scheme to take effect t but that all the British Subjects, without Distinction, may be continued in the free and open Exercise of Trade to all the different Parts of the African Coast which they have 1 ong possessed, and which for many Years past have been by Experience found in the highest Degree beneficial to this Kingdom; and that no Part of this Nation maybe put under any distinguishing Discouragemenis in the Prosecution of any Branch of it: And further alleging. That the BritiPo Forts and Settlements upon the Coast: of Africa may be greatly serviceable to the Trade in general, if put under such Regulations, that all his Majesty's Subjects may equally, without Distindion, enjoy the Benefit thereof, and that his Majesty's Sovereignty may be preserved; but that, if the said Forts and Settlements fnoulci be put under the Management of a particular J oint-Stock. Company, it would be greatly prejudicial to the African Trade; And therefore further praying. That the said. Forts and Settlements may n't be put under the Direction of any particular Company, but put under such. Management as may be conducive to the Good of all Persons trading to Africa, without Distinction; and that such Provision may be made for the Support and Maintenance 0\f the fame, as the House shall think fit: And further alleging, That some of his Majesty's Ships of War> properly Rationed upon the Coait of Africa, might be of great Security and Protection to the Trade.

A Petition of the Gentlemen and principal Traders of the Borough of Newcastle under Line, in the County of Stafford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Trade to the Coast of Afica is highly beneficial to t? is Nation in general; and that this and all other Trades must flourish or decline in proportion as they are left free and open, or restrained, Monopolies cr exclusive Companies in Trade being always found to be a great Hindrance to the Extension and Improvement of it; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that io lock up this Trade in the Hands of a few, exclusive to those to whom the pretent flourishing State of it is chiefly owing, would not only be a great Discouragement to ad Adventurers, but particularly- injurious to those who have ventured their Fortunes tn raising it to such flourishing Condition: And therefore praying, That all his Majesty's Subjects, without Distinction, may be continued in the full Enjoyment of that free and open Exercise of Trade to all the different Parts of the African Coast which they have long possessed; and that such Provision may be made for the Support and Protection of it as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Ashley Cowper Esquire, Clerk of the Parliaments, John Crawfurd Esquire, Puri'uivant or Mefien-ger Extraordinary attending the Great Seal, Edward Wright Esquire, Chaff-wax, Samuel Billingsley, Stationer to the Great Seal, for and on the behalf of themselves, and the rcfl; of the Creditors upon the Office of the Keeper or Clerk of the Hanaper in Chancery, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; fitting forth, That the Revenue of the Hanaper of his Majesty's High Court of Chancery is a very ancient Revenue belonging to the Crown; and the Office ofKeeper orClerk of the said Hanaper is an ancient Office held and enjoyed by Grant from his Majesty, and his Royal Predecessors, Kings and Queens of this Realm j and that the said Revenue consists of certain yearly Rents or Sums reserved or paid out of the Offices commonly called the Alienation Office, the Seal or Green Wax Office, the Six-peny Writ Office, and also of Fees paid upon Grants, Commissions, and other Patents passing under the Great Seal, which are uncertain and contingent; and that such Revenue hath constantly been issued and applied for the Payment of several ancient Fees, Salaries, and Allowances, due to the CJerk of the Parliaments, and other Officers attending the Parliament and the High Court of Chancery, and also to other Officers, for business done for the publick Service of the Kingdom; and likewise for the Discharge of several Bills and Disbursements for Stationary Wares, and other Necessaries, relating to such Business, always paid and allowed out of the Revenue of the said Hanaper, for all which the Keeper or Clerk of the Hanaper passes yearly Accounts upon Oath before the Auditors of the Imprest of his Majesty's Exchequer; and that the said Revenue, by reason of several Acts of Parliament made of latp Years concerning Law Proceedings, and the Change and Alteration of the Course of Business, and other Means, hath not, for divers Years last pall, been sufficient to answer and pay the several Salaries, Allowances, and Disbursements, ilfuing and payable out of the fame; so that there remained due and in Arrear, at Michaelmas 1749, to the Petitioners, and Teveral other Persons infilled to such Salaries, Allowances, and Disbursements, several Sums, amounting, in the Whole, to the Sum of Ten thousand Five hundred and Ninety Pounds Twelve Shillings and Eleven Pence, or thereabouts; and that the Revenue of the said Hanaper will in all Probability ftiil continue to be deficient, so that not only the present Debt upon the said Office will be irrecoverably loft, but great Part of the Salaries, Allowances, and Payments, due and payable to the Petitioners, and the other Persons who have Time out of Mind been |>aid out of the Revenue of the said Office, for Services done to the Publick, will continue to run in Arrear for the future, and be unpaid, unless some Provision be made by Parliament for t heir Relief: And therefore praying. That the House will be pleased to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give them such Relief as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty,

and that by the same Letters Patent it is provided, that if, by any Alteration of the Course and Processof the said Courts, or by Force of any Act of Parliament made or to be made, or by any other Means whatsoevec, it should happen, that the Petitioner should not have or levy so much as should satisfy and pay the said yearly Rents and Payments, and the same should be duly proved before the Lord High Treasurer, or Commissioners of the Trea-stiry, Under-‘l'reafurer, and Chancellor of the Exchequer, or any Two of them, for the Time being, that theh, upon such Proof made, and Allowance thereof had, in every such Case, and at every such Time, the Petitioner should not be compelled or chargeable to pay the said several Rents thereby reserved} but should, upon Oath, be accountable and make Payment, into the said Hanaper, of such Sums of Money only as the Petitioner should have received for the Sealing of any Writs, or other Things, as therein is mentioned; and that upon every such Account and Payment, so to be made as aforesaid, the Pe.‘itioner should be acquitted of and from so much of the said yearly Rents and Payments as, at or before the time of such Account and Payment, should be behind and unpaid: And further setting forth. That by force of several Acts of Parliament made of late Years, and by other Means, the Revenue of the said Office is so decreased, that, for Eleven Years last past, the Fees and Profits thereof have not been near sufficient to satisfy the several yearly Rents reserved by the said Letters Patent, over and above the other Fees, Payments, and Charges therein specified, and the Charges of executing the said Office; inibmurh that there remained behind and unpaid, on the last Day of Michaelmas Term .1749, of the yearly Rents reserved and made payable to the Clerk of the Hanaper, the Sum of Two thousand Eight hundred Thirty-two Pounds Five Shillings and Six Pence; and that there is not the least Expectation that the Revenue of the said Office will increase for the time to come, but on the contrary, that the same will Icffen more and more: And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration the State and Condition of the said Office, and grant the Petitioner such Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. /indrezv Miller, Rope-maker, said. That the new Road from London to his Majesty's Dock-yard at Deptford, the East-IndiaWarehouse at R and his Majesty's

Victualing-Office, is nearer by almost Three Miles than the old Road;

That the Passage from London Bridge to,

A Petition of the Coal Owners, Fitters, Coal-faflors, and Owners of Ships, residing in and near the Town of Sunderland, In the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That a Bill is now depending in this House, and ordered to be read a Third time, for the more effectual repairing and preserving the Piers and Harbour of Whiin the County of York, by laying an additional Duty on all Coals shipped at Nitwcajileupon Tyne, Sunderland, Blyth, Seaton Sluice, Culler-coats, or any other Harbour, Colliery, or Place, reputed to be a Member of the Port of upon Tyne:

And alleging. That the Granting of an additional Duty on all Coal shipped from the several Places or Ports above will be highly prejudicial to the Coal Trade in general, and a very great Hardfnip to the Petitioners, as the Price of Coals will be thereby increased: And further setting forth. That it is intended (as appears by the said Bill) to Voi. *5.

apply Part of the Monty, to arise by the above Duty, in repairing and making more Convenient a Way from the West Pier to the said Town of Whitby, which Way is now commdnly used, when the Tide is out, by Persons travelling from Whitby to Sand's End, Lyth,

Stockton, and many other Parts: And further alleging.

That the Petitioners apprehend the said Bill might, with, equal Propriety and Justice, extend to the Repairing of the Road from Whitby to arty other Town in that County, with the said Duty, as to apply any Part thereof to repair the Way from the said West Pier to the said Town of Whitby, and that the Repairing of the said Way; and purchasing Houses and Ground, tdc. to widen the fame, may be very convenient for Carriages belonging to the Town of Whitby, and Travellers who pass and repass from Sunderland, Lyth, Ghifborough, Stockton, and many other Places, to Whitby or Scarborough, but can be of little or no Use to the Coal-owners, Fitters, Coal-fa6tors, Owners of Ships, and Consumers of Coals; and that, by the above Bill, it is intended the additional Duty on Coals shall be paid, by the Matter or Owner of every Ship, at his shipping or loading Coals at any of the Places or Ports aforesaid; by means whereof the said intended Duty will be paid by all Ships loading at the above Places, though they come not to or near the Port of Whitby, and that this will be a Hardship on the Petitioners, and many others, if the above Bill pass into a Law: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Cout.iel, what they have to offer against the said Bill j or that they may have such further Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Yarmouth An ingrossed Bill for clearing, depthening, repairing Haven, &c. extending, maintaining, and improving, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth-, and for depthening, and making more navigable, the several Rivers emptying themselves into the said Haven; and also for preserving Ships wintering therein from Accidents by Fire; was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Rider, for preventing Annoyances to the said Haven, and directing how Offences of that Kind shall be tried and punished;

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks, which were filled up:

And then the said Clause was read the Third time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill by way of Rider.

In consequence whereof, an Amendment was proposed to be made to the Bill, by leaving out the Clause therein, relating to the said Annoyances, from the Word "not withstanding," in Pr. 30. L. 10. to the Words And "whereas," in Pr. 31. £,.9:

And the Question being put. That the said Clause (land Part of the Bill;

It passed in the Negative.

Whereupon the said Clause was taken out of the Bill, Part thereof being etafed, and the Remainder cut off at the Table.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: Arid that the Title be. An Act for repairing, improving, and maintaining, the Haven and Piers of Great Yarmouth; and for depthening, and making more navigable, the several Rivers emptying themselves into lire said Haven; and also for preserving Ships wintering therein from Accidents by Fire.

Mr. John Crawfurd, Pursuivant or Messenger Extraordinary attending the Great Seal, attending, according to Order, was called in; and, at the Bar, examined touching the Sending of the said Writ to the Sheriff of the County of Middlesex.

And then he withdrew.

The Under-Sheriff of the County of Middlesex at* tending, according to Order, be was called in; and at the Bar, examined touching the issuing of a Precept in pursuance of the said Writ.

And then he withdrew.

The High Bailiff of the City of Westminster, attending, according to Order, was called in; and, being examined at the Bar, acquainted the House, That he is now in the Execution of the said Precept; that he had all along endeavoured to avoid all unnecessary Delay therein; and that if feme Delay has happened in the Scrutiny of the Poll taken at this Election, which he is now proceeding upon, it has been such only as he did not think he had sufficient Powers to prevent or remove.

And then he withdrew.

He was again called in:

And Mr. Speaker (by Direction of the House) recommended some Particulars of his Duty to him; and acquainted him. That if he met with any thing to obstruct him therein, which he could not prevent, he should apply to the House upon it, and might be allured of the Support of the House in the Discharge of his Duty; and that the House expected he would take care in general to expedite the Election as much as possible.

Upon which he expressed his great Readinels to conform himself to the Directions of the House; and laid, That he would use his bell: Endeavours to expedite the Election, and hoped to perform his Duty in general to the Satisfaction of the House.

And then he withdrew.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlettien* and Freeholders, of the Town of Kendall, in the County of Westmrland, was prefehted to the House, and read;

alleging. That the Petitioner* ate concerned to find a Design set on Foot to confine to the Port of London that Trade which has so long, and with such manifest Benefit to these Kingdoms, been carried on from several Out-ports to the African Coast, and from which the Petitioners think it a Detriment to the Community to have any of his MajestyY Subjects excluded, as the Petitioners cannot help thinking all Monopolies prejudicial to the publick Weal: And therefore praying. That a free Navigation to any Part of the said Coast may continuel open to all the Subjects of Great Britain, without a partial Distinttion in favour of any few, how considerable fofevet by their Weight; since a Community, When its Support and Maintenance is considered, ought, as the Petitioners conceive, to be estimated by its Numbers.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Gdrl-sideration of the Committee of the whole House; to whom it is referred to consider further of the Papers' presented to the House upon the 6th Day of this instant February, from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, relating to the Trade to Africa.

A- Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Bir- African mingham, was presented to the House, and read; setting Trade, forth, That the Petitioners are informed a Scheme is proposed to Parliament, by a few West-India Planters in the

City of London, to confine the Trade to the principal Parts of the Coast of Africa, and the Benefit of the 'British Forts and Settlements on that Coast, in the Hands of a Joint-Stock trading Company, to the great Prejudice of the rest of his Majesty's Subjects: And alleging,

That the Petitioners are' fully convinced Freedom of Trade in all its Branches is the best Meahs, nay absolutely necessary at this Day, to promote the Flourishing and Improvement of it in this Kingdom; and that all exetufive

Companies, in proportion to the Extent of them, rriuft inevitably be attended with proportionable mischievous Consequence to the Trade, and this Nation in1 general;

and that the Truth of this has been in no Instancemore fully verified than in our Trade to ,which never flourished while confined to a Company, but always appeared in a very low and languid State in their Hands; but, since rendered open and free to all the Subjects, has been extended to such a Pitch, that the whole Nation sensibly experiences the great Advantages of it; and the said Town in particular for several Years past, from the great Quantities of Iron and Brass Manufactures which they have furnished for all Parts of the Trade on the Coast of Africa: And therefore praying, That this Branch of our foreign Commerce may (till remain in its present Freedom; and that the British Forts and Settlements on the African Coast may be put into such Hands, and under such a Regulation, as to the House shall seem meet, to give every Adventurer an equal Share in the Benefits of them, without Partiality or Distinction.

A Petition of the Traders in the Borough of Tregony, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That by the pernicious and evil Practices now and for several Years past carried on in running Soap from Ireland upon the Coast of Wales, Cornwall, and other Places in the British ChaneL the Petitioners, and others concerned in the Trade and Business of Soap-making, are very'great Sufferers, and have sensibly felt a general Decay in their Trade, to their great Damage and Loss, and to the Diminution of his Majesty's Revenue: That Soap is brought from Ireland in Coasting Vessels, wrapt in Paper in small Parcels, concealed in the Ciclings, and other Parts of the Ship, and lb easily Carried on Shore: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration; and that a Law may be passed to restrain and prevent these evil Practices for the future, either by totally prohibiting the Importation of the said Commodity, or by any other Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Jfbn Robinson, being examined, said, That the Bounty given on the Exportation and Home Consumption of Irish Sail-cloth is a very great Encouragement to the Manufacturers thereof in that Kingdom; and, with the Duty laid on British and foreign Sail-cloth imported into the fame, secures to them their Home Consumpti >0; and as the Manutaft urers of Irish Sail-cloth are furnished at tiieExpenceof the Publick with Work-houses, Looms, Spinning-whteis, a Foreman to the Whitfters, and a Foreman to the Weavers, which he knows to be true, having been offered the same Encouragements if he would have gone thither, and carried his Hands with him; and that, bTides thtfe Advantage^, Labour is much cheaper there than in England; by all which means the can undersell the English in the Plantat:ons, even if the Bounty of 2 d. per Ell given to the British on Exportation was paid.

And Mr. Wallis confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Robinson; and laid, That the British have no Bounty on Home Consumption.

Mr. Philip Elliot, being examined, said, That 10,080 YarJs of Irish Sail-c'oth was consigned to him from Cork in January last; and Quantities thereof are sent to him by Commission, some of which were marked, " Debenture paid," but could not take upon him to say, that it was all marked in that manner: That he received about 46,000 Yards of Sail-cloth \nMay last, and several other Parcels since; and that latterly, for Two or Three Years past, had observed several of them w'ere marked as before-mentioned, and apprehends they w'ere all marked in that manner: That he has fold about 1,100 Bolts or Pieces of it between January 1748 and January 1749, and has now by him upwards of 600 Bolts or Pieces: That all the Sail-cloth, which is consigned to him from Ireland, is certified on Oath, which, without such Certificate, would be seizable; and hath fold within this Year 50 Bolts or Pieces for Exportation.

That the British Sail-cloth is fold considerably cheaper than the Irish; and is of Opinion, that it is owing to the great Numbers which are in the Trade, who are jealous of, and underlell one another.

That upon being asked whether he had fold Irish Sailcloth at a Lois ? said. He could not tell; he is only an Agent, and has Commission for felling the same: That the Price is limited to him, and fells none over or under it.

He was also asked. Whether British Sail-cloth had lately sold to Advantage or Loli ? laid, He was no Judge, but had heard it sold at a Loss: That it is hi Opinion more Hands are employed now than before, the D-minds for British Sail-cloth being greater now than in the War,

it being now chiefly made use of.

He was asked, Why the Demands were greater now ? said, By the Increase of the Numbers of Merchants Ships which have been built here and in the Plantations since the War, who are obliged by Act of Parliament to have the First Suit of Sails of British Canvas.

Mr. Samuel Storke, Merchant, being examined, said. That the British Sail-cloth cannot be exported to the Plantations without the Bounty is duly paid and continued, he having within Twelve Months exported to New England 1,500 Pieces of Russia and only 100 Pieces of British, which is owing to the Cheapness of Russia Sail-cloth: That he formerly, in One Year, exported 1,000 Pieces of British Sail-cloth, and some Part of the Bounty upon that remains unpaid: That the Plantations will be served with Sail-cloth either from Russia, Holland, or Ireland, if the British arc not enabled to fell as cheap at Market as they: And,

1027

Mr. Cookson also said, That if the Bounty was duly Sail-cloth paid and continued, and a further Bounty given, the said Manufae-Manufacture might be carried on as well now as before tur*' the War, it being in great Esteem and much improved; whereby the Manufacturers will be enabled to increase the Exportation, and fell the same as cheap as foreign Sail-cloth is fold for.

Mr. Elias Bland, Merchant, being examined, said, That

British Sail-cloth cannot be exported unless the Bounty is duly paid and continued: That formerly he exported great Quantities to North America; and used to give them Credit, at the Foot of their Account, for the Bounty; and they, knowing that the Bounty was not paid, have ordered foreign Sail-cloth to be sent in lieu thereof.

Mr. Rohinjon also said, That British Sail-cloth cannot be exported as formerly unless the Bounty b*c paid and continued; which if it should be, he made no Doubt but to have a Share in the Trade; for, if it is well manufactured, there will be a Vent for it.

And it appeared to your Committee, That no foreign Sail-cloth will wear like the British, if it be well manufactured.

And, to prove that this Manufactory is at present in a very low State, and must daily decrease.

There were produced several Gazettes, printed in the Years 1743 and 1749, whereby it appeared, That several very considerable Manufacturers had become Bankrupts within 12 Months; and by a List which was also produced, and proved, it appeared, That several others had failed, or left off the Business: And,

Mr. William Richards, oeing examined, said. That be lives at Reading, and has been in the Trade 30 Years; and, when he first came into it, there were not above Five or Six concerned within the Kingdom in this Manufacture, but of late several have been concerned: That about Nine Years since, at the time the Spanish War broke out, he had 500 Families on his Books, employed by him; and those Families might consist of above 2,000 Persons of both Sexes, who lived in and about Reading: That at this time he has not Employment for 100 Families, which may consist of about or 500 Persons; by which it is apparent, that the Trade is greatly decreased, and that not One Half of the Number of Hands are now employed as were before the Spanish War: That the Poor in the Work-houses at Reading used to be employed in this Manufacture, but are now intirely become a Burthen to their several Parishes.

Mr. William Holder, being examined, laid. That he has been in the Trade about 22 Years in London, and about 3 or Years ago he employed between 7 or 800 Persons: That this Manufacture is in great Distress by the Bounty not being regularly paid, therefore it cannot be exported, because it is undersold by foreign Sail-cloth; and there not being a Vent or Encouragement given to export the fame, great Quantities of British Sail-cloth hath been fold for lets than it cost; and, there being large Stocks in Hand, several of the Manufacturers would be glad to fell what they have at prime Cost.

Mr. John Robinson said, That he has carried on this Manufacture at Warrington in Lancash'treabout 30 Years:

When he first begun, he made but little Sail-doth till a Bounty on Exportation was allowed; then he increased the Numbers of his Hands, and had Demands for more than he could make; this was in time of Peace: That; when the additional Bounty was given, the Manufacturers were enabled to export it, and he then increased the Numbers of his Hands again; and in the late War, having large Demands, increased his Hands id more, and employed about 5,000"* Persons of both Sexes; but, since the Peace, several of the Manufacturers have reduced their Hands, and are felling off their Stocks, some at 10 per Cent, others at £. 20 per Cent. Ids than prime Cost, not having any Demand for the Stock in Hand j That he has reduced his Looms and Hands -jds, and would be glad to fell his Stock at prime Cost.

That the Trade to Africa ought never to be taxed with any Duties whatsoever, for the Support and Maintenance of any Forts and Settlements there.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the British Forts and' Settlements on the Coast of Africa are necessary; and may, under proper Management, be rendered useful for the extending and pro ted ing the Trade in general.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to carry on the Trade in the most beneficial manner to these Kingdoms, all his Majesty's Subjects trading to Africa be united in an open Company, without any Joint-Stock, or Power to trade as a Corporation, under proper Regulations; and that the Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa be put under proper Management and Regulation.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the House doth

Mr. James Crokatt, Merchant: Who, being examined,

feid, That he resided in South Carolina upwards of Ten Years; and the Inhabitants of that Colony are frequently under great Difficulties for want of Salt proper to cure and preserv Fish, and other Provisions; which is often lo scarce, and at such exorbitant Prices, that the same has been often sold at 5 s.6 d.per Bushel Sterling, which is 40J. Currency, by reason whereof the Inhabitants are prevented from improving the Advantages Nature has bellowed upon them of Fish, and other Provisions, in great Flenty.

And another great Inconveniency they lie under, is being obliged to buy large Quantities of Salt when cheap, though not immediately wanted, from the Difference of the Price, which has been from 6 to 6s. Sterling per Bushel; and although great Quantities of Beef and Pork are felted there, yet much greater might be, if they could have proper Salt, and cheap; and it is from the Scarcity and Dcarness of the bed Salt, which prevents their Curing of Fish, being supplied with Salt at prdent only from England. Mr. Dinwiddie, being examined, feid, That he was Surveyor-General of the Cudoms for some Yeats for that Part of the Colonies which is distinguished by the South-, ern Didriid of the Continent of America, and extended from Philadelphia to South Carolina, the Bahama Islands, and Jamaica; and observed, in those Places on the Continent, that English S-alt was only made use of to draw the Blood from the Meat when fird cut up, not being drong enough topreserve it for Exportation into hot Climates j but the Meat is afterwards cured w'ith Salt brought from the Iste of Mav, English Salt dissolving very soon; and the Alum, or American Salt, hardens the Meat, and eats up the Fat; that the Salt from Tortuga is too drong for Beef, but does very well for Pork.

That upon being asked, Vi Englisht was mixed with the other Salt brought there, would it not do ? he feid. That he apprehended one was too weak, and the other too drong, but he had never known it tried.

Mr. Philip Lee feid, That Provisions cured with English Salt only are frequently spoiled; and if cured with American Salt, it corrodes the Flesh, and eats the Fat away.

Mr. Shubrick, being examined, feid, That he lived

some time in Carolina, and had cured great Quantities of Provisions for the Use of his Majesty's Navy: That when the Meat was cut up, English Salt was used to dr?iw the Blood from it; afterwards it was cured with American Salt; but, if Liberty was given them to import Salt from the Southern Parts of Europe, it would be preferable to any other Salt: That once, whilst he was there, that Salt was brought, and he preferred it to all the other Salt, it being stronger, went further, coll leis, and did not corrode the Meat.

Then he was asked. Whether that Salt was cheaper than the American Salt ? feid. It was fold much at the same Price.

He was also asked. If the Meat which was cured with that Salt was better than that cured with American Salt? feid. He could not say it was.

That upon being asked, if he had observed that the Meat which was cured with American Salt answers better than the Meat cured with English Salt ? feid, He had observed that it did anfiver better; and that a Bushel of American Salt will go further than a Bushel of English, for the Practice in the West Indies is, to try Salt by Measure, and not by Weight.

That upon being asked as to the Quality of the Salt brought from Turks Island, he said. That Sait is more penetrating than English Salt, it answers better, is stronger, and does not corrode the Meat; nor has the Salt from Tortuga any corrosive Quality.

Mr. John Bacom, being examined, said, That he lived in Maryland 14 Years and purchased great Quantities of Provisions, which was felted with Salt brought from Turks Island, Tortuga, or the Isle of May, and no English Salt was used with it, which he exported to or

Antigua, and never had Complaint of its not being well cured: and, if they can have American, or Salt from the Isle of Alay, they do not use English: That he has never tried English Salt, although he has had 200 Barrels of Beef and Pork failed in One Year.
