Mr. Andrew Pringle, being examined, said. He resided many Years in the West Indies, had been in several Parts of Europe, and seen different Sorts of Sait: That the Salt

made in the Bay of Biscay is of a very good Quality for curing all Sorts of Provisions, as is likewise the Salt made in Portugal, and the Places adjacent, it being all made

with the Sun; and found, that the Grain of the Salt was larger, Quality stronger, and the Colour whiter, than the Salt made in England, which is owing to the Heat of the Sun; and, by what he had seen in the West Indies, that Salt was ffronger, and of a larger Grain, being nearer the Sun, and the Heat more intense; but the Colour of the Portugal and Spanijk Salt is whiter, though the French Bay Salt is not: That he had made his Observations upon Salt made by the Heat of Fire; and, by all his Experience, in curing of Provisions, it is weaker in proportion, taking Quantity for Quantity, and Weight for Vv eight.

That upon being asked his Reasons as to Quantity for Quantity, and Weight for Weight ? he said, That as a Bushel of Spanijk or Portugal Salt will make a Quantity of ffronger Brine than a Bushel of small Salt made by Fire, so too Weight of the same Salt will make a Quantity of ffronger Brine than ioo Weight of small Salt; and he never found that the Salt made from Sea Water was so ffrong as that made with the Sun; for this Reason, As ffrong Pickle and small Salt will not cure Beef, so it is the Largeness of the Grain that makes it most effectual; and there is a Necessity for the Grain of Salt to be large, because small Salt all difiolves.

That the late Mr. Lowndes shewed him some of his Salt, but the Grain was not so large as the Portugal and Spanijk Salt; and he has also seen Mr. Read's Salt, which was good, and of the Size of French Bay Salt, but whiter, though not so white as the and Portugal

Salt.

Mr. George Barrington, being examined, said, That the American Salt, and the Salt brought from the Isle of (which is as big as a Man's Head, that they are obliged to break it to Pieces) are not proper for Curing of Fish, and other Provisions, being corrosive, and eats away the Fat of the Meat; and English Salt being too weak; therefore the properest Salt for those Climates is the nish and Portugal Salt, which is by much the belt; and the Provisions of all Kinds cured with it will keep the Year round, the Inhabitants rather paying for that Salt, could it be had, than to have Salt from the of May for nothing.

other Places that want it, which answers every Use (no Importing other being used at Liverpool for falling Sea Provisions, American which if there was better Salt, they would ule it), besides Colonies, the Isle of May, if open; and, as he believes, Salt may be carried as cheap from thence as from Portugal or Spain, and not any of those Inconvencies can arise, but have the Advantage of carrying Asses, Bullocks, Mules, and Horses, to Barbadoes or Antigua.

Then he was asked. That if he sent a Ship loaden with Corn to Leghorn, whether a Cargo of Salt could not be taken in cheaper at Ivaca for Virginia, than, going round the Isle of May, to take in Salt there for Virginia? said.

That he apprehends there is so little Difference between one and the other, that he did not know which he should chuse; but as he never fends a Ship to the Isle for Salt, where he has it only for Labour, without taking in the Cattle aforesaid, he should chuse to go by the Isle of May, and believes all the Merchants at Liverpool would chuse the fame; and could not tell which Navivation is the cheapest, and whether one is 10 or £.20 more or less than the other.

He was also asked, If Salt was to be had at all times for nothing but Labour at the Isle of May ? said. That there maybe a Difference at some Times of the Year; but the Time when he lends to load Salt, is the Season lor going to the Plantations; and a Ship of about 200 Tons Burthen may be loaden with Salt for about 60 or 70/. and is from 14 Days to Five Weeks taking in her Loading.

Then he was asked. Whether Ships in the rainy Sea-fons are not prevented from getting Salt ? said, He believed so.

And being aflted, Whether Ships going from the Mediterranean, round by the Isle of May, to Virginia, can't smuggle Goods as well as if they carried Salt from the Mediterranean ? laid. He could not tell.

That being asked, Whether, as the Law now Hands, cannot foreign Goods be smuggled into those Colonies which have Liberty of importing Salt, and from thence carried into the other Colonies P said, He believed they might.

Sir, Liverpool, 18th February 1749.

Having received a Letter from Mr. Ralph Barrow at Norwich, of the 17 th inllant, intimating, that Objection is made by some Gentlemen, that the Salt made with them is not so sufficient for curing Fleth Provisiops, and Fish, as the foreign Salt; I have for several Years pad experienced it in curing Provisions for the Navy, ^pd formerly in the Herring Fishery; one Season cured upwards of i,7ood Bands; and at present cures large Quap-tities of Bacon, Hams, Beef, and Pork, for Exportation; and in all these Cafes, finds it to answer extremely well; and therefore is of Opinion, that Salt well made from the pure Spring Brine cannot be outdone. I heartily wish you Health; and am, with due Regard,

Sir,

Your very humble Servant,

Tp Mr. John Hardman, Wm. Garr.

Mr. Hardman, Northwich, February 24th, 1749.

In Answer to your last is that, that we have 97 Pans in the Two Collections, and not Half of them above half-worked, so that a vast deal more might be made; and we have Brine enough to supply double the Quantity, and a deal more; hut as it's not wanted, besides the great Quantity of Salt in Hand, for want of a Demand.

Ralph Barrow.

A Petition of the Ironmongers, Smiths, and others, importing of the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, Iron from on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more Ameris* employed in the Trade and Manufacture of Iron, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That it a Bill for encouraging the Importing of Pig and Bar Iron from Americashould paf* into a Law, under proper Restrictions in regard to the Manufacturing of Iron in America, it will be of great Benefit, as it is apprehended, to the Trade of this Nation, and more especially to the Trade of the said County (on which the Livelihoods of many Thousands here wholly depend) for that it will encourage the Merchants in our American Colonies to take more Goods from this Nation of the Iron Manufacture than they have hither done, because it will enable them to make Returns for those Goods, which is a Difficulty they have laboured under for want of proper Commodities fit for such Remittances; and that it hath been generally allowed, that all the Iron Works in this Kingdom do not supply half the Quantity of Iron sufficient to carry on the Iron Manufacture, and that the Deficiency is brought from other Markets* and that, if a great Part of that Deficiency could be supplied from the American Colonies, the People of this Nation could not be under the Necessity of importing such great Quantities of Swedish Iron, as hath been practised fora long time, for which the Swedes are paid annually large Sums in Specie (they taking very little of our Commodities in Return); and that the Bringing of Iron from the American Colonies cannot affect the Iron Works and Gentlemens Woods in this Kingdom, more than if the like Quantity of Iron was to be brought from any other Country: And therefore praying. That such Encouragement may be given for the Importation of Pig and Bar 1 ron from the American Colonies, as the House shall think proper; but, in regard that many Thousand Families in this Country wholly subsist in the several Branches of the Iron Trade, and mud be ruined if the Manufactory of Iron should be carried into America, further praying.

That the American People may be restrained from erecting any Slitting or Rolling Mills, or any Forges for plating of Iron, and under such other Restraints as may seem 7 meet

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes Westminster within the City and Liberties of Westminster, and of that Small Debt* Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which lies within, or adjoins to, the Parishes of St. Clement Danes and St. Mary le Strand, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That by the Bill, depending in the House, for the more easy and (peedy Recovery of small Debts within the said City, Liberties, and Duchy, the Petitioners are informed One Court and Court-house is intended to be conllituted and established for the Purpose aforesaid:

And alleging, That, in a Place so extremely populous and extensive, One Court and Court-house will be so far from being of publick and general Utility, that it will be attended with great Inconvenience, Delay, and Expence; and that, as the Petitioners desire nothing more than the publick Welfare, they hope they can make it appear clearly to the Satisfaction of the House, that it would tend much more to general Use and Benefit to have at least Four Courts established within the said Chy, Liberties, and Duchy; or, if One Court should be though.t sufficient, that such Court should be held in at least Four different Divisions, whereby Business would be rendered more easy, expedient, and less expensive: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and allow the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, upon the said Bill; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House Hull seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, . be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition.

A Petition of the Tanners of Leather in and about the Impo*t?»g Town of Chesterfield, in the County of Derby, was pre- Iron fi'orn

fented to the House, and read; alleging, That should the America* Bill now depending, for the free Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from America, pass into a Law, the Petitioners are very apprehensive the same will be greatly detrimental to their Properties in many respects, to the Overthrow of their Trade, and the Diminution of his Majesty's Revenues: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as the Nature of their same requires.

A Petition of the Tanners of Leather near the Towns of IVakefield and Leeds, in the County of York, whole

Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are many and great Woods near the said Towns of IVakefield and Leeds, which are springed, and preferred for the Supply of several Furnaces and Forges with Cord-wood, and for the Supply of Oak Bark for the Tanning of Leather: And alleging. That the Petitioners apprehend, that should the Bill now depending in the House, for taking off the Duty on Bar Iron imported into this Kingdom, Irom our Plantations, pass into a Law, the Furnaces and Forges now employed, and using such Cord-wood, will be in a great measure unemployed, since they cannot afford to make Iron upon the same easy Terms on which it may be made in the Plantations, where Cord-wood is so much cheaper than it will be afforded in this Kingdom; the Consequences whereof will be, as the Petitioners fear, that many Spring Woods will be destroyed, and the Petitioners thereby deprived of a regular Supply of Bark necessary for the Tanning of Leather, to the Destruction of that useful Trade, and Ruin of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners are not apprehensive of great Damage arising from the Importation of American Pig Iron Duty-free; for, should such Importation destroy the Furnaces, the Forges now built would be worked the harder, or new ones erected for the Consumption of the Charcoal which the Country can supply: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may have such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Confederation of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Freeholders and Landholders in the County of Stafford, and Persons concerned in the Iron Trade there, was presented to the House, and read alleging. That the Petitioners, having very great Revenues arising out of their Wood-lands and Iron-works, are apprehensive, that should the Bill now depending, for' encouraging the Importation of Iron from , pass

into a Law, the Petitioners will be greatly prejudiced in' both; and the vast Number of People employed and supported by the Petitioners, and others, will, with their Families, be reduced to'Want, and become burthensome to the Petitioners, whole Ability to relieve them will be much lessened, when their Iron-works and Wood-lands are by this means rendered useless and of no Value: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill passing intoaLaw.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be Jheard, by their Cotmfel, before the said Committee, upon their said Petition.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Owners and Proprietors of Wood-lands and Coppices, in the County of -cester, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That should the said Bill pals into a Law, the Petitioners, and many other Persons in the said Country, would be greatly prejudiced thereby, inasmuch as the Estates of the Petitioners in Coppices, and other Woods, which are now very considerable in the said Country, would be so greatly reduced in Value, as scarcely to be sufficient to pay the Land Tax, and other Duties and Payments imposed thereon: And therefore praying th* House to take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to be heard, against the said Bill, by their Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that these Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard, by their Coimfel, before the said Committee, upon, their said Petition.

A Petition of the Merchants, and others. Inhabitants of the Town of Liverpool, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners are fully persuaded, that the Permitting of all his Majesty's Subjects to import into Great Britain Pig and Bar Iron Duty-free from the American Plantations will be attended with many valuable Consequences to the Nation in general, will tend to free us from the Necessity we are now under of being supptied with this Article from those foreign Powers who have the Balance of Trade at pjefent much in their favour, and against us; will greatly serve our Navigation, especially in One important Branch of it; will encourage and promote the Welfare and Prosperity of our Colonies abroad, and may be made highly beneficial to the various Iron Manufactures carried on in the different

Parts of this Kingdom, and in time furnish us (probably on better Terms) with those large Quantities of Bar Iron which are necessary for that valuable Branch of foreign Commerce which we now prosecute to the African Coalt:

And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pals into a Law.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers of Icon, Importing and Ironmongers, of Great Britain, in behalf of them- Iron from selves, and many others, was also presented to the House, America, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners are of Opinion the said Bill will be greatly for the Advantage and Benefit of this Kingdom; as it may, in a Course of Years, be the only Means of rendering Great Britain independent of the Northern Crowns for Supplies of that Commodity, from whence are annually imported about Twenty thousand Tons, the greatest Part of which is paid for in ready Money; particularly to Sweden, from which Kingdom is imported into Great Britain and Ireland more Bat Iron than is taken from them by all besides; and

that the American Bar Iron is good, and applicable to all the Uses of Swedish Iron, as has been heretofore sufficiently made appear; and that the Petitioners, therefore, are of Opinion, that all proper Encouragement should be given for the Making of Bar Iron in America, as it will be the only Method whereby Great Britain may be relieved, and prevent its being distressed for that moll useful Commodity in case of any Rupture between the Northern Powers; and that the Petitioners likewise apprehend, that an Encouragement for the Importation of Bar Iron from America will be the only Means to prevent their manufacturing the re; the Want of which, the Petitioners are of Opinion, has been the chief Occasion of their first entering into it: And therefore praying,

That the said Bill to encourage the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from America; and to prevent the Making of Steel, or setting up Slitting or Rolling Mills in the British Colonies; and to lay such further Restraints on their Manufacturing as to the House shall seem reasonable; may pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

of England in the Name of the Accomptant-General of the Court of Chancery, and placed to the Credit of the Fund for the Relief of the Suitors of the said Court, after Satisfaction of the Demands upon the Offices of the deficient Mailers (which is subject to the Disposition of Parliament) be paid and applied, as will be sufficient to satisfy and discharge the said Debt upon the said Hanaper-Office.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several additional Stamp Duties granted by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for Relief of the Suitors of the High Court of Chancery, and which were afterwards continued by an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for continuing, for the Purposes therein mentioned, the additional Duties upon stamped Vellum, Parchment, and Paper, laid by an Act passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, be revived, and granted to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to prevent any future Deficiency of the Revenue of the Office of the Keeper or Clerk of the Hanaper in Chancery, and to make good the annual Sum of Twelve hundred Pounds, granted in Augmentation of the Revenue belonging to the Office of Mailer of the Rolls, there be paid and applied, out of the Monies arising from the said revived Duties, to the Keeper or Clerk of the Hanaper for the Time being, or his Deputy, a yearly Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Pounds, by equal half-yearly Payments, to be accounted for in the annual Account to be palfed by the said Keeper or Clerk of the Hanaper, before the Auditor of the said Revenue.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Three thousand One hundred and Seven Pounds Nine Shillings, being the Remainder of the said Surplus Calli in the Bank, after deducting the said Sum of Ten thousand Five hundred and Ninety PoundsTwelve Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, in order to be applied in Aid of the said Duties, to make good the said anpual Sum of Three thousand Pounds, granted to his Majesty out of the said Duties.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

That the Resolutions, which, upon Friday the Second Day of this instant , were reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Papers presented to the House, upon the Sixth Day of February last, from the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, relating to the Trade to Africa, and were then agreed to by the House, might be read:

And the same were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as lolloweth; viz.

" Resolved, Nemine , That the Trade to

Africa oughc always to remain free and open.

" Resolved, Nemine , That the Trade to

" Africa ought never to be taxed with any Duties whatsoever, for the Support and Maintenance of any Forts and Settlements there.

" Resolved, Nemine , That the British

" Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa are necessary; and may, under proper Management, be rendered useful for the extending and protecting the Trade in general.

" Resolved, That, in order to carry on the Trade in the most beneficial Manner to these Kingdoms, all his Majesty's Subjects trading to Africa be united in an " open Company, without any Joint-Stock, or Power to " trade as a Corporation, under proper Regulations; and that the Forts and Settlements upon the Coast. of " Africa be put under proper Management and Regulation."

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That any Person or Persons, Bodies Politick or Corporate, who now are, or hereafter may be, interested in, or intitled unto, such Part of the National Debt incurred before Michaelmas 1749, redeemable by Law, which now carries an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, as hath not been subscribed in pursuance of an Act of this present Session of Parliament, for reducing the several Annuities, which carry an Interest after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, to the several Rates therein mentioned; and who do, on or before the Thirtieth Day of May next, subscribe their Names, or signify their Consent to accept of an Interest of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 25th Day of December 1755, ft*bject to the same Provisions, Notices, and Clauses ot Redemption, which their respective Four per Cents are now liable to, shall, in lieu of their present Interest, be intitled unto, and receive, an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum until the 25th Day of December 1750; and, fro n and after the said 25th Day of December 1750, an Interest of Three Pounds Ten Shillings per Centum per Annum until the 25th Day of December 1755; and that no Part of the same shall be liable to be redeemed until after the said 25th Day of December 1755.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Part of the National Debt incurred before Michaelmas 1749, redeemable by Law, which now carries an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, and which shall not be subscribed on or before the Thirtieth Day of May next, be redeemed and paid off.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, and other Proprietors and Possessors of Iron-mines, Wood-lands, Forges, and Furnaces, and other Iron Works, and of those concerned in carrying on the Iron Trade, in the County Palatine of

Lancaster, whole Names are subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That should the Bill, now depending in the House, to encouiage the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from America, pass into a Law, it must not only be the intire Ruin of many of the Petitioners, but of Thousands in the said County, whole lole Livelihood depends on our Iron Trade, Iron Mines, Woodlands, and Iron Works; and that the Petitioners are very sensible, that the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from America into thisKLingdom, Duty-free, must shortly intirely destroy the Forges and Furnaces in the said County, as the American Iron is well known by Experience to be of a limilar Nature and Quality with ours, and therefore must interfere with it; and that the Business ot making Iron has, in the said Cou.ity, been greatly improved, owing

Vol. 25.

to the immense Quantity of Iron Ore produced in the said County, sufficient to supply all England with that Commodity; and that great Numbers of the laborious Sort of People are constantly employed in digging, getting up, and carrying, the said Iron Mine not only to their Iron Works in the said County, but to the Sea Shore there, to be shipped to a great many different Parts of this Kingdom and Ireland, very great Quantities of which are annually exported from the said County to those Parts by many Ships or Vessels, whose chief Employ depends on the said Iron Mine, Iron Works, and Carrying of Bark to Ireland; and that the Petitioners have, with great Care, Industry, and Expence, improved their Lands, which were bairen and rocky, into Wood-lands, confuting of many Thousands of Acres, from which they ex-pected some Recompence to arile from the Profit of the Wood; and that the Petitioners dread being reduced to a very miserable Condition, should their Works be rendered useless, their Iron Mines and Wood-lands of no Value, and Thousands of poor Labourers, with their Families, brought upon their Parishes for want of Employ, who now subsist in a comfortable Way; and that the Petitioners must sustain another great Loss from the Sale of their Bark for carrying on the Leather Trade in England and Ireland, to which last Kingdom very great Quantities have been yearly exported from the said County; and that without being supplied from thence, and other Parts of England, the Petitioners apprehend that Kingdom could not carry on the Tanning Trade, no more than England, should our Woods be grubbed up, as they must be, toniakelomething though little, of the Soil: And therefore the Petitioners, dreading that the ill Consequences, as above set forth, may befal them, besides many Thousands more in this Kingdom, should the said Bill pass into a Law, praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that such Provision may be made for the Preservation and Continuance of the iron Works of this Kingdom as to the House flvll leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Then the House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. John Pitt took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. John Pitt reported front the Committee, That they had heard Counsel and Evidence, and considered the Petitions to them referred, and had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Thursday next, at Twelve of the Clock.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Sir William Calvert report from the Committee, to Prohibiten whom the Petition of the Merchants and Dealers in Linen, of CambricJu. of the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matters of Fact contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

»The Committee find the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition to be as follows:

Mr. Thomas Vigne said. That he had been an Importer of Silesia Lawns and Cambricks upwards of Twenty

Years: That he believes French Cambricks have been imported and worn since the Prohibition, because the

Lawns-, which have been imported to answer the Purposr of Cambricks, have not fold, the Witness having great Quantities in his Hands at this time; and it is the general Opinion of the Trade that French Cambricks have been worn:

That he has dealt chiefly in Silesia Lawns since the Prohibition; and has fold more of them since that Period than he ul'ed to do, but not so many as to answer his Expectation.

And, being asked the Question, he laid. That the Wearing of Muslins, and going without Ruffles, has been a Prejudice to the Sale of Silesia Lawns: That they are like-wife much dearer than they were formerly; for that immediately after the Prohibition, the Demand for them was so great, that it advanced the Price 30 per Cent, and upwards

2 3 Geo. II. 2 2°# Martii. 1067

wards in Foreign Markets: That they are since fallen in their Price, but still continue to be 20 Cent, dearer, on the whole Importation, then thay were before the Prohibition:

That though the Prohibition of Cambricks does not immediately interfere with the coarse Silesia Lawns, yet it has occasioned a Rife in the Price of them; the great Demand for fine ones having made the Manufacturers neglect the low-priced ones:

That the Witness has imported Cambricks since the Prohibition, which he knows to be Cambrick by the Place where 'tis manufactured, and Form and Manner of Making it up: That he has seen Linens, which he thought to be Cambricks, made up in a different manner, and imported since the Prohibition} but that he could not swear they were Cambricks: That his Reason for thinking them so, was, that they looked like Cambricks, and so do all fine Linens that are made; and, if they had been folded in the Cambrick manner, the Witness should have bought them as Cambricks; and, in the manner they were folded, he should have bought them for Silesia Lawns; and that the Price of Cambrick is less than that of a Silesia Lawn of equal Finenels:

That there is a Difference in the-Fabrick of Cambricles, those made at St. Quint in being of a thinner, and those at Valenciennes, of a thicker, Texi ure; and that he has seen

German Linens made to imitate both: That he thinks he has seen German Linens more like each of those Cambricks than the Cambricksaretheoneto the otherjand, if his Correspondent were to fend him Long Lawns instead of Cambricks, if they were the same Length and Breadth, he thinks he might be deceived in them: That he never imported any in that manner, but has been told it has been done, and it is impossible to know a German Lawn from a Cambrick; and that his Reason for saying Cambricks have been imported, was, becaulc he has heard many hate been seized; and that he has likewise heard Cambricks have been imported from under

the Denomination of Silesia Lawns;

That he believes the Manufacture of Silesia Lawns has greatly increased since the Prohibition; but apprehends they have not continued to make the Quantity as at first, because the People of London have not had a Demand for them:

That Cambricks are preferred to Silesia Lawns, because they are cheaper.

And being asked, if there was a Difficulty in distinguishing the Two Species of Goods before the Prohibition ? he said, They did not at that time import fine Silesia Lawns.

Being asked, What are the highest-priced Kentings or Sihjia Lawns that he has seen ? said. He had known Long Lawns fold for £. 15 the Piece, containing 32Yards, which is about 9 s.a Yard; but that he himself never fold any for more than 6j. and a Yard, which might be mistaken for Cambricks of about $s. a Yard.

And being asked, If any Lawns could be mifr

taken for Cambricks above the Price of 5 a Yard ? he said. He apprehended Mhe fined Silesia Lawns might; That the Silesia Lawns he mentioned, of 9 a Yard, would resemble a Cambrick of about a Yard; and that the fined Cambricks are about 12 a Yard.

And being asked, If there was a Possibility to make Lawns resemble the fined Cambricks ? he answered, He could not lay as to the Possibility, but he had not seen or heard of any such: That he apprehends the Lawns cannot interfere with Cambricks of above a Yard, it being impossible to import such as Long Lawns, though he cannot fiiy whether any Cambricks above y a Yard have "been imported as Long Lawns since the Prohibition: If it has been done, it mud have been suspected to have been a Cambrick; but no Man will swear it to be so, as lie as not lung to ground his Judgment upon but the Finenels of the Goods:

That he believes there is at present a Difference between Cambricks above y s.a Yard as Long Lawns, both as to Weight and Fineness; but he thinks it would be itn-Vol. 25.

possible to condemn the fined Cambricks, since, in the Opinion of the Witness, People would not swear them to be such; and that those which have been condemned have been smuggled:

That the Witness imports some Cambricks from Holland, and that Silesia Lawns are likewise imported from thence: That if a Cambrick of 7 a Yard was sent to) him from Harlem, of the same Length, and made up in the same manper, as a Long Lawn, and, as such, charged. 9.*. a Yard, it.would be impossible for him to distinguish the one from the other; and that the only Method of preventing tli$ felling the one for the other, is the Difference of the Numbers and Package:

That the Pridtof Cambricks has rilen since the Prohw hibition, which he al'cribes to the Demand for them, which he has been informed was greater in general than before the Prohibition, but they don't lay particularly from whence that Demand arises j and that, when he mentions the Prohibition, lie, means the Time when the Act took place:

That the gr^ateft Demand, before the Prohibition, was for Cambricks which cod the Importer about a Yard j and that he believes the Proportion of what was fold above ys.a Yard, was about One-third of what was fold under that Price.

Mr. John Payne, being examined, said, That he had been 20 Years concerned in the Linen Trade in general: That he makes no Doubt that Cambricks and French Lawns are clandestinely imported, but thinks he never saw a Piece of German Linen in his Life which he could not distinguish from a French Manufacture: That he thinks he should be a pretty good Judge if it were washed, but could difliDguish it better unwashed: That if a Cambrick were made up of the same Length and Breadth of a Kenting, he thinks he could distinguish it:

That he has lately heard many Doubts, whether a Long Lawn could be distinguished from Cambrick: That, if the Cambrick were to be warehoused, it would be a Means to prevent Frauds, as it would then be always seizable: That he does not know what Proportion the Bonds given for the Re-exportation of Cambrick bear to the Bonds discharged; nor does he know whether there is a Quantity of Cambrick in the Importers Hands sufficient to discharge the remaining Bonds; but he believes some Part of the Cambrick may have been consumed in England, which-were entered for Exportation:

That there is a Difference between Lawn and Cambrick, besides the Bleach, the one being of a silky, the other of a clothy, Nature: That the Silkiness is chiefly owing to the Materials: That Cambricks bleached in Holland are more like Silesia Lawns; but he would not pretend to pass his Judgment on Linen that had been worn.

Mr. Goodchild, being asked. Whether he had ever made any Experiment as to the Weight of Cambricks and Long Lawns ? said, That he had made several for 10 Years last past, having been concerned in a Manufacture of Lawns set up by him at Teddington; and his Reason for weighing them, was, to find how much they were diminished by Bleaching; and that he has found, that all Linens from 27 to 36 Inches wide, which weigh no more than Three Oz. the Yard, are Cambricks or Lawns, or of that Species, and applicable to the same Uses as Cambricks and Lawns, and no other.

Upon the Whole, the Facts are:

That, when the Prohibition of Cambricks took place, great Quantities of Silesia Lawns or Kentings were imported, to supply the Consumption, which continued for some time:

That since that time, and chiefly for the last Six or Eight Months, French Cambricks and Lawns have been ciandeftinely run in; and the Smugglers have offered to insure the Dealers for 8, 9, or to Cent, or even Half the Amount of what the Duty would be in case the Prohibition were taken off:

That some few have been fraudulently entered under the Form of Silesia Linen, and paid the Duty as Narrow Germany, which is One-fifth Part of what would be the Duty on Cambricks, in case the Prohibition were taken off:

That the Witnesses for the Petitioners agreed in general, the Silesia Lawns and low-priced Cambricks were very difficult to be distinguished, if at all; and that, if the Trade in Silesia should improve their Manufacture in Fineness, they might make such as could not be distinguished from the finer Cambricks.

Several eminent Hamburgh Merchants, and several Linen-drapers, being examined by your Committee, asserted. That Silesia Lawns were very distinguishable from French Cambricks in the whole Piece: and in the Shops, before wearing, or being washed or altered; and what proper Regulations would prevent the Importation and Sale, and consequently the Smuggling.

The Petitioners then proposed. That they might have Leave to produce several Pieces of Lawns and

Cambricks, to try whether they could be distinguished, as it had been asserted; which your Committee agreed to: Accordingly, 12 such Pieces as the Petitioners thought proper were produced; and your Committee called in Mr. Payne, Hamburgh Merchant, Mr. Hill, wholesale Linen-draper, and.Mr. Wheeler, Linen-draper, one by one: The Twto former agreed in Opinion exactly as to all of them; and the Third in all but Three or Four, in which he was doubtful. The Particulars are hereunto annexed.

The Petitioners then desired the same as to Remnants, some of which were disguised on purpose, by cutting off the Selvages, whshing, starching, calendering, and tumbling. — These the Linen-drapers declared they could not ascertain; however, the Tryal was made, and the Examination is hereunto annexed.

Proposals for explaining, amending, and enforcing, Two Acts of Parliament, One made in the Eighteenth, the other in the Twenty-first, Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for prohibiting the Wear and Importation of Cambricks and French Lawns.

id, That, from and after the 26 of March 1750, all Cambricks or French Lawns thall, on Importation, be damped, at the End of each Piece, in such a manner as the Commissioners of his Majesty's Customs shalldiredt and appoint; but so as the said Stamp shall describe them to be Cambricks or French Lawns.

2d, That each Bond, that shall hereafter be given upon making the Entry at the Custom-house for the Importation of Cambricks and French Lawns, shall be numbered; and the Stamp to be affixed on each Piece to have the same Number as the Bond; which specified Pieces alone shall be admitted, upon Exportation, to the Discharge of those Bonds c'orresponding with the Numbers, and to no other.

3d, That, on or oefiore the 16th of April 1750, all Cambricks and French Lawns, which have been imported since the 26 March 1747, and on which Bond has been given for the due Exportation within Three Years, and which still remain in this Kingdom, shall be damped, marked, or sealed, in the respective Ports where they were imported, without any Fee or Reward whatsoever, in such manner as the Commissioners of his' Majesty's Customs shall direct; but so that the Pieces may receive as little Damage as possible thereby; and that the Importers, and Persons who produce the same Cambricks, and French LawnS as aforesaid, shall make Oath to the Ident ity of the Goods, expressing therein the Names of tilt Importers, and the respective Time of Importation.

9th, Upon Oath made by One or more credible Person or Persons, that they hav-: Reason to suspect that any Cambricks or French Lawns are in Custody of any Merchant, Draper, Haberdasher, Milliner, Sempstress, Trader, or Dealer, without having such Marks as are required, it shall be lawful for any Two Justices of the Peace to issue their Warrants to any Person or Persons, with the Assistance of a Constable, or other Officer of the Peace, in the Day-time, to search for the fame, and to open Doors, Chests, and Package, and to seize such Goods, and to bring them to the Custom-house Ware-house next adjoining to the Place where they shall be seized; and the Person, in whose Custody such Cambricks or French Lawns shall be found, shall be liable to a Penalty of One hundred Pounds.

9th, That any Person who shall alter, counterfeit, or misapply, any of the Stamps, Seals, or Marks, so to be affixed as aforesaid, and every Aider, Abettor, or Assistant, therein, shall, upon Proof thereof, forfeit the Sum of One hundred Pounds, and stand in the Pillory for Two Hours; and every Person who shall buy or fell any Cambricks or French Lawns marked with a counterfeit Mark, Stamp, or Seal, or which shall have any true Mark, Stamp, or Seal, thereunto affixed or put, which has not been affixed or put thereto by the proper Officer, knowing thereof, and not discovering the fame, shall, over and above the Forfeiture of the Goods, forfeit and pay the Sum of One hundred Pounds.

10th, That whereas, by the Act, made in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, it is expressed, That any Person convicted of felling Cam-bncks or French Lawns after the 24th June 1748, shall be subject to the Penalty of Five Pounds, which, it is apprehended, may be construed to limit the Penalty to that Sum, be the Quantity fold, or offered to Sale, at one time, more or less, and that it could be deemed but as One Offence, it is proposed, That the Penalty shall be Fifty Pounds for every such Offence, and Ten Pounds for every Yard exceeding the Quantity of One hundred Yards so fold, or offered to Sale, and so in proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity than a Yard,

nth, That if any Person, after having made a Seizure of Cambricks or French Lawns, shall offer to compromile or compound for relinquishing of them, he shall forfeit One hundred Pounds, and suffer Twelve Months Imprisonment; the Forfeiture to go Ope Half to the Poor of the Parish where such Offender shall happen to live, and Half to the Informer.

12th, That upon Information given against any Wearer or Seller of Cambricks or French Lawns, before any Justice of the Peace, he shall summon Three Persons, Dealers in Linen being within a convenient Distance from him) to examine them upon Oath, whether the Linen so questioned be or be not Cambrick or French Lawn: If declared in the Affirmative, the Penalty to be immediately levied; or if the Party convicted shall appeal to the Quarter-Sessions, or Judges of Assize, Security be given in double the Sum for his answering to the Appeal, and extraordinary Charges; if the Person convicted shall prove that the Linen so declared to be Cambrick or French Lawn was sold to him under a false Denomination, he shall be exempted from the Penalty, and the Seller to pay a Penalty of One hundred Pounds.

13 th, That no Cambiicks or Lawns, that shall be (eized and forfeited, shall be ufod in this Kingdom, but be exported again, and not fold otherwise than to be exported; and the same shall, immediately on Seizure, be carried to the Custom-house Warehouse, and there sold by Inch of Candle, on Condition to be exported, and not delivered without the Stamps, Marks, or Seals, affixed thereto, and until Security be given that the same be exported, and not landed again in Great Britain or the Isle of Man.

Loading Ports with all possible Expedition, they the said Matters, after such Accounts so regularly settled with their Crimps every Voyage, have leldom inquired after their Bonds: But although, in a general Way, the said Matters have not aiked for their Bonds, it was proved to your Committee, That Application was made by some of the said Matters to James Deacon, late Collector of the Coal Du ties, to know if any Bonds, wherein they were Obligors, retnained unpaid; and that they were told by the said Collector, that all their Bonds were paid which were become due; although there have been found since that time several Bonds uncancelled, which appear to have been due at Times previous to such Inquiry; and the Payment of several Bonds has been since demanded of those very Mailers, who were then told, that there were no Bonds Handing out against them due and unpaid at the time when such Application was made to the said Collector.

That, by Minutes laid before your Committee from the Commissioners of the Customs, it appeared, That the following Orders for the securing and collecting the said Duties, had been at several times made by the said Commissioners for the Time being; That the Collector of the Coal Duties was to call upon the Obligors in the said Bonds for Payment, when the Bonds became due; and, if they were not paid within Fourteen Days, to deliver the said Bonds to the Sollicitor of the Customs, to be put in Suit; and also that no Person should be admitted by them as Securities in new Bonds, who had a former Bond in Suit: And it appeared likewise, by the concurrent Testimony of the Witnesses which were examined by the Committee, That as it was generally known to the whole Trade, that such Rule* above-mentioned were established, and that it was the Duty of the said Officers to conform themselves thereto, the Mailers of Ships had the llrongell Reasons to rest satisfied that the said Bonds were necessarily and regularly discharged by the Crimps; and, had the said Rules and Directions of the Commissioners been faithfully observed, neither the -Crown could have futfered any Loss, nor the Mailers have run any greater Risque than what might have arisen from the Insolvency of a Crimp at the time when such Bond was put in Suit.

That your Committee ffhil, by several Reports and Accounts laid before them, from the Commissioners of the Customs, That, notwithstanding such Rules as aforesaid, upon the Death of James Deacon, late Collector of the Coal Duties, a great Number of uncancelled Bonds was found in his Office, which had become due at different Periods, from the Year 1743, to the Year 1742: That, upon Discovery thereof, the said Commissioners directed a strict Examination into the Offices of the said Collector and Comptroller of the Coal Duties; from which Examination, laid before your Committee, it appears, That the Books of the said Collector and Comptroller had been kept, during that Period of Time, in a moll irregular and conrufed manner; and that the said Officers had been guilty of great Neglect* and Fraud in the managing, collecting, and accounting for, the said Duties, particularly in the following Instances; viz. the giving large Credit to several Crimps, and not putting their Bonds in Suit when due; receiving the large . Sums from the said Crimps upon Account, without a particular Application of the same to their respective Bonds; the making and delivering in fictitious Accounts, by concealing and omitting to insert a true State of Bonds charged in the Weekly Certificates; from which Weekly Certificates, signed by the Collector and Comptroller of the Coal Duties, the Accounts of the said Collector are charged in the Office of the Comptroller-General, and from thence transmitted to the Auditors, with the said Certificates as Vouchers: And all these several Instances of Neglect-and Fraud were confirmed by the Testimony of Charles Ambrose, who had been a Clerk in the Office

of the Comptroller of the Coal Duties for Thirty-four Years; by whole Evidence it appears to your Committee, That, from the Commencement of these Irregulari-Vol. 25.

ties, which he believes might begin to be considerable Untancelled about the Year 1726, to the Death of Deacon in 1742 (which Period includes a Term of Sixteen Years, and up- oa , Uew wards) all the several Accounts of the Duties upon Coals within the Port of London have been charged and patted through all the Offices by falfie Certificates delivered to the Comptroller-General as aforesaid; the same not containing, as they ought to have done, a true State of Bonds charged; and by comparing the Balance of the last Account of the said Deacon, now remaining in the Pipe- Office, whereby he Hands charged, at 1741, fof

Bonds amounting to no more than 12,! 90. 16 with the Value of the outstanding Bonds which were found in his Office uncancelled, and not brought to Account; there appears to have been an Omission of charging Bonds, duringthat Period of Time, to the Amount of 120,000,

and upwards: But although the Debt remaining due uport these Bonds is so considerable and apparent, your Committee find, that it will be very difficult, from the many Errors, Omissions, and fraudulent Practices, of the said Collector, in the Discharge t;f his Office, to ascertain whaf Part of the Debt ought to be charged to the said Cob lector, and what Part to the Crimps; for there is great Reason to believe, from the Reports of the Commissioners of the Customs to the Commissioners of the Treasury, that all the Money received by Deacon was not accounted for; and that it was in the Power of the said,

by omitting to bringto Account atraeState >tthe Bends, to apply the Money receivedupon such Bonds t - his own,

Use; nor can it be ascertained, in many Instances, to what particular Bonds large Sums of Money received by the said Deacon is applicable, the same being received ana -entered upon Account j but, after the Uncled Examination your Committee can make into this intricate Affair, it appears to your Committee, That no Payments have ever been made by the Mailers of Ships themselves, ih Discharge of Bonds taken for the Duties upon Coals, but that all Payments of that Kind have been constantly made by the Crimps; and that the Mailers were neither privy to the said Practices carried on by the Collector and Crimps; nor could propose any Advantage by concealing the fame, if they had suspected any such Practices, having always paid the Duties in manner before Hated, according to theconllant and uniform Practice of the said Trade, from the time that the Duties were first granted by Parliament.

That as no Bonds were ever put in Suit, and the Masters were permitted to enter into new Bonds fronp time to time with the same Crimps, without notice taken by the Collector that any old Bonds, wherein such Mailers were Obligors, remained unpaid — If such Bonds should. now be put in Suit against the Mailers, it will fall upon them to make good a Deficiency intirely unknown to them, and which could not have happened but through the wilful Neglect and evil Practices of the Collector and Comptroller, who were appointed the proper Officers for the securing and col left ing the -said Duties

That by the Death or lnfolvency of John Gibson, William Williford, and Sir Maltas Ry,who appear to be joint Obligors with the ' Matters in the greatest Part of the outstanding Bonds, to the Amount of £. 100,000, and upwards, the Mailers are now deprived of such Re* dress against the said Crimps as they might have obtained if their Bonds had been regularly put in Suit, or the Masters had received Notice in due time that their Bonds were unpaid.

That there are Five hundred Persons, or more, engaged in this Affair, and most of them Matters of Ships now employed in the Coal Trade; and, if these Bonds should be put in Suit against them, they and their Families mutt be intirely ruined, and many of them forced into foreign Countries, to the great Distress of the Coal Trade, from which a considerable Revenue annually ariles for the Service of the Publick.

That, to avoid a Repetition of Facts so fully proved by the F.vidertce on the first-mentioned Petition, your Committee did not examine into the Irregularity of keeping the Accounts in the Office of the Collector of the afore-Ciid Duties, during the time the said James Deacon was Collector.

That, in order to know at what Period of Time Mr. Gibjon first began to pay Money to the Collector upon Account, and not to the Discharge of particular Bond Duties; and whether such Money, so paid upon Account, was adequate to the Credit of the Duties for which the Bonds (landing out against him from time to time were given; your Committee ordered the Commissioners of the Customs to lay before them all Mr. s Cash Books, as also all the Collectors Cash Books with the Receiver-General, from the Year 1723, to the Year 1742: To which Order Answer was returned by their Secretary, That diligent Search had been made at the Custom-house for Mr. Gibjon's Cash Books, and no more could be found than the Three following, for the Years 1739, 1740, 1741, and Part of the Year 1742; and that he did not believe the Commissioners of the Customs were ever possessed of any other Cash Books of the said Gibjon: Then,

Mr. Joseph Luc cock) who had been Clerk to Mr. Gib-

Jon, from the Y'ear 1734, to the Year 1742, being asked,

' If he knew what became of G/^/e#'s "Books and Papers at the time the Extent was taken out by the Commission^-ers of the Customs against the said Gibjon? said. That all the current Books and Papers, which lay in s Compting-house at that time, were seized by virtue of the said Extent; and the rest of the Books and Papers, which were kept in a Room above Stairs, and not discovered, were afterwards seized under a Commission of Bankruptcy taken out against Gibjon by one Mr. Justice Cross, the Assignee: That foine of the last mentioned Books have been since re-seized by a Second Extent, and . carried to the Custom-house; but how many, and what Books in particular these were, the Witness did not know; so that what is become of s Cash Books since they were taken out of his Possession (except those above-men-. tinned, found at the Custom-house) does not appear to your Committee.

Mr. Samuel Maxwell,a Coal-factor, informed your Committee, That he knew the said Mr. Justice Cross: _That he some time ago absconded for Debt; and that he (Maxwell) had conversed with several People lately who have seen him, and who say he is settled in Business at Rotterdam, and that they believe they never return to England.

Mr. Joseph Luccock, being further examined, said. That, during the time he lived with Mr. Gibjon, he, and other Clerks, paid, on s Account, into the

Custom-house, for Coal Duties, 30 or £. 40,000 per Annum, One Year with another: That sometimes he paid Money into the Collector's Office, and sometimes into that of the Receiver General, whose Receipts on those Occasions he used to carry to the Collector's Office, leaving them there as Evidences of his having paid the Money to the Receiver-General: That sometimes he hath paid 7 or £.800 in One Day for Duties: That he paid the Duties regularly; or, if the Payment elapsed One Day, he was obliged to pay the Money the next Morning before the Business came on; being threatened, if he did not, his Mailer should not be allowed a Warrant for the Unloading of any Coal Ship till such Deficiency was discharged:

That the Payments he made on Gibjon % Behalf were always designed by him in Discharge of particular Bonds, and not to be carried to a general Account: That he knew from time to time what Bonds were due, being furnished with Lists of such Bonds from the Custom-house:

That, upon paying the Money, he sometimes received Gibjons Bonds, and sometimes not; and, upon his repeated Requests for such as he did not receive, he has been told, that the Collector was not in the Way, or the Officers were busy, and that they would give such Bonds to his Master; which Answers he used to communicate to Mr. Gibjon: That there are now Three Bonds (landing out against Gibjon, which he ( Lucco) particularly remembers to have paid; and that, notwithstanding many Bonds, paid and demanded by the Witness, remained in the Collector's Office, he always thought he might lately pay his Money, relying on the regular Entries, in his Matter's Books, of Money paid for such Bonds,- and on the Books of the Collector's Office.

Upon the Whole, therefore, the real Debt from Gibjon to the Crown, for Coal Duties, does not appear to your Committee in any other manner than by the Account before-mentioned, contained in the Custom-house Books.

Then a Certificate of the Commissioners, in the Commission of Bankruptcy awarded against Gibjon, was pro duced to your Committee, dated the 5th of 1748, and allowed by the Lord Chancellor; whereby it appeared.

That he had surrendered up all his Estate and Effects whatsoever for the Benefit of his Creditors.

And that the said Gibjon is now a Prisoner in the Fleet, by virtue of the Extent taken out against him by the Commissioners of the Customs. (

In Obedience to the Commands of the House of Commons, I am to acquaint you, that the said House did* on the aoth Day of this instant March, come to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That any Person or Persons, Bodies Politick or Corporate, who now are, or hereafter may be, interested in, or intitled unto, such Part of the national Debt incurred before Michaelmas 174$, redeemable by Law, which now carries an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, as hath not been subscribed in pursuance of

an Act of this present Session of Parliament, for reducing the several Annuities, which carry an Interest after the Rate of Four Pourtds per Centum per Annum, to the several Rates therein mentioned, and who do, on or before the 30th Day of May next, subscribe their Names, or signify their Consent to accept of an Interest of Three -Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from 25th Day of December 1755, subject to the same Provisions, Notices, and Clauses of Redemption, which their respective Four per Cents are now liable to, shall, in lieu of their present Interest, be intitled unto, and receive, an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, until the 25th Day of December 1750; and, from and after the said 25th Day of December 1750, an Interest of Three Pounds Ten Shillings per Centum per Annum, until the 25th Day of December 1755; and that no Part of the same shall be liable to be redeemed until after the said 25th Day of December 1755.

Resolved, That such Part of the national Debt incurred before Michaelmas 1749, redeemable by Law, which now carries an Interest of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, and which shall not be subscribed on or before the 30th Day of May next, be redeemed and paid off.

The Order of the Day being read, for resuming the adjourned Consideration of thfc Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to encourage the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from America; and to prevent the Making of Steel, or setting up Slitting Mills or Rolling Mills in the British Colonies there; was committed;

A Petition of the Mailers, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Adventurers within the City of Bristol, under their Common Sea!, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that a Permission of importing Pig and Bar Iron into Great Britain from the American Plantations, Duty-free, will be attended with many Valuable Consequences to the Nation in general, as it will greatly promote and encourage our Colonies abroad, and thereby our own Manufactures of various Kinds at home; will contiderably relieve us from the Necessity we are now under of being supplied with these Articles from Foreigners, who prohibit many of our Manufactures, receive great Sums in Specie every Year from us, and are ft rift ly united with our Rivals in Trade; and that the Petitioners cannot conceive that the landed Interest of Great Britain will be at all affected by this Permission, as the same Quantity of English Iron will in all Probability be still made use of, the whole Kingdom not producing a Sufficiency for our Use; and the lole Question seeming to be, whether we shall encourage the Commerce of our own Colonies, or that of Foreigners; and that with regard to our own Manufactories of Imall and fine IronWare, the Petitioners are of Opin-on, that there should be a Restriction to prevent any Persons abroad from erecting any Slitting or Rolling Mills, or any Forges for Plating of Iron, whereby that valuable Manufactory here will be preserved to us: And therefore praying, That a Bill may pass this House to permit the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron into this Kingdom from our American Colonies, Duty-free, under a Restriction from erecting the re any Slitting or Rolling Mills, or any Forges for Plating of Iron; and under such other Restrict ions, for preventing any Prejudice to the interest of the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the adjourned Consideration of the said Report is resumed.

Then the House resumed the adjourned Consideration of the said Report.

Importing A Petition of the Matters, Wardens, and Commonalty,

Iron from of Cutlers, in Rallamshire, in the County of York, was

America. presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners are of Opinion, That the BUI, depending in the House, for the Encouragement of the Importation of Pig and Bar Iron from Ameriwill be a national Good, by preserving One of the most valuable Branches of Trade to this Kingdom, without which, the Petitioners apprehend, we shall always be subject to the Interestor Resentment of foreign Powers, to exact what Price and (end what Quantity they please; and that the Iron is at present advanced near Forty Shillings a Ton; and that, by a moderate Computation, there is not more than One-third Part of what is consumed made here; and, in case of a Stop to the Importation thereof in time of War, or by any other means, it must consequently be of very great Prejudice to this Kingdom, particularly to the Manufacturers in the said County, and other Places, by lessening the Quantity of Goods manufactured there (on which fe-veral Thousand Families depend) which will not be equal to the Demand for them; and that, of course, those who can be no longer supplied from hence, must be obliged to procure them from other Parts, or introduce the Making of them for themselves; but that, if the said Bill pafles into a Law, the Petitioners are thereby encouraged to expect, that, by rendering them independent of their arbitrary Neighbours in this respedb, it will enable them to extend their Manufactures, so as wholly to supply those that now only draw from this Kingdom a Part of the Articles they have need of in this way: And therefore praying the House to take such Measures therein, as to secure the Petitioners a sufficient Quantity of Materials for the carrying on their Manufactories, and yet prevent the Removing of them to Ameras the House shall think fit.

Ot'dered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time.

Sail-cloth Mr. f'racy, according to Order, reported, from the Manufacture. Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants, and of the Manufacturers of British Sail-cloth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was referred, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same wete read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Manufacture of British Sail-cloth, which has been greatly extended and improved by the Encouragement and Bounty given by Parliament, has of late greatly decrcafed.

Resolvetd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Fund, out of which the Bounty is given upon the Exportation of British Sail-cloth, hath of late, been deficient, which has contributed to the Decay of the said Manufacture.

Resolvetd \That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the large Bounty, and other Advantages, granted

by the Parliament of Ireland, ori Sail-cloth Made in that Kingdom, of which considerable Quantities have been imported into, and consumed in, Great , are Dif-

couragements to the Improvement of the said Manufacture in this Kingdom, and contribute to the present Decay thereof.

Resolvetd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Bounty upon the Exportation of British Sailcloth, and which is now payable out of the Duty of One Peny per Ell on foreign Sail-cloth imported, do (land charged upon, and be made payable out of, the Customs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty of Four Pence per Yard be laid upon all Sail-cloth of the Value of Fourteen Pence, and upwards, a Yard, and a Duty of Two Pence per Yard upon all Sail-cloth of the Value of Ten Pence, and not exceeding Fourteen Pence a Yard, imported from into Great Britain.

Importing A Petition of the Ironmongers, Hingo-makers, Nail-Iron from makers, Lock-makers, Hoc-makers, Smiths; and others, America. in ' Ashton, Co'wheut, West-Leigh, and Towns'adjacent,

and in Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more employed in the different Branches of the Iron Manufactory, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the Petitioners conceive the Bill, now depending in the House, to encourage the Importation of Pig and Bar I ron from America; and to prevent the Making of

Steel, or erecting Slitting or Rolling Mills and Plating Forges; if properly guarded by the Restrictions proposed, which, the Petitioners apprehend, is intirely to prevent the Americans manufacturing any Wares out of the Bar or Pig, by such Means and in such Manner, as the House shall seem meet, shall pass into a Law, it will greatly tend to the Advantage of the Nation in general, as well as his Majesty's Colonies abroad and our Iron Manufactures in particular; and that the Petitioners have experienced, that what Pig Iron has been imported from America, and made into Bar here, far exceeds the Swedes Iron, which the Petitioners are frequentlyunderaNeceflity to work large Quantities of, and that very much to their Di&dvantage, for want of having a sufficient Supply of English Iron, of which small Quantities are made in proportion to what would be used; and is a very great Encouragement to the Swedes, who take only our Specie in Return; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Importing of Pig and Bar Iron from America would be of great Benefit to our Commerce, and would very much facilitate our Returns from thence, the want of which has been found very detrimental to Trade j whereas eitherof these Articles, being of so extensive and general Ule, are always at a Market; and that, with regard to our Navigation, the Petitioners conceive it would be of singular Advantage, being extremely well suited for Baliaft and Lading, and would expedite the Dispatch of any Commodities we import; and that as the Importation of American Pig and Bar Iron mull; of course take place of the Consumption of Swediflt, these will be as much or more English worked as heretofore, and therefore can be of no Detriment to the Gentlemen Wood^owners in this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time.

Ordered, That the Amendment, made by the Lords, to the Bill, intituled, An Act f >r the Encouragement of the British White Herring Fishery, be now taken into Consideration.

The House accordingly proceeded to take the said Amendment into Consideration.

And the said Amendment was read; and is as fellow-eth; viz.

Pr. 1. L. 2. Leave out and Cod."

The said Amendment being read a Second time, the same appeared to be in the Preamble to the said Bill, in which Mention is made both of the White Herring and Cod Fisheries: And whereas, in several of the Enacting Parts of the Bill, the Fisheries, to which the Encouragement was intended to be given, are not specified, otherwise than by Words of Reference to the Fisheries mentioned in the Preamble, the Purport of the said Amendment was, by leaving out of the Preamble the Mention of the Cod Fisheries, to confine to the White Herring Fishery only such of the Provi lions and Regulations contained in the Bill, as have Reference to the Fisheries mentioned in the Preamble.

And to the end that it might appear what was the Intention of the House with respect to the Fisheries designed to be encouraged:

The King'* After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most peec 'gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followed!; viz. ' . , ' 1

My Lords and Gentlemen, ‘

I cannot put an End to this Session of Parframent, without returning you my hearty Thanks for the Zeal and Dispatch with which you have gone through the publick 'Business. Nothing could have afforded me more Satisfaction, than the Attentfon you have given to those efient ial Points of our fiational Interest which I earnestly record-mended to you at the Opening of the Session; and it is with the great ell Pleasure I have now given iny Assent to those L^Vvs which have been the Refult of your prudent Deliberations for'id&ncing the publick Credit, for promoting the Commerce and Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for encouraging the Industry of my good Subjects.

There" ha^ JSeei^ so little Alteration in the State of Affaits abrdad since your Meeting, that I have feafee any thing to add upon that Head.. My Resolution to adhere strictly to the Engagements I have entered into, and to do every thing in My power to prelcrve the Peace which has been so'happily established, continues the same; and I have received the fulled A durances from my AlUes, of their Disposition to promote this.great End: My sincere Endeavours shall be exerted to cultivate and improve this good Pifposition, that my own Kingdoms as well as the red of Europe, may long enjoy the happy Fruits of the present Tranquillity.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you in a particular manner for the Supplies you. have so readily granted me, and for the publick Spirit you have shewn in laying bold of the very fird Opportunity to reduce the Intered of the national Debt,

without the lead Infringement of Parliamentary Faith.

The Success which has already attended this wifeMealure, is a Proof of the present Credit of this Kingdom, and has laid a sure Foundation for the Continuance of it, and cannot fair to add Strength and Reputation to my Government both at home and abroad.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I make no Doubt but you will carry into your respective Countries the same good Principles and Affections which I have experienced from you here. Let it be your Business to promote Peace and Harmony, and to support and propagate Religion, good Manners, and good Order, amongst my People, whose true and lading Happiness shall be my condant Care.

A Message was brought from the Lords, by Mr. mingham, Deputy Gentleman-Ulher of the Black Rod: Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty's Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable llonle, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for the further Proroguing of the Parliament until Thursday the 17th Day of January next.

And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday the 17th Day of January next.
